15D score as an additive weighted sum of level values

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000241
Type formula
assumes Additive independence of dimensions, Population weights elicited without a duration, A response on every dimension
has calculator text v_H = sum_(j=1)^15 [I_j * w_j]
has common error note Reading every change in score as important. Alanne and colleagues estimated the minimum important change in the 15D score at plus or minus 0.015. A mean change of 0.010 falls within the band described by patients as much the same.
Summing level codes instead of level values. Adding the questionnaire codes 1 to 5, or averaging them, gives a number that is neither a level value nor a preference weight. The codes are first converted to level values and importance weights by the scoring algorithm.
Treating 15D scores as interchangeable with EQ-5D values. The 15D index stops at 0 and cannot value a state as worse than dead, and it was valued with different methods and samples from EQ-5D value sets. NICE's interim methods statement asks for non-EQ-5D measures to be mapped to utility values based on the UK EQ-5D-5L value set when EQ-5D-5L data are not available.
has description in the module Multiplies the value of the level reported on each dimension by the importance weight of that dimension at that level, and adds the products over the 15 dimensions. This is the additive multi-attribute utility model of the 15D valuation system, v_H = sum of I_j(x_j) times w_j(x_j), with the level x_j written into I_j and w_j here.
has formalisation level catalogue record
has implementation 15D score from weight and value rows
has mathematical variable 15D score, Importance weight of dimension j at the reported level, Level value of dimension j
has module record identifier HE-FM-15D-001
has source in the module Alanne S, Roine RP, Räsänen P, Vainiola T, Sintonen H. Estimating the minimum important change in the 15D scores. Quality of Life Research. 2015;24(3):599-606. Generic minimum important change of plus or minus 0.015, estimated in 4,903 hospital patients. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11136-014-0787-4
National Institute for Health and Care Excellence. Interim methods statement: implementing the EQ-5D-5L value set (PMG51). Published 27 August 2026. Statement sections 1.7 and 1.10 (the EQ-5D-5L and UK value set as the preferred approach for adults; non-EQ-5D measures mapped to utility values based on the UK EQ-5D-5L value set when EQ-5D-5L data are not available). https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg51/chapter/statement-on-using-the-eq-5d-5l-value-set
Sintonen H. 15D instrument website (www.15d-instrument.net): Valuation system page. Accessed 29 September 2026. The 15D score formula v_H = sum of I_j(x_j) times w_j(x_j), the anchors (0 dead, 0.0162 unconscious or comatose, 1 no problems on any dimension), level values on a 0 to 1 scale and importance weights summing to 1, elicitation by rating scale and magnitude estimation, and unspecified duration. https://www.15d-instrument.net/valuation-system/
Sintonen H. The 15D instrument of health-related quality of life: properties and applications. Annals of Medicine. 2001;33(5):328-336. The valuation system is an application of multi-attribute utility theory, and the single index score on a 0 to 1 scale is calculated from the descriptive system with population-based preference weights. https://doi.org/10.3109/07853890109002086

340B ceiling price per unit with the penny floor

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000264
Type formula
assumes Quarterly calculation by product, Rules effective from 1 January 2019
has calculator text P_340B = max(AMP - URA, 0.01)
has common error note Reporting a zero or negative ceiling price. When the URA equals or exceeds AMP, the formula gives zero or less. The regulation sets the ceiling at 0.01 dollars in that case, and an analysis that uses a zero acquisition cost understates it.
Using the current quarter's AMP. The ceiling price for a quarter uses the AMP and URA from the preceding calendar quarter. Pairing a quarter's prices with its own AMP misstates the ceiling whenever AMP changes between quarters.
has description in the module 42 CFR 10.10(a) sets the ceiling price as the AMP from the preceding calendar quarter for the smallest unit of measure minus the URA, calculated to six decimal places; HRSA publishes it rounded to two. Under 10.10(b), a calculation below 0.01 dollars gives a ceiling price of 0.01 dollars, the penny pricing policy.

90 per cent confidence interval for the geometric mean ratio

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000267
Type formula
assumes Log-normal pharmacokinetic measures, Equal-tails interval and two one-sided tests, Standard limits for most drugs
has calculator text GMR = exp(d); GMR_L = exp(d - t_crit * SE); GMR_U = exp(d + t_crit * SE)
has common error note Reading the limits as allowing 20 per cent less drug. The limits apply to the confidence interval for the ratio of exposure measures, not to the drug content of the dose. A product whose true ratio sat near 0.80 would usually fail, because its interval would extend below the limit.
Testing the point estimate instead of the interval. A ratio of 0.88 lies within 0.80 to 1.25, but its lower confidence limit of 78.03% does not. The criterion applies to the whole 90% interval.
Using a 95 per cent two-sided interval. A 95% two-sided interval corresponds to one-sided tests at 2.5% and is wider than the interval the guidance specifies for average bioequivalence of AUC and Cmax.
has description in the module The mean difference d between test and reference in natural logs of AUC or Cmax is exponentiated to give the geometric mean ratio, and the limits of the 90% interval are d plus or minus the one-sided 95% t quantile times the standard error, exponentiated. This interval corresponds to the two one-sided tests procedure at the 5% level. Average bioequivalence is concluded when the interval, expressed in per cent and rounded to two decimal places, is at least 80.00 and no more than 125.00.
has formalisation level catalogue record
has implementation 90 per cent interval for the ratio
has mathematical variable Geometric mean ratio of test to reference, Lower 90 per cent confidence limit of the ratio, Mean log difference between test and reference, One-sided 95 per cent t quantile, Standard error of the mean log difference, Upper 90 per cent confidence limit of the ratio

Absence cost by the friction cost method

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000247
Type formula
assumes Friction period for the setting and years, Start date of the absence known, Replacement from the unemployed
definition source Koopmanschap et al. 1995; the Source rows of the Functions and Formulae module record HE-FM-ABSN-003
formalises friction cost method
has calculator text C_FC = min(D_a, D_F) / 7 * H * w * e
has common error note Applying the elasticity twice. The Dutch reference price of 39.88 euros an hour is based on labour costs that already include an adjustment for the elasticity of labour. Multiplying it by a further 0.8 understates the friction cost by a fifth.
Comparing costs across valuation methods. Human capital and friction cost estimates of the same absence can differ several-fold, so productivity costs from studies using different methods, friction periods or hourly values are not directly comparable.
Counting the friction period from the survey date. Capping the absence at the friction period from the start of the recall period, not the start of the absence, counts days already beyond the cap for workers whose absence began earlier.
has Content MathML <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><apply><csymbol cd="relation1">eq</csymbol><ci>C_FC</ci><apply><csymbol cd="arith1">times</csymbol><apply><csymbol cd="arith1">divide</csymbol><apply><csymbol cd="minmax1">min</csymbol><apply><csymbol cd="set1">set</csymbol><ci>D_a</ci><ci>D_F</ci></apply></apply><cn type="integer">7</cn></apply><ci>H</ci><ci>w</ci><ci>e</ci></apply></apply></math>
has description in the module Counts absence only up to the friction period, the time an employer needs to restore production, usually by replacing the worker, and multiplies the counted hours by the value of an hour and by the elasticity of production with respect to working time. Absences shorter than the friction period count in full. When the hourly value already allows for the elasticity, as the Dutch reference price does, e is set to 1.

Absence cost by the human capital approach

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000246
Type formula
assumes Absent time spread evenly over the working week, Output lost for the whole absence
definition source the Source rows of the Functions and Formulae module record HE-FM-ABSN-002
editor note Days are converted to weeks by the constant 7, the number of days in a week, the kind of number HEMO allows.
formalises productivity cost valuation, human capital method
has calculator text C_HC = D_a / 7 * H * w
has common error note Including productivity costs in the NICE reference case. The NICE reference case takes an NHS and personal social services perspective on costs and excludes productivity costs. They can be shown separately as additional information when they may be a critical part of the value of the technology.
Valuing absence by sick pay or benefits. Sick pay and sickness benefits are transfer payments: they change who bears the loss of production, not its size, and are left out of the productivity cost to society.
has Content MathML <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><apply><csymbol cd="relation1">eq</csymbol><ci>C_HC</ci><apply><csymbol cd="arith1">times</csymbol><apply><csymbol cd="arith1">divide</csymbol><ci>D_a</ci><cn type="integer">7</cn></apply><ci>H</ci><ci>w</ci></apply></apply></math>
has description in the module Values every hour of absence at the value of an hour of work. D_a counts calendar days absent, so D_a divided by 7 gives weeks absent, and multiplying by the usual weekly hours and the hourly value gives the cost. The human capital approach usually values time at gross earnings including employer-paid costs such as payroll taxes and benefits, the full cost of employee compensation.

has implementation Human capital absence cost

Absolute and proportional QALY shortfall

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000238
Type formula
assumes Carer QALYs excluded, Same population, starting point and discounting, Value set for population norms
definition source the Source rows of the Functions and Formulae module record HE-FM-ASF-001
feeds Severity QALY weight from the shortfall bands
formalises absolute QALY shortfall estimate, proportional QALY shortfall estimate
has calculator text AS = Q_h - Q_c; PS = (Q_h - Q_c) / Q_h
has common error note Matching on age but not on sex. Life expectancy and utility norms differ by sex, so the DSU guide computes Q_h separately for males and females and weights them by the proportion female in the patient population. A single-sex or whole-population norm misstates Q_h and both shortfall measures.
Undiscounted or non-reference-case discounting. Shortfall calculated from undiscounted QALYs, or at a discount rate other than 3.5%, is on a different scale from the cut-offs of 12 and 18 QALYs and can move a condition into a higher band.
has Content MathML <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><apply><csymbol cd="logic1">and</csymbol><apply><csymbol cd="relation1">eq</csymbol><ci>AS</ci><apply><csymbol cd="arith1">minus</csymbol><ci>Q_h</ci><ci>Q_c</ci></apply></apply><apply><csymbol cd="relation1">eq</csymbol><ci>PS</ci><apply><csymbol cd="arith1">divide</csymbol><apply><csymbol cd="arith1">minus</csymbol><ci>Q_h</ci><ci>Q_c</ci></apply><ci>Q_h</ci></apply></apply></apply></math>
has description in the module Absolute shortfall subtracts the expected remaining QALYs of people with the condition under current care from those of the matched general population. Proportional shortfall divides the same difference by the general-population QALYs. Both look forward from the point at which the technology would be used, so health already lost does not count, and both are discounted at the reference-case rate.
has domain of validity domain of validity of HE-FM-ASF-001
has formalisation level fully formalised
has implementation Shortfall measures in two cells

Absolute and relative health gap between the extreme groups

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000366
Type formula
assumes Health inequality gaps use only the two extreme groups, Ratio-scale health for the relative health gap
has calculator text AG = h_J - h_1; RG = h_J / h_1
has common error note Judging a change in health inequality on one gap measure alone. The two gaps can move in opposite directions. In the article's example a gain of 1 year in every quintile leaves the absolute gap at 10 years while the rate ratio falls from 1.161 to 1.159, and a gain of 2% in every quintile leaves the ratio at 1.161 while the gap widens to 10.2 years. Both are therefore reported, as the WHO handbook recommends.
has description in the module Compares mean health in the most advantaged group J with mean health in the most disadvantaged group 1, as a difference in the units of the health variable and as a ratio without units. The WHO handbook calls these the difference and the ratio; Harper and colleagues call them the rate difference and the rate ratio.

Absolute and relative risk reduction from a relative risk and baseline risk

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000232
Type formula
assumes Relative risk constant across baseline risk, Baseline risk and relative risk over the same period
definition source the Source rows of the Functions and Formulae module record HE-FM-ARR-002
formalises relative riskexternal
has calculator text ARR = p_C * (1 - RR); RRR = 1 - RR
has common error note Substituting a hazard ratio for the relative risk. A hazard ratio is not a ratio of risks. Using it in place of RR is only an approximation, and a poor one when event risks over the horizon are high; the treatment risk comes from applying the hazard ratio to a baseline survival curve, as set out on the Hazard Ratio page.
Treating an odds ratio as a risk ratio. An odds ratio of 0.73 at a comparator risk of 0.3 implies an intervention risk of about 0.238 and an ARR of about 0.0617, as in section 15.4.4.3 of the Cochrane Handbook. Using 0.73 as if it were RR gives 0.081, about 30 per cent too high. The odds conversion is set out on the Network Meta-Analysis page.
Using the trial baseline for a different population. An ARR computed at the trial's comparator risk describes the trial population. Patients at a quarter of that risk gain a quarter of the absolute benefit under a constant relative risk, so the NNT and the cost per event avoided change accordingly.
has Content MathML <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><apply><csymbol cd="logic1">and</csymbol><apply><csymbol cd="relation1">eq</csymbol><ci>ARR</ci><apply><csymbol cd="arith1">times</csymbol><ci>p_C</ci><apply><csymbol cd="arith1">minus</csymbol><cn type="integer">1</cn><ci>RR</ci></apply></apply></apply><apply><csymbol cd="relation1">eq</csymbol><ci>RRR</ci><apply><csymbol cd="arith1">minus</csymbol><cn type="integer">1</cn><ci>RR</ci></apply></apply></apply></math>
has description in the module Applies a relative risk, for example a pooled estimate from a meta-analysis, to an assumed comparator risk for the population of interest. The intervention risk is p_C times RR, so the ARR is p_C times the relative risk reduction 1 minus RR. For a fixed relative risk, the ARR rises in direct proportion to baseline risk: at a relative risk of 0.75 a baseline risk of 0.04 gives an ARR of 0.01, a fifth of the value at 0.20.

has common error note Applying the network odds ratio as a risk ratio. Multiplying 0.25 by 0.8 gives 0.20 rather than about 0.2105. The error grows as the baseline probability rises and can give probabilities above 1 for odds ratios above 1.
has description in the module Applies a treatment effect from a log odds ratio network to a baseline probability on the reference treatment, taken from a separate baseline natural history model. On the logit scale the effect adds, logit(p_k) = logit(p_0) + d_k, with OR_k = exp(d_k); the stated form is the same relation solved for p_k without logarithms. The ARR against the reference is then p_0 minus p_k.

Absolute risk as an incidence proportion

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000230
Type formula
assumes Closed cohort with complete follow-up, Numerator contained in the denominator, Risk stated with its period
has calculator text R = E / N
has common error note Dividing a risk by the number of cycles. Dividing a one-year risk of 0.06 by 12 gives a monthly probability of 0.00500, which over 12 cycles implies a one-year risk of about 0.0584 rather than 0.06. The rate conversion on the Transition Probability page gives about 0.00514.
Dividing by the starting number after losses to follow-up. In the CDC example of 16 cases among 2,100 people followed for four years, dividing by 2,100 gives about 7.6 per 1,000 but understates the risk, because it assumes that people lost to follow-up stayed free of disease for the whole period.
Quoting a risk without its period. A risk of 6 per cent cannot enter a model until it is known whether it applies over one year or five, and risks from studies with different follow-up are not combined without conversion.
Using the complement of Kaplan-Meier survival under competing risks. Where another event, such as death from other causes, can prevent the event of interest, one minus the Kaplan-Meier survival estimate overstates the absolute risk. The cumulative incidence function gives the risk in that setting.
has description in the module Divides the number of new events during the period by the number of people at risk at its start. In epidemiology the same quantity is called the incidence proportion, attack rate or cumulative incidence. It gives the comparator-arm baseline risk that a decision model applies relative treatment effects to.

Actuarial value as the plan-paid share of total allowed cost

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000330
Type formula
assumes Fixed standard population for actuarial value, Allowed costs of covered services only in actuarial value, Spending held fixed when the plan design changes
has calculator text AV = sum_(g=1)^G [n_g * P_g] / sum_(g=1)^G [n_g * X_g]
has common error note Averaging each person's plan share instead of dividing totals. Averaging the plan's share of each person's allowed cost gives about 0.251 in the article's example, against an actuarial value of about 0.740. Spending is skewed, so the ten heaviest users dominate the totals while 90 of the 100 people have less than 74% of their own costs paid and 40 have nothing paid. The actuarial value is a population average and does not predict what any one member will pay.
Comparing actuarial values from different standard populations. A change in the claims data behind the standard population, or a new calculator version, changes the result for an unchanged plan design. Actuarial values from different benefit years or calculator versions therefore cannot be compared as if the plans had changed.
has description in the module Divides the plan's total payment for covered care by the total allowed cost of that care, both summed over a standard population for one benefit year. The population is held as G spending groups of n_g people with the same allowed cost per person, the layout of the article's worked example and of a continuance table. With one person in every group the formula is the article's ratio of summed plan payments to summed allowed costs over N people, and it equals 1 minus the members' share of total allowed cost.

Administrative censoring time and observed follow-up from staggered entry and a data cut-off

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000423
Type formula
assumes Common calendar for entry dates and the cut-off, No loss to follow-up before the cut-off
has calculator text C_i = d - e_i; Y_i = min(T_i, C_i); delta_i = (T_i <= C_i)
has common error note Cut-off date used as every patient's follow-up. Taking the calendar time of the cut-off as the follow-up of every patient ignores staggered entry. Patient 8 of the article's arm would be credited with 36 months of observation instead of 12, and the tail of the curve would appear to rest on far more patients than it does. The 36 months is computed here for illustration.
Median of observed times reported as median follow-up. The median of the observed times counts early deaths as short follow-up. In the article's eight-patient arm it is 15 months, whereas the reverse Kaplan-Meier method, which treats censoring as the outcome, gives a median follow-up of 24 months. Both figures are computed here for illustration and are not printed in the article.
has description in the module The administrative censoring time C_i of patient i is the gap between the calendar date of the data cut-off d and the patient's own entry date e_i. The observed follow-up Y_i is the smaller of the true event time T_i and C_i, and the event indicator delta_i is 1 when the event happened by the cut-off and 0 when the patient was censored. All times after entry are measured from entry or randomisation. When patients can also be lost to follow-up, the censoring time becomes the smaller of d minus e_i and the time of loss, and only the first part is administrative.

Administrative cost ratio as administrative cost over a chosen denominator

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000338
Type formula
assumes Matching period and boundary for administrative cost and its denominator
Payer administration only in a health accounts administrative cost ratio
has calculator text ACR = A / D
has common error note Comparing administrative cost ratios built on different denominators. For the article's insurer, administration over premium is 12.0%, administration over total spending is 13.3% and one minus the medical loss ratio is 18.3%. A gap between two figures built on different bases, or between a figure that includes profit and one that does not, says nothing about which payer runs at lower cost.
Reading a lower administrative cost ratio as greater efficiency. In the article's example a $5 million cut in claims control lowers the ratio on premium from 12.0% to 11.0% while claims rise by $12 million. The ratio sets one input against a scale variable: administration that cuts claims by more than it costs raises the ratio, and a rise in provider prices lowers it with no change in administration.
has description in the module Divides administrative cost over a period by a denominator for the same period: premium revenue for an insurer (written ACR_P in the article), the payer's total spending on claims, quality improvement and administration (ACR_S), or current health expenditure for a country. The result is a proportion, usually reported as a percentage, and two ratios are comparable only when both parts are defined in the same way.

Age-weighted continuously discounted years lived with disability per incident case

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000688
Type formula
assumes Constant disability weight over the case and discounting from onset
Incidence perspective for age-weighted years lived with disability
has calculator text YLD_awd = DW * (K * C * exp(r * a) / (r + beta)^2 * (exp(-(r + beta) * (L + a)) * (-(r + beta) * (L + a) - 1) - exp(-(r + beta) * a) * (-(r + beta) * a - 1)) + (1 - K) / r * (1 - exp(-r * L)))
has common error note Age at the end of the case entered as its duration. L is the duration, not the age at which the case ends. Entering 45 for the case with onset at 35 counts 45 years of illness and gives about 15.86 years lived with disability instead of 6.955 (computed here for illustration).
Disability weight applied to the age-weighted term only. The weight multiplies the whole expression. Leaving the (1 minus K) term unweighted at K = 0.5 gives about 7.80 years for the case with onset at 35 instead of 6.07 (computed here for illustration), and at K = 0 it counts the illness as if it were death.

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000687
Type formula
assumes Continuous discounting from the time of death at one rate, Age-weighted discounted DALYs as a historical convention
has calculator text YLL_awd = K * C * exp(r * a) / (r + beta)^2 * (exp(-(r + beta) * (L + a)) * (-(r + beta) * (L + a) - 1) - exp(-(r + beta) * a) * (-(r + beta) * a - 1)) + (1 - K) / r * (1 - exp(-r * L))
has common error note Age-weighted discounted values compared with later unweighted estimates. GBD from 2010 onwards and WHO after its 2012 decision use neither age weights nor discounting. Comparing the 36.44 years for a death at 5 in the article's illustration with an undiscounted 75 years from a later study attributes to a change in health a difference that is the change in convention, the article's second misreading.
Factor e to the ra dropped from the age-weighted term. The age-weighted term is valued at the time of death, which the factor e to the ra restores after the integral is taken from birth. Without it a death at 5 counts about 31.36 years instead of 36.44, and a death at 40 about 7.0 instead of 23.22 (computed here for illustration), so the error grows with the age at death.
has description in the module Gives the years of life lost for one death at age a with L standard years remaining, each year weighted by HE-FM-AGW-001 and discounted continuously at rate r from the time of death, in the form the WHO environmental burden of disease guide gives for a single death. The first term is the age-weighted integral, scaled by K, and the second term, with weight 1 minus K, is the continuously discounted years of HE-FM-YLL-003, so K = 0 returns that record and HE-FM-DISC-003 with an amount of 1 and its continuous rate rho set equal to r. With r = 0.03 and K = 1 it gives the YLL per death of the standard GBD 1990 DALY, which GBD 2010 and WHO later dropped. The undiscounted case is HE-FM-AGW-002.

Aggregate stop-loss carrier payment and employer retention for one contract year

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000333
Type formula
assumes Claims accumulate net of specific stop-loss recoveries, Claims inside the aggregate stop-loss contract basis
has calculator text L = min(max(S - A, 0), M); R = S - L
has common error note Accumulating gross claims towards the aggregate attachment point. For illustration, suppose Employer 1's gross claims were $2,100,000 with $120,000 recovered under the specific cover, leaving $1,980,000 net. Applying the aggregate rule to gross claims gives a payment of $225,000 instead of $105,000, so total recoveries are counted as $345,000 rather than $225,000. The $120,000 already paid by the specific layer is reimbursed twice.
Treating the aggregate attachment point as a cap on the employer's cost. The attachment point limits retained claims only within the contract and only up to the maximum payment. In the second worked example the employer retains $2,050,000, which is $175,000 above the attachment point, before adding premiums, excluded services and claims that fall outside the incurred and paid basis.
has description in the module Gives the aggregate stop-loss carrier's payment for a contract year as the excess of the employer's net claims over the aggregate attachment point, capped at the policy's maximum aggregate payment, and the employer's retained claims as the remainder. Net claims S are the sum over covered members of each member's eligible claims net of specific stop-loss recoveries, so the calculator takes the total directly. The functions min and max return the smaller and the larger of their arguments. With no maximum the retained claims equal the smaller of S and A, so they never exceed the attachment point.

Type formula

has calculator text delta = AIC_i - AIC_min
has common error note Interpreting a single AIC value on its own. An AIC of 1210.4 says nothing by itself, because individual AIC values contain an arbitrary constant and change with the sample size. Only differences between models fitted to the same data can be read.
Settling a near-tie by the smallest AIC. A difference of 1.2 between the log-normal and the generalised gamma does not separate them. A near-tie signals structural uncertainty, which belongs in scenario analysis rather than being settled by the smallest number.
has description in the module Rescales each model's AIC to its distance from the smallest AIC in the candidate set, so the best model scores 0 and the arbitrary constant cancels. On Burnham and Anderson's rule of thumb, a difference of 2 or less indicates substantial support, 4 to 7 considerably less, and above 10 almost none.

Akaike information criterion from the maximised log-likelihood

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000275
Type formula
assumes Candidate models fitted to identical survival data, Parameter count includes every estimated parameter, Candidate set chosen before fitting
has calculator text AIC = 2 * k - 2 * lnL
has common error note Comparing AIC across models fitted to different data. AIC values from curves fitted to different patients, endpoints or data cuts are not comparable, because each likelihood describes different observations. When treatment arms are fitted separately the rankings may disagree, and NICE DSU TSD 14 advises the same type of distribution in both arms unless there is strong evidence that an alternative is more plausible.
Reading the lowest AIC as evidence of plausible extrapolation. AIC measures fit to the observed data only. In a simulated example in NICE DSU TSD 21, the log-normal had the lowest AIC, yet the two models with the lowest AIC gave the poorest 40-year extrapolations. The clinical plausibility of the extrapolated hazard has to be assessed separately.
has description in the module Akaike's criterion charges a penalty of 2 for each estimated parameter. A more complex model is therefore preferred only if each extra parameter raises the maximised log-likelihood by more than one unit. Because it compares maximised likelihoods rather than testing one model against another, it can rank survival distributions that are not nested within one another.

Akaike weight of a candidate model

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000277
Type formula
assumes Weights conditional on the full candidate set
has calculator text w = exp(-delta / 2) / S
has common error note Dropping the factor of one half from the weight. Using exp(-delta) instead of exp(-delta/2) exaggerates the lead of the best model. In the six-curve example it raises the log-normal weight from about 0.44 to about 0.64 and cuts the Weibull weight from about 0.066 to about 0.014.
Reading the largest Akaike weight as plausibility of the extrapolation. An Akaike weight of 0.44 for the log-normal describes its fit to the observed trial data relative to the other candidates. It says nothing about whether the curve's hazard beyond follow-up is clinically plausible, which has to be assessed against external evidence.
has description in the module Converts AIC differences into weights that sum to 1 across the R candidate models. The weight w_i equals exp(-delta_i/2) divided by S, where S is the sum of exp(-delta_r/2) over all R candidates. It is read as the weight of evidence that the model is the best approximating model in the set, given the data. Adding or removing a candidate changes every weight.

All-cause bathtub hazard as background plus excess hazard

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000354
Type formula
assumes Background hazard fixed from population rates, Excess hazard of zero or above in a bathtub model
has calculator text h_all = h_bg + h_exc
has common error note Excess hazard extrapolated below zero. A fitted excess hazard that keeps falling can turn negative in the extrapolated period, pulling the all-cause hazard below population mortality and inflating survival in the tail.
General population rates for a cohort with more comorbidity. Taking the background hazard from national life tables when patients carry more comorbidity than the general population understates expected mortality, and the late arm of the bathtub then rises too slowly.
has description in the module Splits the all-cause hazard into a background hazard from population mortality and an excess hazard attributed to the disease or procedure. When the excess hazard declines after the early period, the background hazard, which rises with age, supplies the late arm of the bathtub. On the survival scale the same relation makes all-cause survival equal to background survival multiplied by relative survival. The per-cycle probability follows from h_all with the conversion HE-FM-TP-001.

All-cause cycle death probability from independent background and disease-specific death probabilities

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000695
Type formula
assumes Background and disease deaths as independent competing risks within the cycle
Disease probability that excludes deaths already in the life table
Background probability read at attained age in every cycle
has calculator text p_all = 1 - (1 - p_bg) * (1 - p_dis)
has common error note All-cause hazard ratio applied to background deaths. Applying a treatment hazard ratio to p_all also cuts background deaths, which the treatment cannot affect. With the article's annual rates and an illustrative hazard ratio of 0.70, the treated all-cause probability is 0.169311 when the ratio is applied to p_all through HE-FM-HR-004, against 0.173041 when it is applied to p_dis alone (computed here for illustration).
Background and disease death probabilities added. Adding the two probabilities counts twice the people who would have died of both causes in the cycle. For the article's annual rates the error is small, 0.236087 against 0.232794, but with illustrative probabilities of 0.10 and 0.30 at older ages the sum is 0.40 against 0.37 (computed here for illustration).
Life-table probability layered on an all-cause trial probability. Combining p_bg with a disease probability that already contains other-cause deaths counts background mortality twice. In the article's illustrative cure model life years to 30 years fall from 11.93 to 10.05, an understatement of 1.87 years, or 16%. A trial curve can take background mortality only as a floor, which HE-VT-BTH-008 checks.
has description in the module Combines the probability of dying of other causes in a cycle, read from the life table at the cohort's attained age, with the probability of dying of the disease in the same cycle. A person survives the cycle only by escaping both, so the all-cause probability is 1 minus the product of the two survival probabilities. When both come from constant rates over the same cycle with HE-FM-TP-001, the result equals the probability from the summed hazard of HE-FM-BTH-005, the total compound rate that Sonnenberg and Beck form by adding the excess rate to the baseline rate. HE-FM-TP-004 splits the result between background and disease death states where a model keeps them apart.

Analysed final-visit mean after LOCF as a mixture of the earlier and final means

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000616
Type formula
assumes Final-visit values missing completely at random for the LOCF mixture mean
All imputed values carried from one earlier visit
has calculator text mu_tilde = tau * mu_last + (1 - tau) * mu_end; bias_mu = tau * (mu_last - mu_end)
has common error note Calling LOCF conservative in a deteriorating condition. When the outcome worsens over time, mu_last is above mu_end and the bias tau times their difference is positive in every arm, so LOCF makes each arm look better than it is. The EMA guideline describes LOCF in Alzheimer's disease as very likely to be overly optimistic in both arms, and not appropriate where active-arm participants withdraw earlier.
Treating LOCF as unbiased because data are missing completely at random. Random dropout does not remove the bias: in the article's treatment arm dropout is unrelated to utility, yet LOCF overstates the 12-month mean by 0.016 because the mean falls between 6 and 12 months. The completers alone would recover the true mean of 0.64 in this case. The National Research Council panel notes that LOCF is sometimes mistakenly considered valid under missing completely at random or missing at random data.
has description in the module When a fraction tau of final-visit values is missing completely at random and replaced by values from an earlier visit, the completed final-visit data are a mixture of two distributions. Their expected mean, mu_tilde, is tau times the mean at the earlier visit plus one minus tau times the true final-visit mean (Lachin 2016, equation 1). The bias, mu_tilde minus mu_end, is tau times the change in the mean between the two visits, so it is zero only when the mean does not change after the last observed visit.

Type formula
assumes Occupancy, stay and turnover rate from the same counts, A 365-day year for the annual bed turnover rate
has calculator text T = 365 * o / L_bar
has common error note Bed turnover rate from averaged occupancy and stay. Averaging hospital-level ratios does not reproduce the ratio of group totals. Applying the formula to Aloh and colleagues' mean occupancy of 42.14% and mean stay of 8.15 days gives about 18.9 patients per bed, against their reported mean turnover of 21.27, because each mean is an average across hospital-years. Pooled figures come from summed discharges, bed-days and beds.
Occupancy entered as a percentage in the bed turnover rate. Entering occupancy as 85 instead of 0.85 multiplies the result by 100, giving 6,205 patients per bed a year at a 5-day stay instead of 62.05.
has description in the module Expresses the annual turnover rate through bed occupancy and average length of stay. It follows from dividing both sides of the throughput identity on the Average Length of Stay page (HE-FM-ALOS-002) by the number of beds, with o equal to U divided by 365 times B_bar and L_bar equal to U divided by D. A high turnover rate can come from short stays, from full beds or from both, so the rate is ambiguous on its own. On a Pabón Lasso chart, which plots T against o, each line from the origin joins points with the same L_bar.

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000497
Type formula
assumes Difference-in-differences effect applied to the population covered
Difference-in-differences effect persists over the year costed
has calculator text C_net = C_prog + tau * N / 1000 * c_event
has common error note Dropping the per 1,000 scaling of a difference-in-differences rate. Multiplying minus 3.0 by 200,000 instead of 200 claims 600,000 fewer admissions, a thousandfold overstatement.
Ignoring spillovers to other services or payers when costing a difference-in-differences effect. If comparison areas also benefit or patients are displaced into them, the estimate is biased and the cost change misallocated; Meacock and colleagues stress positive and negative spillovers and who receives any savings.
has description in the module Turns an estimated change in an event rate per 1,000 people into events per year for the population covered and values them, then adds the policy's running cost. A negative result is a net saving. Health effects are valued separately in a cost-effectiveness analysis, and the estimate's standard error should be carried into probabilistic analysis.

Annualised capital charge net of discounted resale value

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000622
Type formula
assumes Annualised sums falling at the end of each year of use
Annualisation rate equal to the evaluation's real discount rate
Resale value counted whether or not the asset is sold
Replacement price for capital bought in earlier years
Same service in every year of the useful life
has calculator text A = (1 - (1+r)^(-n)) / r; E = (K - S * (1+r)^(-n)) / A
has common error note Nominal annualisation rate applied to real prices. Annualising with a nominal rate, which includes expected inflation, while prices are held in one price year overstates the opportunity cost of capital and so the annual charge. The rate and the prices are both real or both nominal.
Purchase price and annualised charge counted for the same asset. A model that enters the purchase price in the year of purchase and also adds an annualised charge for the same asset counts the capital twice. The same applies to published unit costs that already include an annualised building element.
Subtracting an undiscounted resale value before annualising. Netting the full GBP 5,000 resale value off the camera's price, rather than its present value of about GBP 4,210, gives about GBP 9,967 a year instead of GBP 10,142. The shortfall is r times S, GBP 175, the yearly cost of the funds still tied up in the resale value.
has description in the module Divides the purchase price, net of the resale value discounted over the useful life, by the annuity factor A, the present value of one unit of currency received at the end of each of n years. The result is the economic cost of using the asset for one year, covering both the value used up and the opportunity cost of the funds tied up in it. Rearranged, E equals K minus S divided by A, plus r times S, so the resale value attracts only a yearly holding charge of r times S and no wear.

Setting the type argument of PMT to 1 treats each sum as paid at the start of the year and gives about GBP 10,700 a year for the camera instead of GBP 11,074. Annuity-due instalment for a one-off therapy price

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000285
Type formula
assumes First annuity instalment paid at treatment, Fixed financing rate and equal annuity instalments
has calculator text A = P * i / ((1 - (1+i)^(-n)) * (1+i))
has common error note End-of-year annuity used when the first instalment is paid at treatment. Applying the ordinary annuity formula, without the division by (1 + i), to a schedule whose first payment falls at treatment overstates every instalment by a factor of (1 + i). In the £1 million example it gives about £230,975 instead of £219,976, and the five payments then have a present value at 5% of £1.05 million rather than the price.
has description in the module Gives the equal instalment paid at the start of each year, the first at the point of treatment, so that the n payments have the same present value at the financing rate i as the upfront price P. It is the present value of an annuity due rearranged for the payment. When payments fall at the end of each year instead, the final division by (1 + i) is dropped, which gives the ordinary annuity used to annualise capital costs.

Antithetic variance reduction factor and equivalent independent sample size

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000322
Type formula
assumes Equal cost of original and mirrored antithetic evaluations
Within-pair correlation above -1 for the antithetic efficiency factor
has calculator text VRF = 1 / (1 + rho); n_eq = n / (1 + rho)
has common error note Carrying a best-case antithetic gain over to a full model. The 2.8-fold gain in the survival example comes from one smooth monotone input and is close to a best case. A 2010 type 2 diabetes simulation reported that antithetic variates cut the replications needed for predicted QALYs by 53%, which implies a variance factor of roughly 0.47, about a 2.1-fold gain.
Reading an antithetic variance cut as the same cut in standard error. A 64% cut in variance, a factor of 0.3551, lowers the standard error by only about 40%, because the standard error scales with the square root of the variance: 0.188 against 0.316 years in the survival example.

A factor above 1 means pairing helps and a factor below 1 means it harms.

Approximate Bayes factor from a difference in BIC

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000400
Type formula
assumes BIC approximates the log Bayes factor, not the Bayes factor itself
Closer approximation under a unit-information prior
Kass and Raftery categories as a descriptive scale
has calculator text B_12 = exp((BIC_2 - BIC_1) / 2)
has common error note Exponentiating the whole BIC difference without halving it. Taking exp of the whole difference squares the approximate Bayes factor. For the exponential against the generalised gamma, a difference of 7.83 would give about 2,515 instead of about 50, far into the range the table calls very strong.
Treating BIC differences either side of a category edge as different verdicts. A BIC difference only approximates twice the log Bayes factor, so differences of 1.9 and 2.1, which fall either side of the first category edge, carry practically the same evidence. Treating them as different verdicts reads more precision into the scale than it holds.
has description in the module Kass and Raftery show that the Schwarz criterion is a rough approximation to the log Bayes factor, so twice the natural log of the Bayes factor in favour of model 1 over model 2 is approximately BIC_2 minus BIC_1. Exponentiating half the difference gives an approximate Bayes factor. On the Kass and Raftery scale, a difference of 0 to 2 is not worth more than a bare mention, 2 to 6 is positive, 6 to 10 strong and above 10 very strong evidence against the higher-BIC model.

Approximate confidence interval for a hazard ratio from the log scale

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000471
Type formula
assumes Approximate normality of the log hazard ratio
Estimate and standard error from the same model and reference group
has calculator text HR_L = exp(beta - z * SE_beta); HR_U = exp(beta + z * SE_beta)
has common error note Adding standard errors on the hazard ratio scale. Adding and subtracting 1.96 times 0.155839 to 0.70 gives about 0.3946 to 1.0054, an interval that crosses 1, instead of 0.5158 to 0.9501 on the log scale (computed here for illustration). The standard error belongs to the log hazard ratio.
Inverting the hazard ratio without inverting and swapping its limits. When a report gives the comparator against treatment, the reciprocal of the hazard ratio and of its limits is taken, and the limits change places: 0.70 (0.5158 to 0.9501) becomes about 1.4286 (1.0525 to 1.9387), computed here for illustration.
has description in the module Builds the interval on the natural log scale, where ratio measures are analysed, by adding and subtracting z standard errors to the log hazard ratio, and exponentiates the two limits. The interval is symmetric about the log hazard ratio and asymmetric about the hazard ratio itself. The log hazard ratio and its standard error come from a Cox model (HE-FM-HR-002) or from event counts and person-time (HE-FM-HR-005); z is 1.96 for a 95% interval.

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000401
Type formula
assumes Equal prior probability for every candidate curve in the BIC probabilities
Probability of the quasi-true model within the set
has calculator text Delta_i = BIC_i - BIC_min; p_i = exp(-Delta_i / 2) / S
has common error note Comparing BIC posterior probabilities across different candidate sets. Because the probabilities sum to 1 over the candidates, dropping the exponential from the 120-death example raises the generalised gamma from about 0.521 to about 0.526, and dropping the Weibull instead raises it to about 0.844. Probabilities from analyses with different candidates cannot be compared.
Reading a BIC posterior probability near 1 as a plausible extrapolation. A probability near 1 means that one model stands out on the data within follow-up, not that it will extrapolate well. NICE DSU TSD 14 treats AIC and BIC as measures of internal validity only, so the extrapolated tail is judged on external data, clinical plausibility and expert judgement.
has description in the module Converts BIC differences into approximate posterior probabilities for each candidate model, assuming every model has the same prior probability. S is the sum of exp(-Delta_r / 2) over all R candidate models, so the probabilities add to 1 across the set. Burnham and Anderson view such model weights as a step towards model averaging.

AR(1) correlation between measurements s visit steps apart

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000305
Type formula
assumes Equally spaced visits for the AR(1) step form, AR(1) correlation depends only on the distance between visits, Pure AR(1) correlation decays towards zero
has calculator text r = rho^s
has common error note Assuming AR(1) correlation dies out over long follow-up. Pure AR(1) drives the correlation between distant visits towards zero, yet stable differences between patients keep utilities correlated over long follow-up. Fitting pure AR(1) to such data misdescribes the correlation between baseline and late visits; a random intercept with AR(1) residuals often fits better.
Confusing an AR(1) residual structure with a lagged outcome model. An AR(1) residual structure describes the dependence left after the mean model and keeps the regression coefficients marginal. Including the previous outcome as a covariate answers a conditional question, a distinction Liang and Zeger drew between their marginal approach and conditional models.
Reading an omitted trend as AR(1) serial correlation. An unmodelled trend or seasonal pattern leaves residuals that are correlated over time, which can look like autoregressive correlation. The mean model is checked first, for example with residual plots and the partial autocorrelation function, before an autoregressive error is added.
has description in the module Gives the correlation between two outcomes of the same patient, for example utilities or costs, measured s equally spaced visits apart, when the correlation between adjacent visits is rho. With rho between 0 and 1 the correlation is highest for adjacent visits and falls geometrically towards zero as the gap grows. For four visits the correlation matrix has 1 on the diagonal, rho beside it, then rho^2 and rho^3 in the corners.

Extrapolating a baseline above general population values. PMG36 section 4.3.7 asks that baselines extrapolated over long horizons reflect the decline in quality of life in the general population and do not exceed general population values at a given age, based on a recent source.
has description in the module Ara and Brazier's regression of EQ-5D index scores from the 2003 and 2006 Health Survey for England gives mean general population utility as a quadratic in age with a shift for men. Applying a proportional decrement m to this baseline, as the multiplicative rule does, makes the absolute loss shrink as the baseline falls with age, whereas a fixed additive decrement costs the same at every age. The equation is shown for illustration; PMG36 asks for a recent source, and the norms used should match the instrument and value set of the other utilities.

Arc cross-price elasticity between two observed price and quantity pairs

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000488
Type formula
assumes Only the price of good j changes between the two arc cross-price observations
Cross-price elasticity price measured where the prescribing or buying decision is made
has calculator text eps_arc = ((Q_i1 - Q_i0) / (Q_i1 + Q_i0)) / ((P_j1 - P_j0) / (P_j1 + P_j0))
has common error note Assuming every branded pack lost becomes a generic pack gained. In the article's example 1,200 branded packs are lost but only 1,000 generic packs gained; holding total use fixed would put generic use at 7,200. A budget impact model that ignores the cross response altogether, keeping generic use at 6,000, overstates the payer's saving by 2,000 pounds a month, about 6 per cent of the true saving.
Dividing by starting values instead of averages in an arc cross-price elasticity. Using 6,000 and 8 as bases gives 0.1667 / 0.50, or 0.33, and reversing the start gives 0.1429 / 0.3333, or 0.43; neither is the arc value of 0.38.
has description in the module Divides the change in the quantity of good i, as a proportion of the average of its two values, by the change in the price of good j, as a proportion of the average of its two prices. Using averages gives the same answer whichever observation is treated as the start; the factors of 2 in the averages cancel. With i equal to j the same formula gives the arc own-price elasticity, as in the RAND form HE-FM-MH-003.

Atkinson equally distributed equivalent health at epsilon of 1

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000294
Type formula
assumes Health above zero for the geometric-mean EDE, Equal weight per person or group in the geometric-mean EDE
definition source the Source rows of the Functions and Formulae module record HE-FM-ATK-003
editor note The geometric mean takes logarithms of health in years and exponentiates their mean, which keeps the unit of health but which the dimension rule of the 0.1 runner cannot follow.
formalises equity weighting
has calculator text h_EDE = exp(sum_(i=1)^n [log(h_i)] / n)
has common error note Zero or negative values in the geometric-mean EDE. Applying the geometric mean to a health measure that can be zero or negative, such as QALYs gained or net health benefit, fails: Excel GEOMEAN returns #NUM!, and a single zero computed by hand gives an EDE of zero and an index of 1. The formula needs levels of health, such as QALE, not changes.
has Content MathML <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><apply><csymbol cd="relation1">eq</csymbol><ci>h_EDE</ci><apply><csymbol cd="transc1">exp</csymbol><apply><csymbol cd="arith1">divide</csymbol><apply><csymbol cd="arith1">sum</csymbol><apply><csymbol cd="interval1">integer_interval</csymbol><cn type="integer">1</cn><ci>n</ci></apply><bind><csymbol cd="fns1">lambda</csymbol><bvar><ci>i</ci></bvar><apply><csymbol cd="transc1">ln</csymbol><apply><csymbol cd="hemo1" cdbase="https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/cd">element</csymbol><ci>h_i</ci><ci>i</ci></apply></apply></bind></apply><ci>n</ci></apply></apply></apply></math>
has description in the module Gives the equally distributed equivalent health when epsilon equals 1, where the general formula HE-FM-ATK-002 is undefined. The EDE is then the geometric mean of the n health values, the nth root of their product, written here as the exponential of the mean natural logarithm. The function log is the natural logarithm. It corresponds to Atkinson's logarithmic welfare function and is the limit of the general formula as epsilon tends to 1.

editor note The equally distributed equivalent raises health in years to the power 1 minus epsilon and back, so it is homogeneous of degree 1 in health and keeps its unit, which the dimension rule of the 0.1 runner, built for whole-number powers, cannot follow.
h_i and h_EDE are quality-adjusted life expectancy, so QALYs. The equally distributed equivalent holds for any health measure on a ratio scale.
formalises equity weighting, relative inequality aversion parameter
has calculator text h_EDE = (sum_(i=1)^n [h_i^(1-epsilon)] / n)^(1/(1-epsilon))
has common error note Setting epsilon to exactly 1 in the general Atkinson EDE formula. At epsilon of 1 the outer exponent one over one minus epsilon divides by zero, and Excel returns #DIV/0!. The EDE at epsilon of 1 is the geometric mean, HE-FM-ATK-003, which is the limit of this formula as epsilon tends to 1.
Treating groups of unequal size as equal in the Atkinson EDE. Entering one value per group when the groups differ in size gives each group the same weight. With baseline QALE of 60 and 72 years and the less healthy group making up 20% of the population, the share-weighted EDE at epsilon of 2 is about 69.23 years, whereas entering the two values once each gives about 65.45 years.

Each h_i is the health of one person, or of one of n groups of equal size.

Atkinson index from equally distributed equivalent health

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000292
Type formula
assumes EDE and Atkinson index computed at the same epsilon, Positive ratio-scale health in the Atkinson index, Relative inequality concept of the Atkinson index
has calculator text A_epsilon = 1 - h_EDE / h_bar
has common error note Choosing the programme with the lower Atkinson index. The index measures inequality, not social welfare, so the option with the lower index is not necessarily preferred. In the article's example at epsilon of 1, programme U has the higher index, about 0.00438 against 0.00391 for T, yet also the higher EDE, about 66.0095 against 65.9912 years, so U is still ranked first at that epsilon. Decisions rest on the EDE or an inequality-adjusted net health benefit.
Reading the Atkinson index as a gap between groups. An index of 0.04 does not mean that the less healthy group has 4% less health than the mean. It means that an equal distribution at 96% of current mean health would be judged as good as the current one at the chosen epsilon, and the same distribution gives a different index at another epsilon.
has description in the module Compares the equally distributed equivalent health at a chosen epsilon, from HE-FM-ATK-002 or HE-FM-ATK-003, with mean health. The index is one minus their ratio, so it lies between 0, complete equality, and 1. Atkinson's own reading is that a value of 0.3 means an equal distribution would need only 70% of present national income to give the same social welfare; in health, an index of 0.04 means an equal distribution at 96% of current mean health would be judged as good.

ATT as the treated-mix weighted sum of subgroup effects

Type formula
assumes Subgroup effect applies to its treated members, Treatment probabilities from the practice described
has calculator text ATT = sum_(x=1)^K (P_x * e_x * CATE_x) / sum_(x=1)^K (P_x * e_x)
has common error note Using the ATT for a whole-population decision. The ATT of 0.31 QALYs and £3,700 gives about £11,935 per QALY and an incremental net monetary benefit of £4,050 at £25,000 per QALY. A decision to treat the whole population needs the ATE instead: about £15,455 per QALY and £2,100. Matched analyses often report the ATT, so the estimand is checked before the figures enter a model.
has description in the module Computes the average treatment effect on the treated (ATT) from the same subgroup effects as HE-FM-ATE-001, reweighted to the subgroup mix of the patients who were actually treated. The product P_x times e_x is the share of the whole population that is treated and in subgroup x, and dividing by the sum of these products gives each subgroup's share of the treated group. When treatment is more likely where the effect is larger, the ATT exceeds the ATE.

AUC as the trapezoidal area under the empirical ROC curve

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000297
Type formula
assumes ROC points at every distinct threshold in order
has calculator text AUC_trap = sum_(k=1)^K [(FPR_end_k - FPR_start_k) * (TPR_start_k + TPR_end_k) / 2]
has common error note Using rectangles instead of trapezoids through tied scores. Drawing the tie as a step gives a rectangle in place of the diagonal segment. Moving across before up gives 0.875 for the ten-patient curve, and moving up before across gives about 0.917, against about 0.896 from the trapezoid. These are the pessimistic and optimistic segments that Fawcett describes for equally scored cases.
has description in the module Adds the areas of the trapezoids beneath the empirical ROC curve, which plots sensitivity (the true positive rate) against the false positive rate (one minus specificity) at every threshold. Each segment between consecutive points contributes its width on the false positive axis multiplied by the mean of its two heights. Vertical segments add nothing, and the diagonal segment drawn through tied scores supplies the half credit of the pair count, so the result equals HE-FM-AUC-001.

AUC estimated by counting case and non-case pairs

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000296
Type formula
assumes Binary outcome known for every person in the AUC sample, Higher score means higher risk in the AUC pair count
has calculator text AUC = (n_conc + 0.5 * n_tie) / (n_1 * n_0)
has common error note Counting tied pairs as wins or losses in the AUC. In the ten-patient example, counting the tie at 0.30 as concordant gives 22 divided by 24, about 0.917, and dropping it gives 21 divided by 24, or 0.875. Only the half credit reproduces the area under the empirical ROC curve, about 0.896.
Reading a high AUC as evidence of calibration. The AUC depends only on the order of the scores. Adding 0.10 to every predicted risk in the ten-patient example leaves the AUC at about 0.896, but the mean predicted risk moves from 0.34 to 0.44 against an observed event rate of 0.40, and at an illustrative treatment threshold of 0.35 the number of patients flagged rises from 4 to 6. At an illustrative £400 per patient flagged, treatment costs per ten patients rise from £1,600 to £2,400. Calibration is checked separately before predicted risks enter a cost-effectiveness model.
Reporting the AUC of a score coded in the wrong direction. If a lower score indicates higher risk but the count treats higher scores as higher risk, the result is one minus the correct AUC: about 0.104 instead of 0.896 for the ten-patient example. An estimate well below 0.5 is a prompt to check the direction of the score.
has description in the module Compares every person with the outcome with every person without it. A pair in which the person with the outcome has the higher score counts 1, a tied pair counts one half, and the total is divided by the number of such pairs. This is the article's double sum of psi(s_i, s_j) over all n_1 times n_0 pairs, written with pair counts, and it is the quantity estimated by the Wilcoxon rank statistic.

Average annual inflation rate between two consumer price index values

Annualising that one month gives minus 6.2% a year, while the 12-month change to January 2024 was 4.0% (131.5 against 126.4), both computed here from the published rounded indices. Section 11.3 of the manual warns that one or two months of change may mislead.
Total CPI change divided by the number of years. Dividing the 21.65% rise between the two financial-year averages by 4 gives 5.41% a year, against a compound average of 5.02% (computed here for illustration). Compounding the simple rate over four years gives a ratio of 1.2347 in place of 1.2165.
Years entered in place of months in the average CPI rate. Entering n = 4 for four years in place of 48 months makes the exponent 3 and gives 80.0% a year for the financial-year example in place of 5.02% (computed here for illustration).
has description in the module Turns the ratio of a later index value I_2 to an earlier value I_1, n months apart, into the constant annual rate that compounds to the same change, the equation section 11.3 of the ONS technical manual gives for an annual average inflation rate over any period other than a year. With n = 12 it is the change on the figure 12 months earlier, the annual inflation rate of section 11.2. The ratio I_2 / I_1 is the I_b / I_a of HE-FM-COST-002, which uprates a cost and is not repeated here. The financial-year averages that the article compares are built in HE-CF-CPI-002.

Average cost-effectiveness ratio against doing nothing

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000324
Type formula
assumes Doing nothing as the real alternative, Positive health gain over doing nothing, Stated and estimated do-nothing baseline
has calculator text ACER_i0 = (C_i - C_0) / (E_i - E_0)
has common error note Choosing the option with the lowest average ratio. Ranking mutually exclusive options by average ratio ignores what the extra health from the more effective option costs. At £40,000 per QALY the lowest average ratio still picks A at £5,000, but the ICER of B against A is £35,000, below the threshold, and net monetary benefit is £15,000 for B against £14,000 for A, so B is the right choice.
Reading a table of average ratios as a funding ranking. Average ratios from separate studies each rest on their own baseline, population and time horizon, so placing them side by side and funding from the lowest upwards compares unlike quantities.
Testing an average ratio against the threshold when another option exists. An average ratio below the threshold shows cost-effectiveness only if doing nothing is the sole alternative. In the article's example B costs £15,000 per QALY gained against no treatment, below £20,000, but its ICER against A is £35,000 per QALY, so adopting B on its average ratio approves a poor-value option.
has description in the module Divides the cost of option i minus the cost of doing nothing by its health effect minus the health effect of doing nothing. It is the pairwise ICER (HE-FM-ICER-001) with doing nothing as the comparator, so it is informative when doing nothing is the real alternative and misleading when another option is available. When C_0 and E_0 are both zero it equals the total-form ratio HE-FM-ACER-001.

Average per-cycle death probability across three tunnel states and a long-term state

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000586
Type formula
assumes Average specific to one cycle and one entry history, Weights from the occupancy at the start of the cycle
has calculator text q_bar = (m_T1 * q_1 + m_T2 * q_2 + m_T3 * q_3 + m_L * q_L) / (m_T1 + m_T2 + m_T3 + m_L)
has common error note Averaging the tunnel death probabilities without weights. The simple mean of 0.20, 0.08, 0.04 and 0.03 is 0.0875, against the weighted 0.0925 in the article's year 4 example, and the unweighted figure does not move as the mix of durations changes (computed here for illustration).
Carrying one scenario's average into a single memoryless state. Fixing 0.0925 as the probability of a single post-infarction state fits only that cycle at 5 per cent incidence. The same tunnel gives 0.20 after one year, and 0.0885 or 0.0940 after four years at incidences of 10 or 3 per cent, so a strategy that changes incidence changes the right value.
has description in the module Gives the share of people in a tunnelled clinical state who die in the next cycle, as the occupancy-weighted mean of the probabilities in T1, T2, T3 and L. Here m_T1 to m_L are the values m_(T_k,t) and m_(L,t) of HE-FM-TUN-001 at one cycle, and q_k equals 1 minus s_k when death is the only exit. The average depends on when people entered, which is why a single memoryless state with a cycle-specific probability cannot reproduce a tunnel once entry is staggered. Longer tunnels add one term to each sum for each extra state.

Averaged-cohort gap in constant-risk life expectancy for two strata

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000707
Type formula
assumes Constant death probability within each stratum run to absorption, Fixed and exhaustive stratum shares at model start, Undiscounted life expectancy in the averaged-cohort gap
has calculator text q_bar = w * q_1 + (1 - w) * q_2; L_strat = w * (1 / q_1 - 0.5) + (1 - w) * (1 / q_2 - 0.5); L_avg = 1 / q_bar - 0.5; gap_L = L_strat - L_avg
has common error note Averaged-cohort ICER taken as confirmed by the mean of stratum ICERs. With a one-off cost c, a constant utility u and a proportional cut e, each constant-risk stratum has an ICER of c(1 minus e)q divided by ue (derived here), proportional to q, so the ICER of one cohort at the mean probability equals the share-weighted mean of the stratum ICERs. In the article's example the averaged cohort's GBP 15,000 equals the simple mean of GBP 5,000 and GBP 25,000. The agreement is a property of this model and checks nothing, since both differ from the population ICER of GBP 8,333 per QALY that the share-weighted gains of HE-FM-ATE-001 give with HE-FM-ICER-001; HE-ER-CHN-002 shows why subgroup ICERs are not averaged.
Death rates averaged in place of probabilities for an averaged cohort. Converting 0.05 and 0.25 to rates, averaging them and converting back gives a probability of about 0.156 and a life expectancy of about 5.91 years, still 49% below the stratified 11.5 years (computed here for illustration). Changing the scale on which the input is averaged leaves the bias in place; running the strata separately removes it.
Expecting a proportional cut to gain most where death risk is highest. Run as separate cohorts, the article's strata gain 5.0 life years from a 20% cut at an annual death probability of 0.05 and 1.0 at 0.25, each gain the difference of two values of L(q), although the absolute risk reduction of HE-FM-ARR-002 in one cycle is 0.01 in the first stratum and 0.05 in the second. At a constant probability the gain equals e divided by (1 minus e) q (derived here), so at a fixed proportional cut it falls as baseline risk rises, and ranking strata by the one-cycle absolute reduction reverses their ranking by lifetime life years gained.
Half cycle subtracted on one side of an averaged-cohort comparison. Setting a stratified result counted at the start of each cycle with no half-cycle subtraction, 12 years, against an averaged cohort that has it, 6.17 years, overstates the gap by half a cycle, 5.83 against 5.33 years. Both sides need the same counting weights, as in HE-FM-CSIM-001.
Second-order approximation read as the averaged-cohort gap. Applying HE-FM-EV-002 to 1/q at the mean probability of 0.15, with a second derivative of about 592.6 and a variance of 0.01 across the two equal strata, gives a gap of about 2.96 years against the exact 5.33, 44% too small (computed here for illustration). With strata this far apart the higher-order terms are large, so the closed form or separate stratum runs give the estimate.
has description in the module Gives the population mean life expectancy when each of two strata with constant per-cycle death probabilities q_1 and q_2 is run as its own cohort and weighted by its share, the life expectancy of one cohort run at the share-weighted mean probability, and the difference between them. Each stratum result is the article's L(q), 1/q minus one half, the one-state case of HE-FM-ABS-001 with the half-cycle subtraction of HE-CF-MKCH-001, and the weighting is that of HE-FM-ATE-001. The half cycle cancels in gap_L, which equals w(1 minus w)(q_1 minus q_2) squared divided by q_1 q_2 q_bar (derived here), so the gap is never negative and is zero only when the strata share one probability or one stratum holds the whole cohort. The averaged cohort therefore never overstates life expectancy in this model and understates it whenever both strata are present with different probabilities, the bias that TSD 15 section 3.1 describes for an outcome that is non-linear in a patient characteristic; HE-FM-EV-002 approximates the same gap by a second-order term, whereas this form is exact.

has common error note Checking appearances but not pairings. A design in which every object appears four times can still show some pairs together more often than others. The pair count, not only the appearance count, needs to be equal for the design to be balanced.

Whole-number values of r and lambda are needed for such a design.

Bang and Tsiatis simple weighted estimator of mean cost with censored data

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000526
Type formula
assumes Censoring independent of the cost and survival process
Restricted period with enough complete cases for the weighted cost estimator
has calculator text mu = (1 / N) * sum_(i=1)^N [Delta_i * A_i / S_c_i]
has common error note Averaging observed costs over all patients. The full-sample mean counts censored patients' partial costs as complete and is biased downwards; in heart failure data with 32 per cent censored over 1,080 days it gave 30,420 Canadian dollars against 36,490 from reweighted estimators.
Relying on the simple weighted estimator under heavy censoring. Only complete cases carry information, so the estimator becomes unstable as censoring grows; in simulations it substantially overestimated true costs with 53 per cent censoring.
Running a Kaplan-Meier analysis on cumulative cost. Treating cost as the time scale assumes cost at censoring is independent of cost at death, but with a constant spending rate R the two are R times the censoring time and R times the death time, so survival methods are not valid for cost.
has description in the module Estimates mean cost over a restricted period from all N patients, counting only complete cases (death or full follow-up to the limit) and weighting each by the inverse of the Kaplan-Meier probability of remaining uncensored at its time, with censoring treated as the event. Censored patients contribute through the weights given to complete cases with longer follow-up. Survival methods applied directly to cumulative cost are not valid, because cost at censoring and cost at death are linked through the same patient's spending.

Basic reproduction number from the final attack rate of a completed epidemic

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000329
Type formula
assumes Final size relation assumptions for estimating R_0, Completed epidemic and an infection-based final attack rate
has calculator text R_0 = -log(1 - z / s_0) / z
has common error note Estimating R_0 from a clinical attack rate. Illustrative figures: if only half of the infections in the article's example caused symptoms, a clinical attack rate of 0.40 would imply R_0 of about 1.28 instead of 2.
Ignoring prior immunity when estimating R_0 from a final attack rate. Treating the final attack rate of 0.358 from a population with 30% immune as though everyone had been susceptible gives R_0 of about 1.24 instead of 2.
has description in the module In the simple susceptible, infectious and recovered model, the final attack rate z of an epidemic satisfies the final size relation z = s_0(1 minus exp(minus R_0 z)), where s_0 is 1 when almost everyone is susceptible at the start. Taking logarithms of 1 minus z/s_0 = exp(minus R_0 z) rearranges the relation to give R_0 from an observed final attack rate. The function log is the natural logarithm.

Basic reproduction number of a two-group next-generation matrix as its dominant eigenvalue

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000701
Type formula
assumes Next-generation matrix evaluated at the disease-free state with non-negative entries
has calculator text T_K = k_11 + k_22; D_K = k_11 * k_22 - k_12 * k_21; R_0 = (T_K + sqrt(T_K^2 - 4 * D_K)) / 2
has common error note Largest diagonal entry of a next-generation matrix read as R_0. For the article's matrix the larger diagonal entry, 0.8, suggests that spread dies out, while R_0 is about 1.268 because cases pass between the groups, so judging each group on its own transmission misses the threshold crossing.
Square root dropped from a host and vector reproduction number or used for a host coverage target. Van den Driessche notes that the literature often omits the square root for vector-host models, which keeps the threshold at 1 but changes the value, so the two forms cannot be compared across studies. In the illustrative host and vector matrix the product 2 would replace 1.414. Neither value gives a host coverage target through the threshold formula of HE-FM-BRN-003. Vaccinating a proportion p of hosts scales the host row of K by 1 minus p and gives R_0 of the square root of 2(1 minus p), which falls below 1 only when p exceeds 50%, while 1 minus 1/1.414 would suggest about 29.3% (computed here for illustration). Van den Driessche restricts herd immunity to control aimed at all individuals and uses type reproduction numbers for control aimed at one host type.
has description in the module When infected people differ by group or stage, element k_ij of the next-generation matrix K is the expected number of new cases in group i caused by one newly infected person in group j, as Diekmann, Heesterbeek and Roberts define it, and R_0 is the dominant eigenvalue of K, the definition proposed by Diekmann, Heesterbeek and Metz. For a compartmental model van den Driessche writes K as F times the inverse of V, with F the rates of new infections and V the other transitions, and R_0 as its spectral radius. For two groups the dominant eigenvalue is the larger root of lambda^2 minus T_K lambda plus D_K = 0, with T_K the trace and D_K the determinant, and the term under the square root equals (k_11 minus k_22)^2 plus 4 k_12 k_21, which is never negative for a matrix of non-negative entries. When D_K is zero, as for a matrix of rank one, R_0 is the trace. Larger matrices are handled by HE-CF-BRN-001.

The abstract, which defines the expected number of secondary cases produced by a typical infected individual during its entire period of infectiousness in a completely susceptible population as the dominant eigenvalue of a positive linear operator. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00178324
Diekmann O, Heesterbeek JA, Roberts MG. The construction of next-generation matrices for compartmental epidemic models. Journal of the Royal Society Interface. 2010;7(47):873-885. Section 1, which defines element K_ij as the expected number of new cases with state-at-infection i generated by one individual just infected in state-at-infection j; section 2.1, equation 2.12, which obtains the dominant eigenvalue of a 2 by 2 matrix from its trace and determinant and notes that R_0 equals the trace when det K = 0; and section 3.2, which defines R_0 as the largest eigenvalue, R_0 = rho(K). https://doi.org/10.1098/rsif.2009.0386
van den Driessche P, Watmough J. Reproduction numbers and sub-threshold endemic equilibria for compartmental models of disease transmission. Mathematical Biosciences. 2002;180:29-48. The abstract, which presents a precise definition of R_0 for a general compartmental model based on ordinary differential equations, shows that the disease-free equilibrium is locally asymptotically stable if R_0 is below 1 and unstable if it is above 1, and illustrates the definition with multigroup, staged progression and vector-host models. https://doi.org/10.1016/s0025-5564(02)00108-6
van den Driessche P. Reproduction numbers of infectious disease models. Infectious Disease Modelling. 2017;2(3):288-303. Section 3, which splits the infected compartments into new infections F and other transitions V at the disease-free equilibrium, states that F is entrywise non-negative and V a non-singular M-matrix, that the (i, j) entry of F V^-1 is the expected number of secondary infections in compartment i produced by an individual introduced in compartment j and that R_0 = rho(F V^-1), with Theorem 1 linking R_0 below 1 to local stability; section 4.1, which states that herd immunity is applicable if a control strategy is aimed at all individuals and introduces type reproduction numbers for control aimed at one host population; and section 5, which gives the square root form for a vector-host model and notes that the square root is often omitted in the literature. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.idm.2017.06.002
