Basic reproduction number of the SIR model as transmission rate times mean infectious period

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000697
Type formula
assumes Closed homogeneously mixing SIR population behind beta over gamma, Constant recovery rate implying an exponential infectious period
has calculator text D = 1 / gamma; R_0 = beta * D
has common error note Infectious period of 10 days entered as the recovery rate. Typing 10 days into the recovery rate cell gives R_0 = 0.3/10 = 0.03 instead of 3 for the article's infection, which would show an epidemic-prone infection as one that dies out at once.
Same basic reproduction number read as the same speed of spread. R_0 carries no time unit. Two infections with R_0 of 3, one with a 10-day and one with a 3-day mean infectious period (beta of 0.30 and 1.0 per day), have early growth rates of 0.2 and about 0.667 per day by the SIR relation r = gamma(R_0 minus 1), and doubling times of about 3.47 and 1.04 days (computed here for illustration). Delamater and colleagues stress that R_0 does not show whether secondary cases appear within a day or months later.
has description in the module In the simple susceptible, infectious and recovered (SIR) model, one infectious person in a fully susceptible population causes new infections at rate beta and stays infectious for a mean time D equal to 1/gamma, so R_0 is beta times D, or beta/gamma. Van den Driessche derives R_0 as the product of the transmission rate and the mean infectious time and shows that R_0 = 1 is a sharp threshold, with the number infectious falling steadily to zero below it and first rising above it. The WHO guide writes the same quantity for a homogeneously mixing population as p c D, the probability of transmission per contact times the contact rate times the duration of infectiousness, so beta here corresponds to p times c. Models with a latent stage, demography or several groups take R_0 from the next-generation matrix of HE-FM-BRN-005.

has implementation SIR basic reproduction number from named rate cells

has source in the module Delamater PL, Street EJ, Leslie TF, Yang YT, Jacobsen KH. Complexity of the basic reproduction number (R0). Emerging Infectious Diseases. 2019;25(1):1-4. The abstract, which states that R_0 is not a biological constant for a pathogen, a rate over time or a measure of disease severity, and the section Various Names for R0, which states that R_0 does not indicate whether new cases occur within 24 hours of the initial case or months later and is most accurately described in terms of cases per case. https://doi.org/10.3201/eid2501.171901
World Health Organization. WHO guide for standardization of economic evaluations of immunization programmes, 2nd edition (WHO/IVB/19.10). Geneva, WHO, 2019. Section 6.1.1, which writes R_0 = pcD for a homogeneously mixing population without immigration or emigration, with p the probability of transmission following exposure, c the average number of new contacts per unit of time and D the duration of infectiousness, and states that the reproduction number depends on infectious disease characteristics (p and D) and population characteristics (c and x). https://iris.who.int/handle/10665/329389
van den Driessche P. Reproduction numbers of infectious disease models. Infectious Disease Modelling. 2017;2(3):288-303. Section 2.1, which defines R_0 = beta S_0/gamma for the SIR model as the product of the transmission rate, the mean infectious time 1/gamma and S_0, notes that R_0 is independent of the fraction dying from the disease, states that R_0 = 1 acts as a sharp threshold between the disease dying out and causing an epidemic, and gives R_0 = beta S_0/(d + gamma) once births and natural deaths are included. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.idm.2017.06.002

Type formula
assumes Proposed price and basket prices on one basis, Price exactly at the basket ceiling accepted
has calculator text T = k * P_ref; D = P_prop - T
has common error note Basket ceiling read as a change in the value of the drug. The ceiling falls by 17.5, from 131.25 to 113.75, between Baskets A and B with no change in the drug or its evidence. A cost-effectiveness model that uses the ceiling as the drug price states the basket, the price type, the exchange-rate rule and the aggregation formula and tests other prices in sensitivity analysis, as the article recommends.
Multiplier applied to the lowest basket price. Applying 1.25 to Basket A's lowest price of 80 gives a ceiling of 100 instead of 131.25 under the article's mean-based rule, so the proposed price of 130 would be cut by mistake (computed here for illustration).
has description in the module Multiplies a basket reference price by a multiplier k to give a ceiling and subtracts the ceiling from a proposed domestic price. A positive margin means the price is above the ceiling and is cut or reviewed, and a margin of zero or below means it is accepted. The article's illustrative rule takes k = 1.25 on the basket mean, modelled on Japan's foreign average price adjustment, whose adjusted price is HE-FM-BOC-005, while the PMPRB test is k = 1 on the highest international price. The reference price comes from HE-FM-BOC-003 or HE-CF-BOC-002.

Basket mean, lowest and highest price from five converted reference prices

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000704
Type formula
assumes All five basket countries priced, Same product and price type across the basket
has calculator text P_mean = (c_1 + c_2 + c_3 + c_4 + c_5) / 5; P_low = min(min(min(min(c_1, c_2), c_3), c_4), c_5); P_high = max(max(max(max(c_1, c_2), c_3), c_4), c_5)
has common error note Larger basket assumed to give a lower reference price. Adding a sixth country priced at 130 to Basket A raises the mean from 105 to about 109.17 while the lowest price stays at 80 (computed here for illustration). Under a lowest-price rule an added country can never raise the benchmark, as the article notes, while under the mean or the median it can.
Missing basket price entered as zero. Recording the unlaunched country of Basket B as 0 gives a mean of 77 and a lowest price of 0, against 96.25 and 80 when it is left out, and a ceiling at 1.25 times the mean of 96.25 in place of 120.31 (computed here for illustration).
has description in the module Combines the converted prices c_1 to c_5 of a five-country basket, each from HE-FM-BOC-001, into the mean, the lowest and the highest price, three of the aggregation rules f in the article's P_ref. Kanavos and colleagues report that the lowest price in the basket is often used and that the average or the median is not uncommon, and Rémuzat and colleagues found the average price in use in 15 European countries and the lowest price in 7. The highest price is the PMPRB's highest international price. The median, baskets of other sizes and countries without a price are handled by HE-CF-BOC-002, and HE-FM-BOC-004 turns a reference price into a ceiling.

The function exp is the exponential function; the reverse step is theta_j equal to the natural log of p_j divided by one minus p_j.

Bathtub hazard as the sum of two Weibull hazards

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000353
Type formula
assumes Independent additive components of a bathtub hazard, Distinct shapes for the two Weibull components
has calculator text h_t = lambda_1 * gamma_1 * t^(gamma_1 - 1) + lambda_2 * gamma_2 * t^(gamma_2 - 1); S_t = exp(-(lambda_1 * t^gamma_1 + lambda_2 * t^gamma_2))
has common error note Mixing two Weibull distributions to obtain a bathtub hazard. Averaging two Weibull survival curves with mixing weights is a mixture model, not a sum of hazards. Demiris and colleagues cite reliability work showing that a mixture of two Weibull distributions cannot give a bathtub-shaped hazard, whereas a sum of Weibull hazards can.
has description in the module The poly-Weibull model of Demiris, Lunn and Sharples adds a falling Weibull hazard, with shape gamma_1 below 1, to a rising one, with shape gamma_2 above 1, so the total hazard falls at first and rises later. Survival is the exponential of minus the summed Weibull cumulative hazards, which is the product of the two component survival curves. The symbol ^ denotes a power.

Baumol component of real health spending growth in OBR projections

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000365
Type formula
assumes Constant Baumol coefficient across the projection, Baumol component as one part of other cost pressures
has calculator text B = beta * g_econ
has common error note Adding a full technology driver on top of the Baumol component. The OBR assumes that most spending growth from new technology is already captured by a mixture of its Baumol and income effects, leaving only a small residual of 0.13 percentage points. Adding a separate full technology driver to B and the income effect counts much of the same growth twice.
Reading the Baumol component as a change in the GDP share. B is a contribution to the annual growth rate of real health spending, not a change in health spending as a share of GDP. The 0.72 points in the OBR baseline are one input to a projection in which the share of GDP depends also on demography, incomes and GDP growth.
has description in the module Gives the contribution of the Baumol effect to annual real growth in health spending as a coefficient times projected economy-wide productivity growth. The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) uses this top-down form, with an OECD estimate of the coefficient, within the other cost pressures that it adds to demographic and income effects.

has description in the module Schwarz's criterion replaces the AIC penalty of 2 per parameter with the natural logarithm of the sample size, so the penalty grows with n. With 300 patients it is about 5.70 per parameter, and BIC leans towards simpler distributions. NICE DSU TSD 14 recommends presenting AIC and BIC, or other suitable tests of internal validity, when survival models are compared. The function log is the natural logarithm.

Aloh and colleagues cite a suggested ideal turnover interval of 1 to 3 days, but the buffer a hospital needs depends on how variable its demand is. In Bagust and colleagues' simulation, risks of having no bed for an emergency admission became discernible above about 85% average occupancy, which at a 5-day stay is an interval of about 0.88 days.
Occupancy entered as a percentage in the turnover interval. Entering occupancy as 85 instead of 0.85 at a 5-day stay returns about minus 4.94 days, an impossible negative interval, instead of about 0.88 days.
has description in the module Expresses the turnover interval through occupancy and average length of stay. Adding the stay and the interval gives 365 divided by the annual turnover rate, so each bed cycles through one stay and one empty interval per patient, and the stay is the share o of that cycle. On a Barber-Johnson diagram, which plots L_bar against TI, lines from the origin join points of equal occupancy and diagonals with equal intercepts join points of equal turnover.

Bed turnover rate from discharges and average available beds

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000384
Type formula
assumes Discharges and beds from the same bed stock, Bed turnover rates compared over equal periods
has calculator text T = D / B_bar
has common error note Bed turnover rate from opening and closing bed counts. A hospital with 400 beds on the first and last days of the year, but with a 60-bed ward closed for 73 days in between, had 388 beds available on an average day. The mean of the opening and closing counts, 400, gives a turnover rate of 62.05 for 24,820 discharges instead of about 63.97, understating bed use.
Counting ward transfers as bed turnover discharges. Counting ward transfers or consultant episodes instead of whole stays inflates D. Adding 2,482 transfers to the baseline's 24,820 discharges would raise the turnover rate from 62.05 to about 68.3 with no extra patient treated. Readmissions raise D in the same way, so turnover is read alongside the readmission rate.
has description in the module Divides the discharges of a period, including deaths, by the average daily number of available beds over the same period. The result is the number of patients each bed served, a partial productivity ratio of one output, discharges, to one input, beds. NHS Wales reports it as the bed use factor (indicator IP03). B_bar is the mean of the daily bed counts, which the computational function under this formula derives from those counts.

Bed-days chosen under a mixed payment with a linear marginal benefit of care

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000545
Type formula

has calculator text q = max(0, (b_0 - (1 - r) * c / alpha) / b_1)
has common error note Holding the cost of a bed-day fixed when more cost is reimbursed. The formula fixes c, but Ma and Mak note that cost reimbursement mutes cost incentives, so raising r can raise the cost per day itself; the article's example omits this cost-reduction effort.
Treating the index of agency as known to the payer. The stay depends on alpha, which the payer cannot observe directly; Ellis and McGuire suggest inferring it from the ratio of the demand and supply elasticities to reimbursement, a measure they note is precise only under conditions unlikely to hold exactly.
has description in the module Ellis and McGuire's first-order condition alpha b(q) = (1 minus r) c sets the weighted marginal benefit of care equal to the cost the provider bears. With the marginal benefit falling in a straight line, b(q) = b_0 minus b_1 q, the condition solves for the stay; the max function returns no care when even the first unit is not worth its cost to the provider. The article's patient benefit B(q) = 1200q minus 50q squared gives b_0 = 1,200 and b_1 = 100.

Section 3: under prospective payment with constant marginal cost the condition is a b(q) = c (eq. 8). Section 4: under mixed reimbursement the first-order condition is a b(q) = (1 minus r)c (eq. 13). Beta parameters for a probability from binomial event counts and a conjugate prior

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000390
Type formula
assumes Binomial evidence for a beta fit from counts, Observation period of the counts matching the model cycle, Prior for small or zero event counts stated
has calculator text alpha = alpha_0 + r; beta = beta_0 + n - r; E_p = alpha / (alpha + beta)
has common error note Beta fitted to a zero event count without a prior. With no deaths among 120 patients the counts rule gives Beta(0, 120), which is not a valid distribution, and Excel BETA.INV returns the #NUM! error. A uniform prior gives Beta(1, 121) instead, with a mean of about 0.008.
Entering the number at risk as the second beta parameter. Setting beta to n rather than n minus r counts every patient as a non-event. For 24 progressions among 120 patients, Beta(24, 120) has a mean of about 0.167 instead of 0.20, and the error grows with the event proportion.
has description in the module Updates a beta prior for a probability with r events among n patients at risk. Because the beta is the conjugate prior for a binomial probability, the result is again a beta distribution. With the limiting prior alpha_0 = beta_0 = 0 the rule reduces to alpha equal to the number of events and beta equal to the number of non-events, n minus r, so the mean is the observed proportion r/n. A uniform prior, alpha_0 = beta_0 = 1, adds one to each parameter.

Section 2.4, pp. 34-35, which shows that a Beta(alpha, beta) prior with y successes in n binomial trials gives the posterior Beta(alpha + y, beta + n minus y) and calls this conjugacy; and Appendix A, p. 584, which gives Beta(1, 1) as the uniform distribution and alpha = beta = 0 as a noninformative choice. https://doi.org/10.1201/b16018

Beta shape parameters from a reported mean and standard error by the method of moments

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000391
Type formula
assumes Existence condition for a beta moments fit, Beta moments fit checked for parameters below one, Standard error of the mean as the beta moments input
has calculator text alpha = mu * (mu * (1 - mu) / s^2 - 1); beta = (1 - mu) * (mu * (1 - mu) / s^2 - 1)
has common error note Beta moments fit used without checking for parameters below one. A mean of 0.10 with a standard error of 0.25 gives Beta(0.044, 0.396). About three quarters of its draws fall below 0.01 and about 4% above 0.9, so a probability with a mean of 0.10 is sampled mostly at the extremes, which rarely matches the evidence.
Patient-level standard deviation entered in a beta moments fit. For a binary outcome with mean 0.20, the standard deviation across patients is the square root of 0.20 times 0.80, which is 0.40. Entered as s, it makes alpha + beta exactly zero, so no beta distribution exists; with other data a patient-level standard deviation gives a distribution far too wide for parameter uncertainty.
has description in the module Sets the beta mean and variance equal to a reported mean probability and the square of its standard error and solves for the two parameters. The sum alpha + beta equals mu (1 minus mu) divided by s squared, minus one, and alpha and beta are that sum multiplied by mu and by 1 minus mu. A solution exists only when s squared is below mu (1 minus mu).

Between-group minimal important difference from mean changes in two anchor groups

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000575
Type formula
assumes Anchor correlated with the change score, Both anchor groups from the same cohort and interval
has calculator text MID_between = d_M - d_S
has common error note Ignoring the choice of anchor category. De Vet and colleagues show that the estimate can differ by a factor of about 2.5 depending on whether the first category above no change or moderate to much improvement is chosen, and that the choice cannot rest on statistical grounds.
Using the within-person mean change for a difference between arms. Terwee and colleagues point out that a difference between patients reporting a little better and about the same is a minimal important difference between groups, not a within-person minimal important change; in the article's example these are 6.0 and 8.0 points.
has description in the module Subtracts the mean change of patients who rate themselves about the same from the mean change of patients who rate themselves a little better (or a little worse, for deterioration). The mean change of the minimally improved group on its own is the Jaeschke estimate of a within-person change; the difference between the two groups is, in the terms of Terwee and colleagues, a minimal important difference between groups, the quantity suited to a difference between trial arms.

Bias of the LOCF between-arm difference with unequal dropout fractions

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000617
Type formula
assumes Dropout completely at random within each arm for the LOCF difference
Arm means taken from complete follow-up for the LOCF bias
has calculator text Delta_tilde = (tau_T * mu_T_last + (1 - tau_T) * mu_T_end) - (tau_C * mu_C_last + (1 - tau_C) * mu_C_end); Delta = mu_T_end - mu_C_end; bias_Delta = tau_T * (mu_T_last - mu_T_end) - tau_C * (mu_C_last - mu_C_end)
has common error note Applying the equal-dropout direction rule when dropout differs by arm. Lachin's rule, an LOCF difference too large when the earlier difference exceeds the final one, assumes the same fraction missing in both arms. In the article's example the true difference widens from 0.04 to 0.06, so the rule predicts an understatement, yet with 40% against 10% dropout LOCF overstates the difference by 0.010.
Using a pooled dropout fraction for both arms in the LOCF bias. Replacing the arm-specific fractions with a pooled 25% for the article's example, with arms of equal size, gives a bias of 0.25 times (0.04 minus 0.06), or minus 0.005, an apparent understatement, instead of the overstatement of 0.010 (computed here for illustration). Each arm's error has to use its own fraction.
has description in the module Applies the mixture mean of HE-FM-LOCF-001 to each arm with its own fraction imputed and subtracts. The analysed difference, Delta_tilde, departs from the true final difference, Delta, by the treatment arm's bias minus the control arm's bias. With unequal fractions that rule no longer holds.

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000399
Type formula
assumes One event count applied to every candidate survival curve, Event count reflects how fast the information grows
has calculator text BIC_d = -2 * lnL + k * log(d)
has common error note Mixing patient and event counts across candidate curves. Computing some candidates with the patient count and others with the event count distorts the comparison. In the 400-patient example, a Weibull BIC of 1059.98 from the patient count set against a generalised gamma BIC of 1056.96 from the event count puts the generalised gamma 3.02 ahead, positive evidence on the Kass and Raftery scale, instead of 0.61 ahead under one consistent count.
Using the events of both arms for a single-arm BIC. When arms are fitted separately, the count for each fit is the number of events in that arm. Taking the events of both arms for a model fitted to one arm overstates the penalty for that fit and pushes BIC further towards the simpler curves.
has description in the module Volinsky and Raftery's revision for censored survival data replaces the number of patients in the BIC penalty with the number of uncensored events d. With heavy censoring d is much smaller than the number of patients, so each parameter costs less and BIC moves closer to AIC. The function log is the natural logarithm.

Break-even activity volume and margin of safety for a health service paid per unit

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000465
Type formula
assumes Costs linear and fixed or variable within the relevant range, Fixed costs constant only up to capacity
has calculator text Q_star = F / (P - V); MS = (Q_e - Q_star) / Q_e
has common error note Ignoring a step in fixed costs above capacity. Using the one-team cost structure for 4,500 attendances suggests a surplus of £135,000, but the second team's £120,000 leaves £15,000 (computed here for illustration). The article shows that expansion beats staying at 4,000 attendances, with its £90,000 surplus, only above 5,333 attendances.
Judging extra activity against average cost. At 3,600 attendances the average cost per attendance, including a share of fixed costs, is £145, so an extra contract paying £120 per attendance looks loss-making, yet within capacity each extra attendance adds £50 to the surplus because only the £70 variable cost changes (computed here for illustration).
Rounding a fractional break-even volume down. With two teams the day unit makes a loss of £30 at 4,333 attendances and a surplus of £60 at 4,334, so a fractional break-even volume is rounded up (computed here for illustration).
has description in the module Applies the cost-volume form of break-even analysis from management accounting to a service paid a fixed price or tariff per unit of activity. Each unit contributes the price less the variable cost, so the break-even volume is the fixed cost for the period divided by the contribution per unit, and the margin of safety is the share by which expected activity could fall before the service makes a loss. When fixed costs step up with capacity, as when a second team is needed, the calculation is repeated for each block of capacity.

Break-even and cost-neutral unit prices of a health technology

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000464
Type formula
assumes Price enters the incremental cost linearly, Other inputs held at their base-case values, Break-even price compared with the net price paid by the NHS
has calculator text p_star = (lambda * Delta_E - Delta_C_0) / u; p_0 = -Delta_C_0 / u
has common error note Comparing the break-even price with the list price. PMG36 bases reference-case analyses on the prices paid in the NHS, including patient access schemes, so a list price above the break-even price does not show that the net price is too high.
Leaving cost offsets out of the break-even price. Setting the break-even price to the threshold times the QALY gain alone gives £10,000 per course in the article's example instead of £13,000, because the £3,000 of net care avoided is left out; adding the negative Delta_C_0 instead of subtracting it gives £7,000 (computed here for illustration).
Reading the break-even price as a fair or target price. At the break-even price the health gained is just offset by the health displaced elsewhere, so the net health benefit to the health system is zero and, as Claxton and colleagues argue, the benefit of the innovation goes to the manufacturer as revenue. A price below it shares that benefit with the health system.
Treating a cost-effective price as a cost-neutral price. At £25,000 per QALY the break-even price of £13,000 is £10,000 above the cost-neutral price of £3,000, so a technology priced at its break-even level still adds cost: £10 million in discounted lifetime costs for a cohort of 1,000 patients in the article's example. Whether that can be afforded is a budget impact question.
has description in the module Splits the incremental cost per patient into the acquisition cost of the technology, u units at unit price p, and every other cost difference, Delta_C_0, which is negative when the technology avoids more cost than it adds. Setting incremental net monetary benefit, lambda times Delta_E less (u times p plus Delta_C_0), to zero gives the break-even price, the highest unit price at which the technology is cost-effective at threshold lambda. Setting the incremental cost alone to zero gives the cost-neutral price. The gap between them, lambda times Delta_E divided by u, is the money value of the health gain per unit, so for a technology that improves health the break-even price lies above the cost-neutral price. With u equal to 1 the break-even price is the payer's maximum price per patient of HE-FM-BARG-002. Solving the same condition for the effect gives Delta_C divided by lambda, the health displaced of HE-FM-CET-002.

Brier score from patient-level predicted risks and outcomes

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000406
Type formula
assumes Binary outcome known for every patient at the horizon, Brier score as a property of a model in one population
has calculator text BS = sum_(i=1)^N [(p_i - y_i)^2] / N
has common error note Comparing raw Brier scores across populations with different event rates. A non-informative model scores 0.25 at a 50% event rate but 0.090 at a 10% rate, so a raw score from a low-risk primary care population can look better than one from a high-risk hospital population without any difference in model quality. The scaled score on this page corrects for the event rate.
Reading a low Brier score as evidence of clinical value. A lower score indicates more accurate probabilities but does not show whether using the model leads to better decisions. Assel, Sjoberg and Vickers found that when prevalence was low the score could favour a highly specific test where high sensitivity was needed, and recommended decision-analytic measures such as net benefit.
has description in the module Averages the squared differences between each patient's predicted probability of the event and the observed outcome, coded 1 for an event and 0 otherwise. The score runs from 0 for perfect predictions to 1 for predictions that are confidently and completely wrong, and its square root is a typical distance between prediction and outcome on the probability scale.

Bucher adjusted indirect comparison through a common comparator

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000234
Type formula
assumes Independent sources of direct evidence, Additive scale and one direction convention, Transitivity across the two sets of trials

has common error note Comparing active arms across trials. Pooling the active-treatment arms of different trials and comparing them directly discards randomisation and is prone to bias. Bucher and colleagues describe this naive approach as offering no advantage over observational data.
has description in the module Estimates the effect of C relative to B from trials of B against A and trials of C against A. Working with within-trial contrasts preserves randomisation, unlike a comparison of active arms taken from different trials.

Budget implied by a fixed cost-effectiveness ratio across four independent programmes

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000720
Type formula
assumes Critical ratio as the threshold at which the two rules agree for divisible programmes
Ties at the threshold count as adopted under the fixed ratio rule
has calculator text a_1 = (Delta_C_1 <= lambda * Delta_E_1); a_2 = (Delta_C_2 <= lambda * Delta_E_2); a_3 = (Delta_C_3 <= lambda * Delta_E_3); a_4 = (Delta_C_4 <= lambda * Delta_E_4); B_lambda = a_1 * Delta_C_1 + a_2 * Delta_C_2 + a_3 * Delta_C_3 + a_4 * Delta_C_4
has common error note Adopting the marginal programme in full at the critical ratio. Setting the threshold at the critical ratio of GBP 20,000 per QALY and adopting every programme at or below it funds all of D and spends GBP 1,150,000, GBP 250,000 more than the budget. Under a fixed budget the tie at the critical ratio is settled by the share of HE-FM-CELT-001, not by the threshold.
Setting the threshold below the critical ratio under a fixed budget. A threshold of GBP 15,000 per QALY adopts A, B and C and leaves GBP 150,000 of the GBP 900,000 unspent, which at D's GBP 20,000 per QALY would have bought 7.5 QALYs (computed here for illustration).
has description in the module Under the fixed ratio rule a programme is adopted when its ICER does not exceed a threshold lambda, tested here as Delta_C_i at most lambda times Delta_E_i, which is an incremental net monetary benefit of HE-FM-NMB-002 of zero or above. Each a_i is 1 for an adopted programme and 0 otherwise, and B_lambda adds up the incremental costs of the adopted programmes, the budget the threshold implies. Sacristán and colleagues state that the fixed ratio rule and the fixed budget rule coincide if this implied budget is the same as the budget constraint of the fixed budget rule. A B_lambda above the budget means the threshold adopts more than the budget pays for, and one below it leaves money that could buy more health.

Budget neutrality multiplier and adjusted conversion factor after a revaluation of relative value units

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000549
Type formula
assumes Projected volumes held fixed in the budget neutrality calculation, Adjustment made only above the 20 million dollar limit
has calculator text BN = (q_A * R_A_old + q_B * R_B_old) / (q_A * R_A_new + q_B * R_B_new); CF_adj = CF_old * BN
has common error note Overlooking the 2026 efficiency adjustment behind the budget neutrality increase. For 2026 CMS cut the work units of non-time-based services by 2.5 per cent, exempting time-based services such as evaluation and management visits, and an estimated 0.49 per cent adjustment for finalised changes in work units for some services raised the factor, so exempt services gained without any change in their own units.
Pairing one year's relative values with another year's factor. Each year's factor is set for that year's relative values; combining 2025 units with the 2026 factor double counts or misses the budget neutrality adjustment.
Reading a higher conversion factor as a rise in every fee. After the cut, service A's fee rises from 66.00 to 66.47 dollars but service B's falls from 132.00 to 131.29, because its own units fell by more than the factor rose; budget neutrality redistributes payment rather than adding to it.
has description in the module When relative value units are revised, the conversion factor is scaled so that the projected volume of services, priced at the new units, costs the same as before. The multiplier is the ratio of total weighted units before to after the change, so a cut to some services' units raises the factor and with it the fee of every service whose units were not cut. Two services are written out so that the calculator can run; SUMPRODUCT in Excel takes any number. This is the article's simplified version: CMS estimates the adjustment from prior-year utilisation and handles several adjustments in sequence.

Case fatality rate among confirmed cases

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000450
Type formula
assumes Deaths restricted to the counted cases, Every counted case resolved and detection consistent
has calculator text CFR = D / N_c
has common error note Applying a confirmed-case fatality rate to all infections. A CFR among confirmed cases goes with confirmed cases. In the article's example five infections per confirmed case give an infection fatality ratio of 0.006 against a CFR of 0.030, so applying the CFR to all infections multiplies deaths by five, and applying the infection fatality ratio to confirmed cases divides them by five.
Reading a mid-outbreak crude case fatality rate as final. At week 8 of the article's illustrative outbreak the crude estimate is 0.020 against a final 0.030. In its cost-effectiveness example the crude figure gives about £16,667 per QALY instead of about £11,111, because it counts too few deaths averted.
Treating a four-week case fatality rate as annual. The article's 3% refers to deaths within four weeks of becoming a case. Rescaled with HE-FM-TP-003 to weekly cycles it gives about 0.0076 a week. Treated as an annual probability over 52 weekly cycles it gives about 0.00059 a week, and a four-week illness then carries a death risk of about 0.23%, roughly one thirteenth of the intended value.
has description in the module Divides the deaths from the disease among the counted cases by the number of cases that meet the case definition. The numerator is restricted to deaths among the cases in the denominator, so the CFR is a proportion rather than a true rate. It applies over the period in which those deaths were counted, which a precise definition states, for example a one-month CFR.

Type formula
assumes Base rate set on the same scale as the case weights, Add-on and outlier payments outside the case payment formula
has calculator text P_i = w_g * B * a_h
has common error note Reading a case payment as the resource cost of an admission. A case payment is a payer's price, moved by stabilisation caps, efficiency factors and add-ons. NHS England states that its prices are calculated on the basis of average costs (NHS England 2026). Average cost per case can differ markedly from the marginal cost of the cases a technology adds or avoids, so a payment rate suits a budget impact analysis better than a measure of opportunity cost.
has description in the module Converts a case weight into money by multiplying it by a base rate, the money paid per unit of weight, and by any adjustment factor for the hospital. In the Medicare inpatient prospective payment system, the base payment rate, with its labour-related share adjusted by the area wage index, is multiplied by the DRG relative weight. Summed over a hospital's cases, the payment equals its casemix multiplied by the base rate and the adjustment.

Casemix-adjusted cost ratio of a hospital

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000448
Type formula
assumes Comparable coding and complexity within groups across hospitals, Weights, reference cost and hospital cost on one costing basis
has calculator text CM_h = sum_(g=1)^G [n_hg * w_g]; R_h = C_h / (CM_h * c_bar)
has common error note Ranking hospitals on crude cost per case. Crude cost per case is £3,300 for Hospital X and about £6,243 for Hospital Y, so Y looks nearly twice as costly. Per weighted case the order reverses, £4,400 for X and £3,800 for Y, and the cost ratios are 1.10 and 0.95. The crude comparison favours X only because it treats mostly cheap cases.
Reading a casemix-adjusted cost ratio as efficiency. The ratio compares cost for a given mix of cases, not health produced. A hospital can score below 1 through generous coding or shorter stays with worse outcomes, so coding, complexity within groups and outcomes are checked before a ratio is read as efficiency.
has description in the module Divides a hospital's actual total cost by the cost expected if each of its cases cost the reference amount for its group. The ratio has the form of an indirect standardisation, as in the SMR (an analogy drawn here). CM_h is the hospital's casemix, the sum of the weights of its cases, so the ratio equals cost per weighted case divided by the reference cost of one unit of weight. A value above 1 means spending above the reference for that casemix. HE-FM-ALOS-004 applies the same structure to bed-days.

Ceiling on the ENBS of a study design from population EVPI

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000661
Type formula
assumes EVPI and EVSI on the same population and threshold, Same study cost in the ceiling as in the ENBS
has calculator text ENBS_ub = EVPI_pop - C_n
has common error note Population EVPI above the study cost read as proof that the study is worthwhile. With an illustrative discounted population of 4,000, population EVPI is GBP 1,600,000, above the GBP 1,460,000 cost of the article's 600-patient trial, yet its ENBS is minus GBP 260,000 (computed here for illustration). Population EVPI is a ceiling, and only ENBS for a feasible design shows that a study repays its cost.
has description in the module No finite study delivers perfect information, so the population EVSI of any design is at most population EVPI (HE-FM-VOI-002) and the ENBS of a design costing C_n cannot exceed population EVPI less that cost. When the ceiling is zero or below for every feasible design, research is not worthwhile and the value of information process stops before any EVSI is computed, the first screen in the sequence set out by the ISPOR task force. A positive ceiling is necessary but not sufficient, so ENBS itself is still required.

Chain-linked consumer price index from the December level and two annual links

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000715
Type formula
assumes December level and links from one CPI series and class, Chain-linked CPI series not a fixed basket over several years
has calculator text I_t = I_Dec * L_Jan / 100 * L_t / 100
has common error note CPI link movements added as index points. Adding the link movements of minus 0.4 and plus 1.5 points to the December level of 120.0 gives 121.1 in place of 121.3128 (computed here for illustration). Chaining is multiplicative, so a rise of 1.5% in the link is worth 1.8 points at a level of 120.
CPI links multiplied without dividing by 100. Each link is on a base of 100. Multiplying 120.0 by 99.6 and 101.5 without the two divisions gives 1,213,128 in place of 121.3128 (computed here for illustration).
has description in the module Builds a long-run index level for month t of year y from the published level for December of year y minus 1 on the 2015 = 100 reference, the January index of year y on the previous December = 100, and the index for month t on January of year y = 100. Section 3.6 of the ONS technical manual sets out the two-link product for the CPI and CPIH, whose weights are updated twice a year, and prints it as the product of the three index values with no divisor. Each link is stated on a base of 100, so here each is divided by 100 before it multiplies the December level (derived from the link bases), as the manual's RPI chaining formulas in section 12.4.2 and its July 1987 example in section 11.2 divide the link by 100. For January itself L_t is 100. A series chained once a year, such as the RPI, is entered with L_Jan = 100 and the long-run level of its January link month in I_Dec. Ratios of chained levels such as the D7BT series are what HE-FM-COST-002 takes.

Section on methods used to create the data, which states that the indices are annually chain-linked with each year's series taking the value 100 in the most recent January, and the coherence section, which states that the CPIH, CPI and RPI differ in both coverage and methodology. https://www.ons.gov.uk/economy/inflationandpriceindices/methodologies/consumerpriceinflationincludesall3indicescpihcpiandrpiqmi
Office for National Statistics. Consumer Prices Indices Technical Manual, 2019. Newport, Office for National Statistics, 2019, page last revised 26 March 2025. Section 3.6, chaining, which states that the CPIH and CPI are chain-linked twice every year, with a January index based on the previous December = 100 and a further index for February to December based on January = 100, and gives the chained class index as the product of the December level on 2015 = 100 and the two links, printed without a divisor of 100. Section 11.2 chains the RPI for July 1987 (101.8 on January 1987) to 394.5 on January 1974 and reports a change of 4.4% from 384.7 in July 1986. Section 11.6 unchains by dividing by the January (or previous December) index and multiplying by 100, and section 12.4.2 chains the RPI each January with the January link divided by 100. https://www.ons.gov.uk/economy/inflationandpriceindices/methodologies/consumerpricesindicestechnicalmanual2019

Change in a programme's discounted cost per QALY when the whole programme is delayed under differential rates

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000572
Type formula
assumes Whole programme shifted with unchanged amounts and rates
has calculator text F_s = ((1 + r_H) / (1 + r_C))^s; ICER_s = ICER_0 * F_s
has common error note Concluding that a programme should be postponed because its ratio falls. The fall comes from the discounting arithmetic, not from the programme; Gravelle and Smith argue that the paradox reveals a difficulty with cost-effectiveness analysis that is irrelevant to the choice of the health rate, and Attema and colleagues note that infinite postponement was never observed in the UK before 2004 or in the Netherlands since 2004.
Moving the discount base year before the start of a programme. Attema and colleagues warn that placing the base year before the actual start lowers the ratio when costs are discounted more than effects, the same arithmetic as the delay factor, so a fixed rule such as the year of treatment initiation is needed.
has description in the module Moving every cost and QALY of a programme s years later multiplies its discounted cost by (1 + r_C)^(-s) and its discounted QALYs by (1 + r_H)^(-s), so the ratio is multiplied by ((1 + r_H) / (1 + r_C))^s. The factor is below one whenever the health rate is below the cost rate, so the ratio improves with every year of delay, the postponement paradox of Keeler and Cretin; under equal rates it is one.
has formalisation level catalogue record
has implementation Delay factor and delayed ratio from named cells

has module record identifier HE-FM-DDIS-004

Section Discounting of Costs and Health Effects: Brief History: the cost-effectiveness ratio of a given intervention will improve with each year it is postponed; infinite postponing was never observed in practice, including the UK before 2004 and the Netherlands since 2004. Change in consumer surplus from a price change on a linear demand curve

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000261
Type formula
assumes Straight-line demand between the old and new prices, Small income effects
has calculator text Delta_CS = (P_0 - P_1) * (Q_0 + Q_1) / 2
has common error note Counting only the saving on the original quantity. Multiplying the 10-pound cut by the original 4 visits gives 40 pounds and misses the 5-pound surplus on the extra visit. For a price rise the same shortcut overstates the loss.
has description in the module When demand is linear between the old and new prices, the change in consumer surplus is the trapezoid between the two prices out to the demand curve: the price change multiplied by the average of the quantities bought before and after. The result is positive for a price fall and negative for a rise. It is the Marshallian approximation to CV and EV and lies between them for a single price change.

Change in mean health, EDE health and Atkinson index of a programme against its comparator

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000675
Type formula
assumes Programme and comparator EDE at the same inequality aversion
Distributions hold only unfair variation before the EDE is taken
Same population and groups for both distributions in a DCEA comparison
has calculator text d_mu = mu_1 - mu_0; d_EDE = EDE_1 - EDE_0; d_P = d_mu - d_EDE; dEDE_pop = N_pop * d_EDE; d_A = (1 - EDE_1 / mu_1) - (1 - EDE_0 / mu_0)
has common error note Applying the EDE formula to net health changes instead of health levels. The harmonic mean of the article's per-person changes of minus 0.004 and 0.016 years is about minus 0.0107 years, a figure with no meaning, because the EDE needs positive levels of health. The change in EDE health is the EDE of the programme's distribution less the EDE of the comparator's.
Setting the per-person change in EDE health against a population total. At epsilon of 2 the change of 0.004843 years per person is 484.3 EDE QALYs across 100,000 people. Setting the per-person figure beside the 600 QALYs of total net health benefit suggests that inequality absorbs almost all the gain, when the inequality cost takes about 19% of it.
has description in the module Takes the mean health and the equally distributed equivalent health of the programme's distribution and of the comparator's, both at the same inequality aversion epsilon from the live records HE-FM-ATK-002 or HE-FM-ATK-003, or HE-CF-ATK-001 for groups of unequal size, and returns the change in mean health, the change in EDE health per person and across the population, the change in the inequality cost and the change in the Atkinson index. The inequality cost is mean health less EDE health, the health per person that a decision maker with that aversion would give up for full equality, so the change in EDE equals the change in mean health less the change in the inequality cost. A positive change in EDE health means the programme is preferred to the comparator at that epsilon. Each Atkinson index is HE-FM-ATK-001, and only the difference between the two is new here.

Chi-square probability density with k degrees of freedom

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000416
Type formula
assumes Independent standard normal terms behind the chi-square density
has calculator text f_x = x^(k/2 - 1) * exp(-x / 2) / (2^(k/2) * Gamma(k/2))
has common error note Reading the chi-square density as a p-value. The density at the observed statistic is not a probability. For the Weibull against exponential statistic of 9.0 on one degree of freedom the density is about 0.0015, whereas the p-value, the area of the right-hand tail, is about 0.0027.
has description in the module Gives the density of the chi-square distribution at a value x above zero. Gamma(.) is the gamma function, which equals (m minus 1)! for a whole number m and the square root of pi at one half. With k = 2 the density reduces to one half of exp(minus x/2), the exponential density with mean 2.

editor note HEMO computes the upper-tail probability Q_z from z with the standard normal distribution function and writes the constant pi, where the module takes Q_z as an input and writes pi as 3.14159265, so that a test cannot give a Q_z that does not match z.
The general EVSI is an expectation over the study data of a maximum of posterior expectations, which the 0.1 grammar does not evaluate. This closed form for two options with normal incremental net benefit is the formalised member of the family, so HEMO-HOOK-19 is stated in part.
formalises EVSI estimate
has calculator text s = sqrt(s2); z = abs(m0) / s; phi_z = exp(-z * z / 2) / sqrt(2 * pi); Q_z = 1 - Phi(z); EVSI = s * (phi_z - z * Q_z)
has calculator text in the module s = sqrt(s2); z = abs(m0) / s; phi_z = exp(-z * z / 2) / sqrt(2 * 3.14159265); EVSI = s * (phi_z - z * Q_z)
has common error note Cumulative normal probability used in place of the upper-tail probability. Entering Phi(z), about 0.807 for 100 per arm, as Q_z gives about minus GBP 245 per patient, a negative EVSI that cannot occur.
Prior variance used in place of the preposterior variance in the closed form. Putting the prior variance of 1,000,000 into the formula returns per-person EVPI, about GBP 197.80, whatever the trial size, so a trial of 100 per arm is credited with more than three times its EVSI of about GBP 61.68.

has description in the module Applies the unit normal loss integral to the preposterior distribution of incremental net benefit, which is normal with the prior mean m0 and the preposterior variance s2 of HE-FM-EVSI-002. EVSI is the expected gain from switching away from the option preferred now in the results that reverse the sign of the posterior mean, s times phi_z less the absolute value of m0 times Q_z, where z is the absolute prior mean in preposterior standard deviations. phi_z is the standard normal density written out with exp and sqrt, and Q_z is the standard normal upper-tail probability at z, entered from Excel's 1-NORM.S.DIST(z,TRUE) because the calculator has no normal distribution function. With s2 equal to the prior variance the same expression gives per-person EVPI under normality, the bound in HE-FM-VOI-001.

Cobb-Douglas gross investment in health from medical care, own time and schooling

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000734
Type formula
assumes Cobb-Douglas class with constant returns in medical care and own time
Factor-neutral schooling effect and a suppressed intercept in gross investment
Medical care as the single purchased health input with no joint production
has calculator text I = exp(rho_H * E) * M^(1 - K) * TH^K
has common error note Cross-sectional regression of health on medical care read as the production function. Fitting the production function by ordinary least squares across people gives a coefficient on medical care that Grossman shows is biased downward, because people with high unobserved depreciation demand more care and hold less health, and unmeasured differences in efficiency bias it the same way. Grossman notes that two-stage least squares with wealth, wage rates and the price of care as instruments can give consistent estimates, provided the instruments are valid and explain enough of the variation in care. A negative association between care and health across people does not by itself show that the elasticity 1-K is zero or negative.
Gross investment in health read as the health stock. I is the flow added to the stock in the period, not the stock. In the article's example 20 units of gross investment take a stock of 100 with depreciation of 0.15 to 105 through HE-FM-DFH-001, so the 3.05% rise in I from one more year of schooling raises next period's stock by 0.61 units, about 0.6% (computed here for illustration).
Total years of schooling used as E with a suppressed intercept. Because the intercept that Grossman's estimating form leaves unstated is absorbed into the reference level, rho_H E is a shift from that level. Entering 12 years of schooling in place of 0 for the article's reference person raises I to 28.67 against 20, 43% too high (computed here for illustration), while the comparison the article draws, one more year against the reference, gives 20.61.
has description in the module Gross investment is the efficiency factor exp(rho_H E) times medical care raised to the power 1-K times own time raised to the power K, the exponential form of Grossman's estimating equation ln I = rho_H E + (1-K) ln M + K ln TH. The exponents sum to one, so doubling both inputs doubles I, and 1-K is the elasticity of gross investment with respect to medical care. Schooling enters as a factor-neutral efficiency shift, so one more year multiplies I by exp(rho_H) for the same inputs, a rise of about 3.05% when rho_H is 0.03. The result I is the gross investment of HE-FM-DFH-001.

Cochran's Q statistic for an aggregate data meta-analysis

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000300
Type formula
assumes Common-effect weights and estimate in Cochran's Q
has calculator text Q = sum_(i=1)^k [(y_i - theta_F)^2 / v_i]
has common error note Choosing the pooling model from the Q test. The chi-squared test based on Q has low power when studies are few or small, so a non-significant result is weak evidence that the studies share one effect. Switching between common-effect and random-effects pooling on the test result alone lets an underpowered test decide the treatment effect that enters the model.
has description in the module Sums each study's squared deviation from the common-effect estimate, weighted by the inverse of its variance. Under the common-effect model Q follows approximately a chi-squared distribution with k-1 degrees of freedom, so values well above k-1 suggest heterogeneity. Q is the input to I-squared and to the DerSimonian and Laird estimate of tau2.

Coefficient of variation of a bootstrap standard error from B replicates

Type formula
assumes Large-sample approximation for the replicate count
has calculator text CV_B = sqrt(CV_inf^2 + (E_delta + 2) / (4 * B))
has common error note Setting the replicate count for an interval by the standard error rule. The 50 to 200 replicates that suffice for a standard error are too few for bias-corrected intervals, for which Efron and Tibshirani give about 1,000 as a rough minimum, or for a percentile interval, about 250. The count is set by the most demanding output.
has description in the module Efron and Tibshirani's approximation splits the variability of a bootstrap standard error into the sampling variability of the ideal value and the simulation noise from using B replicates. The second term shrinks as B grows, which is why 50 to 200 replicates are adequate for a standard error in most situations.

Cohen's d from two group means and the pooled standard deviation

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000444
Type formula
assumes Equal spread in the two populations, Same direction of scale in every study, Uncorrected for small-sample bias
has calculator text s_p = sqrt(((n_1 - 1) * s_1^2 + (n_2 - 1) * s_2^2) / (n_1 + n_2 - 2)); d = (xbar_1 - xbar_2) / s_p
has common error note Cohen's d and Hedges' g used interchangeably. Reporting a standardised effect without saying whether it is the uncorrected d or Hedges' adjusted g, the Cochrane standardised mean difference, leaves the reader unable to reproduce it. The difference is small above about 20 participants but should still be stated.
Comparing Cohen's d across populations with different spread. The same six-point difference gives a d of 0.75 in a narrow trial population with a standard deviation of 8 and 0.40 in a broad pragmatic population with a standard deviation of 15, computed here for illustration. A larger d does not by itself mean a larger benefit.
Standard errors entered as standard deviations. Dividing the difference by a pooled standard error instead of the pooled standard deviation inflates d by about the square root of the group size. In the article's trial, 11.0454 divided by the square root of 30 is about 2.0166, which would give a d of about 2.98 instead of 0.54, computed here for illustration.
has description in the module Divides the difference between two observed group means by the pooled standard deviation of the two groups, the usual sample estimate of Cohen's d. The pooled standard deviation weights each group's variance by its degrees of freedom. The sign carries the direction of the effect, so instruments that run in opposite directions have to be aligned first. The function sqrt is the square root.

Cohort recursion through a chain of one-cycle tunnel states and a long-term state

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000584
Type formula
assumes Each tunnel state lasts exactly one cycle, Duration effect over a whole number of cycles, Every route into the clinical state enters the first tunnel state
has calculator text m_(T_1,t+1) = sum_(i=1)^n_S_tunnels [m_(i,t) * p_(i,T_1)]; m_(T_(k+1),t+1) = m_(T_k,t) * s_k; m_(L,t+1) = m_(T_K,t) * s_K + m_(L,t) * s_L
has common error note Entrants reaching the clinical state without passing through the first tunnel state. If one route into the clinical state, such as a second strategy's event pathway, sends people to L or to a later tunnel state, those people skip the high early risk and their clock is wrong. Every column of entry probabilities has to point at T1.
Giving a tunnel row the diagonal pattern of an ordinary state. Putting the probability of surviving T1 on the T1 diagonal rather than in the T2 column keeps survivors in T1 at the first-year risk for ever. In the article's example 512 people are alive after three years in place of 706.56 (computed here for illustration).
Too few tunnel states for the duration effect. Ending the tunnel after two states starts the long-term risk a cycle early. With the article's probabilities, two tunnel states followed by a long-term state at 0.03 leave 713.92 people alive after three years in place of 706.56 (computed here for illustration), and the error grows with each missing state.
has description in the module Moves the cohort one cycle through a tunnel of K one-cycle states T_1 to T_K feeding a long-term state L. New entrants from every state with a route into the tunnel collect in T_1; everyone in T_k who neither dies nor leaves by another route moves to T_(k+1), so no one stays in a tunnel state for a second cycle; survivors of T_K join those who stay in L. These are the tunnel rows of the expanded transition matrix written out, with a zero on each tunnel diagonal. Summing T_1 to L gives the clinical state for reporting, while each column keeps its own cost and utility.

Combined disability weight for a person with two conditions under the multiplicative model

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000504
Type formula
assumes Multiplicative combination of disability weights for comorbid health loss
Weights from the same set and on the same scale
has calculator text DW_12 = 1 - (1 - DW_1) * (1 - DW_2)
has common error note Adding weights for people with several conditions. Addition overstates health loss and can exceed 1 for severe combinations; WHO notes that at the oldest ages summed YLDs may approach or exceed the person-years lived.
Applying the multiplicative disability weight rule to dependent conditions. The multiplicative rule is applied to co-occurrence simulated under independence; Vos and colleagues note that YLDs might be slightly overestimated where one disease makes another more or less likely.
has description in the module Combines two weights so that the second condition removes its share of the health remaining after the first: one minus the product of one minus each weight. The result is below the sum of the two weights and never exceeds 1. GBD 2010 applied this rule to every combination of sequelae in its comorbidity simulation.

Common-effect inverse-variance pooled estimate and standard error

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000299
Type formula
assumes All studies estimate one common effect, Estimates on a scale with approximately normal sampling error
has calculator text theta_F = sum_(i=1)^k [y_i / v_i] / sum_(i=1)^k [1 / v_i]; SE_F = sqrt(1 / sum_(i=1)^k [1 / v_i])
has common error note Pooling hazard ratios or odds ratios on the ratio scale. Averaging ratio measures directly treats a halving and a doubling of the hazard asymmetrically: two equally weighted hazard ratios of 0.5 and 2.0 average 1.25 on the ratio scale but 1.0 when pooled as logarithms and transformed back. Standard errors derived from a confidence interval also apply to the log scale only.
Weighting studies by one over the standard error. The inverse-variance weight is 1 over the square of the standard error. Weighting by 1 over the standard error gives weights of 5, 10 and 4 in the three-trial example and a pooled log hazard ratio of about -0.2684 (hazard ratio 0.765) instead of -0.1872 (0.829), because the most precise trial is under-weighted.
has description in the module Pools the study estimates y_i with weights equal to the inverse of their variances v_i, under the assumption that every study estimates the same underlying effect. The weight of study i is 1/v_i, and the standard error of the pooled estimate is the square root of one over the summed weights. For a ratio measure the result is on the log scale and is exponentiated for presentation.

Compensated cross-price elasticity from the gross elasticity by the Slutsky equation

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000491
Type formula
assumes Elasticities and budget share measured at the same point
Smooth demand at a utility-maximising choice for the Slutsky cross-price decomposition
has calculator text eps_c_ij = eps_ij + w_j * eta_i
has common error note Classing goods as substitutes from a gross elasticity alone. Gross substitution need not be reciprocal and can differ in sign from the compensated effect, as the second example shows; substitutes in the Hicksian sense are defined on compensated demand.
Subtracting the income term instead of adding it to a gross cross-price elasticity. Writing eps_c_ij = eps_ij minus w_j eta_i doubles the income effect in the wrong direction; in the second example it gives minus 0.4 instead of plus 0.2.
has description in the module Separates a gross (uncompensated) cross-price elasticity, which mixes substitution with an income effect, into its compensated part. In elasticity form the Slutsky equation is eps_ij = eps_c_ij minus w_j times eta_i, so the compensated elasticity adds back the budget share of good j times the income elasticity of good i. With a small budget share, as for most co-payments, the two nearly coincide.

Compensating and equivalent variation from the expenditure function

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000260
Type formula
assumes Income unchanged by the policy, Known preferences
has calculator text CV = e0_u0 - e1_u0; EV = e0_u1 - e1_u1
has common error note Assuming CV and EV are equal for health. The two coincide only without income effects. They differ most for goods with few substitutes, and a person's own health is one.
Using a stated willingness to accept as a compensating variation for a gain. For a gain, CV is the maximum willingness to pay and EV the minimum willingness to accept to forgo it. Mixing the two measures across gainers and losers in one comparison changes the result when income effects are large.
has description in the module For a change in prices with income unchanged, the compensating variation is the income that could be taken away after the change while leaving the person at the original utility level u0; the equivalent variation is the income that would have to be given before the change to reach the new utility level u1. Each is a difference in the minimum expenditure needed to reach a utility level at old and new prices: CV = e(p0,u0) minus e(p1,u0) and EV = e(p0,u1) minus e(p1,u1). The formula takes the four expenditure values as inputs.

Compensating variation for a health change under log-income utility

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000466
Type formula
assumes Health state fixed for the person after the change, Utility additive in log income and health
has calculator text CV = Y * (1 - exp(-b * Delta_h))
has common error note Ranking several options by compensating variation. In the Equivalent Variation article's two-treatment example, compensating variation puts treatment A (£4,178.76) above treatment B with a £3,900 copayment (£3,875.45), although the person prefers B. Each compensating variation is measured from its own option's position; equivalent variation (HE-FM-EVAR-002) ranks the options as the person does.
Reporting willingness to pay to avoid a loss as its compensating variation. For the loss of 0.15 the compensating variation is -£4,855.03 (as in the Equivalent Variation article's loss example), the least compensation the person would accept. Reporting £4,178.76, the most the person would pay to avoid the loss, as its compensating variation mixes in the equivalent variation.
Using the linear value for a large health change. Valuing the gain of 0.15 at income times b times the change gives £4,500, about 7.7% above the compensating variation of £4,178.76 and about 7.3% below the equivalent variation of £4,855.03 (computed here for illustration).
has description in the module With utility equal to the natural log of income plus b times a health index h, the compensating variation of a change in h solves ln(Y less CV) plus b times h_1 equals ln Y plus b times h_0. Because utility is concave in income, the money value is not proportional to the health change: for a gain it is below the linear value Y times b times Delta_h, and for a loss its absolute value is above it. HM Treasury's wellbeing guidance gives the same form for the compensating surplus of a large change in life satisfaction, with b equal to the coefficient on the outcome divided by the coefficient on log income, and presents it as a sensitivity test for the high end of the range, not the central value.

Compensating variation from a multinomial logit model by the log-sum formula

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000467
Type formula
assumes Logit errors and utility linear in income for the log-sum formula, Change small relative to income for the log-sum formula
has calculator text CV = (log(sum_(j=1)^J1 [exp(1)^V1_j]) - log(sum_(j=1)^J0 [exp(1)^V0_j])) / alpha
has common error note Dividing the improved alternative's utility gain by alpha. In the first example the service's utility rises by 0.4, which divided by alpha gives £40 per person, about 50% above the log-sum value of £26.71, because about 38% of choosers took the opt-out before the change (computed here for illustration).
Reading a log-sum result as a pure compensating variation. Because alpha is constant, the log-sum figure is the compensating and the equivalent variation at once and cannot show any gap between willingness to pay and willingness to accept.
Using the cost coefficient itself as alpha in the log-sum formula. With the cost coefficient of -0.01 in the denominator the first example gives -£26.71, a loss for an improvement (computed here for illustration). Alpha is the negative of the cost coefficient.
has description in the module Values a change in the attributes of the alternatives, or in the set of alternatives, in a discrete choice experiment or another logit model. Expected utility from the choice is the log of the sum of the exponentiated representative utilities, and the change in it is converted to money by dividing by the marginal utility of income, the negative of the coefficient on the cost attribute. Train attributes the closed form to Williams and to Small and Rosen; it holds for independent extreme value errors and utility linear in income, so it gives a single figure that is both the compensating and the equivalent variation, per person per choice occasion.

Concentration index of health for grouped data

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000370
Type formula
assumes Ratio-scale nonnegative health for the concentration index, Ranking by socioeconomic position for the concentration index, Between-group inequality only in the grouped concentration index
has calculator text C = 2 * cov_hr / mu
has common error note Reading a smaller concentration index as narrower absolute health inequality. The concentration index is a relative measure. Under Programme A it falls from 0.0294 to 0.0290 while the absolute gap stays at 10 years and the slope index at 12.5 years, because adding the same amount to everyone changes the index without changing any absolute difference.
Treating a zero concentration index as no socioeconomic health inequality. An index of zero can arise because the concentration curve lies on the line of equality or because it crosses the line and the areas on each side cancel out. The curve is examined alongside the index before concluding that there is no socioeconomic-related inequality.
has description in the module Gives the concentration index from the covariance between health and fractional rank in the socioeconomic distribution. For grouped data the fractional rank of each group is the cumulative population share up to the midpoint of the group, and the mean and covariance are weighted by population share, so cov_hr is the same covariance as in the slope index. The index is positive when health is concentrated among the better-off and negative when it is concentrated among the worse-off.

Conditional posterior mean of the mean effect given the between-study variance

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000380
Type formula
assumes Normal summary likelihood with known within-trial variances in a Bayesian meta-analysis
Flat or vague prior on the mean effect in a Bayesian meta-analysis
Exchangeable trial effects in a Bayesian random-effects model
has calculator text m_mu = sum_(i=1)^k [y_i / (s_i^2 + tau2)] / sum_(i=1)^k [1 / (s_i^2 + tau2)]; sd_mu = sqrt(1 / sum_(i=1)^k [1 / (s_i^2 + tau2)])
has common error note Entering standard errors where squared standard errors are needed in a Bayesian meta-analysis. The weights need the squared standard errors. Entering 0.20, 0.15, 0.30 and 0.25 as if they were variances gives a conditional posterior mean of about -0.2505 with a standard deviation of about 0.2403 at tau2 = 0.0193, instead of -0.2390 and 0.1268, and makes tau2 look small against the within-trial variation.
Reporting the posterior of mu at one fixed tau as the full posterior. The formula conditions on one value of tau2 and ignores uncertainty about it. At tau2 = 0.0193 a 95% interval of the conditional posterior gives odds ratios of about 0.614 to 1.010, while the article's full posterior gives 0.593 to 1.032 under the Turner prior and 0.432 to 1.352 under the vague U(0, 2) prior on tau. The gap widens when the prior on tau allows large values.
has description in the module Gives the posterior mean and standard deviation of the mean effect mu when the between-study variance tau2 is held at one value and mu has a flat prior. Each trial is weighted by 1/(s_i^2 + tau2), so the arithmetic is that of random-effects inverse-variance pooling (HE-FM-ADMA-005), read here as a conditional posterior. A full Bayesian analysis averages this result over the posterior for tau, as in the computational function attached to this formula.

Constant hazard fitted to early follow-up of a bathtub-hazard cohort

Type formula

has calculator text lambda_hat = D / PY; S_t = exp(-lambda_hat * t); E_T = 1 / lambda_hat
has common error note Accepting a constant hazard because five-year survival matches. A fit that matches the Kaplan-Meier curve at the end of follow-up can still misplace deaths and the tail. In the article's example the exponential gives five-year survival of 0.7030 against 0.7136, yet overstates mean survival by 3.61 life-years (14.19 against 10.58), most of it after year fifteen.
has description in the module Fits an exponential model to follow-up that covers only the early part of a bathtub hazard. The fitted hazard is the deaths divided by the person-years at risk, the rate formula of the Adverse Event Rate page (HE-FM-AER-002), and the exponential model then implies survival exp(-lambda_hat t) and mean survival 1 divided by lambda_hat. Comparing these with the bathtub values shows how a constant hazard misplaces deaths and overstates the tail.

Continuous discount rate equivalent to an annual discount rate

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000521
Type formula
assumes Annual discount rate applied as compound annual discounting, Same discount rate for costs and health unless stated
has calculator text rho = log(1 + d); DF_t = exp(-rho * t)
has common error note Assuming a reference-case rate other than the one stated. The NICE reference case discounts costs and health effects at the same rate of 3.5 per cent a year, which corresponds to a continuous rate of about 0.0344; alternative analyses at 1.5 per cent need their own rho.
Using the annual rate as the continuous rate. exp(minus 0.035 times 10) gives 0.7047 instead of 0.7089, so every discounted total is slightly too low; in a continuous discount function the rate is not the same as in the discrete form.
has description in the module Converts an annual (discrete) discount rate d into the continuous rate rho that gives the same discount factor at every time, so that exp(minus rho t) equals (1 plus d) to the power minus t. Continuous-time models integrate costs and QALYs against exp(minus rho t), so rho, not d, belongs in the exponent.

has calculator text r = phi^d
has common error note Counting visit steps for unequally spaced AR(1) visits. In an illustrative 0, 3, 6, 12-month schedule with 0.7 per visit step, the baseline and 12-month utilities are three steps apart and receive 0.343, whereas elapsed time at 0.49 per year gives 0.49. Because each step is given the correlation of a 6-month gap, step counting understates the correlation for every pair that spans either 3-month interval.
Entering months against a yearly AR(1) correlation. In an illustrative calculation, using a gap of 6 months with phi defined per year gives 0.49 raised to the power 6, about 0.0138, instead of 0.7. The time unit of d has to match the unit of phi.
has description in the module Uses elapsed time instead of visit steps, so a 3-month gap and a 6-month gap receive different correlations. phi is the correlation between two measurements one time unit apart and d is the elapsed time between them in that unit. With equally spaced visits it reduces to HE-FM-AR1-001, with rho equal to phi raised to the visit interval.

Continuously discounted DALYs of a cohort with deaths and disability beginning at time zero

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000646
Type formula
assumes Deaths and onset of illness both at time zero in a discounted cohort DALY
Continuous discounting at one rate with no age weighting
has calculator text f_L = (1 - exp(-r * L)) / r; f_T = (1 - exp(-r * T)) / r; DALY_d = D * f_L + S * DW * f_T
has common error note Discounted cost per DALY averted compared with undiscounted results. Discounting raises the article's cost per DALY averted from USD 500 to about USD 744, so a discounted ratio set against an undiscounted one, or against burden estimates that use a 0% rate, misstates the difference between programmes. WHO-CHOICE presents health benefits both undiscounted and discounted at 3%.
Discrete annual factors used in place of continuous discounting for cohort DALYs. Counting each year at its start and discounting by 1/(1.03)^t gives factors of 25.254 and 8.786 and 979.54 DALYs for the untreated cohort, about 2% more than the continuous 960.37 (computed here for illustration). Larson regards differences of this size as minor, but the convention is stated and used in both scenarios.
has description in the module Replaces the L standard years lost per death and the T years lived with the condition by their present values under continuous discounting at rate r, (1 minus e to the minus rL) over r and (1 minus e to the minus rT) over r, as in HE-FM-YLL-003 and HE-FM-YLD-002. Fox-Rushby and Hanson define DALYs for economic evaluation as the present value of future years of life lost plus the present value of future years lived with disability, and the original DALY used a 3% rate. Discounting shrinks the long stream of years lost to a death more than the shorter stream of illness, so it lowers the weight of deaths prevented. The function exp is the exponential function.

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000620
Type formula
assumes Even flow within each year of a continuously discounted stream, Continuous rate taken from the annual rate in force
definition source the Source rows of the Functions and Formulae module record HE-FM-DISC-003
has calculator text rho = log(1 + r); Q_c = q * (1 - exp(-rho * T)) / rho
has common error note Annual discount rate used as the continuous rate for an even flow. Putting 0.035 in place of rho for the article's gain gives about 14.86 discounted QALYs instead of 14.97 (computed here for illustration). The annual and continuous rates differ, and the continuous rate is the natural log of (1 + r).
Continuous QALY totals set against end-of-year cost totals. Discounting QALYs continuously while costs or the comparator use end-of-year counting mixes conventions. In the article's example the cost per QALY at 3.5% falls from about GBP 20,389 to GBP 20,041, about 1.7% lower (computed here for illustration), only because of the convention.

has description in the module Treats the amount q as arising evenly through each year instead of at one point, and integrates it against the continuous discount factor exp(minus rho t) from 0 to T. The continuous rate rho, the natural log of (1 + r), gives the same factor at every whole year as the annual rate r, so the result lies between the end-of-year and start-of-year totals of HE-FM-DISC-001 and HE-FM-DISC-002. The function log is the natural logarithm.

Continuously discounted years lived with disability per incident case and for a cohort of new cases

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000582
Type formula
assumes Continuous discounting from the year of onset without age weighting
has calculator text YLD_case = DW * (1 - exp(-r * L)) / r; YLD_d = I * YLD_case
has common error note Applying a 3 per cent discount to prevalence-based YLDs. A prevalence-based count records only the health loss lived in the reference year and has no future stream to discount; discounting belongs to the incidence-based count or to a model of an intervention's future effects.
Discounting YLDs from onset and YLLs from death. WHO records that in the original DALY the discounting of YLDs started at the year of incidence and that of YLLs at the year of death, an inconsistency avoided when GBD 2010 and WHO dropped discounting from burden estimates.
Mixing continuous discounting of health with discrete discounting of costs. Larson shows that counting each of 10 years at the start of the year and discounting at 3 per cent gives 8.786 against the continuous 8.639, a difference of 1.7 per cent; a cost-effectiveness analysis with DALYs should state which convention it uses and apply it to costs and health alike.
has description in the module Under the pre-2010 convention each new case's future years with the condition were discounted from onset. With continuous discounting at rate r and no age weighting, L years at weight DW are worth DW times (1 minus e to the minus rL) over r present years, so a long-lasting condition loses most in the conversion.

Continuously discounted years of life lost per death and for a group of deaths

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000604
Type formula
