Discounted years of life lost for evaluation and historical comparison only
has calculator text YLL_death = (1 - exp(-r * L)) / r; YLL_d = N * YLL_death
has common error note Comparing discounted years of life lost with current GBD or WHO estimates. GBD 2010 calculated YLLs without discounting and WHO adopted a 0 per cent rate after 2012, so a discounted figure, such as the article's 2,902.9 against 5,169.1, is not comparable with current burden tables.
Mixing continuous and discrete discounting of years of life lost. Counting each of 10 lost years at the start of the year and discounting at 3 per cent gives 8.786 against the continuous 8.6394, a difference of 1.7 per cent. Larson regards the difference as minor, but an analysis should state which convention it uses.
Treating discounting of years of life lost as neutral between ages. Discounting compresses the difference between young and old deaths: in the article's example the older deaths rise from 25 to 37 per cent of the total. The rate therefore changes cause rankings as well as totals.
has description in the module Before GBD 2010 the standard DALY discounted future years at 3 per cent a year. With continuous discounting from the time of death and no age weighting, the L standard years remaining at the age of death are worth (1 minus e to the minus rL) over r present years, so discounting reduces the loss from a young death much more than from an old one. The function exp is the exponential function.

Copas probit probability that a study with standard error s is published

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000901
Type formula
assumes Probit selection on the reported standard error with fixed selection parameters
Precision coefficient at zero or above in the Copas selection equation
Standard error on the pooling scale in the Copas selection index
has calculator text u = gamma_0 + gamma_1 / s; P = Phi_u
has common error note Phi of the Copas intercept read as the probability for the least precise study. Phi(gamma_0) is the limit for an infinitely large standard error, not the probability for the least precise study in the meta-analysis. In the article's moderate scenario Phi(-1.062) is 0.144, while the small trials with standard error 0.40 are published with probability 0.35. The metasens manual calls the cumulative normal of gamma0 approximately the probability that a small study is published, which holds only when gamma_1 / s is close to zero for that study; here it is 0.68 (derived). The copas software reports selection as the probability of publishing the study with the largest standard error, which is Phi(gamma_0 + gamma_1 / s) at that standard error, 0.35 here.
Variance used in place of the standard error in the Copas selection index. Writing gamma_1 / s^2 instead of gamma_1 / s inflates the index of every study with a standard error below 1. In the article's moderate scenario the large trial's probability becomes 1.000 instead of 0.95 and the small trial's 0.7356 instead of 0.35, so a scenario meant to leave 65% of small trials unpublished leaves about 26% unpublished (computed here for illustration).
has description in the module Under the selection equation of the Copas model a study is published when a latent propensity Z = gamma_0 + gamma_1 / s + delta is above zero, with delta standard normal, so its marginal probability of publication is the standard normal distribution function at the index u = gamma_0 + gamma_1 / s. Phi(gamma_0) is the probability of publishing a study with an infinitely large standard error, and gamma_1 sets how fast the probability rises as the standard error shrinks. The site calculator has no normal distribution function, so Phi_u is entered as a named input from NORM.S.DIST(u, TRUE) or pnorm(u), the convention of HE-FM-MCID-004. That record's normal share above a threshold returns the same number with a threshold of zero, a standard deviation of 1 and a mean of u; the Copas form adds the index in the study's precision with its two selection parameters.
has formalisation level catalogue record
has implementation Copas publication probability of one study from named cells
has mathematical variable Copas selection intercept for one study's publication probability
Copas precision coefficient for one study's publication probability
Copas probability that one study is published
Mean publication propensity of one study in the Copas model
Reported standard error of one study in the Copas selection equation
Standard normal distribution function at the Copas publication index
has module record identifier HE-FM-COPAS-001
has source in the module Carpenter J, Rücker G, Schwarzer G. copas: an R package for fitting the Copas selection model. The R Journal. 2009;1(2):31-36 (full text read). Section Copas selection model, equations (2) to (4), states that study i is observed or published if Z_i = gamma_0 + gamma_1 / s_i + delta_i is above zero, with fixed gamma_0 and gamma_1, so that the marginal probability that study i is observed is Pr(Z_i > 0) = Phi(gamma_0 + gamma_1 / s_i), with Phi the standard normal cumulative distribution function. The text interprets Phi(gamma_0) as the marginal probability of publishing a study with infinite standard error and says gamma_1 is associated with the change in publication probability with increasing precision. https://doi.org/10.32614/RJ-2009-012
Duan R, Piao J, Marks-Anglin A, Tong J, Lin L, Chu H, Ning J, Chen Y. Testing for publication bias in meta-analysis under Copas selection model. arXiv preprint arXiv:2007.00836. 2020 (full text read). Section 2.1, Copas selection model, states that gamma_0 controls the overall proportion of selection and gamma_1 how selection depends on the size of the study, that the sign of gamma_1 is expected to be positive since larger studies are more likely to be accepted for publication, and gives Pr(Z_i > 0 | s_i) = Phi(gamma_0 + gamma_1 / s_i). https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.00836
Schwarzer G, Carpenter JR, Rücker G. metasens, Statistical Methods for Sensitivity Analysis in Meta-Analysis. R package version 1.5-3, 2025 (reference manual read). Function copas, Details, writes the selection model as Z = gamma0 + gamma1 / (SE(i)) + delta(i) and states that the software chooses a grid of gamma0 and gamma1 values corresponding to a range of selection or publication probabilities for the study with the largest treatment effect standard error. The arguments describe gamma0 as the constant in the probit selection model for study publication and gamma1 as the coefficient of study precision (1/standard error). https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/metasens/metasens.pdf

has common error note Ignoring readmission bed-days after a shorter stay. If the shorter stroke stay raised readmissions by 2 percentage points, 300 × 0.02 = 6 extra readmissions at an illustrative 8 days each use 48 bed-days, offsetting 16% of the 300 released, and each brings the costly early days of a new admission.
Reporting average bed day cost as a cash saving. In the illustrative stroke example, £135,000 at the average cost would be reported as saved although only £30,000 is variable. The remaining £105,000 is saved only if beds close, or becomes value only if the freed beds treat other patients. Page, Barnett and Graves found chief executives valued a ward bed day at about a quarter of its accounting cost.
has description in the module Values the bed-days released when the average stay of a patient group falls, at a stated cost per bed day. The answer depends on which cost is used: an average cost gives the apparent saving, a marginal cost the cash saving.

Type formula

has common error note Market-rate and PPP conversions mixed in one comparison. Turner and colleagues treat US dollars at market rates and international dollars as different output currencies, either or both of which a study may report. Adding or ranking costs from several countries when some were converted at market rates and others at PPPs gives figures in no single unit, so one method is used for each comparison and named.
PPP ratio inverted. Multiplying by the source factor and dividing by the target factor gives about 1,142.86 in place of 875 in the illustrative example, 31% too high (computed here for illustration). Since both factors are local currency per international dollar, the source factor always divides.
has Content MathML <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><apply><csymbol cd="relation1">eq</csymbol><ci>C_t</ci><apply><csymbol cd="arith1">times</csymbol><apply><csymbol cd="arith1">divide</csymbol><ci>C_s</ci><ci>PPP_s</ci></apply><ci>PPP_t</ci></apply></apply></math>
has description in the module Divides a cost in the source currency by the source country's PPP conversion factor, which gives international dollars, and multiplies by the target country's factor, which gives the target currency. Both factors are local currency units per international dollar, so the route through international dollars follows from their units (derived here), and a target factor of 1 returns international dollars. The World Bank describes PPPs as eliminating differences in price levels between countries in the process of conversion, and the CCEMG-EPPI-Centre Cost Converter page notes that pure exchange-rate conversion, the market rate of HE-FM-BOC-001, does not. Where the cost also comes from another price year, the year is moved first with HE-FM-COST-002 and HE-CF-BOC-001 sets out the two orders.

Cost efficiency and its decomposition into technical and allocative efficiency

Type formula

has calculator text CE = C_min / C_obs; TE_I = C_tec / C_obs; AE = C_min / C_tec
has common error note Comparing scores across different frontiers. Scores are relative to the frontier of the sample, inputs, outputs and model used. A score of 0.85 in one study cannot be compared with 0.85 in another built from different units or variables.
Reading input-mix allocative efficiency as programme allocation. A score of 0.9 for AE says that the hospital's input mix costs 10% more than necessary at its prices. It says nothing about whether resources are allocated to the right services or programmes.
has description in the module Compares three costs of producing the unit's observed output at its input prices: the actual cost, the cost of the technically efficient input bundle found by shrinking all inputs in proportion to the frontier, and the minimum cost with the least-cost mix of inputs. Cost efficiency is the minimum cost over the actual cost; input-oriented technical efficiency is the technically efficient cost over the actual cost; allocative efficiency in this production-frontier sense, the choice of input mix at given prices, is the minimum cost over the technically efficient cost. Cost efficiency equals technical efficiency multiplied by allocative efficiency.

Cost per relative value unit for a category of outpatient care in the HERC average cost method

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000550
Type formula
assumes One cost per unit for each category of care, Resource use proportional to Medicare relative values
has calculator text CF_c = X_c / R_tot; C_i = CF_c * R_i
has common error note Costing a procedure with its global fee. HERC advises applying separate relative values for a procedure and the visits before and after it rather than a global fee, so that the estimate reflects the visits that actually occur, and the facility practice expense values for care in VA medical centres.
Using one cost per unit across all categories of care. HERC assigns every VA visit to one of 12 categories and finds a factor for each, so a single system-wide rate would move cost between categories whose costs relative to Medicare differ.
has description in the module Keeps Medicare's relative values as the measure of resource use but replaces Medicare's price level with a health system's own spending: total spending on a category of care divided by the total relative value units of its encounters gives a cost per unit, and each encounter is costed at that rate times its units. This is the article's simplified stylisation of the method used by HERC, the health economics unit of the US Department of Veterans Affairs, which in practice scales a hypothetical Medicare reimbursement for each visit so that the estimates tally to national VA spending.
has formalisation level catalogue record
has implementation Category cost per unit and encounter costs from named cells
has mathematical variable Cost per relative value unit for a category of care, Actual spending on a category of outpatient care, Estimated cost of one outpatient encounter, Relative value units of one outpatient encounter, Total relative value units of encounters in a care category
has module record identifier HE-FM-CVF-004
has source in the module HERC, US Department of Veterans Affairs. Estimating Medicare Payments. Web page, accessed 3 October 2026 (full text read). Medicare Basics: to find the cost of outpatient services HERC recommends Medicare reimbursement rates, with relative values converted to a reimbursement by a conversion factor; Global Fees: apply separate RVUs for the procedure and the pre-procedure and post-procedure visits rather than global fees; Facility vs non-facility RVUs: apply the facility weights for care at VA medical centres. https://www.herc.research.va.gov/include/page.asp?id=estimate-medicare-payments
HERC, US Department of Veterans Affairs. HERC Outpatient Average Cost Data. Web page, accessed 3 October 2026 (full text read). Methods: every VA visit is assigned to one of 12 categories of outpatient care; for each category a specific factor converts the relative value to a VA cost estimate, assuming the resources used are proportionate to the Medicare relative values. Data Overview: the estimates represent the hypothetical Medicare reimbursement given the procedure codes of the visit, adjusted so that they tally to actual national VA expenditures for that type of care. https://www.herc.research.va.gov/include/page.asp?id=outpatient

Count-based D1 value set form with interaction terms in place of a constant

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000723
Type formula
assumes Counts beyond the first dimension and no linear I2 term
Coefficient signs as estimated, entered as disutility coefficients
Equivalence of the D1 form and a constant form
has calculator text D_1 = max(n_2 + n_3 - 1, 0); I_2 = max(n_2 - 1, 0); I_3 = max(n_3 - 1, 0); U = 1 - (beta_MO + beta_SC + beta_UA + beta_PD + beta_AD) - a_D1 * D_1 - a_I22 * I_2^2 - a_I3 * I_3 - a_I32 * I_3^2
has common error note Counting every dimension with a problem in D1. D1 counts dimensions beyond the first. Counting all of them gives a single-problem state a D1 credit it should not have, so with the illustrative coefficients 21111 scores 0.97 in place of 0.85 and 22222 scores 0.69 in place of 0.57 (computed here).
Scoring a D1 value set with the constant and N3 formula. Entering a D1 set's level decrements into HE-FM-EQ3L-001 with a zero constant and N3 drops all the count terms. With the illustrative coefficients 22222 then scores 0.25 in place of 0.57 and 33333 minus 1.50 in place of minus 0.30 (computed here), so a D1 set needs its own scoring rule, as HE-AS-EQ3L-003 states.
has description in the module Scores an EQ-5D-3L profile with the D1 form that Shaw, Johnson and Coons used for the US time trade-off set. There is no constant and no N3 term. The level decrements are subtracted as in HE-FM-EQ3L-001, and the interaction effects of problems on several dimensions enter through counts beyond the first, D1 for dimensions with any problem, I2 for dimensions at level 2 (squared) and I3 for dimensions at level 3 (linear and squared). HE-AS-EQ3L-003 records that this form cannot be scored with the constant and N3 formula, and Rand-Hendriksen and colleagues show that it equals a constant model with every level decrement shifted by the D1 coefficient. The coefficients in the examples are illustrative, not the published US values.

Coverage reached by voluntary vaccination when families weigh private cost against expected loss from infection

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000927
Type formula
assumes Families compare expected loss with private cost at the steady-state infection risk
No voluntary vaccination once the cost ratio reaches the risk with no vaccination
has calculator text r = c / L; v_vol = 1 - 1 / (R_0 * max(1 - r, 1 / R_0))
has common error note Bauch and Earn's interior equilibrium used when nobody vaccinates. Eq. 17 holds only when r is below 1 minus 1/R_0. With R_0 of 5, a cost ratio of 0.9 gives 1 minus 1/(5 × 0.1), or minus 1, and a cost ratio of 1.2 gives 2, neither a coverage; the equilibrium in both cases is 0, which the max term in the formula returns.
Resource cost used in place of the family's private cost in voluntary uptake. Free provision changes the cost the family sees, not the cost to society. Entering the full GBP 250 resource cost when the family bears only GBP 100 predicts coverage of 0.6 in place of 0.75, a shortfall from the threshold of 0.2 in place of 0.05, four times too large.
has description in the module A family that bears a private cost c per vaccination, counting any price and its own time and travel, and expects a loss L if the child is infected vaccinates while L times pi exceeds c, so in a homogeneous population uptake settles where the unvaccinated child's lifetime risk equals r = c/L. Solving pi(v) = r with HE-FM-VEXT-001 gives v_vol = 1 minus 1/(R_0(1 minus r)), the convergently stable Nash equilibrium P* of Bauch and Earn's vaccination game with r read as their relative risk r_v/r_i, and, with P/(theta H) equal to r, theta times d(P)/mu, the share immunised under the demand d(P) of Goodkin-Gold and colleagues, which for a fully protective vaccine is the share vaccinated. When r is at least the risk with no vaccination, 1 minus 1/R_0, nobody vaccinates, and writing max(1 minus r, 1/R_0) in the denominator returns that 0 and avoids a division by zero for r of 1 or more (derived; it equals the piecewise result on a grid of R_0 and r). For any r above zero v_vol is below the threshold H of HE-FM-BRN-003, Bauch and Earn's result that voluntary vaccination cannot eradicate the disease, and free provision lowers c and raises v_vol without reaching H while any private cost remains.

has source in the module Bauch CT, Earn DJ. Vaccination and the theory of games. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America. 2004;101(36):13391-13394. Section The Vaccination Game, subsections Description of Game and Characterization of Nash Equilibria, which give the payoff E(P, p) = minus r P minus pi_p(1 minus P) with relative risk r = r_v/r_i (Eq. 2) and state that if r is at least pi_0 the convergently stable Nash equilibrium is never vaccinate and otherwise vaccinate with a probability P* above 0 and below 1; section Incorporation of an Epidemic Model, which gives the mixed equilibrium obtained by solving r = pi_P* as P* = 1 minus 1/(R_0(1 minus r)) (Eq. 17); section Results and Discussion, which states that for any perceived relative risk r above 0 the expected uptake is below the eradication threshold and that parents can be expected to play a pure nonvaccinator strategy if r > pi_0, that is if r > 1 minus 1/R_0 (Eq. 18); and the Appendix, which shows that the Nash equilibrium is the unique solution of pi_P* = r when r < pi_0. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0403823101
Goodkin-Gold M, Kremer M, Snyder CM, Williams HL. Optimal vaccine subsidies for endemic and epidemic diseases. NBER Working Paper 28085. Cambridge, MA: National Bureau of Economic Research; 2020. Section 2.2, Consumer Demand, which states that consumers buy the vaccine when its marginal private benefit exceeds the price, that when some but not all buy they must be indifferent so that the price equals the marginal private benefit, and gives the demand d(P) = (mu/theta)(1 minus 1/((1 minus P/(theta H)) R_0)) (equation 17) with its boundary cases (equation 18); and section 2.5, Perfectly Competitive Equilibrium, which sets the price at the cost c, bounds case LR2 by R_0 at most 1/(1 minus c~), with c~ = c/(theta H), a case in which the marginal private benefit is below c even if no other consumer buys and the vaccine quantity stays 0, and states that some but not all newborns buy in the next range of R_0, case LR3. https://www.nber.org/papers/w28085

Covered days in the PDC observation period from shifted same-drug fills

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000456
Type formula
assumes Index date as day 1 of the PDC period, Shifted fills of one drug do not overlap
has calculator text C = sum_(i=1)^n [(E - a_i + 1) * (E - a_i + 1 > 0) * (E - a_i + 1 < S_i) + S_i * (E - a_i + 1 >= S_i)]
has common error note Counting supply that runs past the PDC end date. Adding the full days' supply of every fill gives 210 days for the article's history and a ratio of about 1.167, which is the fixed-interval medication possession ratio (HE-FM-MPR-001), instead of 150 covered days and a PDC of about 0.833. The 60 days of supply after day 180 hide the 30-day gap.
Summing covered days across different drugs in a PDC class measure. Two drugs in a class taken together, each covering days 1 to 90 of a 180-day period, give 180 summed days and a PDC of 1, against 90 covered days and a PDC of 0.5 when a day counts once if at least one drug is available (computed here for illustration).
has description in the module Adds, over the n fills of one drug after shifting, the days of each fill's supply that fall on or before the last day of the period. Shifting leaves the fills without overlap, so the sum counts each day once; a fill that starts after the end day adds nothing, and supply running past the end day is ignored. Day numbers run from the index date as day 1, so every fill starts on or after day 1 and the end day E equals the number of days in the period. Each comparison in parentheses inside the bracket equals 1 when it is true and 0 otherwise, so a fill adds its full supply when the supply ends on or before the end day, only the days up to the end day when it runs past it, and nothing when it starts after the end day.

Critical ratio of the fixed budget rule as the highest ICER among four funded programmes

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000718
Type formula
assumes Ratios ascending and positive with funding flags from the budget fill
Budget that binds on the league table for the critical ratio
has calculator text lambda_c = max(max(max(f_1 * r_1, f_2 * r_2), f_3 * r_3), f_4 * r_4)
has common error note Treating the critical ratio as fixed when the budget changes. In the article's table the critical ratio is GBP 12,500 per QALY at a budget of GBP 700,000 and GBP 20,000 at GBP 900,000. A ratio read at one budget and applied as a threshold after the budget changes adopts or rejects the wrong programmes, so it is recomputed with the fill at each budget.
Using one critical ratio for budget cuts and increases at a row boundary. With a budget of GBP 750,000 that exactly exhausts C, a cut of GBP 50,000 loses 4 QALYs at C's GBP 12,500 per QALY, while an increase of GBP 50,000 gains only 2.5 QALYs at D's GBP 20,000 (computed here for illustration). At a row boundary the health lost from a cut and the health gained from an increase are read from the two neighbouring rows.
has description in the module Reads the critical ratio lambda_c, which Sacristán and colleagues define as the ICER of the least cost-effective intervention adopted, from four programmes in ascending ICER order. Each f_i is 1 when programme i receives a share above zero in HE-FM-CELT-001, in full or in part, and 0 otherwise, and each r_i is that programme's ICER from HE-FM-ICER-001, so the largest product is the ratio of the last programme funded. Sacristán and colleagues describe this ratio as the cost-effectiveness threshold that represents the opportunity cost of funding new programmes. While the marginal programme still has an unfunded part, one more unit of budget buys 1 divided by lambda_c units of health, the shadow price of the budget in the sense Dakin and Tsiachristas give, and lambda_c is then the threshold k of HE-FM-CET-001 for a small change in budget (derived).

has source in the module Dakin H, Tsiachristas A. Rationing in an era of multiple tight constraints: is cost-utility analysis still fit for purpose? Applied Health Economics and Health Policy. 2024;22(3):315-329. Section 2.1, headed Constrained optimisation, which defines shadow prices as the change in outcome from a one unit increase in the constraint, and section 2.2 on the league table, which sorts items by the reciprocal of the ICER. The equality of the shadow price of the budget and the reciprocal of the critical ratio is derived here, not stated in the paper. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40258-023-00858-w
Marseille E, Larson B, Kazi DS, Kahn JG, Rosen S. Thresholds for the cost-effectiveness of interventions: alternative approaches. Bulletin of the World Health Organization. 2015;93(2):118-124. Section League tables, which states that since the length of the list of interventions deemed cost effective varies according to the budget, league tables combine considerations of cost-effectiveness with affordability, and that the last, least cost-effective intervention in the table to be adopted is more likely to approximate society's willingness to pay for health benefits than the open-ended set of commitments implied by global thresholds. https://doi.org/10.2471/BLT.14.138206
Sacristán JA, Abellán-Perpiñán JM, Dilla T, Soto J, Oliva J. Some reflections on the use of inappropriate comparators in CEA. Cost Effectiveness and Resource Allocation. 2020;18:29. Introduction, which states that under the fixed budget rule, or league table approach, interventions are ranked in increasing order of ICER and successively included until the budget is exhausted, and that the ICER of the least cost-effective intervention adopted indicates the critical ratio, a term they attribute to Weinstein and Zeckhauser 1973, or the cost-effectiveness threshold representing the opportunity cost of funding new programmes. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12962-020-00226-8

Cross-set gap in a utility gain split into constant, dimension and N3 terms

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000721
Type formula
assumes Both national value sets of the constant and N3 main-effects form
Same profile pair, levels and coefficient signs under both value sets
has calculator text g_A = c_A * (I_0 - I_1) + v_A_MO + v_A_SC + v_A_UA + v_A_PD + v_A_AD + gamma_A * (N3_0 - N3_1); g_B = c_B * (I_0 - I_1) + v_B_MO + v_B_SC + v_B_UA + v_B_PD + v_B_AD + gamma_B * (N3_0 - N3_1); dg = g_A - g_B
has common error note Charging the Zimbabwe constant to full health in a gain to 11111. Jelsma and colleagues' Table 6 lists a predicted value of 0.90 for 11111, which is their constant 0.900 with no level effect subtracted (derived). Using that value for the end state of a return to full health out of 21121 gives a gain of 0.123 in place of 0.223 under the Zimbabwe set and inflates the UK and Zimbabwe gap to 0.150 in place of 0.050 (computed here). Fixing 11111 at 1, through I = 0, keeps every set on the scale anchored at full health.
Reading a cross-set gain gap as a difference in dimension weights. Two sets can agree closely on every dimension and still give very different gains because of a profile-wide term. For the move out of 21232 into 11121 the four dimension differences between the UK and Zimbabwe sets add up to only 0.059, while the UK N3 decrement adds 0.269, so 82% of the gap of 0.328 comes from a term the Zimbabwe set does not have (computed here). Splitting the gap by term shows this before the gap is put down to national preferences about pain or mobility.
has description in the module Scores the same move between two EQ-5D-3L states under two national value sets of the constant and N3 form of HE-FM-EQ3L-001 and finds where the difference between the two gains comes from. Under each set the gain is the constant times the change in the any-problem indicator, plus the decrement relieved on each of the five dimensions, plus the N3 decrement times the change in the N3 indicator; this is the difference of two HE-FM-EQ3L-001 scores, written term by term (derived). Subtracting the two gains shows how much of the gap each dimension and each profile-wide term carries. When neither state is full health the constant cancels within each set, as HE-AS-EQ3L-009 notes, so the gap rests on the dimension weights and the N3 term alone.

Crude-versus-adjusted ranking reversal condition for two providers' costs

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000748
Type formula
assumes Index ratio read as like for like only under proportional cost deviations
Same national unit costs and cost basis for both providers' indices
Ties in the crude or the adjusted cost ranking
has calculator text rho = (A_1 / n_1) / (A_2 / n_2); mu = (E_1 / n_1) / (E_2 / n_2); RI = rho / mu; rev = (rho - 1) * (RI - 1) < 0
has common error note Mixing per-case crude costs with total expected costs in the mix ratio. If Hospital A treated half as many cases with the same mix and unit costs, its crude cost per case would stay 3,360 GBP, but a mix ratio taken on total expected costs, 1,600,000 / 6,200,000 = 0.258, in place of expected cost per case gives an index ratio of about 2.21 instead of 1.105 (computed here for illustration). The case numbers cancel only when both ratios are taken per case or both on totals.
Reading a ratio inflated by under-coding as worse performance. Mohammed and colleagues give a hypothetical pair of hospitals that are identical in case mix, care and deaths, 1,500 each, where hospital B under-records comorbidities. B's expected deaths fall to 743 and its standardised mortality ratio rises to 202 against 100 for A, a ratio of about 2.02 between the two hospitals with no difference in care. A ratio of cost indices moves the same way when one provider records its cases in lighter groups than the other, so RI between providers with different coding depth is checked against coding audits before it is read as a cost difference.
Reading a reversal of indirectly standardised indices as a like-for-like cost difference. Two illustrative hospitals with A's and B's mixes and identical unit costs in every group, 2,200 GBP for simple and 8,000 GBP for complex cases, score indices of 105.0 and about 100.97, so A looks about 4% dearer and the crude ranking reverses, yet direct standardisation on the pooled mix (HE-FM-INEQ-001) gives both 4,810 GBP per case (computed here for illustration). The 10% excess on simple cases weighs more in A's simple-heavy mix, so an index ratio is checked against direct standardisation before it is read as a cost difference for the same patients.
Reading an index ratio widened by recoding as a cost difference. In step 5 of the article's illustrative example Hospital B records 100 of its simple cases as complex, with the same care and the same 5,890,000 GBP of cost. Its expected cost rises by 100 × 6,000 = 600,000 GBP to 6,800,000 GBP, so mu falls from about 0.516 to about 0.471 and the index ratio rises from about 1.105 to about 1.212, while rho stays at about 0.570. B's index falls from 95 to about 86.6, a change equal to the old index times the added expected cost over the new one, 95 × 600,000 / 6,800,000 = 8.38 points (derived here). The recoded index is HE-FM-CWT-003 recomputed on the new counts, the effect HE-AS-CWT-006 warns of, so an index ratio is read against coding audits before it is credited to efficiency.
Reading two providers' crude cost ratio as relative efficiency. In the article's example B's crude cost per case is 75% above A's (5,890 / 3,360 = 1.753), while A's index is 10.5% above B's (105 / 95 = 1.105). The crude gap reflects B's larger share of complex cases, a mix ratio of 0.516, and points the wrong way.
has description in the module Compares two providers on crude cost per case and on the indirectly standardised cost index. The crude cost ratio rho is the product of the index ratio RI and the ratio mu of expected cost per case, the part of the crude gap that the case mix accounts for, so RI is rho divided by mu and equals I_1 / I_2 for the indices 100 A_h / E_h, which are 100 times R_h of HE-FM-CWT-003. The adjusted ranking reverses the crude one when rho minus 1 and RI minus 1 have opposite signs, which holds exactly when rho lies strictly between mu and 1 (derived here and checked numerically on 200,000 random inputs). A crude cost advantage therefore survives adjustment only when it is larger than the advantage in expected cost per case, and two providers with the same mix, mu equal to 1, cannot reverse. A tie in either ranking is not counted as a reversal.

Cumulative hazard from a survival probability

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000473
Type formula
assumes Single event type for the cumulative hazard and survival link, Survival estimated with non-informative censoring
has calculator text H_t = -log(S_t); F_t = 1 - S_t
has common error note Base-10 logarithm in place of the natural logarithm. Excel's LOG function is base 10. Minus LOG(0.4493) gives about 0.3475 instead of the cumulative hazard of 0.8000, and every later conversion through EXP is then wrong (computed here for illustration).
Reading the cumulative hazard as the proportion who have had the event. A cumulative hazard of 1.118 is not a 112% probability, and one of 0.5 corresponds to an event probability of about 0.39, not 0.5. Treating H_t as a probability overstates the share who have had the event, more so as H_t grows.
has description in the module Takes minus the natural logarithm of the probability of being event free beyond time t, which gives the cumulative hazard at t, and sets it beside the probability of having had the event by t. The two agree only when both are small: the cumulative hazard has no upper limit and passes 1 when survival falls below exp(minus 1), about 0.3679, while the event probability never exceeds 1. The reverse step is S_t = exp(minus H_t).

Current health expenditure as a percentage of gross domestic product

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000924
Type formula
assumes Current health expenditure counted on the health accounts boundary
One database and one release for a comparison of GDP shares
Same country, year and currency in both parts of the GDP share
has calculator text S = CHE / GDP * 100
has common error note Health spending share of GDP formatted as a percentage after multiplying by 100. HE-IM-HGDP-001 already multiplies by 100, so a result cell set to the Excel Percentage format shows the United Kingdom 2019 share as 997.95%, or 998% with no decimals, rather than 9.98. Either keep the factor of 100 with a General or Number format, or drop it and use the Percentage format, but not both.
Reading a low GDP share as low spending per person. In the 2023 GHED figures Ireland spent 6.6% of GDP on health against 11.0% in the United Kingdom, yet its current health expenditure per person was 8,269 international dollars at purchasing power parity against 6,365, about 30% higher. The OECD notes that in Ireland and Luxembourg a significant part of GDP is repatriated profits not available for national consumption, and that gross national income may be a more meaningful denominator there. Levels per person are compared through HE-FM-BOC-002, not through S.
Reading a rise or fall in the GDP share as a change in health spending. Between 2021 and 2022 Norway's share fell to 7.91% from 9.81% while its health spending in kroner rose by a factor of 1.0684, because GDP rose by a factor of 1.3259, and the ratio of the two shares, 0.8058, equals the ratio of the two growth factors (derived). The United Kingdom's share rose by a factor of 1.2129 in 2020 with spending up by a factor of 1.1421 and GDP down by a factor of 0.9416. A change in S has to be read with the change in CHE and in GDP beside it.
Spending and GDP taken from different years in the GDP share. Dividing the United Kingdom's 2020 health spending of 254,603 million pounds by the 2019 GDP of 2,233,921 million pounds gives 11.40% instead of the 12.10% of HE-EX-HGDP-002, because the 2020 fall in GDP is left out (derived). The same mistake arises when a GDP series is revised after the spending figures were taken, so both parts should come from one release.
has description in the module Divides current health expenditure by gross domestic product for the same country and year and multiplies by 100. The WHO Global Health Expenditure Database defines its indicator che_gdp in this way, with both parts held in million current national currency units, so no exchange rate or purchasing power parity enters the share. The OECD uses the same ratio in Health at a Glance and keeps GDP as the denominator for every country. The share moves whenever either part moves, so a value read on its own says nothing about the level of spending.

The Data sheet gives the United Kingdom and Norway values used in the worked examples and tests, and the 2023 shares and per person values for Ireland and the United Kingdom. The database home page notes that WHO adjusts and estimates national figures and that country data may still differ in definitions, data collection methods, population coverage and estimation methods. https://apps.who.int/nha/database/Home/IndicatorsDownload/en

Cycle transition probability from the rise in cumulative hazard across a cycle

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000474
Type formula
assumes Clock measured from the origin of the fitted curve, Fitted curve describes the modelled population, Single exit from the state for the cumulative hazard conversion
has calculator text p_t = 1 - exp(-(H_t - H_prev))
has common error note Using cumulative event probability as a per-cycle probability. Taking 1 minus S(t) as the probability for the cycle ending at t applies the risk accumulated since time zero to one cycle: 0.2464 in year 2 instead of 0.1671 in the article's example.
Using cumulative hazard increments as cycle probabilities. Treating each rise in H as the cycle probability overstates deaths in every cycle: in the article's example, survival at year 6 falls to 0.1786 instead of the fitted 0.2300. The gap grows with cycle length and risk.
has description in the module Gives the probability that a person event free at the start of a model cycle has the event by its end, from the cumulative hazard at the end of the cycle and at its start. Because survival is exp(minus H), the ratio S(t) / S(t minus Delta) is exp of minus the rise in H, so the conversion is exact for any hazard shape and the cohort trace reproduces the fitted curve. Time t runs from the origin of the fitted curve, so in a cohort model it is the time since model start at the cycle's end. With a constant hazard it reduces to HE-FM-TP-001.

DALYs averted and cost per DALY averted by a programme against its comparator

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000645
Type formula
assumes Programme averts DALYs at a positive extra cost, Same cohort, horizon and conventions in both DALY scenarios
definition source the Source rows of the Functions and Formulae module record HE-FM-DALY-003
feeds Cost per DALY averted converted at a market exchange rate
has calculator text DALY_av = DALY_0 - DALY_1; ICER = (C_1 - C_0) / DALY_av
has common error note Denominator taken as the programme's DALYs less the comparator's. Copying the QALY form E_1 minus E_0 with DALYs gives 552 less 1,440, or minus 888, and a ratio of minus USD 500, which reads as a programme that saves money and loses health. With a loss measure the comparator's DALYs come first.
Multiples of GDP per capita applied as a decision rule for cost per DALY averted. Calling the article's USD 500 per DALY averted cost-effective because it lies below one or three times GDP per capita applies a rule that Bertram and colleagues, writing for WHO in 2016, said should not be used alone as a decision rule for funding. The 2021 WHO-CHOICE update recommends against using any threshold as a decision rule.
Reading a cost per DALY averted against a cost per QALY threshold. A cost per DALY averted is not read directly against a threshold set per QALY gained. Deadweight loss of an untaxed negative externality with linear curves

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000428
Type formula
assumes Linear curves between the efficient and untaxed quantities, Welfare measured as consumer benefit less social cost
has calculator text Q_0 = (a - c) / b; Q_star = (a - c - m) / (b + g); DWL = 0.5 * (Q_0 - Q_star) * (m + g * Q_0)
has common error note Deadweight loss read as the total external cost. The triangle is the loss from the units consumed beyond Q_star. The external cost imposed by all 160 thousand units is much larger, but most of it comes from units whose benefit exceeds their social cost, which the tax keeps.
Triangle height taken from the external cost at the efficient quantity. Using the marginal external cost at Q_star, 3.20 pounds, as the height of the triangle gives 51.2 instead of 64 thousand pounds in the article's example. When the external cost rises with consumption, the height is the gap at Q_0. The 51.2 is computed here for illustration.
has description in the module Without a tax, every unit between Q_star and Q_0 costs society more than it is worth to consumers. With linear curves the loss is a triangle: its base is Q_0 minus Q_star, and its height is the gap between marginal social cost and marginal private benefit at Q_0, which equals the marginal external cost at Q_0 because marginal private benefit equals c there. The Pigouvian tax removes the whole triangle.

Tax revenue and insurer payments are transfers; only the triangle is a loss to society.

The coinsurance case written in terms of the coinsurance rate is HE-FM-MH-001.

Decision curve threshold probability from the benefit to a case and the harm to a non-case

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000501
Type formula
assumes Threshold benefit and harm the same for every case and non-case, Threshold benefit and harm in a common unit
has calculator text p_t = L / (G + L)
has common error note Choosing a threshold to suit the model. The threshold comes from the benefits and harms of the intervention, not from the curve; picking the threshold where a model looks best overstates its value.
Swapping benefit and harm in the threshold probability. Writing p_t = G / (G + L) turns the 25 per cent threshold of the first example into 75 per cent, so a model would be judged at the wrong end of the range.
has description in the module Sets the threshold at which a rational decision maker is indifferent between intervening and not, given the expected benefit of intervening for a patient who has or will have the event and the expected harm of intervening for one who does not. Equivalently the odds p_t / (1 minus p_t) equal L / G. Harm can include money, time, stress and adverse health effects, as long as G and L share a unit.

Journal of Clinical Oncology. 2016;34(21):2534-2540. doi:10.1200/JCO.2015.65.5654. Section on decision curves: a classic result in decision theory says a rationally chosen risk threshold is R = C/(B + C), equivalently R/(1 minus R) = C/B, where B is the expected benefit of intervention for a case and C the expected cost to a control, interpreted broadly (money, time, stress, negative health effects); every case is assumed to have the same B and every control the same C. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4962736/
Vickers AJ, Elkin EB. Decision curve analysis: a novel method for evaluating prediction models. Medical Decision Making. 2006;26(6):565-574. doi:10.1177/0272989X06295361. Introductory theory, Equation 1: p_t a + (1 minus p_t) b = p_t c + (1 minus p_t) d gives (a minus c)/(d minus b) = (1 minus p_t)/p_t, where a, b, c and d are the values of a true positive, false positive, false negative and true negative. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2577036/
Vickers AJ, Van Calster B, Steyerberg EW. Net benefit approaches to the evaluation of prediction models, molecular markers, and diagnostic tests. BMJ. 2016;352:i6. doi:10.1136/bmj.i6. Net benefit and risk prediction: if no more than 10 men should undergo biopsy to find one man with high grade cancer, the harm of delaying diagnosis is nine times greater than that of an unnecessary biopsy. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4724785/

Delta-method confidence interval for an ICER

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000289
Type formula
assumes Effect difference well away from zero for the delta method
Non-zero cost and effect differences in the relative variance form
has calculator text R = Delta_C / Delta_E; SE_R = abs(R) * sqrt(SE_C^2 / Delta_C^2 + SE_E^2 / Delta_E^2 - 2 * Cov_CE / (Delta_C * Delta_E)); R_L = R - z * SE_R; R_U = R + z * SE_R
has common error note Reading a negative delta-method limit as a cost saving. A negative limit such as -£6,296 per QALY does not identify a cheaper and more effective option. A negative ICER arises both for a cheaper, more effective option and for a dearer, less effective one, in opposite quadrants of the cost-effectiveness plane.
Taking the delta-method upper limit as the plausible maximum ICER. In the article's trial the delta method puts the upper limit at £39,600 per QALY whereas Fieller's interval reaches about £96,786, because a much smaller QALY gain remains plausible and would push the ratio up sharply. Polsky and colleagues found that the Taylor series method underestimated the upper limit.
Trusting the delta-method interval when the effect difference is not significant. With a QALY standard error of 0.06 the delta method returns about -£6,296 to £46,296 per QALY, which looks informative, while Fieller's confidence set is every value below about -£110,622 together with every value above about £6,177. The data cannot place an upper limit on the ICER, and the symmetric interval hides that.
has description in the module Linearises the ratio of the two estimated differences around their point estimates to obtain a large-sample standard error for the ICER, then forms a symmetric Wald interval around the ratio. The function abs returns the absolute value, so the standard error stays positive when the ICER is negative. The method is also called the Taylor series method.

Demographic projection of service use from age-specific base-year rates

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000532
Type formula
assumes Age-specific use rates held at base-year levels, Base-year activity measures use under base-year supply, Age groups cover the whole population once
has calculator text U_t = P_1 * r_1 + P_2 * r_2 + P_3 * r_3
has common error note Converting the forecast to beds with one average length of stay. Beds follow from admissions times average stay over 365 times occupancy (HE-FM-ALOS-002 solved for beds), but older patients stay longer: for emergency admissions in England in 2022 the Health Foundation reported 12.5 days for those aged 85 and over against 5.1 days at 16 to 44, so one average understates bed growth when the case mix ages.
Holding age-specific rates fixed as survival improves. Zweifel, Felder and Meiers found that health care expenditure in the last eight quarters of life depended on remaining lifetime rather than calendar age beyond 65, so constant age-specific rates can overstate the effect of ageing; in the example a modest fall in older-group rates cuts the forecast from 24,950 to 23,905.
Projecting with one crude rate for the whole population. Base-year use of 22,500 over 250,000 people is 0.09 per person; applied to 257,000 people it gives 23,130 admissions and misses the 1,820 that come from the shift towards older groups (computed here for illustration).
Reading a utilisation forecast as a forecast of need. Wright and colleagues report that geographical variation in hospital admission rates is explained more by the supply of beds than by mortality, so rates extrapolated from activity data carry past supply forward and can lock in supplier-induced demand.
has description in the module Applies the base-year use rate of each age group to that group's projected population and adds the results. The article's form sums over any number of age groups; three are written out here so that the calculator can run. Only the size and age structure of the population change; the rates stay at base-year levels unless a scenario changes them. Converting the forecast to beds is HE-FM-ALOS-002 solved for beds.

Destination probabilities under constant competing hazards

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000217
Type formula
assumes Constant cause-specific hazards, Absorbing destinations within the cycle
has calculator text p_1 = h_1 / (h_1 + h_2) * (1 - exp(-(h_1 + h_2) * Delta)); p_2 = h_2 / (h_1 + h_2) * (1 - exp(-(h_1 + h_2) * Delta)); p_stay = exp(-(h_1 + h_2) * Delta)
has common error note Converting each competing rate with the single-event formula. Using p equal to 1 minus exp of minus h_k times Delta for each exit ignores that people who leave by one route are no longer at risk of the other. With both hazards equal to 1 per cycle, each exit would receive about 0.632 and the probability of remaining would be about minus 0.264, which is impossible. The joint formula gives about 0.432 for each exit and about 0.135 for remaining.
has description in the module Splits the probability of leaving a state within an interval between two absorbing destinations with constant cause-specific hazards h_1 and h_2. The total exit probability depends on the summed hazard, and each destination receives its share h_1 or h_2 of that sum.

Direct unfairness measure of health inequity

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000431
Type formula
assumes Additive attribution of the health gap to causes for direct unfairness
Fairness judgements stated before direct unfairness is computed
has calculator text I_DU = sum_(j=1)^J [u_j * Delta_j]
has common error note Counting the unexplained remainder under direct unfairness. Adding the 2.4-point remainder turns the direct unfairness figure of 4.0 points into 6.4 points, which is the fairness gap result, not direct unfairness. The two measures treat the remainder differently and are labelled accordingly.
Reporting direct unfairness without the fairness judgements behind it. Reclassifying smoking from a restricted to a free choice halves the result from 4.0 to 2.0 points with the same data. A figure reported without the classification of each cause cannot be interpreted.
has description in the module Fleurbaey and Schokkaert define direct unfairness through the variation that remains when every legitimate source of difference is held at a common reference value, written h_i^DU = f(c_i, l_bar) in the article's simplified notation. Applied to a gap between two groups that has been attributed additively to causes, holding the legitimate causes constant leaves only the parts attributed to causes judged illegitimate, so the inequity is the sum of those parts. The unexplained remainder is dropped, which treats it as acceptable. This group-gap formula is this page's simplification: Fleurbaey and Schokkaert define a hypothetical distribution across individuals and then apply an inequality index to it.

Directly age-standardised rate for comparing social groups

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000430
Type formula
assumes One standard population for every social group compared
Age classed as a legitimate source of difference in the inequity analysis
Same age bands and comparable age-specific rates in every social group
has calculator text R_g = sum_(k=1)^K [w_k * r_gk]
has common error note Comparing crude rates of social groups with different age structures. Crude rates weight each group's age-specific rates by its own age structure, so part of the comparison reflects age. In the article's example the crude gap is 4.8 points against a standardised gap of 6.4 points, because the deprived group is younger.
Reporting a standardised health gap without its standard population. The standardised gap depends on the standard. With a standard of 50% under 50 and 50% aged 50 and over, computed here for illustration, group D's rate is 26.0% and group A's 19.0%, a gap of 7.0 points instead of 6.4. The standard is stated with the result.
has description in the module Weights the age-specific rates of one social group by the age structure of a common standard population, so that groups with different age structures are compared as if they had the same one. In a health inequity analysis this removes the part of a difference that is due to age, which Whitehead places partly under natural, biological variation and so treats as a legitimate source of difference. The weights sum to 1. With a group's own age shares as the weights, the same sum returns the group's crude rate.

Dirichlet posterior parameter, mean and beta marginal for one destination from transition counts and a Dirichlet prior

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000574
Type formula
assumes Counts from the population, starting state and interval of the model
Zero prior valid only when every destination was observed
has calculator text alpha_j = a_j + n_j; b_j = A_0 + N - alpha_j; E_j = alpha_j / (A_0 + N)
has common error note Building a row from a percentage and an assumed sample size. Multiplying a published percentage by an assumed number of patients sets the precision alpha_0 by assumption, which sits uneasily with NICE's requirement that distributions are not chosen arbitrarily but represent the available evidence.
Giving prior weight to a transition that cannot happen. A uniform prior over a row that includes an impossible move, such as a return from death, makes that probability positive in every draw; structural zeros are left out of the row instead.
Replacing a zero count with a small arbitrary number. Substituting, say, 0.01 for a zero count makes the spreadsheet run but hides the prior it implies; the article asks for the prior to be reported, and a uniform prior adds one to every destination, not to the zero cell alone.
has description in the module A Dirichlet prior combined with multinomial counts gives a Dirichlet posterior in which each parameter is its prior parameter plus its count. The posterior mean of one destination is that parameter over the prior total plus the number of patients, and the destination's probability on its own follows Beta(alpha_j, alpha_0 minus alpha_j), whose second parameter is written b_j here. A zero prior reproduces the observed proportions; a prior of one per destination is uniform over all valid rows.

has description in the module Samples one row of a transition matrix for a state with three exits by drawing an independent gamma variable for each destination, with shape equal to that destination's count plus any prior and a scale of one, and dividing each draw by their total. Each component has a beta marginal: the second probability from Dirichlet(90, 24, 6) follows Beta(24, 96).

has common error note Expecting discounting to leave a one-off treatment ratio unchanged. A common rate leaves the ratio unchanged only when costs and QALYs fall in the same years in the same proportions, as for a lifelong drug. With the whole cost in year 0 the ratio rises by about 63% at 3.5% over 30 years.
Reading the 1.5 per cent ratio as the reference-case result. Lowering the rate from 3.5% to 1.5% cuts the article's ratio from about GBP 20,389 to GBP 15,615. The 1.5% result is a non-reference-case analysis, and NICE also asks for a highly plausible case that the benefit is maintained.

Discounted fundamental matrix of a time-homogeneous Markov chain at a constant discount rate

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000592
Type formula
assumes Constant transition matrix and constant discount rate for the discounted matrix
Absorbing chain for the discounted fundamental matrix
Start-of-cycle counting with an undiscounted first cycle in the discounted fundamental matrix
has calculator text N_disc = (I - Q / (1 + r)^Delta)^(-1); t_disc = N_disc * c
has common error note Annual discount factor applied to shorter Markov chain cycles. With six-month cycles the per-cycle factor is 1.035 to the power 0.5, about 1.0173. Dividing Q by 1.035 discounts every half-year as if it were a full year and understates discounted life expectancy.
Discounting undiscounted Markov chain life expectancy as one lump. Discounting the 16 undiscounted years from Well as if they all fell at year 16 gives 9.2273, and treating them as 16 certain years from the start gives 12.5174. Both miss the 10.7260 of N_disc, because survival time is spread over many cycles and the discount factor is not linear in time.
Mixing counting conventions with the discounted fundamental matrix. Counting membership from the end of the first cycle, with factor 1.035 to the power minus 1 for the first cycle counted, drops the undiscounted starting cycle and gives 9.7260 from Well, exactly one cycle less than t_disc. That total should not then also have half a cycle subtracted, which would count the same timing adjustment twice.
has description in the module Discounting membership at the start of cycle k by (1 + r) to the power minus k Delta multiplies every cycle by the same factor, so the discount folds into Q and the series of discounted powers of Q sums to a matrix inverse. Entry i, j of N_disc is the expected discounted number of cycles spent in transient state j by a person starting in transient state i, with the starting cycle counted in full and undiscounted. The row sums t_disc are the discounted expected cycles before absorption, which with death as the only absorbing state is discounted life expectancy in cycles. With r equal to zero the formula returns the fundamental matrix of HE-FM-ABS-001.

has implementation Discounted fundamental matrix and its row sums in Excel
has mathematical variable Annual discount rate for a Markov chain fundamental matrix, Cycle length in years for discounting a Markov chain, Column of ones for Markov chain discounted row sums, Discounted fundamental matrix of a Markov chain, Discounted expected cycles before absorption in a Markov chain, Identity matrix for the discounted fundamental matrix, Transient block of a Markov chain for discounted occupancy
has module record identifier HE-FM-MKCH-001
has source in the module Grinstead CM, Snell JL. Grinstead and Snell's Introduction to Probability. The CHANCE Project version of 4 July 2006, based on the 2nd edition published by the American Mathematical Society (full text read). Chapter 11 Markov Chains, section 11.2 Absorbing Markov Chains: Theorem 11.3 (Q to the power n tends to 0), Theorem 11.4 (I minus Q has an inverse N and N = I + Q + Q^2 + ..., proved from Q^n tending to 0) and Theorem 11.5 (t = Nc). Section 11.5 notes that the series converges because Q^n tends to 0, so it acts like a convergent geometric series. The discounted matrix follows by replacing Q with Q divided by the discount factor, whose powers also tend to 0; this step is the Markov Chain article's derivation and is not stated by Grinstead and Snell. https://math.dartmouth.edu/~prob/prob/prob.pdf
Sonnenberg FA, Beck JR. Markov models in medical decision making: a practical guide. Medical Decision Making. 1993;13(4):322-338. doi:10.1177/0272989X9301300409 (full text read). The Half-Cycle Correction: the fundamental matrix representation is equivalent to counting state membership at the beginning of each cycle, and the correction for a matrix solution is subtraction of one half cycle from the membership of each starting state. Discounting: because of the time variance, discounting cannot be used when the fundamental matrix solution is used; the Markov Chain article qualifies this for a constant geometric discount. https://doi.org/10.1177/0272989X9301300409

Discounted general-population QALYs from a life table

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000239
Type formula
assumes Period life table and population utility norms, Deaths spread evenly within each year
has calculator text Q_hs = sum_(t=0)^T [L_t * U_t / (1 + r)^t]
has common error note Discounting from calendar age instead of the starting age. The exponent counts years from the starting age, so the first year is undiscounted. Using age x itself as the exponent discounts every year by a further i years and shrinks Q_h far below the cut-offs.
has description in the module Sums, over each year of remaining life from the starting age, the expected years lived multiplied by the age-specific utility norm and discounted to the starting age. Here t counts years from the starting age i, so t equals x minus i for age x, and the sum runs to the last age in the life table, usually 100. It is carried out separately for each sex, and the two results are weighted by the proportion female to give Q_h.

Discounted QALYs from a cure fraction under constant background and excess hazards

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000597
Type formula
assumes Constant background and excess hazards for the closed-form cure QALYs
Constant utilities by cure status over the lifetime
Continuous discounting equivalent to the annual cure model discount rate
has calculator text QALY_d = pi * u_C / (mu + r) + (1 - pi) * u_U / (mu + lambda + r)
has common error note Annual discount rate used as the continuous rate in cure QALYs. Putting 0.035 in place of log(1.035) in the denominators gives 13.33 discounted years for cured patients instead of 13.44, and 3.508 QALYs at pi = 0.25 instead of 3.530, so every discounted total is slightly too low.
Discounting cure model survival at the mean survival time. Applying one discount factor at the mean, 25 years times 1.035 to the power minus 25, gives about 10.58 discounted years for cured patients instead of 13.44, because deaths are spread around the mean and earlier years carry more weight. The discount belongs inside the area, as exp(minus r t) times the survival curve.
has description in the module Values each group's survival with a constant utility and discounts it continuously at rate r. With exponential survival the area under exp(minus h t) times exp(minus r t) is 1/(h plus r), so each group's discounted mean is one over its total hazard plus r. With r = 0 and both utilities 1 the formula returns T_bar of HE-FM-CRM-003. The continuous rate equivalent to an annual rate d is r = log(1 plus d), HE-FM-CONT-003.

Discounted QALYs in a progressive illness-death model with continuous discounting

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000522
Type formula
assumes Constant rates and utilities over a lifetime horizon
Progressive illness-death model starting Well for discounted QALYs
has calculator text QALY_d = u_W / (q_WS + q_WD + rho) + u_S * q_WS / ((q_WS + q_WD + rho) * (q_SD + rho))
has common error note Discounting the undiscounted state times as a lump. Multiplying 3.714 undiscounted QALYs by a single factor, such as the factor at the mean survival time, does not reproduce the integral, because discounting acts on every instant of the time in each state.
Using the annual rate in place of rho. Putting 0.035 for rho gives about 3.283 QALYs instead of 3.289 (computed here for illustration); small here, but the gap grows with longer survival and higher rates.
has description in the module Solves the article's integral of state utilities times state occupancy times exp(minus rho t) in closed form when rates are constant: discounting adds rho to every exit rate, so discounted time Well is 1 / (q_WS plus q_WD plus rho) and discounted time Sick is q_WS / (q_WS plus q_WD plus rho) / (q_SD plus rho). Weighting by utilities gives discounted QALYs; state costs in place of utilities give discounted costs.

The closed form in this record is that integral with constant rates and a factor exp(minus rho t), derived for this record and checked numerically. https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/msm/vignettes/msm-manual.pdf

Type formula

definition source the Source rows of the Functions and Formulae module record HE-FM-DISC-001
formalises constant rate discounting method
has calculator text Q = q * (1 - (1 + r)^(-T)) / r
has common error note Inflation added to the discount rate for a real cost stream. Discounting real costs of GBP 1,000 a year for 30 years at 5.5%, the 3.5% rate plus 2% inflation, gives about GBP 14,534 instead of GBP 18,392 at 3.5% (computed here for illustration). The Green Book states that the two rates should not be added together.
Year 0 included in an end-of-year discounted stream. Running the year index from 0 to 30 adds a 31st year. For 0.8 QALYs at 3.5% the total becomes about 15.51 instead of 14.71 discounted QALYs (computed here for illustration). A stream of T years counted at the end runs from year 1 to year T.
Zero rate entered in the closed-form discounted annuity. The closed form divides by r, so a rate of zero returns #DIV/0! in Excel instead of the undiscounted total q times T. An undiscounted result, which PMG36 asks for in its disaggregated table and the Dutch guideline as a scenario, uses q times T, the factor-by-factor sum or Excel PV, which accepts a zero rate.
has Content MathML <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><apply><csymbol cd="relation1">eq</csymbol><ci>Q</ci><apply><csymbol cd="arith1">divide</csymbol><apply><csymbol cd="arith1">times</csymbol><ci>q</ci><apply><csymbol cd="arith1">minus</csymbol><cn type="integer">1</cn><apply><csymbol cd="arith1">power</csymbol><apply><csymbol cd="arith1">plus</csymbol><cn type="integer">1</cn><ci>r</ci></apply><apply><csymbol cd="arith1">unary_minus</csymbol><ci>T</ci></apply></apply></apply></apply><ci>r</ci></apply></apply></math>
has description in the module Gives the present value of the same amount q in each of T years when each year's amount is counted at the end of that year, so the first year carries the factor 1/(1 + r) and the last 1/(1 + r)^T. The fraction (1 minus (1 + r) to the power minus T) divided by r is the sum of the T yearly discount factors, the annuity form in the article's worked example. It tends to T as r falls towards zero, where the closed form itself cannot be evaluated.

has common error note Ignoring treatment process decrements over long horizons. Brennan and Dixon's review found process utility values for different drug delivery methods from 0.02 to 0.27; a decrement of 0.02 lasting as long as a ten-year treatment is 0.2 QALYs (computed here for illustration).
Subtracting a decrement the baseline utility already contains. TSD 12 warns that decrements for grade 1 to 2 adverse events need care because the cohort behind the main utilities may already include patients who had them; utilities collected during treatment can likewise already reflect treatment burden.

Drug cost of one administration with whole single-use vials and with vial sharing

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000567
Type formula
assumes One vial size and no sharing of opened vials
has calculator text C_vial = n_v * p_v; C_share = D * p_v / v; C_waste = C_vial - C_share
has common error note Costing single-use vials per mg used. Bach and colleagues note that leftover drug in a single-dose vial still has to be paid for even when discarded, and NICE's PMG24 asks for drug wastage to be taken into account in drug costs; per-mg costing prices the article's 150 mg course at 5,400 instead of 7,200 pounds.
Treating the available vial sizes as fixed. Hatswell and Porter estimated, with UK population data, that supplying pembrolizumab in 70 mg and 100 mg vials instead of 50 mg and 100 mg would cut wastage from 13.3 per cent to 8.7 per cent, so the vial sizes assumed can change drug costs.
has description in the module When the dose is set by weight or body surface area and the drug comes in single-use vials, the amount paid for is the vials opened: n_v is the dose divided by the vial content rounded up to a whole number. With vial sharing, or payment per mg used, the cost is in proportion to the dose, and the difference is the cost of the drug discarded. The calculator has no rounding-up function, so n_v is entered.
has formalisation level catalogue record
has implementation Whole-vial, shared and wasted drug cost from named cells
has mathematical variable Content of one single-use vial, Cost of drug discarded at one administration, Drug cost of one administration with whole vials, Drug cost of one administration with vial sharing, Number of single-use vials opened for one administration, Price of one single-use vial, Prescribed dose for one administration
has module record identifier HE-FM-DOSE-003
has source in the module Bach PB, Conti RM, Muller RJ, Schnorr GC, Saltz LB. Overspending driven by oversized single dose vials of cancer drugs. BMJ. 2016;352:i788. doi:10.1136/bmj.i788 (full text read). Opening section: patients' body sizes are unlikely to match the amount of drug in a single-dose vial, so there is nearly always some left over, and the leftover drug still has to be paid for, even when discarded. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.i788
Hatswell AJ, Porter JK. Reducing drug wastage in pharmaceuticals dosed by weight or body surface areas by optimising vial sizes. Abstract (Results): changing the available vial sizes for pembrolizumab (50 mg and 100 mg vials) to 70 mg and 100 mg could cut wastage from 13.3 per cent to 8.7 per cent, using UK population data. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40258-018-0444-0
National Institute for Health and Care Excellence. Single technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies evaluation: user guide for company evidence submission template (PMG24). Drug cost per cycle scaled by relative dose intensity

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000568
Type formula
assumes Drug cost in proportion to the dose delivered under RDI scaling, RDI from the trial that supplies the efficacy
has calculator text C_drug = C_planned * RDI
has common error note Applying RDI to a per-mg cost under whole-vial pricing. A 150 mg administration at an RDI of 0.90 delivers 135 mg, which still needs two 100 mg vials at 600 pounds, while the per-mg scaling gives 540 pounds, so the saving is overstated (computed here for illustration).
Leaving the RDI calculation undocumented. Dasgupta and colleagues found RDI or a dose delay factor in 63 of 265 NICE solid-tumour appraisals, with RDI from 85 to 100 per cent and widely varying methods; excluding the RDI adjustment generally raised ICERs by 5 to 10 per cent, and committees frequently questioned the transparency of RDI calculations and the assumptions on delayed or missed doses and wastage.
has description in the module Relative dose intensity (RDI) is the delivered dose per unit of time divided by the planned dose per unit of time, and models multiply the cost of the planned dose for a cycle by it to reflect dose reductions, delays and missed doses.
has formalisation level catalogue record
has implementation Drug cost after relative dose intensity from named cells

A review of the utilization of relative dose intensity and dose delay factor in health technology appraisals of oncology drugs in solid tumors. Advances in Therapy. 2025;42(11):5313-5340. doi:10.1007/s12325-025-03358-6 (abstract read). Abstract (Results): of 265 HTAs sourced to 31 March 2024, 63 included RDI or dose delay factor variables; RDI ranged from 85 to 100 per cent across all HTAs; approaches to calculating and applying RDI varied widely; committees frequently raised concerns about the transparency of RDI calculations and assumptions on delayed or missed doses and wastage; excluding RDI adjustments generally increased ICERs by 5 to 10 per cent. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12325-025-03358-6

Economically justifiable price per unit and per patient at one threshold

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000613
Type formula
assumes Price enters the incremental cost linearly in an EJP calculation
Inputs of an EJP from one comparator, perspective and discount rate
EJP compared with the net price paid
has calculator text EJP_patient = lambda * Delta_E - Delta_C_other; EJP = EJP_patient / U
has common error note Adding the other incremental costs in the EJP. Adding Delta_C_other to lambda times Delta_E instead of subtracting it gives GBP 860 per pack for Drug X instead of GBP 740, a price at which the ICER is GBP 28,750 per QALY, above the threshold (computed here for illustration). Savings enter Delta_C_other as negative amounts and raise the EJP; added costs lower it.
Mixing per-patient and per-unit EJPs. Drug X's per-patient EJP of GBP 18,500 and its EJP of GBP 740 per pack describe the same ceiling. Comparing the per-patient figure with a pack price, or dividing by a unit count that differs from the one in the model, misstates the price: over 30 packs with no extra QALYs the EJP per pack falls to about GBP 616.67.
Reading the EJP as a target price. At the EJP the health gained is just offset by the health displaced elsewhere, so the net health benefit to the payer is zero and the value of the gain goes to the manufacturer as revenue, as Claxton and colleagues and the York glossary state. The EJP is a ceiling for the net price, NICE does not use a precise maximum acceptable ICER (PMG36 section 6.3.1), and meeting the EJP does not guarantee a positive recommendation.
has description in the module Splits the incremental cost per patient into the medicine's acquisition cost, U units at the price EJP, and every other cost difference, Delta_C_other. Setting the ICER, EJP times U plus Delta_C_other, all divided by Delta_E, equal to the threshold lambda and solving gives the per-patient EJP, lambda times Delta_E minus Delta_C_other: the most the payer could spend on the medicine for each patient. Dividing by U gives the EJP per unit, so with U equal to 1 the two results coincide. When Delta_C_other equals or exceeds lambda times Delta_E both are zero or negative, and no positive price makes the medicine cost-effective at that threshold.

has common error note Discounting at equal rates while expecting the threshold to grow. Claxton and colleagues show that, with a fixed budget and decisions based on incremental ratios, discounting costs and health at the same rate is correct only if the threshold stays constant.
Taking the effective cost rate to be the consumption rate. Attema and colleagues give the health rate as the consumption rate minus g_v and the cost rate as the health rate plus g_k, so the effective cost rate equals the consumption rate only if the threshold and the consumption value of health grow at the same rate.
has description in the module With a fixed budget, a cost in year t displaces health equal to the cost divided by the threshold in that year, and the forgone health is then discounted at the health rate. If the threshold grows at g_k a year, a pound spent later displaces less health, so costs carry an effective rate r_C_star with one plus r_C_star equal to (one plus r_H) times (one plus g_k), approximately the health rate plus the threshold growth.

Effective reproduction number as the basic reproduction number times the susceptible proportion

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000698
Type formula
assumes Homogeneous mixing and few infectious people for the effective reproduction number
Immune people fully protected for the effective reproduction number
has calculator text R_t = R_0 * x_t
has common error note Current reproduction number quoted as the basic reproduction number. An estimate of R_t made after immunity has built up understates R_0. Reading the article's R_t of 1.65 as R_0 gives a herd immunity threshold of 1 minus 1/1.65, about 0.394, instead of 0.667 (computed here for illustration), so the coverage target would be set far too low.
has description in the module Once part of the population is immune, each case meets fewer people who can be infected. The WHO guide gives R_t = R_0 x_t for a homogeneously mixing population, where x_t is the proportion of the population still susceptible at time t, and Pitman and colleagues define the effective reproduction number in the same way. Vaccination and past infection lower x_t and so R_t, while R_0 stays the same because its definition assumes a fully susceptible population. R_t above 1 means new infections per generation are rising and below 1 falling. With an all-or-nothing vaccine of effectiveness E given to a proportion V before any spread, x_t equals 1 minus V times E, which is the starting susceptible proportion s_0 of HE-CF-ATR-001 when V times E is entered there as the fully protected proportion.

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000546
Type formula
assumes Index of agency from 0 to 1 for the efficient share, Zero margin on an efficient stay as the normalisation
has calculator text q_eff = (b_0 - c) / b_1; r_star = 1 - alpha; P = (1 - r_star) * c * q_eff
has common error note Ignoring what the blend does to cost control. Partial reimbursement weakens the incentive to reduce the cost of each day, which the formula holds fixed; Ma and Mak report that cost reimbursement fails the internalisation principle for cost effort, so the efficient share for quantity is not efficient for cost.
Treating the blend as better by construction. The blend restores the efficient stay only when r matches the provider's alpha; at alpha of 0.8 a half-reimbursed blend would give 9.5 days instead of eight (computed here for illustration), so a share chosen without evidence on agency can overshoot as well as undershoot.
has description in the module Efficiency requires the patient's marginal benefit to equal the marginal cost of care. Comparing this with the provider's condition (HE-FM-CTH-002) gives Ellis and McGuire's optimal reimbursed share r_star = 1 minus alpha, so the provider's own cost share equals the index of agency. The fixed part is then set so that the payment for an efficient stay equals its cost, the article's choice; Ellis and McGuire note that the prospective amount can be lowered as r rises to keep the same total payment per case.

has common error note Cost of waiting left out under only in research. Ignoring the people who wait outside the study keeps the 600-patient trial as the efficient design at GBP 940,000. Under only in research it is worth GBP 540,000 and the 300-patient trial, worth GBP 570,000, is the better choice.
Waiting cost charged when the new treatment is expected to be worse. If the expected incremental net benefit were minus GBP 200, people outside the study would receive standard care, the expected best option, and lose nothing by waiting. Using the absolute value would wrongly subtract GBP 400,000 for 2,000 people waiting (computed here for illustration).
has description in the module Subtracts from the population EVSI of a design its expected study cost and the net benefit forgone by people treated outside the study while it runs, when the new treatment is available only in research. When the new treatment is expected to be better, with INB above zero, each of the N_w people waiting forgoes INB. When it is not, standard care outside the study is already the expected best option and waiting costs nothing in this sense. Under approval with research N_w is zero and the result equals the ENBS of HE-FM-ENBS-001, so the same trial can have a different ENBS under the two arrangements.
