People treated before the study reports counted as beneficiaries. If 2,000 of the article's 8,000 people would be treated before the 600-patient trial reports, only 6,000 can benefit and ENBS falls to GBP 340,000 instead of GBP 940,000 (computed here for illustration). Eckermann and Willan reduce the number who benefit by those treated inside and outside the trial until its evidence is available.
Study cost set against per-person EVSI instead of population EVSI. Comparing the per-person EVSI of GBP 300 for the article's 600-patient trial with its cost of GBP 2,000 per participant suggests the study cannot pay its way, yet its ENBS is GBP 940,000. The cost belongs against the population value, after scaling and discounting.

has common error note Reading an EQ-5D-5L profile in reverse dimension order. The five digits run mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain or discomfort and anxiety or depression. Reading 23245 backwards scores 54232, 0.350 under the England set instead of 0.247, because the dimensions carry different decrements.
Taking 0.950 as the England EQ-5D-5L value of state 21111. The abstract of Devlin and colleagues gives 0.950 for states 11211 and 21111, but Table 3 of the same paper lists 0.942 for 21111, which follows from the Table 2 decrement of 0.058 for slight mobility problems, and 0.950 for 11211 and 12111. Using 0.950 for 21111 overstates it by 0.008, and the other single slight-problem states are lower still, 0.937 for 11121 and 0.922 for 11112.
Treating crosswalk values as the England EQ-5D-5L value set. The crosswalk of van Hout and colleagues 2012 maps five-level responses onto three-level values and is not a value set elicited for five-level states. Table 3 of Devlin and colleagues shows it giving 0.877 for 21111 against 0.942 in the England set, and 833 of the 3,125 states, 26.7%, below zero against 159, 5.1%, so mixing the two within one analysis changes utilities by far more than rounding.
has description in the module Scores a profile with the EQ-5D-5L value set for England published by Devlin and colleagues in 2018, 1 minus the Table 2 decrement for the level reported on each dimension, with no separate constant decrement. Each bracket is the lookup of HE-FM-EQ5L-001 with that dimension's England coefficients. The lowest value is minus 0.285 for 55555, the highest below full health is 0.950, and 159 of the 3,125 states score below zero. NICE does not use this set for reference-case analyses, and the set NICE now names is not formalised here.

has calculator text e_ij = n_ii * p_ij; L_j = 1 / (1 - p_jj); T_ij = e_ij * L_j; h_ij = p_ij / (1 - p_ii)
has common error note Ignoring returns to Well after recovery in a Markov chain episode count. Taking the time at risk in Well as 1 divided by 0.15, or 6.67 years, leaves out the years spent in Well after recovering, giving 0.67 episodes and 2.22 years Ill in place of 1.2 episodes and 4 years.
Reading Markov chain mean episode length as mean time ill per person. The mean of 3.33 years applies to each episode. A third of people starting in Well never fall ill, and those who do may have several episodes, so the mean time Ill among people who ever fall ill is 4/0.6667 = 6 years, and the mean over everyone starting in Well is 4 years.
has description in the module Splits the expected time that a person starting in transient state i spends in another transient state j into the expected number of separate episodes in j and the mean length of each episode, and gives the probability of ever entering j. Each cycle begun in i leads into j with probability p_ij, so the expected number of entries is n_ii, the expected cycles in i from the fundamental matrix of HE-FM-ABS-001, times p_ij; n_ii already includes the cycles spent in i after each return from j. Each episode lasts a geometric number of cycles with mean 1 divided by 1 minus p_jj.

Subtracting the illustrative 0.27 for both level 3 dimensions of 31131 gives minus 0.30 instead of minus 0.03, and under the UK tariff charging it five times for 33333 gives minus 1.670 instead of minus 0.594, so the most severe states are understated.
Reading the minus 0.594 floor as a property of the EQ-5D-3L instrument. The lowest value belongs to the value set and not to the questionnaire. Scoring 33333 with the Dutch time trade-off coefficients of Lamers and colleagues 2006 tabulated in the EuroQol reference volume gives minus 0.329, against minus 0.594 with the UK tariff, so a negative mean utility partly reflects the set used.

has common error note Adding the lower EQ-5D-5L level decrements to the reported one. Each coefficient in a five-level value set table is the whole decrement for its level. Adding the England mobility coefficients for levels 2, 3 and 4 for a severe mobility problem gives 0.341 instead of 0.207, and the England worked example for 23245 subtracts a single coefficient per dimension.
Reading the EQ-5D-5L level one place too high. Treating the level as a position in the list of four coefficients, without the zero for level 1, picks the next coefficient up. For England mobility a severe problem then costs 0.274 instead of 0.207, a slight problem 0.076 instead of 0.058, and level 5 has no coefficient left, so CHOOSE returns an error value.
has description in the module Returns the decrement that a five-level value set attaches to the level reported on one dimension. Level 1 carries no decrement, and each of levels 2 to 5 has its own coefficient, which is the full decrement for that level and not a step to be added to the lower ones. The level indicators are written with min and max so that the site calculator picks exactly one coefficient for a whole-number level. Five such lookups, one per dimension, give the decrements beta_d of the article's additive form U(s) = 1 minus their sum, scored for a whole profile in HE-CF-EQ5L-001.

Equity switching weight at which a programme breaks even

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000642
Type formula
assumes Positive cost and QALY gain for a break-even weight, Break-even weight depends on the value of a QALY, Break-even weight read against the weights available
has calculator text w_star = Delta_C / (lambda * Delta_E)
has common error note Break-even weight for a programme that loses health. With an illustrative extra cost of GBP 30,000 and a QALY loss of 0.1 at GBP 35,000 per QALY, the formula returns about minus 8.57, which has no meaning as a weight. A weight above 1 enlarges a loss, so the break-even weight is computed only for a QALY gain.
Judging the break-even weight at one value of a QALY only. Subgroup A's weight of 1.7 clears the break-even weight of about 1.43 at GBP 35,000 per QALY but not the 2.0 needed at GBP 25,000. Reporting only the upper value suggests the severity weight is enough across the whole NICE range.
has description in the module Sets the weighted net health benefit to zero and solves for the weight, giving the incremental cost divided by lambda times the QALY gain, which is the unweighted ICER divided by lambda. A weight at or above w_star makes the programme acceptable at lambda, so the value states how much concern for the group is needed to justify a programme that is not cost-effective without weights. A value below 1 means the programme is cost-effective unweighted.

Equity-efficiency impact plane quadrant of a programme against its comparator

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000676
Type formula
assumes Comparator at the origin of the equity-efficiency impact plane
Inequality index oriented so that a higher value means more inequality
Points on an axis of the impact plane follow the dominance tie rule
Total health on the impact plane counted net of the opportunity cost
has calculator text WW = (d_H >= 0) and (d_I <= 0) and (d_H > 0 or d_I < 0); LL = (d_H <= 0) and (d_I >= 0) and (d_H < 0 or d_I > 0); WL = (d_H > 0) and (d_I > 0); LW = (d_H < 0) and (d_I < 0)
has common error note Reversing the orientation of the inequality index on the impact plane. Measuring the gap as the more deprived group's health less the other group's turns the article's widening of 0.020 years into minus 0.020 and moves the programme out of the win-lose quadrant into the win-win one, reporting a fall in inequality that did not happen.
Treating a win-lose programme as one to reject. The quadrant shows that a trade-off exists and leaves open which objective prevails. The article's programme is win-lose, yet at the cited public aversion of 10.95 it still raises EDE health by 31.8 EDE QALYs under equal sharing, so the decision rests on HE-FM-DCEA-002 or on an explicit judgement about the trade-off.
has description in the module Places a programme on the equity-efficiency impact plane from the sign of its change in total health, net of the health opportunity cost, and the sign of its change in an inequality index, with the comparator at the origin. A win-win programme raises total health and lowers inequality and a lose-lose programme does the reverse, while win-lose and lose-win programmes need a trade-off analysis such as the change in EDE health of HE-FM-DCEA-002. The sources name the four quadrants without classifying a point on an axis, so the formula applies the tie rule of the live dominance record HE-FM-DOM-001, with less inequality taking the place of lower cost. No change on one axis with an improvement on the other counts as win-win, the mirror case counts as lose-lose, and no change on either axis gives no quadrant.

Equity-weighted ICER for one group and the equivalent threshold

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000640
Type formula
assumes Positive QALY gain and cost for the equity-weighted ICER, One weight for the whole group in the equity-weighted ICER, Equity weighting leaves cost and displaced care unchanged
has calculator text ICER_w = Delta_C / (w * Delta_E); lambda_w = w * lambda
has common error note Applying the equity weight to the ICER and to the threshold together. Comparing the weighted ICER of GBP 29,412 with the raised threshold of GBP 59,500 applies the weight twice. It is the same as a weight of 2.89 on the unweighted ICER (1.7 × 1.7 = 2.89), well above the largest NICE severity weight. Either the ICER or the threshold carries the weight, not both.
Reading the equity-weighted ICER as the cost per QALY gained. The weight moves subgroup A from GBP 50,000 to about GBP 29,412 per weighted QALY, but each QALY gained still costs GBP 50,000 and displaces the same care. Reporting GBP 29,412 as the cost per QALY hides the health given up to act on the severity judgement.
has description in the module Divides the incremental cost by the weighted QALY gain of a group that carries a single weight w. Because the weight is the same for everyone in the group, the weighted ICER equals the unweighted ICER divided by w, and judging it against a threshold lambda gives the same decision as judging the unweighted ICER against w times lambda. The second part of the formula returns that equivalent threshold, the route the Norwegian committee proposed in 2014 through differential threshold ranges by severity.

has common error note Dividing the displaced health by the equity weight. Weighting the displaced health as well, by dividing the GBP 30,000 by 1.7 times GBP 35,000, gives about 0.5158 QALYs per patient for subgroup A instead of 0.1629. Only the QALY gain carries the weight.
Reporting only the weighted net health benefit. For the 300 patients of subgroup A at GBP 35,000 per QALY, the weighted net health benefit is about 48.9 QALYs, while the unweighted value is about minus 77.1 QALYs, a fall in total population health. PMG36 section 6.3.2 asks for both so that this loss stays visible.
has description in the module Converts the incremental cost into the health displaced elsewhere, Delta_C divided by lambda, and subtracts it from the weighted and from the unweighted QALY gain. The displaced health is not weighted, so the two results differ by w minus 1, times Delta_E. A negative unweighted value with a positive weighted value marks a programme that lowers total population health and would be recommended only on the strength of the equity judgement.

Type formula

has common error note Averaging per-patient weighted gains across groups of unequal size. Averaging the per-patient weighted gains of 1.02 and 0.8 QALYs and multiplying by 1,000 patients gives 910 weighted QALYs instead of 866. Subgroup A is only 30% of the patients, so each group's weighted gain has to be multiplied by its own number of patients before the groups are added.
Weighting severity and unmet need as two separate concerns. PMG36 states that the extent of unmet health need is reflected within the severity definition (section 6.2.12). A weight of 1.7 for severity combined with a further 1.2 for unmet need multiplies the gain by 2.04 and counts the same shortfall twice.

has description in the module Multiplies the incremental QALY gain in each group by that group's equity weight to give the group's equity-weighted value, and adds these values over the groups that the programme affects. The calculator form is written for two groups, V_1 and V_2, and each further group adds one more term w_g times Delta_E_g to the sum. A weight above 1 counts each QALY gained in a priority group as more than one QALY, and a weight of 1 leaves a group's gain unchanged. The result replaces the unweighted QALY gain in the ICER and in net health benefit, so the comparison with costs follows the usual rules once the weights are fixed.

Equivalent annual cost of a capital asset

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000244
Type formula
assumes Constant annual payments at the end of each year, Replacement cost for existing assets, Share attributed to the evaluated service
has calculator text E = (K - S / (1 + r)^n) / ((1 - (1 + r)^(-n)) / r)
has common error note Straight-line depreciation as the annual cost. Dividing 500,000 pounds by 8 years gives 62,500 pounds a year, which omits the opportunity cost of the capital tied up in the asset and understates the equivalent annual cost of about 72,738 pounds at 3.5%.
has description in the module Spreads the cost of a capital asset, such as equipment or a building, over its useful life as an equal annual amount whose present value equals the purchase cost less the discounted resale value. The annuity factor A(n,r), one minus (1 + r) to the power minus n, all divided by r, is the present value of 1 a year for n years at rate r. Unlike straight-line depreciation, the equivalent annual cost includes the opportunity cost of the funds tied up in the asset.

Equivalent variation for a health change under log-income utility

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000468
Type formula
assumes Health state not purchasable by the person
Utility additive in log income and health, valued at the status quo
has calculator text EV = Y * (exp(b * Delta_h) - 1)
has common error note Describing the equivalent variation of a gain as willingness to pay. For the gain of 0.15, £4,855.03 is the least the person would accept to forgo it. The most the person would pay for it is the compensating variation, £4,178.76; equivalent variation is willingness to pay only for a loss.
Expecting a logit log-sum value to show the equivalent variation gap. A log-sum figure from a discrete choice model assumes a constant marginal utility of income, so it is the equivalent and compensating variation at once and cannot reproduce a gap such as the £676.27 in this example.
Using the linear value in place of the equivalent variation of a large change. Valuing the gain of 0.15 at income times b times the change gives £4,500, £355.03 or about 7.3% below the equivalent variation of £4,855.03 (computed here for illustration).
has description in the module With utility equal to the natural log of income plus b times a health index h, the equivalent variation solves ln(Y plus EV) plus b times h_0 equals ln Y plus b times h_1. For a gain it exceeds both the linear value Y times b times Delta_h and the compensating variation of the same gain; for a loss of the same size it equals minus the compensating variation of the gain, so the two measures swap values between a gain and a loss. HM Treasury's wellbeing guidance gives the same form for the equivalent surplus of a large change in life satisfaction and notes that, under its ln(income) formulae, the equivalent surplus always exceeds the compensating surplus for a gain.

Valuing treatment B at the status quo income of £30,000 gives an equivalent variation of about £10,495.76 instead of £5,231.31, overstating it by the £3,900 copayment multiplied by the exponential of 0.30 (computed here for illustration).
Ranking options by compensating variation instead of equivalent variation. Compensating variation puts treatment A (£4,178.76) above treatment B (£3,875.45), contradicting the person's preference: a direct comparison shows the person would pay up to a further £278.76 to receive B rather than A.
has description in the module Values an option that moves both the health index and the person's income, for example a treatment with a copayment, from the same status quo income Y_0 and health. Solving ln(Y_0 plus EV_k) plus b times h_0 equals ln Y_k plus b times h_k gives the formula. Because each option is valued at the same status quo, the option with the larger equivalent variation gives the higher utility, the ranking property that compensating variation lacks when there are income effects. With Y_k equal to Y_0 the formula reduces to HE-FM-EVAR-001.

Erlang loss refusal probability, annual refusals and achieved occupancy of a six-bed unit

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000928
Type formula
assumes Poisson arrivals at a constant rate in the six-bed loss model
Refused patients leave the six-bed unit and do not wait
Any length of stay distribution with the same mean in the six-bed loss model
Six interchangeable staffed beds and arrivals counted as demand
has calculator text a = lambda * L_bar; P_block = (a^6 / 720) / (1 + a + a^2 / 2 + a^3 / 6 + a^4 / 24 + a^5 / 120 + a^6 / 720); R = 365 * lambda * P_block; o_ach = a * (1 - P_block) / 6
has common error note Offered load over beds read as the achieved occupancy of a loss unit. Dividing the offered load by the beds ignores the bed-days refused patients never use. For the coronary care unit a / 6 is 0.994, while the achieved occupancy is 0.733 (computed here), so a plan that reads the first figure as occupancy hides a quarter of its patients being turned away.
Poisson overflow used in place of the Erlang loss probability. The probability that a Poisson count with mean a exceeds six, the complement of the Poisson sum up to the capacity that HE-CF-ARRP-001 uses for hourly arrivals, counts refused patients as if they still occupied beds. For the coronary care unit it gives 0.388 against the loss probability of 0.262, about 48% too high (computed here).
Recorded admissions entered as the arrival rate of the six-bed loss model. Hospital systems record admissions, not refused patients, so admissions understate demand wherever beds run short. For de Bruin and colleagues' coronary care unit, entering the roughly 2.60 patients a day actually admitted (computed here from 3.52 arrivals with 26.2% refused) in place of 3.52 gives a refusal probability of 0.147 in place of 0.262 and about 139 refusals a year in place of 337. De Bruin and colleagues estimate the arrival rate from the average number of occupied beds instead.
Refusal probability read as the chance of waiting for a bed. P_block counts patients turned away. If patients who find the unit full wait instead, the M/M/s probability of delay in Green's equation 11-1, which assumes exponential stays, applies and is higher; for the illustrative six-bed unit with a load of 2.96 it is 0.094 against a refusal probability of 0.050 (computed here). The article's 95-bed unit shows the same gap, a 6.8% chance of waiting against 1.14% refused.
has description in the module Gives, for a unit of six staffed beds with Poisson arrivals, the share of arriving patients who find all six beds occupied and are refused, the Erlang loss formula of de Bruin and colleagues written out term by term, with the offered load a equal to arrivals per day times the mean stay. Refusals a year are the annual arrivals times that share, and the achieved occupancy is the load actually carried, a times one minus the refusal probability, over the six beds, de Bruin and colleagues' occupancy rate for the loss model, which takes the form of HE-FM-ALOS-002 solved for o with the patients admitted, not the patients arriving, as the discharges. Achieved occupancy is always below a / 6 because refused patients use no bed-days. The model needs only the mean stay, not the shape of the length of stay distribution. Other numbers of beds follow the same pattern with terms up to a^N / N!, which HE-CF-CAPP-001 computes by recursion.

Erreygers corrected concentration index for a bounded health variable

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000608
Type formula
assumes Fixed bounds of the measurement scale for the Erreygers correction
Value judgement behind choosing the Erreygers correction
has calculator text E = 4 * mu * C / (b - a)
has common error note Reading the Erreygers corrected index as a measure of relative inequality. If illness prevalence doubles in every quintile of the article's example, to 0.80, 0.60, 0.50, 0.30 and 0.20, the standard index stays at minus 0.25 but the corrected index doubles from minus 0.24 to minus 0.48 (computed here for illustration). A larger corrected index can therefore come from a proportional rise in illness with no change in relative inequality, in line with Wagstaff's point that the index measures absolute inequality.
Using the observed range in place of the scale bounds in the Erreygers correction. Taking a and b as the lowest and highest quintile prevalences in the article's example, 0.10 and 0.40, divides by 0.30 in place of 1 and gives minus 0.8 in place of minus 0.24 (computed here for illustration). The bounds belong to the measurement scale and stay fixed across the populations being compared.
has description in the module Multiplies the standard concentration index by 4 times the mean and divides by the range of the measurement scale, b minus a. Because C equals 2 cov_hr / mu, the corrected index also equals 8 times the covariance of health and fractional rank divided by b minus a, a scaled version of the generalised concentration index mu C. Erreygers designed it to satisfy four requirements: transfer, level independence, cardinal invariance and mirror. For a binary variable a is 0 and b is 1.

Euler step of one compartment from its inflows, outflows, births and deaths

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000708
Type formula
assumes Flows held constant within each step and steps short enough to keep compartments non-negative
has calculator text x_next = x_now + (F_in - F_out + b - d) * dt
has common error note Internal flow taken from its source compartment but not added to its destination. Each internal flow appears twice, as an outflow of one compartment and an inflow of another. Taking the article's 29.7 day-1 infections from the susceptibles but leaving them out of the infectious compartment gives 90 infectious people instead of 119.7 and a population of 9,970.3 instead of 10,000 after one day, a loss that a mass-balance check on the compartment totals catches at once.
has description in the module Over a short step of length dt the number in a compartment changes by the flows into it from other compartments, less the flows out of it to other compartments, plus births or immigration into it, less deaths or emigration out of it, each held at its value at the start of the step. This is the article's balance equation for dx_j/dt advanced by one Euler step. Each internal flow leaves one compartment and enters another, so summed over all compartments the internal flows cancel and the population total changes only by births less deaths times dt, and stays fixed in a closed population (derived from the balance equation). Hethcote's endemic SIR model is a case with external flows, with births at rate mu N entering the susceptible class and deaths at rates mu S, mu I and mu R leaving the three classes, so that the population size stays constant. The SIR form of the step is HE-FM-CMPM-004.

EVPI as the probability of a wrong current decision times the mean loss when wrong

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000653
Type formula
assumes Error probability and loss from the same draws and threshold as EVPI
Ties counted as correct decisions in the EVPI error split
has calculator text EVPI = P_err * L_wrong
has common error note Reading the error probability alone as the cost of uncertainty. Between GBP 25,000 and GBP 35,000 per QALY the error probability in the article's example halves, 40% at the lower value and 20% at the higher, while EVPI falls by more than two thirds, 0.06 QALYs at the lower value and about 0.017 at the higher. The probability of a wrong decision says nothing about the size of the loss.
Reporting the mean loss when wrong as EVPI. Dividing the total loss of 0.30 QALYs in the article's example by the 2 draws with a loss gives 0.15 QALYs, the loss when wrong, not the EVPI of 0.06. The loss is averaged over all draws, or the loss when wrong is multiplied by P_err.
has description in the module Splits the mean opportunity loss into how often the option chosen on current evidence is not the best option, P_err, and the mean loss in the draws where it is not, L_wrong. The product equals EVPI because the draws where the chosen option is best add no loss. P_err is one minus the acceptability of the chosen option (HE-FM-CEAC-003), so the formula links the acceptability curve to EVPI and shows why a small chance of a costly error can give a larger EVPI than a large chance of a small one.

Type formula

has calculator text P_pos = p * q + (1 - p) * (1 - q); pF_pos = p * q / P_pos; pF_neg = p * (1 - q) / (1 - P_pos); B_pos = pF_pos * NB_BF + (1 - pF_pos) * NB_BU; B_neg = pF_neg * NB_BF + (1 - pF_neg) * NB_BU; V_S = P_pos * max(NB_A, B_pos) + (1 - P_pos) * max(NB_A, B_neg); V_0 = max(NB_A, p * NB_BF + (1 - p) * NB_BU); EVSI = V_S - V_0
has common error note Keeping the current choice after an unfavourable study result. Valuing S1 as if B were kept after every result gives 0.48 times GBP 1,256.25 plus 0.52 times about GBP 859.62, which is the GBP 1,050 of the current decision, so EVSI comes out as zero for any study. The value of S1 lies entirely in switching to A after a negative result, 0.52 times about GBP 140.38, or GBP 73 per patient.
Reading EVSI as a forecast that the study will favour the new option. A high EVSI does not predict a positive result. In the example the positive result of S1 leaves the decision unchanged and adds nothing, and all GBP 73 per patient comes from the negative result that reverses adoption.
has description in the module Evaluates the EVSI expectation exactly when the proposed study can give only two results and the choice is between standard care A and a new option B whose net benefit depends on whether B works (state F) or not (state U). Bayes theorem turns the prior probability p of state F and the chance q that the result points the right way into the probability of each result and the posterior probability of F after it. The better option is chosen after each result, and the expected value of choosing after the study, V_S, is compared with the value of choosing now, V_0. A result adds value only when it changes the choice, so EVSI is zero when every result leaves the current choice in place and equals EVPI when q is 1.

has common error note Converting each rate separately into a probability. Treating each rate as the only risk gives 1 minus exp(minus 0.30), about 0.2592, for Sick and 0.0488 for death, and a lifetime model with half-cycle counting that overstates life expectancy by 0.300 years, about 6 per cent, in the article's example; this traditional conversion is applicable only to two-state models.
Entering a rate as a probability. Using the Well to Sick rate of 0.30 as an annual probability overstates it against the single-risk 0.2592 and the exact 0.2062; conversions between time units go through rates, and probabilities should never be called rates.
Using the competing-risk split for an annual illness-death matrix. The split gets staying Well right but counts only the 0.0422 direct deaths, missing the 0.0469 who fall Sick and die within the year; the annual model with half-cycle counting then gives 5.486 life-years against the true 5.000.
has description in the module Gives the closed-form matrix exponential for a three-state model in which Well people can fall Sick or die and Sick people can die, with no recovery. Staying Well depends on the total exit rate; being Sick at the end of the interval allows for people who fall Sick and then die within it; the remainder is death by either route. The single-rate conversion is HE-FM-TP-001 and the competing-risk split HE-FM-TP-004; neither includes the two-step path through Sick.

Expected arrivals over a window with two arrival-rate periods

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000316
Type formula
assumes Rate constant within each arrival period, Independent arrivals in separate intervals
has calculator text m = lambda_1 * t_1 + lambda_2 * t_2
has common error note One gap distribution fitted to pooled busy and quiet periods. Because the gaps of a time-varying Poisson process are neither independent nor identically distributed, a single exponential or other distribution fitted to gaps pooled across the peak and the night describes neither period. Rates are estimated for each period from arrivals divided by observed time.
Pooling the same hour across weeks with different rates. Combining counts for a fixed hour and weekday over several weeks whose arrival rates differ makes the pooled counts more variable than a Poisson count, so a test can reject the Poisson model for the wrong reason. Kim and Whitt list this overdispersion, data rounding and subintervals over which the rate varies too much as causes of false rejection.
has description in the module Gives the expected number of arrivals in a non-homogeneous Poisson process whose rate is constant within each of two periods, such as day and night. In general the expected count is the area under the rate curve, the integral of lambda(u) from a to b; for a rate that is constant within periods the integral becomes the sum of rate times length over the periods. The count over the window is then Poisson with mean m, so the Poisson probability formula on this page applies with m in place of lambda times t.

Expected cost and health outcome at a chance node

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000441
Type formula
assumes Chance-node branches mutually exclusive and exhaustive, Branch probabilities conditional on the pathway to the node, Chance-node values right to left
has calculator text C_n = sum_(j=1)^k [p_j * C_j]; E_n = sum_(j=1)^k [p_j * E_j]
has common error note Averaging subgroup ICERs at a chance node. A ratio cannot be rolled back. Computed here for illustration: in the article's example, testing against treating nobody saves £150 and gains 1.8 QALYs among people with the disease, and costs £600 more and loses 0.03 QALYs among people without it. Averaging the two subgroup ratios with weights 0.2 and 0.8 gives about minus £16,017 per QALY, whereas the ICER formed from the expected values, HE-FM-ICER-001, is about £1,339 per QALY. Net monetary benefit (HE-FM-NMB-001) can be averaged at the node because expectation is linear.
Cost counted on a branch and again at the terminal node. Attaching a cost to a branch and also including it in the terminal value of the same pathway counts it twice. Computed here for illustration: if the £300 test cost were attached to the test branch while every terminal value already included it, the test strategy's expected cost would rise from £950 to £1,250 and its ICER against treating nobody from about £1,339 to about £2,232 per QALY.
has description in the module Replaces a chance node with the probability-weighted averages of the costs and of the health outcomes at the ends of its k branches. Costs and health outcomes are averaged separately because they are measured in different units; in a cost-utility analysis the health outcome is usually QALYs. When a branch leads to a further chance node, its C_j and E_j are the expected values already calculated at that node.

Expected cycles before absorption from the fundamental matrix

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000228
Type formula
assumes Absorbing chain, Counting convention, Time-homogeneous transition matrix
has calculator text t_abs = (I - Q)^(-1) * c
has common error note Including the absorbing state in Q. If the Dead row and column are left in Q, I minus Q has a row of zeros and cannot be inverted; Excel MINVERSE returns #NUM!.
Reading t_abs as a corrected or discounted life expectancy. t_abs counts every cycle begun alive in full. Applying a half-cycle correction to a cohort that starts alive and is fully absorbed reduces it by half a cycle, to 9.5 cycles from Well in the example, and discounting reduces it further.
Using a fundamental matrix with age-dependent mortality. A lifetime model with background mortality rising by age has a different matrix in each cycle. Inverting the matrix of one cycle gives the life expectancy of a cohort whose risks never change.
has description in the module Inverts I minus Q to obtain the fundamental matrix N, whose entry in row i and column j is the expected number of cycles spent in transient state j by a person starting in transient state i, counting the starting cycle. Multiplying N by a column of ones sums each row, giving the expected number of cycles before absorption from each starting state. With death as the only absorbing state, this is the undiscounted expected number of cycles alive.

Expected improvement of a candidate run for a loss that is minimised

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000531
Type formula
assumes Normal posterior for the loss at the candidate, Phi_z evaluated at the z of the same candidate
has calculator text z = (L_best - mu_n) / s_n; EI = (L_best - mu_n) * Phi_z + s_n * exp(-z^2 / 2) / 2.5066283
has common error note Applying the maximisation form to a loss. Frazier states expected improvement for maximising an objective; used unchanged for a loss, with the gap taken as posterior mean minus best value, it rewards candidates predicted to fit worse and gives about 3.87 instead of 2.17 at 0.04.
Reading the candidate with the highest expected improvement as the answer. Expected improvement picks the next run, not the optimum: the run it chose at 0.04 had a loss of 3.52, and the search ends only when a stopping rule or the run budget is reached.
Using the best observed loss with a noisy microsimulation. With noisy runs the lowest observed loss is itself uncertain; implementations typically use the lowest posterior mean at the evaluated values in its place.
has description in the module Values a candidate by how far its loss is expected to fall below the best loss so far, given a normal posterior with mean mu_n and standard deviation s_n. The first term rewards candidates predicted to fit well and the second rewards uncertainty. The site's calculator has no normal distribution function, so Phi_z, the standard normal distribution function at z, is entered as an input (NORM.S.DIST(z, TRUE) in Excel, pnorm(z) in R); the normal density is computed as exp(minus z^2 / 2) / 2.5066283, the constant being the square root of 2 times pi.

has common error note Averaging an expected loss over the losing draws only. Dividing the adoption losses in the article's example, 1.4 QALYs in total, by the 4 draws in which adoption loses gives 0.35 QALYs, the loss when wrong of HE-FM-EVPI-003, not the expected loss of 0.28, the slip that HE-ER-EVPI-005 describes for EVPI. An expected loss is averaged over all draws, including those with no loss.
Choosing the option most likely to be cost-effective instead of the smaller expected loss. In the article's example usual care is the better option in four draws out of five, but keeping it has an expected loss of 0.48 QALYs per patient against 0.28 for adopting the new treatment. Choosing by the probability of 0.8 gives up 0.2 QALYs per patient of expected net health benefit, the HEMA point that the probability alone can point to the option with the lower expected net benefit, and the trap HE-ER-ENB-001 shows in money terms.
has description in the module With a new option and a comparator whose net health benefit is set to zero, the loss from adopting the new option in a draw is the incremental net health benefit forgone when it is negative, and the loss from keeping the comparator is the gain forgone when it is positive. EL_new and EL_comp average these losses over all five equally likely draws, the two-option case of the expected loss of each strategy in equation 3 of Alarid-Escudero and colleagues, whose expected loss curves give the loss of every option as HE-FM-CEAC-002 gives the probability of every option. For the option chosen on current evidence the loss is the mean opportunity loss of HE-FM-EVPI-001, so the smaller of the two equals the per-person EVPI of HE-FM-EVPI-001 and HE-FM-EVPI-002, and the larger is the figure that HE-ER-EVPI-001 warns must not be reported as EVPI. Their difference D_EL equals the mean incremental net health benefit, because the positive part of a number less the positive part of its negative is the number itself (derived, the two-option case of equation 4 of Alarid-Escudero and colleagues), so the option with the smaller expected loss is the option with the higher expected net health benefit (HE-FM-ENB-002).

Expected lowest cost, expected price and winner's margin in a second-price reverse auction with uniform costs

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000950
Type formula
assumes Independent uniform private costs on a common range in a reverse auction
Truthful second-price bidding with no binding price ceiling and at least two bidders
Risk-neutral symmetric suppliers for the first-price equality of the expected price
has calculator text E_c1 = c_low + (c_high - c_low) / (N + 1); E_p = c_low + 2 * (c_high - c_low) / (N + 1); M_w = E_p - E_c1
has common error note Expected lowest cost taken as the tender price. The purchaser pays the second-lowest cost under the second-price rule, or a bid above cost under the first-price rule, never the winner's cost. Budgeting at the expected lowest cost of 2.75 in place of the price of 3.50 understates spend by 0.75 per pack, GBP 750,000 on the article's 1,000,000 packs (computed here).
Number of rivals used in place of the number of bidders. N counts every bidding supplier, the winner included. Entering the two rivals of a three-supplier tender gives an expected price of 4.00 in place of 3.50 and a margin of 1.00 in place of 0.75 (computed here).
Selling-auction weight applied to procurement costs. Klemperer's expected revenue of a selling auction, v_low + ((n minus 1) / (n + 1)) (v_high minus v_low), is the expected second-highest value. Copying it to costs gives the expected second-highest cost, not the second-lowest. With three suppliers the two coincide at 3.50, so the article's example does not reveal the slip, but with five suppliers it gives GBP 4.00 in place of GBP 3.00 and it rises, rather than falls, as bidders are added (computed here).
has description in the module A purchaser buys from the lowest of N bidding suppliers whose unit costs are independent draws from a uniform distribution on the interval [c_low, c_high]. Under the second-price rule each supplier bids its cost and the winner is paid the second-lowest bid, so the expected price is the expected second-lowest cost. Klemperer prints the expected k-th highest of n uniform draws as v_low + ((n + 1 minus k) / (n + 1)) (v_high minus v_low); the lowest cost is the N-th highest and the second-lowest the (N minus 1)-th highest, which give E_c1 and E_p. By revenue equivalence the first-price rule has the same expected price (HE-FM-AUCT-002). The winner's expected margin is the gap between the two, (c_high minus c_low) / (N + 1) (derived), and both the price and the margin fall towards c_low and zero as N rises.

Author's copy dated May 1999, posted on the author's Nuffield College page (full text read), which states that it is published in Journal of Economic Surveys 1999;13(3):227-286, doi:10.1111/1467-6419.00083 (journal version not seen; page numbers below are the author's copy's). Appendix D (Examples Using the Uniform Distribution), page 57, states that the expected k-th highest value among n values independently drawn from the uniform distribution on [v_low, v_high] is v_low + ((n + 1 minus k) / (n + 1)) (v_high minus v_low), and, under the heading Bidding with Independent Private Values, Revenue Equivalence, and Marginal Revenues, for risk-neutral bidders with independent private values, that everyone bids her true value in a second-price auction, so the seller's expected revenue is the expected second-highest value, v_low + ((n minus 1) / (n + 1)) (v_high minus v_low). Section 5 (Risk Aversion) states that risk aversion has no effect on a bidder's optimal second-price strategy. The procurement forms E_c1 and E_p are the printed fact with k = N and k = N minus 1; the reverse-auction reading is derived here. https://www.nuff.ox.ac.uk/users/klemperer/survey.pdf
Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences. Improvements to auction theory and inventions of new auction formats. Scientific background on the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel 2020. 12 October 2020 (full text read). Section 2.2 (Private Values) describes Vickrey's model of statistically independent private valuations with risk-neutral, ex-ante symmetric bidders, states that in the second-price auction each bidder's dominant strategy is to bid exactly what the object is worth to her, and that all four standard formats yield the same expected revenue, the revenue-equivalence theorem. Under the heading Extensions and Further Research in the same section it states that Vickrey proved the theorem for a uniform distribution of values in 1961, and section 2.1 (A General Framework) states that first-price auctions are common vehicles for procuring goods and services and for awarding public contracts. https://www.nobelprize.org/uploads/2020/09/advanced-economicsciencesprize2020.pdf

Expected net monetary benefit from probabilistic simulations

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000205
Type formula
assumes Distributions that represent the evidence, Enough simulations for a stable mean, Adoption follows the highest mean, Same parameter draw for every option
has calculator text ENB_j = sum_(n=1)^N [lambda * E_jn - C_jn] / N
has common error note Adopting the option that wins most simulations. The option with the highest probability of being cost-effective can have the lower expected net benefit. In the worked examples, A has the higher net benefit in 60% of simulations, but adopting it forgoes £2,200 per patient on average compared with B.
Reporting a deterministic result as expected net benefit. For a nonlinear model the output at the mean inputs differs from the mean of the outputs. Under a constant hazard equally likely to be 0.1 or 0.3 per year, mean survival at the mean hazard of 0.2 is 5 years, while the mean of the two survival times, 10 years and about 3.33 years, is about 6.67 years.
Running each option on different draws. Sampling parameters independently for each option breaks the pairing across options, removes the correlation between their net benefits and inflates the Monte Carlo error in the difference that drives the decision.
has description in the module Averages option j's net monetary benefit over N probabilistic simulations, each valuing the simulated health effect at threshold lambda and subtracting the simulated cost. Because net benefit is linear in cost and effect, the result equals lambda times the mean effect minus the mean cost from the same simulations. The option-level formula on the net monetary benefit page is the deterministic counterpart.

Expected number of unpublished studies implied by Copas selection parameters for two standard error groups

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000902
Type formula
assumes Selection parameters fixed when counting implied unpublished studies
Studies in each Copas group share one standard error
Unpublished studies per published study in the Copas count
has calculator text u_1 = gamma_0 + gamma_1 / s_1; u_2 = gamma_0 + gamma_1 / s_2; P_1 = Phi_1; P_2 = Phi_2; M = n_1 * (1 - P_1) / P_1 + n_2 * (1 - P_2) / P_2
has common error note Average publication probability used for the Copas unpublished count. Because (1 minus P) / P is convex in P, giving all twelve trials of the moderate scenario their average probability of 0.45 returns 14.67 unpublished trials instead of 18.68, about a fifth too few (computed here for illustration). The count has to be built group by group or study by study.
One grid point's implied count taken as the number of missing studies. M follows from the assumed selection, not from the data. In the article's illustration the moderate and severe scenarios imply about 19 and about 57 unpublished trials, yet with the correlation re-estimated both reproduce the group means, so the published trials cannot choose between them. The count is a figure to set against trial registries, which Huang and colleagues use to inform the model.
Total studies run reported as the Copas unpublished count. n / P counts the published studies as well as the unpublished ones. In the moderate scenario about 30.68 trials would have been run, of which 18.68 are unpublished; reporting 30.68 adds the twelve published trials to the count.
has description in the module Copas and Shi translate a pair of selection parameters into the expected number of unpublished studies, M, the sum over the published studies of (1 minus P_i) / P_i, with P_i the publication probability of HE-FM-COPAS-001 at study i's standard error. The formula is written for two groups of published studies that share a standard error within each group, n_1 at s_1 and n_2 at s_2, as in the article's example of two large and ten small trials; each further standard error adds a term of the same form, which the R and Python code of HE-CF-COPAS-001 handles. Each published study with probability P stands in expectation for (1 minus P) / P unpublished studies of the same precision, so groups with a low publication probability dominate M; in the article's moderate scenario 18.57 of the 18.68 come from the ten small trials. The step that turns P into M is the same algebra as the bed turnover interval of HE-FM-BTO-004 in another setting; the Copas content is the chain from gamma_0, gamma_1 and the standard errors.

Expected outcome per person from a cohort simulation trace with counting weights and discounting

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000443
Type formula
assumes Mutually exclusive, exhaustive and homogeneous cohort states, Counting rule stated with the cycle length, Rewards per cycle include the cycle length
has calculator text Y = sum_(t=0)^T [w_t * delta_t * m_t * r]
has common error note Counting rule left unstated in a cohort simulation. End-of-cycle counting gives 2.3616 expected years in Healthy in the article's example, about 10.7% below the continuous-time area, and start-of-cycle counting gives 2.952, about 11.6% above it. The errors need not cancel in incremental results, so the rule has to be stated.
Half-cycle weight dropped at the end of a truncated horizon. Applying the half weight only at t = 0 when the horizon stops at four cycles gives 2.8616 years in Healthy instead of 2.6568, computed here for illustration. Over a horizon that is not lifetime, the final cycle also takes a half weight.
Simpson weights with an odd number of cycles. Simpson's 1/3 rule needs an even T. With three cycles the pattern of one third, four thirds, two thirds and one third sums to two and two thirds instead of 3, computed here for illustration, so the count is too low.
has description in the module Sums the reward earned by the cohort in each recorded cycle, m_t r, after multiplying it by a within-cycle counting weight w_t and a discount factor delta_t. Here m_t is the row of the cohort trace at cycle t and r the column of rewards per cycle in each state, so m_t r is the reward per person at cycle t; where only one state carries a reward, m_t r is that state's proportion times its reward, the form used in the worked examples. The counting weights for the common rules are: end of cycle 0 at t = 0 and 1 afterwards; start of cycle 1 up to T minus 1 and 0 at T; half-cycle correction (trapezoidal rule) one half at t = 0 and t = T and 1 in between; Simpson's 1/3 rule, for T even, one third at t = 0 and t = T, four thirds at odd t and two thirds at even t. The half-cycle and Simpson weights appear here only as counting options; the Half-Cycle Correction page covers the correction itself.

Expected overstatement of a population standardised effect by Cohen's d in small samples

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000743
Type formula
assumes Normal outcomes and a known population effect for the expected bias of d
Degrees of freedom set by the standard deviation in the expected bias of d
has calculator text J = 1 - 3 / (4 * m - 1); E_d = delta / J; Bias_d = E_d - delta
has common error note Bias of Cohen's d taken as delta times one minus J. The reduction from d to g is d times one minus J, but the expected bias of d is delta times (1/J minus 1), which is larger. At 4 degrees of freedom the first reading gives 20% instead of 25%, and at 20 degrees of freedom about 3.8% instead of about 3.9%, computed here for illustration.
Expecting pooling of many small studies to remove the bias of Cohen's d. Hedges shows that the average of uncorrected estimates from many small studies is not a consistent estimator of delta, because each estimate carries the same bias while the variance of the average falls, so the average estimates the wrong quantity more precisely. Ten studies with 4 degrees of freedom each and a delta of 0.5 have an expected average d of about 0.627 whatever their number, computed here for illustration with the exact factor.
has description in the module Gives the mean of the uncorrected estimate d over repeated samples when the population standardised difference is delta, using Hedges' result that this mean is delta divided by the exact factor, here replaced by the approximate J of HE-FM-HEDG-001. Bias_d is the amount by which d overstates delta on average. The relative overstatement Bias_d over delta depends only on m, and with the approximate J it is about 25% at 4 degrees of freedom, about 4% at 20 and under 0.4% at 198 (computed here). It describes the estimator before any correction and does not shrink when more small studies are averaged.

Expected present value of an outcomes-based annuity payment schedule

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000287
Type formula
assumes Outcomes-based payments stop once response is lost, Outcomes-based instalment fixed at the start
has calculator text EPV = sum_(t=0)^T [S_t * A / (1+r)^t]
has common error note Payment probabilities that differ from those in the health model. Weighting payments by response probabilities from a different source from those that drive the QALYs breaks the link between paying and benefiting. The model can then credit benefit for which nothing is paid, or charge for benefit that it does not count.
Year-on-year continuation probabilities entered as payment probabilities. S_t is the probability from treatment that instalment t is payable. If a source reports the share of responders at one payment date who still respond at the next, those conditional values have to be multiplied together first. Entering conditional values of 0.90, 0.85, 0.80 and 0.75 directly gives about £888,304 in the worked example, against about £777,765 with the cumulative values 0.90, 0.765, 0.612 and 0.459.
has description in the module Values a schedule in which each later instalment is due only if the patient still meets a pre-agreed response criterion on that date. The sum runs over the years t from 0, the payment at treatment, to T, the year of the last instalment, which is the number of instalments minus 1. Each instalment A is weighted by the probability S_t that it falls due and discounted at the evaluation rate r. The probabilities should be the same ones that drive the modelled health benefit, so that a patient who stops responding stops generating both QALYs and payments.

Expected profit per member from an enrolled risk mix

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000439
Type formula
assumes Expected cost of each risk group unchanged by selection, Costs of attracting the risk mix not deducted, Same payment for every member of the payment cell
has calculator text pi_bar = R - sum_(k=1)^K [m_k * EC_k]; Pi = N * pi_bar
has common error note Crediting the risk-mix profit to efficiency. In the article's example the plan's £500 per member comes entirely from enrolling fewer chronically ill members; it treats each type of member at the same expected cost as any other plan. Comparing average costs across plans without adjusting for the mix credits the plan with savings it did not make.
Treating the risk-mix profit as the net gain from selection. The £500,000 is an upper bound. Attracting a healthier mix has costs, and Brown and colleagues note that money spent on screening, such as targeted advertising, may not benefit members.
has description in the module The payment per member minus the average expected cost of the members a plan actually enrols, where the payment is the same for every member of the payment cell and the plan's mix of risk groups may differ from the cell's population. The profit comes entirely from the mix, since the expected cost of each type of member is unchanged. Multiplying by the number of members gives the plan's total expected profit, which is an upper bound on the gain from selection because attracting the mix has costs of its own.

Expected profit per member under a fixed or risk-adjusted payment

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000438
Type formula
assumes Payment fixed in advance of the member's actual costs, Plan information on expected cost beyond the payment formula
has calculator text pi_i = R_i - EC_i
has common error note Reading a concentration of healthy members as proof of cream skimming. A positive average expected profit shows that a plan has healthier members than its payment assumes, not that the plan selected them, since healthier people may choose some plans for their own reasons. Evidence of selection by the plan needs a design that separates insurer behaviour from consumer choice, such as an audit study.
Using realised instead of expected costs in the cream-skimming profit. A member who happens to have a costly year is not thereby unprofitable in expectation. Selection acts on predictable differences, so the profit is computed with expected costs given what the plan can observe, not with costs realised after the event.
has description in the module The payment received for a member, whether a community-rated premium, a capitation payment or a risk-adjusted payment, minus the member's expected cost of care, written pi_i = R_i minus E[C_i] in the article. A plan has an incentive to attract members with a positive expected profit and deter those with a negative one whenever it can tell them apart and influence who joins. Under community rating with no risk equalisation the payment is the premium, and the expected profit equals the cross-subsidy of HE-FM-CRAT-002.

Expected QALY loss from adverse events per patient

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000274
Type formula
assumes Health state utilities free of adverse event effects, Short-lived adverse events as one-off decrements
has calculator text Q_AE = sum_(k=1)^K [p_k * u_k * tau_k]
has common error note Adding adverse event disutilities to on-treatment utilities. When the health state utilities were measured in patients on treatment, they may already include the effect of adverse events, and subtracting a separate disutility per event can count the same loss twice.
Entering the adverse event duration in days. Multiplying the decrement of 0.10 by 14 days rather than by 14/365 of a year gives a loss of 1.4 QALYs per episode instead of about 0.00384, more than a year of full health for a two-week event.
has description in the module Multiplies the probability of each adverse event type by the utility decrement during an episode and by the episode's duration in years, and adds the products over the K event types. The result is subtracted from the QALY total of the arm as a one-off decrement.

Expected response at a dose under the sigmoid Emax model

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000565
Type formula
assumes Monotonic sigmoid curve fitted over the doses that matter, Population-average response on the sigmoid Emax curve
has calculator text E_D = E_0 + E_max * D^h / (ED_50^h + D^h)
has common error note Costing a dose that lies on the plateau. The ICH E4 guideline records that drugs have often been marketed first at doses later recognised as excessive, well onto the plateau of the dose-response curve; a plateau dose adds cost and harm without adding benefit, as the step from 150 mg to 200 mg (41,786 pounds per extra responder) shows in the article.
Estimating ED50 from a narrow dose range. Mawdsley and colleagues found in their triptan example that, with a limited dose range, the ED50 parameter of an Emax model proved difficult to estimate reliably; they borrowed strength by treating Emax or ED50 as exchangeable across agents in a class.
Judging a dose by its average cost per extra responder. In the article the average ratio rises only from 18,000 to 22,500 pounds between 100 mg and 200 mg while the incremental ratio from 150 mg to 200 mg is 41,786 pounds; the choice of dose rests on the incremental ratio between adjacent doses.
has description in the module The sigmoid Emax model, the standard four-parameter dose-response curve, rises from the placebo response E_0 towards E_0 plus E_max, reaching half the maximum added effect at the dose ED_50; the Hill coefficient h sets how steeply it rises around ED_50, and with h = 1 it reduces to the hyperbolic Emax model. Because acquisition cost usually rises in proportion to dose while the effect flattens, each extra milligram buys less response than the one before once the dose is past the steep part of the curve.
has formalisation level catalogue record
has implementation Sigmoid Emax response from named cells
has mathematical variable Expected response at a dose of a sigmoid Emax curve, Dose given in a sigmoid Emax curve, Dose giving half the maximum added effect, Hill coefficient of a sigmoid Emax curve, Maximum added effect of a sigmoid Emax curve, Placebo response of a sigmoid Emax curve
has module record identifier HE-FM-DOSE-001

Reference manual, help page drmodels (full text read). drmodels: the sigmoid Emax model is f(d) = E_0 + E_max d^h / (ED_50^h + d^h), an extension of the hyperbolic Emax model by a parameter h that determines the steepness of the curve at the ED50; e0 is the placebo effect, ed50 the dose giving half of the asymptotic maximum effect and h the Hill parameter. https://cran.r-project.org/package=DoseFinding

CPT: Pharmacometrics and Systems Pharmacology. 2016;5(8):393-401. doi:10.1002/psp4.12091 (full text read). Section on model-based meta-analysis: the Emax model is widely used to model drug effect as a function of dose; Emax corresponds, physiologically, to the drug saturating the body's receptors and ED50 is the dose at which half the maximum effect is reached. Expected response for a tumour-type mix from basket estimates

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000360
Type formula
assumes Basket estimates transfer to the same tumour types in practice, Tumour-type shares describe the treated population
has calculator text R = sum_(j=1)^J [pi_j * p_est_j]
has common error note Dropping unrepresented tumour types from the basket mix. Rescaling the shares of the represented baskets to sum to 1 assumes that tumour types absent from the trial respond like the weighted average of those present. In TA630 the committee noted that it would need to accept that unrepresented solid tumours, for which there were no data, would respond to larotrectinib. Murphy and colleagues instead used the hierarchical model's predictive distribution, a mean response of 56.9% with a 95% credible interval of 0.2% to 99.9% for an unrepresented histology.
Using the pooled basket trial response as the population estimate. The pooled trial figure implies 50 responders per 100 patients treated, against 30 with the separate basket estimates weighted to the illustrative NHS mix. A response-based economic model fed the pooled figure overstates benefit when the trial over-represents tumour types that respond well.
has description in the module Weights each basket's response estimate by the share of that tumour type in the population expected to be treated, rather than by its share of trial enrolment. With enrolment shares and the observed proportions the result equals the pooled trial response, which reflects whoever was easiest to recruit. The same weighting applies to separate or partially pooled basket estimates.

Expected survival and event probability under a gamma-distributed constant hazard

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000600
Type formula
assumes Hazard constant over the horizon in every draw, Gamma distribution of the hazard in shape and scale form, Uncertain hazard shared by the whole cohort
has calculator text S_bar = (1 + s * t)^(-k); p_bar = 1 - S_bar
has common error note Averaging hazard draws before converting them to probabilities. Averaging sampled hazards and converting the average reproduces the deterministic 0.3935. The conversion has to be applied to each draw before averaging, or the closed form used.
Converting the mean hazard to a probability and calling it the expected probability. Applying 1 minus exp(minus h t) at the mean hazard gives 0.3935 in place of 0.36, about 393 rather than 360 fractures per 1,000 people and about £402 more cost per person, an overstatement of about 9 per cent of the expected value.
Entering the gamma rate where the scale is expected. With a rate of 20 entered as the scale, the formula returns an expected five-year probability of about 0.9999 instead of 0.36. The parameterisation of each software function has to be checked before the hazard distribution is set up.
has description in the module When a constant hazard h is uncertain and follows a gamma distribution with shape k and scale s, so that its mean is k times s and its variance k times s squared, the expected value of exp(minus h t) is the gamma Laplace transform evaluated at t, and the expected event probability over the horizon t is one minus that value. It replaces the deterministic 1 minus exp(minus h t) at the mean hazard (HE-FM-TP-001), which overstates the expected probability because the probability is concave in h. The same identity gives population survival under a gamma frailty with a constant baseline hazard.

Expected total cost of a two-arm study with the opportunity loss to participants

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000659
Type formula
assumes Participants on the option expected to be better lose nothing, Stated perspective for the cost of a study
has calculator text C_n = C_F + c_V * n + s_inf * n * abs(INB)
has common error note Opportunity loss to participants left out of the study cost. Dropping the GBP 100,000 participant loss from the article's 1,000-patient trial raises its ENBS to GBP 600,000 instead of GBP 500,000, an overstatement of 20%. Rothery and colleagues include the opportunity cost to people while the research is under way in the cost of research.
Participant loss charged to every participant. Charging the GBP 200 loss to all 1,000 participants of the article's largest trial doubles the loss to GBP 200,000 and cuts its ENBS to GBP 400,000 instead of GBP 500,000 (computed here for illustration). Only those on the option expected to be inferior forgo benefit.
has description in the module Adds the three cost components that Fenwick and colleagues list, a fixed cost, a variable cost for each participant and the opportunity cost for participants who receive the option expected to be inferior while the study runs. Each such participant forgoes the absolute value of the expected incremental net benefit per person on current information, so with a share s_inf of the n participants on that arm the loss term is s_inf times n times abs(INB). The result is the C_n entered in HE-FM-ENBS-001.

Expected undiscounted time in the Well and Sick states with constant rates

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000520
Type formula
assumes Constant rates over a lifetime horizon without discounting, Sick entered only from Well and at most once
has calculator text L_W = 1 / (q_WS + q_WD); L_S = q_WS / (q_WS + q_WD) / q_SD; LE = L_W + L_S
has common error note Applying mean sojourn times when risk depends on time in state. 1 / rate is the mean of an exponential stay, which requires a constant rate; where risk changes with time already spent in a state, tunnel states, a semi-Markov model or individual simulation are needed.
Taking 1 / q_WS as the expected time before falling Sick. 1 / 0.30 gives 3.33 years, but people also leave Well by dying, so the mean stay in Well is 1 / 0.35, about 2.86 years, and only 86 per cent of them ever fall Sick.
has description in the module Gives life expectancy in a progressive illness-death model directly from the rates. A stay in a state with constant total exit rate lasts 1 over that rate on average (the mean sojourn time); the share of people leaving Well who go to Sick is q_WS over the total Well exit rate, and each spends on average 1 / q_SD in Sick. The sum is life expectancy, the value a cycle model of the same process should reproduce.

Expected value of a product of two correlated quantities

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000598
Type formula
assumes Means and covariance taken from one joint distribution, Finite variances for the product identity
has calculator text E_NU = E_N * E_U + Cov_NU
has common error note Combining admission counts and unit costs from separate sources as if independent. When counts and unit costs come from different studies, the covariance cannot be estimated and is set to zero without being stated. The resulting expected cost rests on an independence assumption that patient-level data recording both quantities could check.
Multiplying mean admissions by mean cost per admission. Multiplying the two means drops the covariance: £4,500 in place of £4,800 per patient in the article's example, an understatement of 6.25 per cent of the expected cost that carries into every budget built on it.
has description in the module Gives the expected value of a product, such as the number of admissions times the cost per admission, from the two means and their covariance. The identity is exact for any joint distribution with finite variances. The product of the means equals the expected product only when the covariance is zero, for example when the two quantities are independent; a positive covariance raises the expected product above the product of the means and a negative one lowers it.

Expected wait before service in a single-server queue with Poisson arrivals

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000319
Type formula
assumes Poisson arrivals, exponential service and one server, Steady state with arrivals below service capacity
has calculator text rho = lambda / mu; W_q = rho / (mu - lambda)
has common error note Applying the single-server wait when arrivals exceed capacity. With 3 arrivals an hour and a service rate of 2.5, the formula gives minus 2.4 hours. The queue has no steady state and grows through the session, so the result has to come from a time-dependent model or simulation.
Reporting the wait before service as the time in the system. W_q excludes the service itself. In the 80% example the expected wait is 1.6 hours, while the expected time from arrival to leaving is 2 hours, the wait plus the mean service time of 0.4 hours.
has description in the module Gives the expected time a patient waits before service starts in a single-server queue with Poisson arrivals at rate lambda and exponential service at rate mu, in steady state with lambda below mu. The utilisation rho is computed first and then used in the wait. As rho approaches 1 the expected wait grows without limit, so a small rise in arrivals near full utilisation produces a large rise in waiting.

The 44 months before entry for patients D, E and F could not end in a recorded death; including them lowers the rate from about 0.47 to 0.33 per person-year and lengthens the fitted mean by 11 months, and cost or event rates per person-year are diluted the same way.
Fitting a parametric curve without entry times. Stata's streg manual states that each subject contributes its density or survival conditional on the entry time; a fit that leaves out the entry term treats late entrants as observed from the origin and carries the bias into the extrapolated tail.

It is maximised by the number of events over the person-time from entry to exit, and the fitted mean time from the origin is 1 / lambda.

Exponential event time by inverse transform

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000225
Type formula
assumes Constant hazard for the event, Next-event advance of the clock, Independent or deliberately shared random numbers
has calculator text T_j = -log(U) / lambda_j
has common error note Assigning every patient the mean time. Using 1 divided by the rate as every patient's event time removes between-patient variation. When costs or QALYs depend non-linearly on event time, for example through discounting or a time horizon, the average result is then biased.
Leaving obsolete events on the calendar. If events scheduled before death are not cancelled, the model can accrue follow-up costs or progression after the absorbing event.
Using a per-cycle probability as the hazard. lambda_j is a rate. Entering a probability per cycle, or a rate in a different time unit, gives sampled times on the wrong scale. A rate per year yields times in years.

Exponential residual time and median sojourn in a Markov state with a constant exit rate

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000672
Type formula
assumes Exit rate and times in one unit for the exponential Markov sojourn
Total exit rate constant over time since entry to the Markov state
has calculator text S_res = exp(-lambda * (tau + s)) / exp(-lambda * tau); t_med = log(2) / lambda
has common error note Mean sojourn taken from one exit rate when a Markov state has competing exits. With an illustrative death rate of 0.05 and progression rate of 0.10 a year, the mean stay is 1 divided by 0.15, about 6.67 years, not the 20 years implied by the death rate alone, because every exit ends the stay (HE-FM-TP-004 and HE-FM-CONT-002).
Median exponential sojourn taken as half the mean. At 0.05 a year half the mean is 10 years, but the median is log 2 divided by 0.05, about 13.86 years, so the shortcut understates it by about 28% (computed here for illustration). The median is about 0.693 of the mean at any constant rate.
has description in the module The continuous-time counterpart of HE-FM-MKA-002. With a constant total exit rate lambda the time spent in the state is exponential, with survival exp(minus lambda t) and mean 1 divided by lambda as in HE-FM-BTH-003 and HE-FM-CONT-002, which are not restated. S_res, the conditional survival ratio of HE-FM-LTR-001 applied to exponential survival, is the probability of staying a further time s after a time tau already spent, which equals exp(minus lambda s) whatever tau is, and t_med is the time by which half of all stays have ended. Grinstead and Snell state that the exponential is the only continuous density with the memoryless property, so in continuous time a constant exit rate and a stay that ignores time already spent go together. In a cycle model the stay probability is exp(minus lambda Delta), 1 minus the exit probability of HE-FM-TP-001, and t_med divided by Delta equals d_star of HE-FM-MKA-001.

Extended dominance condition for three ordered options

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000200
Type formula
assumes Dominated options removed first, Adjacent options, recalculated after each removal, Equal sequential ratios
has calculator text D_M = (C_M - C_L) / (E_M - E_L) - (C_H - C_M) / (E_H - E_M)
has common error note Not recalculating after a removal. Keeping ICERs computed before a removal leaves comparisons with an option that is no longer adjacent. In the example, the ICER for D is recalculated against B, £18,000 per QALY, rather than kept at about £13,333 against C.
Relying on a common baseline. An option can have an acceptable ICER against a common baseline and still be extendedly dominated, because the baseline comparison ignores the next option on the frontier.
Testing before dominated options are removed. Sequential ICERs calculated while a dominated option remains can be negative or misleading, so the extended dominance check gives unreliable results.
has description in the module Subtracts the sequential ICER of the next more effective option from the sequential ICER of the middle of three consecutive options, ordered by expected effect. The middle option is extendedly dominated when the difference is greater than zero.

assumes Constant demand slope, Price reduction as the only change
has calculator text Delta_q = D * (p - c * p); WL = 0.5 * D * (p - c * p)^2
has common error note Assuming the loss is proportional to the price reduction. Doubling the price reduction doubles both the extra use and the height of the triangle, so the loss rises fourfold. A linear extrapolation from one coinsurance rate understates the loss at lower rates.
has description in the module When demand for care is linear with slope D, a fall in the price the patient faces from p to c × p raises use by D × (p minus c × p). Substituting into the triangle gives a welfare loss of one half of D × (p minus c × p) squared. The loss therefore rises with the square of the price reduction: halving the coinsurance rate from 0.5 to 0.25 more than doubles it.

Fairness gap measure of health inequity

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000432
Type formula
assumes Additive attribution of the health gap to causes for the fairness gap
Same gap and decomposition for the fairness gap and direct unfairness
has calculator text I_FG = Delta - sum_(j=1)^J [(1 - u_j) * Delta_j]
has common error note Subtracting the illegitimate parts in the fairness gap. The hypothetical distribution removes the illegitimate causes, so its gap holds the legitimate parts, and the fairness gap subtracts those. Subtracting the illegitimate parts instead returns the remainder: with smoking judged unfair, 6.4 minus 4.0 gives 2.4 points, which is not the inequity.
Treating the fairness gap and direct unfairness as interchangeable. In the article's example the two measures differ by the 2.4-point remainder in every scenario: 6.4 against 4.0 points with smoking judged unfair, and 4.4 against 2.0 points with smoking judged a free choice. Fleurbaey and Schokkaert note that the two approaches generally give different results.
has description in the module Fleurbaey and Schokkaert define the fairness gap as the difference between the actual distribution and a hypothetical one in which every illegitimate source of difference is set to a common reference value, written h_i^FG = h_i minus f(c_bar, l_i) in the article's simplified notation. Applied to a gap between two groups that has been attributed additively to causes, removing the illegitimate causes leaves only the legitimate parts in the hypothetical gap, so the inequity is the whole gap minus those legitimate parts. The unexplained remainder stays in the result, which treats it as unfair. This group-gap formula is this page's simplification: Fleurbaey and Schokkaert define the fairness gap distribution across individuals and then apply an inequality index to it.

Feldstein and Gruber reduction in the deadweight loss of insurance when coinsurance rises

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000478
Type formula
assumes Care supplied at constant cost with uninsured price normalised to 1
Out-of-pocket spending below any cap
Risk-bearing change evaluated separately
has calculator text dDWL = (E_0 - E_1) * (1 - P_1) + 0.5 * (P_1 - P_0) * (E_0 - E_1)
has common error note Reading the fall in spending as the welfare gain. In the article's example spending falls by 50,000 pounds but the gain is 35,000. At an elasticity of 0.5, Feldstein and Gruber found that a deductible of 15 per cent of income cut spending more than 50 per cent coinsurance up to the same 15 per cent limit (USD 1,629 against USD 1,426 per insurance unit) but reduced deadweight loss less (USD 735 against USD 1,045).
Treating the triangle gain as the whole effect of more cost sharing. Higher coinsurance also exposes people to more financial risk. A case for more cost sharing needs that change alongside the reduction in deadweight loss.
has description in the module Measures the fall in the deadweight loss of insurance-induced care when the coinsurance rate rises from P_0 to P_1. Care is measured in units whose price without insurance is 1, so quantities are spending at full cost. The reduction is a rectangle, the forgone care times the gap between its cost and the new patient price, plus a triangle above it. With a constant elasticity eta, E_1 = E_0 * (P_0 / P_1)^eta, and the triangle term then treats demand as straight between E_1 and E_0, an approximation.

Cambridge, MA: MIT Press; 1995. p. 103-130. Section 4.1 and Figure 1: raising the coinsurance rate from P0 to P1 reduces the deadweight loss by the area BCDE, equal to (E0 minus E1) times (1 minus P1) plus 0.5 times (P1 minus P0) times (E0 minus E1), with E1 = E0 (P0/P1) raised to the absolute price elasticity. Section 4.3 and Table 5: zero elasticity gives no gain; 50 per cent coinsurance with an out-of-pocket limit of 10 per cent of income reduces deadweight loss by USD 534 per insurance unit at an elasticity of 0.33 and USD 902 at 0.5; with a 15 per cent limit the reduction at 0.5 is USD 1,045, against USD 735 for a deductible of 15 per cent of income, which cuts spending more (USD 1,629 against USD 1,426). https://www.nber.org/system/files/chapters/c10892/c10892.pdf

has calculator text a = Delta_E^2 - z^2 * SE_E^2; b = -2 * (Delta_C * Delta_E - z^2 * Cov_CE); c = Delta_C^2 - z^2 * SE_C^2; R_L = (-b - sqrt(b^2 - 4 * a * c)) / (2 * a); R_U = (-b + sqrt(b^2 - 4 * a * c)) / (2 * a)
has common error note Reading the two roots as an interval when a is negative. With a QALY standard error of 0.06, a is about -0.00383 and the roots are about £6,177 and -£110,622 per QALY. The roots bound the interval when a is positive.
