Fixed bed cost per discharge from the bed turnover rate

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000388
Type formula
assumes Bed cost shared equally across discharges, Bed cost unchanged as turnover changes
has calculator text c_D = C_bed / T
has common error note Reporting a lower bed cost per discharge as a cash saving. In route A the bed cost per discharge falls by about £290, which across the original 24,820 discharges looks like £7.2 million saved. No cash is saved: the £48 million bed cost is unchanged and the gain is the health benefit of 4,380 extra patients, net of the variable cost of treating them. Only route B, closing 60 beds, avoids £7.2 million a year.
Valuing bed-days freed by higher turnover at accounting cost. Page, Barnett and Graves argue that the economic cost of a bed day, not its accounting cost, is the better value for resource decisions. Bed-days freed by higher turnover are valued at their opportunity cost, the benefit to the extra patients admitted, unless beds close.
has description in the module Spreads the annual cost of a staffed bed that does not vary with patient numbers over the patients the bed served in the year, as in top-down costing. A higher turnover rate lowers this average only because the same cost is shared among more patients; whether cash is saved depends on what happens to the freed capacity.

Fixed-interval medication possession ratio

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000458
Type formula
assumes Dispensed supply taken as directed, Window long enough after the first dispensing
has calculator text MPR_fixed = sum_(i=1)^n [S_i] / D
has common error note Reading an MPR above 0.8 as continuous supply. The article's patient has an MPR of about 1.167, or 1.000 capped, while 30 of the 180 days (16.7%) had no medicine and the PDC is about 0.833. Every version of the MPR passes an 80% threshold, so a dichotomised MPR hides the gap.
Summing supply across drugs in a class for the MPR. When the MPR is calculated for a class, a switch between drugs with an overlap, or two drugs taken together, adds both supplies to the numerator. Two drugs from the same class each dispensed for 90 days on day 1 of a 90-day window give an MPR of 2 for 90 days of treatment (computed here for illustration).
has description in the module Divides the total days' supply of the fills dispensed in the observation period by the number of days from the first dispensing to the end of the period, the most common variant in the review by Raebel and colleagues. Time after the last refill counts in the denominator, so stopping treatment lowers the ratio. Supply that runs past the end of the period still counts unless the analyst truncates it, so the ratio can exceed 1.

Force of infection and new infection flow under frequency-dependent transmission

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000709
Type formula
assumes Homogeneous mixing and contacts that do not grow with population size
Force of infection read as a rate and converted to a probability only through the hazard
has calculator text lambda = beta * I / N; F_SI = lambda * S
has common error note Frequency-dependent transmission rate entered into the mass action form. Entering the article's beta of 0.3 per day into beta S I without dividing by N gives 297,000 new infections a day in a population of 10,000 instead of 29.7. Hethcote shows that the mass action coefficient eta equals beta/N, here 0.00003 per person per day, so a coefficient taken from one form is rescaled before use in the other.
Susceptible count used in place of the whole population in the force of infection. Dividing by S instead of N gives 0.3 times 100/9,900, about 0.00303, and 30.0 infections on the article's day 1, 1% too many, and the error grows as susceptibles are used up. With 5,000 susceptibles left and 100 infectious the wrong force is 0.006, twice the correct 0.003 (computed here for illustration).
has description in the module The force of infection is the rate at which each susceptible person is infected. Under frequency-dependent, or standard, transmission it is the transmission rate beta times the infectious proportion I/N, and new infections per unit time are lambda times S, the flow from the susceptible to the infectious compartment. The WHO guide writes the incidence as lambda X = p c (Y/N) X, so beta here corresponds to p times c, the probability of transmission per contact times the contact rate. Because lambda rises and falls with I, a model that recalculates it at every step is dynamic and one that holds it fixed, or takes it from a run without the programme, is static (HE-FM-CMPM-005). Hethcote contrasts this standard incidence with the mass action form eta I S, for which beta equals eta N, the form van den Driessche writes as beta S I with force of infection beta I. The per-person probability of infection within a step under a constant lambda follows HE-FM-TP-001.

Section 2.1, Formulating Epidemiology Models (pages 602 and 603), which defines the standard incidence (beta I/N) S as the number of new cases per unit time, with beta the average number of adequate contacts of a person per unit time, compares it with the simple mass action law eta I S, for which beta = eta N, and concludes that the standard incidence is more realistic for human diseases. https://doi.org/10.1137/S0036144500371907
World Health Organization. WHO guide for standardization of economic evaluations of immunization programmes, 2nd edition (WHO/IVB/19.10). Geneva, WHO, 2019. Section 6.1.2, Incidence and the force of infection, which defines the force of infection lambda as the probability per unit of time that a susceptible person becomes infected, the per-susceptible rate of infection, and gives the incidence of new cases as lambda X = p c (Y/N) X, with X the number of susceptible people, Y the number of infectious people, N the total population, p the probability of transmission given contact and c the number of contacts. https://iris.who.int/handle/10665/329389

Section 2.1, SIR epidemic model, which models transmission by mass action with the term beta S I, beta being the transmission rate constant and beta I the force of infection, in the equations dS/dt = minus beta S I, dI/dt = beta S I minus gamma I and dR/dt = f gamma I. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.idm.2017.06.002

Force of infection on one group from infectious people in two mixing groups

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000710
Type formula
assumes Random mixing within each group and a transmission matrix fixed over the period
has calculator text lambda_1 = beta_11 * I_1 / N_1 + beta_12 * I_2 / N_2
has common error note Group infectious counts divided by the whole population instead of the group size. Dividing I_b by N rather than N_b understates the force on the group whose own prevalence is high. In the illustrative children and adults example it gives 0.0032 instead of 0.0115 per day, about 72% too low, and in the random-mixing example 0.00168 instead of 0.003 (computed here for illustration).
has description in the module When the population is split into groups, such as age or risk groups, each compartment is stratified by group and the force of infection on susceptible people in group a sums the transmission from the infectious people of every group, each weighted by a transmission rate beta_ab and the infectious proportion I_b/N_b of group b. Written out for two groups the formula gives lambda_1, and lambda_2 follows by exchanging the indices 1 and 2. Hethcote's SEIR model with age groups writes the force of infection on group i as a contact-weighted sum over the infectious fractions of all groups, with separable contact rates, which is the case beta_ab = b_a b~_b N_b/N of the matrix form here (derived); a full matrix of beta_ab, the article's notation, allows any pattern of mixing. When beta_1b equals beta times N_b/N for both groups, mixing is random and lambda_1 reduces to beta I/N of HE-FM-CMPM-002 (derived). The reproduction number of a stratified model is the dominant eigenvalue of its next-generation matrix, HE-FM-BRN-005 and HE-CF-BRN-001.

Foreign price or cost converted to the home currency at a market exchange rate

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000702
Type formula
assumes Exchange rate quoted as home currency per unit of foreign currency
Rate period stated and applied to every price from one country
definition source the Source rows of the Functions and Formulae module record HE-FM-BOC-001
formalises currency conversion
has calculator text c_i = p_i * e_i
has common error note Exchange rate applied in the wrong direction. Multiplying by a rate published as local currency units per US dollar, in place of dividing by it, turns 120 at 0.800 into 96 US dollars instead of 150, a 36% understatement (computed here for illustration). For a currency quoted at thousands of units per US dollar the result is wrong by the square of the rate.
Exchange rate taken from a different period than the price. Turner and colleagues report that the market rate for Myanmar moved from 5.44 kyat per US dollar in 2011 to 640.65 in 2012. Converting 1,000 kyat at the 2011 rate gives about US$183.82 and at the 2012 rate about US$1.56, a factor of about 118 (computed here for illustration), so the rate period is matched to the price and reported.

Funded share of a league-table programme from the budget left after the programmes ranked above it

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000717
Type formula
assumes Independent programmes each measured against the comparator it would replace
Positive increments in ascending ICER order, with ties and cost-saving programmes
Divisible programmes at a constant cost per unit of health with no interdependence
has calculator text x_i = min(1, max(0, (B - S_prev) / Delta_C_i)); h_i = x_i * Delta_E_i; S_i = S_prev + Delta_C_i
has common error note Counting a programme's own cost in the cumulative cost above it. Using the cumulative cost through each programme in place of the cost above it moves every row's budget test down one programme. In the article's table C then receives 0.6 of its cost and D nothing, so GBP 650,000 is spent, GBP 250,000 is left over and the budget buys 82 QALYs in place of 97.5 (computed here for illustration).
Entering a programme at its ratio against no treatment when it would replace a funded service. The article's programme N costs GBP 700,000 and gives 50 QALYs, GBP 14,000 per QALY against no treatment, which places it between C and D and ahead of D in the fill. It would replace the funded service M (GBP 400,000, 40 QALYs), so its incremental ratio from HE-FM-ICER-001 is GBP 30,000 per QALY and it belongs below D. Switching spends GBP 300,000 for 10 QALYs, while the same sum on D buys 15, so the error loses 5 QALYs, the incremental net health benefit of HE-FM-CET-002 at the GBP 20,000 critical ratio. The test of Birch and Gafni, as Dakin and Tsiachristas describe it, also rejects the switch, since freeing GBP 300,000 from the funded programmes gives up at least 19.5 QALYs, the funded part of D and GBP 150,000 of C, against the 10 gained (computed here for illustration).
has description in the module Funds programme i, the i-th in ascending order of ICER, in full when the budget left after the programmes ranked above it covers its incremental cost, in part when it covers some of that cost, and not at all when nothing is left. The share x_i is the budget left, B less the cumulative cost S_prev of the programmes above, divided by Delta_C_i and held at least 0 and at most 1, and the health it buys is x_i times Delta_E_i. Applied down the table this is the league-table rule of Marseille and colleagues, which Sacristán and colleagues call the fixed budget rule and Dakin and Tsiachristas identify as the greedy algorithm for the knapsack problem, with the marginal programme part-funded as in the article's worked example. S_i carries the cumulative cost to the next row, and HE-CF-CELT-001 fills the whole table.

has source in the module Dakin H, Tsiachristas A. Rationing in an era of multiple tight constraints: is cost-utility analysis still fit for purpose? Applied Health Economics and Health Policy. 2024;22(3):315-329. Section 2.2, headed Cost-effectiveness league tables, a greedy algorithm, which states that given one constraint the league table ranks proposed and current interventions by ICER and adopts interventions from the lowest ICER upwards until the budget is exhausted, equivalent to the greedy algorithm for the knapsack problem, which sorts items by the reciprocal of the ICER. Section 2.3 describes the alternative of Birch and Gafni, which adopts a proposed intervention only if current interventions can be discontinued to free enough funds to cover its cost while generating fewer QALYs than it does. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40258-023-00858-w
Marseille E, Larson B, Kazi DS, Kahn JG, Rosen S. Thresholds for the cost-effectiveness of interventions: alternative approaches. Bulletin of the World Health Organization. 2015;93(2):118-124. Section League tables, which states that if all of the interventions considered are at least somewhat scalable they can be ranked into a league table by their ICERs, and that the approach rests on the principle that for any budget health outcomes are maximised if selection begins with the option with the lowest ICER and moves down the list, to successively higher ratios, until the budget is exhausted. Table 1, the WHO-CHOICE malaria table, compares each option after the first with the next cheapest intervention. https://doi.org/10.2471/BLT.14.138206

Gamma shape and scale for a utility decrement fitted by moments

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000392
Type formula
assumes Decrement approach used when a normal or beta does not fit the mean utility
Scale parameterisation of the gamma decrement
has calculator text mu_D = 1 - mu_U; k = mu_D^2 / s^2; theta = s^2 / mu_D
has common error note Gamma rate entered where Excel GAMMA.INV expects a scale. The third argument of GAMMA.INV is a scale. Entering the rate 1/theta, about 140.6 in the severe-state example, gives a mean decrement of about 17,800 instead of 0.90.
Sampled gamma decrement used as the utility itself. The gamma draw is the decrement. Using it directly as the utility turns a severe state with a mean utility of 0.10 into one with a mean of 0.90; the sampled utility is one minus the draw.
has description in the module Describes a mean utility as a decrement from full health, one minus the utility, and fits a gamma distribution to the decrement by matching its mean and standard error. The shape is the squared mean decrement over the squared standard error and the scale is the squared standard error over the mean decrement. Each sampled utility, one minus a gamma draw, is at most one with no lower limit, which suits states where a mean utility below zero is plausible.

Gamma unit deviance and deviance residual of one patient's cost in a generalised linear model

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000556
Type formula
assumes Positive costs with fitted means from a gamma GLM, Unweighted and unscaled gamma deviance residuals
has calculator text d = 2 * ((y - mu) / mu - log(y / mu)); r_D = (y - mu) / abs(y - mu) * sqrt(d)
has common error note Computing gamma deviance residuals for zero costs. The log of y / mu is undefined at a cost of zero, so the residual cannot be computed; Mihaylova and colleagues describe two-part models in which a logit or probit first part estimates the probability of any cost and a GLM models the positive costs.
Expecting the gamma deviance residuals to sum to zero. The Pearson residuals of an intercept-only fit sum to zero, but in the article's example the deviance residuals sum to about minus 0.526, so a residual plot need not centre on zero and an offset alone does not signal misfit.
Ranking cost outliers by the Pearson residual. In the article's three-patient example the Pearson residual puts the 6,000 pound patient first (+1.000) and the deviance residual puts the 1,000 pound patient first (minus 0.929), because the gamma deviance judges the ratio of observed to fitted cost on roughly a log scale; Stata's glm postestimation manual notes that Pearson residuals often have markedly skewed distributions for non-normal families.
has description in the module For a gamma GLM of positive costs, the unit deviance compares the observed cost with its fitted mean through the proportional gap minus the log of their ratio, so it depends only on y / mu. The deviance residual takes its square root with the sign of y minus mu, and the squared residuals add up to the model deviance. In the Math line the sign is written (y minus mu) / |y minus mu|; at y = mu the residual is 0 by convention, a case the calculator cannot show because it divides by zero there.

has implementation Gamma unit deviance and deviance residual from named cost cells
has mathematical variable Gamma unit deviance of one patient's cost
Fitted mean cost of one patient from the gamma model
Deviance residual of one patient's cost under the gamma model

has module record identifier HE-FM-DEVR-001
has source in the module Mihaylova B, Briggs A, O'Hagan A, Thompson SG. Review of statistical methods for analysing healthcare resources and costs. Health Economics. 2011;20(8):897-916. doi:10.1002/hec.1653 (full text read). Section 1: cost and resource use data often show substantial positive skewness and heavy tails, with a mass at zero for non-users. Section 3.1.3: GLMs are used for costs (for example a gamma specification) and resource use (Poisson and negative binomial). Section 3.1.6: in a two-part model a logit or probit first part estimates the probability of any cost and the second part models costs among those with any. https://doi.org/10.1002/hec.1653
StataCorp. Stata Base Reference Manual, Release 19: glm postestimation. College Station, TX: Stata Press; 2025 (full text read). Methods and formulas: the deviance residual is sign(y minus mu) times the square root of the squared deviance residual, and the Pearson residual divides y minus mu by the square root of the family variance function. Options: deviance residuals are recommended by McCullagh and Nelder (1989) and are approximately normally distributed if the model is correct; Pearson residuals often have markedly skewed distributions for non-normal family distributions. https://www.stata.com/manuals/rglmpostestimation.pdf
StataCorp. Stata Base Reference Manual, Release 19: glm. College Station, TX: Stata Press; 2025 (full text read). Methods and formulas: the squared deviance residual for the gamma family is minus 2{ln(y/mu) minus (y minus mu)/mu}; for the Poisson family it is 2 mu when y is zero and 2{y ln(y/mu) minus (y minus mu)} otherwise; the overall deviance reported by glm is the weighted sum of the squared deviance residuals. https://www.stata.com/manuals/rglm.pdf

Gaussian process posterior mean and variance of the loss after two noise-free runs

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000530
Type formula
assumes Noise-free model runs, Fixed prior mean, variance and length-scale for the posterior
has calculator text a_1 = (c_1 - c_12 * c_2) / (1 - c_12^2); a_2 = (c_2 - c_12 * c_1) / (1 - c_12^2); mu_n = mu_0 + a_1 * (y_1 - mu_0) + a_2 * (y_2 - mu_0); var_n = sf2 * (1 - (c_1 * a_1 + c_2 * a_2))
has common error note Ignoring simulation noise in a microsimulation. Treating noisy losses as exact makes the surrogate pass through the noise and report zero uncertainty at evaluated values; a noise variance on the diagonal (HE-AS-BOPT-005) avoids this.
Reading the surrogate as the disease model. The posterior describes the loss, not the model's outputs, and can take impossible values: after another iteration in the example the posterior mean at 0.030 is about minus 1.09 (computed here for illustration).
has description in the module Writes the posterior mean and variance at an untried value in closed form when two runs have been made without noise. The weights a_1 and a_2 solve the two-by-two correlation system of the runs; the posterior mean moves the prior mean towards the observed losses by those weights, and the posterior variance is the prior variance less the part the runs explain. Correlations come from the kernel (HE-FM-BOPT-002); for more runs or noisy runs the matrix form is HE-CF-BOPT-001.

GBD age-weight function with its age and value of peak weight

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000685
Type formula
assumes Age weight as a continuous function of exact age, Standard GBD constants for the age-weight function
has calculator text W = C * x * exp(-beta * x); x_peak = 1 / beta; W_peak = C / beta * exp(-1)
has common error note Peak of the age weight read as the age of greatest loss per death. The weight peaks at 25, but a death at 25 loses fewer age-weighted years than a death in childhood, because the child's lost years pass through the whole high-weight span. Up to an illustrative age of 80 and without discounting, a death at 25 loses about 58.50 age-weighted years against 84.07 at age 5 and 85.88 at birth (HE-FM-AGW-002, computed here for illustration), the article's first misreading.
Shape parameter changed without recalibrating the scaling constant. Murray notes that if beta is altered the constant C would necessarily change as well. Keeping C = 0.1658 with beta = 0.05 lowers every weight, and the undiscounted age-weighted loss from a death at 5 up to age 80 falls from 84.07 to about 58.49 (computed here for illustration), a change produced by the constant, not by the new shape.
has description in the module Gives the weight on a year of life lived at age x as C times x times e to the minus beta x, the exponential form Murray used for the original DALY. The weight is zero at birth, rises through childhood and declines slowly after its peak, which falls where the slope C e to the minus beta x times (1 minus beta x) is zero, at the age 1/beta. The weight at the peak is C/(beta e). With the standard constants of 0.1658 and 0.04 the peak is at age 25 with a weight of about 1.525, as in the article.

Generalised hyperbolic discount factor of Loewenstein and Prelec

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000632
Type formula
assumes Positive parameters of the generalised hyperbola, Generalised hyperbola parameters in the time unit of the delay
has calculator text D_G = (1 + alpha * t)^(-beta / alpha)
has common error note Division by alpha dropped from the generalised hyperbola exponent. Writing (1 + alpha t) to the power minus beta gives about 0.889 two periods ahead with alpha = 0.4 and beta = 0.2, instead of 0.745 (computed here for illustration), and loses the constant-rate limit.
Generalised hyperbola beta confused with the quasi-hyperbolic present-bias factor. The article warns that the two betas differ. Entering a present-bias estimate of 0.7 as the generalised beta with alpha = 0.4 gives about 0.555 one period ahead, against 0.693 for the quasi-hyperbolic form with beta = 0.7 and delta = 0.99 (computed here for illustration).
has description in the module Raises 1 + alpha t to the power minus beta divided by alpha, the form that Frederick and colleagues attribute to Loewenstein and Prelec. Beta sets the overall level of discounting and alpha how far the curve departs from a constant rate. Setting beta equal to alpha returns the simple hyperbola of HE-FM-HYPD-001, and as alpha approaches zero the weight approaches exp(minus beta t), the continuous constant-rate factor (HE-FM-CONT-003 gives the continuous rate for an annual rate). The beta here is not the present-bias factor of HE-FM-HYPD-004.

Geographically adjusted Medicare physician fee schedule amount for a service in a locality

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000547
Type formula
assumes Participating supplier and services outside anaesthesia, Published indices used as given, Same year for relative values, indices and conversion factor
has calculator text Fee = (W * GPCI_W + PE * GPCI_PE + MP * GPCI_MP) * CF
has common error note Applying the qualifying participant factor to every service. The 2026 rule sets 33.5675 for qualifying participants and 33.4009 for everyone else, and CMS generally views the non-qualifying factor as the default because many practitioners do not qualify; using the higher factor overstates most payments by about 0.5 per cent (computed here for illustration).
Averaging the three indices without weights. Applying the simple mean of 1.02, 1.15 and 0.80 (0.99) to Service A's 2.30 units gives 76.05 dollars instead of 82.83 (computed here for illustration), because practice expense, the component with the highest index, carries more than half of the service's units.
Pricing anaesthesia with the general conversion factor. Anaesthesia services have their own 2026 factors, 20.5998 and 20.4976, with anaesthesia-specific adjustments, so the general factor does not apply to them.
has description in the module Each of the three relative value components of a service is multiplied by its geographic practice cost index for the payment locality, and the adjusted total is multiplied by the conversion factor. The regulation writes the same amount as total relative value units times a geographic adjustment factor (GAF) times the conversion factor, where the GAF weights each index by the component's share of the total. In the article's notation Fee is P_s,l and PE and MP are E_s and M_s. The amount is for a participating supplier; a non-participating supplier receives 95 per cent of it.

Geometric distribution of cycles spent in a Markov state on one visit with a constant stay probability

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000670
Type formula
assumes Cycle of entry counted in the length of a Markov state visit
One uninterrupted visit described by the geometric Markov sojourn
Stay probability unchanged across the cycles of one Markov state visit
has calculator text f_d = p_ii^(d - 1) * (1 - p_ii); G_d = p_ii^(d - 1); F_d = 1 - p_ii^d; d_star = log(0.5) / log(p_ii)
has common error note Mean stay of a memoryless Markov state read as its typical stay. A geometric stay is skewed to the right. With p_ii = 0.90613 the mean is about 10.65 cycles but the median is 8, and 62.7% of stays have ended within 10 cycles (computed here for illustration), so quoting the mean as the typical stay overstates it.
One-cycle shift between counting conventions for a Markov state stay. The mean stay counting the cycle of entry is 1 divided by 1 minus p_ii, 8.333 cycles for the event-free state at 0.88, while a trace counted at the end of each cycle from model start credits p_ii/(1-p_ii), 7.333. Comparing a mean taken under one convention with a model run under the other misstates the stay by a full cycle, about 12% here.
has description in the module Gives the probability that one visit to state i lasts exactly d cycles, at least d cycles or at most d cycles, counting the cycle of entry, when the probability of staying for another cycle is the same p_ii in every cycle of the stay. Each cycle acts as a trial in which the person leaves with probability 1 minus p_ii, so the stay ends at the first exit and its length has the geometric distribution of Grinstead and Snell. Its mean, 1 divided by 1 minus p_ii, is the mean episode length L_j of HE-FM-MKCH-002 and is not restated. The median is the smallest whole number of cycles at or above d_star, the first d at which F_d reaches one half; when d_star is itself a whole number F_d equals exactly one half there and that number is the median.

has implementation Geometric Markov sojourn probabilities and median stay from named cells
has mathematical variable Constant stay probability in the geometric Markov sojourn, Length in cycles of a geometric Markov sojourn, Median threshold of a geometric Markov sojourn, Probability that a Markov state visit lasts exactly d cycles, Probability that a Markov state visit lasts at least d cycles, Probability that a Markov state visit has ended within d cycles
has module record identifier HE-FM-MKA-001
has source in the module Grinstead CM, Snell JL. Grinstead and Snell's Introduction to Probability. The CHANCE Project version of 4 July 2006, based on the 2nd edition published by the American Mathematical Society. Chapter 5, section 5.1, Geometric Distribution, pages 184 to 186, which defines T as the number of trials up to and including the first success with P(T = j) = q^(j-1) p for j = 1, 2, 3 and onwards, gives P(T > k) = q^k in Example 5.1, and simulates T as the least integer at or above log(1 minus rnd) divided by log q, the rule applied here to the median with rnd at one half. Taking the exit from the state as the success gives p = 1 minus p_ii. https://math.dartmouth.edu/~prob/prob/prob.pdf
Sonnenberg FA, Beck JR. Markov models in medical decision making: a practical guide. Medical Decision Making. 1993;13(4) 322-338. Page 326, The Markov Property, which states that the behaviour of the process after any cycle depends only on its description in that cycle, so that the process has no memory for earlier cycles and all patients in a state have the same prognosis whatever their previous histories, and page 325, Types of Markov Processes, which calls the process with transition probabilities constant over time a Markov chain. The geometric length of a stay follows from these statements and is not itself stated in the paper. https://doi.org/10.1177/0272989X9301300409

Type formula

has calculator text Gini = 2 * AUC - 1
has common error note Confusing the discrimination Gini index with the inequality Gini coefficient. The Gini index of an ROC curve measures how well a score ranks cases above non-cases. The Gini coefficient used in studies of income or health inequality measures the spread of a distribution across a population, so values of the two cannot be compared or substituted for each other.
has description in the module Converts the AUC to the Gini index, defined as twice the area between the ROC curve and the diagonal, using the relation that the Gini index plus 1 equals twice the AUC. The index is 0 for no discrimination and 1 for perfect discrimination. It is a different quantity from the Gini coefficient of income or health inequality.

Gradient of an IQWiG efficiency frontier segment and the net cost at which a new intervention reaches the extended last segment

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000667
Type formula
assumes Benefit on an approximately cardinal scale for the efficiency frontier
Last segment drawn with absolute and extended dominance applied
Price judged by the version 6.1 extension of the last segment
has calculator text g = (B_j - B_i) / (K_j - K_i); lambda_g = 1 / g; K_max = K_j + (B_new - B_j) / g
has common error note Extending an earlier segment of the efficiency frontier. If an earlier segment joins EUR 5,000 and 25 points to EUR 8,000 and 40 points, its gradient is 0.005 points per euro. Extending it beyond EUR 8,000 and 40 points gives EUR 12,200 for the new intervention with 61 points, EUR 4,200 below the EUR 16,400 from the last segment (computed here for illustration). Only the last segment applies.
Reading an efficiency frontier gradient as a cost per unit of benefit. A gradient of 0.0025 points per euro is benefit per cost, the reciprocal of EUR 400 per point. A steeper segment means greater efficiency, the opposite direction to an ICER, where a lower ratio is better.
has description in the module In the IQWiG efficiency frontier benefit B is on the vertical axis and total net cost per patient K on the horizontal axis, the reverse of the usual cost-effectiveness plane, so the gradient g of a segment is the incremental benefit per incremental cost and its reciprocal lambda_g is the sequential ICER of HE-FM-CEA-001. General Methods version 6.1 extended the last segment to judge a new intervention with more benefit and more cost than the comparators, and took the reciprocal of its gradient as the threshold for the net health benefit used to derive a price. K_max is the net cost per patient at which a new intervention with benefit B_new lies on that extension, where its net health benefit is zero. Version 8.0 (section 4.15) states that extending the last segment is no longer necessary, so K_max is a version 6.1 calculation.

has calculator text V_X = P_1 * d_1X^(-beta) + P_2 * d_2X^(-beta) + P_3 * d_3X^(-beta); V_Y = P_1 * d_1Y^(-beta) + P_2 * d_2Y^(-beta) + P_3 * d_3Y^(-beta); A_1 = S_X * d_1X^(-beta) / V_X + S_Y * d_1Y^(-beta) / V_Y; A_2 = S_X * d_2X^(-beta) / V_X + S_Y * d_2Y^(-beta) / V_Y; A_3 = S_X * d_3X^(-beta) / V_X + S_Y * d_3Y^(-beta) / V_Y
has common error note Friction coefficient borrowed without checking how the gravity scores rank. At a beta of 1 the article's neighbourhoods rank A, B, C (4.440, 2.978 and 2.672 per 10,000) and at a beta of 2 they rank A, C, B (5.615, 2.997 and 2.293), while the 2SFCA at 30 minutes ranks B first (computed here). The order that guides a siting or funding decision therefore depends on beta. Wang 2012 notes that beta might be region specific and that the best decay function cannot be settled without real utilisation data.
Gravity sum computed without the population demand potential. Leaving out V_X and V_Y gives the simple gravity form, which Guagliardo notes models supply only. At a beta of 1 it returns 0.9, 0.56 and 0.444 for A, B and C (computed here), GPs per minute rather than GPs per head, and the scores do not change when more people compete for a practice; Guagliardo's example is two providers at the same distance, one serving 1,000 people and one 5,000, which the simple form scores alike.
Zero or token travel time for a neighbourhood that contains a practice. Entering 0 minutes between A and X, where A contains practice X, makes 0 to the power minus beta undefined for any beta above zero, and Excel returns #DIV/0! in DemandPotentialX and in all three scores, which divide by it; a blank time cell counts as 0 and gives the same, and at a beta of 0 Excel returns #NUM! instead (checked in Excel). Entering 1 minute in place of the article's 10 raises A's score at a beta of 1 to 7.875 per 10,000 from 4.440 and lowers B's to 1.463 from 2.978 (computed here), so the time within a neighbourhood is an input that drives the result.
has description in the module Each practice's demand potential adds the neighbourhood populations weighted by travel time raised to the power minus beta, so nearer residents compete for its GPs more than distant ones. Each neighbourhood's score adds, over both practices, the practice's GPs weighted the same way and divided by its demand potential. Every practice counts, with no threshold, and a larger beta makes distance matter more. It is Wang's equation 1 and Luo and Wang's equation 6, the improved gravity model that Guagliardo attributes to Joseph and Bantock, written for the article's example, and HE-CF-ACCS-002 computes it for any number of sites. The scores are in GPs per head, and their population-weighted mean equals total GPs over total population, as for HE-FM-ACCS-001.

Full text read (PMC394340), formula images included. Section Measuring spatial accessibility, the simplest gravity formula, A_i as the sum over j of S_j divided by d_ij to the power beta, the note that it models supply only with no adjustment for demand and the example of two providers serving 1,000 and 5,000 people, the population demand adjustment factor V_j of Joseph and Bantock as the sum over k of P_k divided by d_kj to the power beta, and the improved gravity model, A_i as the sum over j of S_j divided by d_ij to the power beta times V_j, all printed as unnumbered expressions, with the note that beta is usually unknown and must be estimated empirically. https://doi.org/10.1186/1476-072X-3-3
Luo W, Wang F. Measures of spatial accessibility to healthcare in a GIS environment: synthesis and a case study in Chicago region. Environment and Planning B: Planning and Design. 2003;30(6):865-884. Author manuscript read (HHS Author Manuscripts, PMC8238135); the published version, doi 10.1068/b29120, not seen. Section The Gravity-Based Method and a Synthesis, equation (6), the gravity-based index as the sum over physician locations of S_j d_ij to the power minus beta divided by V_j, with V_j the sum over population locations of P_k d_kj to the power minus beta, after equation (5), Hansen's form without V_j; it states that the population-weighted average of the index equals the physician to population ratio of the whole area and shows the 2SFCA to be a special case by recoding travel times to 1 within d_0 and infinity beyond. Section The Case Study and Sensitivity Analysis tests seven values of beta of 1.0 to 2.2, cites 1.85 from a commuting study, reports larger variances at larger beta and higher gravity scores than 2SFCA scores in areas with low accessibility, and notes the trade-off between the number of physicians and travel time at a beta of 1. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8238135/
Wang F. Measurement, optimization, and impact of health care accessibility: a methodological review. Annals of the Association of American Geographers. 2012;102(5):1104-1112. Section Health Care Accessibility Measures Synthesized, equation (1), with P_k, S_j, d, beta and the numbers of physician and population locations n and m defined, the description of the model as the ratio of supply to demand each discounted by a distance factor, the note that beta requires additional data and work to define and might be region specific, and the statement that the best decay function cannot be settled without analysing real utilisation. Standard STPR schedule used for health effects in a Green Book appraisal. A health effect in year 50 then carries a factor of 0.1973 (Table A.1) in place of 0.4955 (Table A.2), about two fifths of the weight the guidance gives it, since paragraph 2.17 applies the health rate in every year.

Green Book social time preference rate from its Ramsey components with the health discount rate

Normative status of the Ramsey components of time preference
has calculator text rho = delta + L; W_e = mu * g; STPR = rho + W_e; r_HD = STPR - W_e
has common error note Green Book health rate taken as pure time preference alone. Discounting health at 0.5% drops catastrophic risk from the time preference term. A QALY in year 20 then keeps a weight of 0.9051 against 0.7425 at the 1.5% health rate (computed here for illustration), as in step 3 of the article's worked example.
Green Book health rate used in a NICE reference case. Discounting QALYs at 1.5% in place of the 3.5% of PMG36 section 4.5.1 puts a weight of 0.7425 on a QALY in year 20 against 0.5026, about 48% more discounted health (computed here for illustration), which lowers the cost per QALY of programmes with distant gains.
Treasury 3.5% read as the public's impatience. Only 0.5 of the 3.5 points is pure time preference. Setting it to zero lowers the rate to 3.0% (Table 3.B), so a value in year 20 keeps a weight of 0.5537 instead of 0.5026 (Annex A Tables A.3 and A.1), far from the full weight of 1 that a rate of zero would give.
has description in the module Adds pure time preference delta and catastrophic risk L to give time preference rho, and adds the wealth effect, the elasticity of marginal utility mu times the growth rate g of real per capita consumption, to give the social time preference rate, as in paragraphs 2.2 to 2.8 of the Treasury's supplementary guidance on discounting (February 2026). With the Table 2.A values for years 1 to 30 the two parts are 1.5% and 2.0% and the rate is 3.5%. The health discount rate r_HD leaves out the wealth effect (paragraph 2.16), so it equals rho, 1.5%, which is broader than pure time preference because it keeps catastrophic risk. Freeman, Groom and Spackman, in their report for HM Treasury, and Attema and colleagues write the same sum as the Ramsey rule.

has common error note Applying the proportional loading as a markup on the net premium. Multiplying the net premium by 1.10 gives £13.20 rather than £13.33. A 10% share of £13.20 is £1.32, leaving £11.88 for claims, so the scheme is short by £0.12 per member, about £24,000 a year across 200,000 members.
Treating the gross premium as the expected cost of care. The gross premium includes expenses and the security margin. Using £13.33 as the cost of the physiotherapy benefit in an economic model overstates the expected claims of £12 per member by the loading.

Grossman demand for the health stock as a ratio between two states with the implied gross investment

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000903
Type formula
assumes Pure investment model with a zero real-own rate of interest in the health stock demand
Constant elasticity of the marginal efficiency schedule from Grossman's healthy-time function
Net investment small relative to depreciation for the gross investment ratio
has calculator text H_ratio = (W_1 / W_0)^eps * (pi_1 / pi_0)^(-eps) * (delta_1 / delta_0)^(-eps); I_ratio = (delta_1 / delta_0) * H_ratio
has common error note Fall in the health stock demanded read as a fall in gross investment and care. In the article's example the stock demanded falls by about 29% when depreciation doubles, yet gross investment, and with it care, rises by about 41%. Grossman shows that when eps is below one gross investment and the depreciation rate are positively correlated over the life cycle while gross investment and the stock of health are negatively correlated, so less health demanded does not mean less care bought.
Positive real-own rate of interest left out of the cost of health capital. The formula assumes a zero real-own rate. If r minus pi_tilde were 0.03, doubling depreciation to 0.04 from 0.02 would raise the cost of capital to 0.07 from 0.05, a factor of 1.4, and with eps of 0.5 the stock demanded would fall to 0.8452 of its level, a fall of 15.5% against the 29.3% that the zero-rate formula gives (computed here for illustration with the cost of capital of HE-FM-DFH-002).
Price of medical care used in place of the marginal cost of gross investment. pi is the unit cost of HE-FM-HPF-003, not the price of care. With K of 0.5 a 10% rise in the price of care raises pi by 4.88%, so with eps of 0.5 the stock demanded falls by 2.35%, while entering the price ratio as the cost ratio gives a fall of 4.65%, about twice as large (computed here for illustration). HE-ER-DFH-004 makes the same point for the pure investment condition.
has description in the module Grossman's demand function for the health stock, ln H = eps ln W minus eps ln pi minus eps ln delta with the intercept suppressed, is written as the ratio of the stock demanded after a change to the stock demanded before it, so that the intercept cancels. With pi held fixed a 1% rise in the wage raises the stock demanded by eps percent, while a 1% rise in the marginal cost of gross investment or in the depreciation rate lowers it by eps percent. The wage also raises pi through the own time input, so with pi taken from HE-FM-HPF-003 the net wage elasticity of the stock is (1-K) eps and schooling raises it by rho_H eps per year, Grossman's reduced form for health. The second step applies HE-FM-DFH-001 with net investment small, so gross investment is about delta H and its ratio is the depreciation ratio times H_ratio (derived here), which for a change in delta alone is (delta_1 / delta_0) to the power 1-eps and rises with depreciation when eps is below 1. The function follows from the pure investment condition HE-FM-DFH-002 once the marginal efficiency schedule has the constant elasticity eps.

Grossman reduced-form demand for medical care with its wage, price, schooling and depreciation elasticities

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000904
Type formula
assumes Cobb-Douglas gross investment with a unit elasticity of substitution in the derived demand for care
Pure investment model, zero real-own rate and small net disinvestment in the derived demand for care
Money price of care and two inputs in the derived demand for care
Factor-neutral schooling in the derived demand for care
has calculator text e_MW = (1 - K) * eps + K; e_MP_scale = -(1 - K) * eps; e_MP_subst = -K; e_MP = e_MP_scale + e_MP_subst; s_ME = rho_H * (eps - 1); e_Mdelta = 1 - eps; M_ratio = exp(e_MW * log(W_1 / W_0) + e_MP * log(P_1 / P_0) + s_ME * (E_1 - E_0) + e_Mdelta * log(delta_1 / delta_0))
has common error note Coefficient on log depreciation read as the percentage change for a doubling. The coefficient 1-eps applies to ln delta, so with eps of 0.5 a doubling of depreciation raises care by exp(0.5 times ln 2), 41.4%, not by 50%, which overstates the rise by about a fifth (computed here for illustration). The article takes the same route, 0.347 and its exponential.
Negative health coefficient in a conditional demand for care read as evidence against derived demand. Grossman states that when the conditional demand for care is estimated with health treated as exogenous, the initial depreciation rate in the disturbance is positively correlated with care and negatively with health, so the coefficient of health is biased downward and could well be negative. In HE-EX-DDHC-005 the same doubling of depreciation gives 41% more care with 29% less health (HE-EX-DDHC-001).
Price elasticity of care taken as the substitution part or the scale part alone. With eps of 0.5 and K of 0.4 the price elasticity of care is -0.7. Using the substitution part alone, -0.4, understates the response by 43%, and using the scale part alone, -0.3, by 57% (computed here for illustration). The scale part is the response of the health stock demanded to the price of care, so a care elasticity estimated with health held fixed leaves it out (derived here).
has description in the module Grossman's reduced-form demand function for medical care, ln M = [(1-K) eps + K] ln W minus [(1-K) eps + K] ln P plus rho_H (eps minus 1) E plus (1-eps) ln delta, with intercepts suppressed and the small net disinvestment term left out, is written as the ratio of care demanded after and before a change. It follows from the health stock demand of HE-FM-DDHC-001, gross investment of about delta H from HE-FM-DFH-001, the unit cost pi of HE-FM-HPF-003 and the least-cost care M = (1-K) C / P of HE-FM-HPF-002, and every coefficient contains eps, the parameter of the demand for health. The price elasticity splits into a scale part, minus (1-K) eps, through the smaller health stock demanded when care is dearer, and a substitution part, minus K, towards own time. Schooling changes care by rho_H (eps minus 1) per year and depreciation by the elasticity 1-eps, so with eps below 1 the more educated use less care and people whose health depreciates faster use more. For a change in the price of care alone the ratio is HE-FM-XPE-003 with the own-price elasticity e_MP.

Group health after a programme net of the group's share of the health opportunity cost

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000674
Type formula
assumes Groups cover the whole general population in a DCEA, Opportunity cost shares add to one in a DCEA, Health opportunity cost of a DCEA at a stated value of a QALY
has calculator text NHB_1 = dQ_1 - o_1 * H_d; NHB_2 = dQ_2 - o_2 * H_d; h1_1 = h0_1 + NHB_1 / N_1; h1_2 = h0_2 + NHB_2 / N_2; NHB_tot = NHB_1 + NHB_2
has common error note Reading the equity impact of a DCEA from gross QALY gains. Before the opportunity cost is counted, the more deprived group in the article's example gains 400 QALYs, 0.008 years per person, yet after its equal share of the 1,200 displaced QALYs it loses 0.004 years per person. A programme whose benefits reach a disadvantaged group can still leave that group worse off once the displaced care is counted.
Splitting the opportunity cost equally per group when groups differ in size. With illustrative groups of 20,000 and 80,000 people, sharing 1,200 displaced QALYs equally per head puts 240 on the smaller group, whereas a half and half split puts 600 on it. With a gain of 400 QALYs the smaller group's net health benefit is 160 QALYs under per-head sharing and minus 200 under the half split, so the error turns a gain into a loss.
has description in the module Subtracts each group's share of the health opportunity cost from the QALYs the group gains, giving the group's net health benefit, and divides that by the number of people in the group to move the group's baseline health per person to its health under the programme. The health opportunity cost H_d is the incremental cost divided by the value of a QALY, the live record HE-FM-CET-002, and the shares o_1 and o_2 say who bears it. Because the shares add to 1, the total of the group net health benefits equals the total QALY gain less H_d, so the distribution of the opportunity cost changes who gains while total health stays the same. The line shows two groups, the more deprived group 1 and the less deprived group 2, and each further group adds a pair of terms of the same form.

Group-time average treatment effect for one adoption cohort against never-treated units

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000496
Type formula
assumes Parallel trends between each cohort and the never-treated group, Staggered adoption that stays on and is not anticipated
has calculator text ATT_gt = (Y_g_t - Y_g_base) - (Y_n_t - Y_n_base)
has common error note Using already-treated units as controls under staggered adoption. Two-way fixed effects regressions under staggered adoption include comparisons in which already-treated units serve as controls; when effects change over time some of these comparisons receive negative weights, and the coefficient can even take the opposite sign to every underlying effect.
Using the cohort's own first period as the base. The base is the last period before adoption, g minus 1; a base further back adds any pre-policy differential trend to every effect.
has description in the module Compares the change in mean outcome for units first treated in period g, from the last period before adoption (g minus 1) to period t, with the same change for units never treated. Estimating one effect per cohort and period avoids the comparisons with already-treated units that bias the two-way fixed effects coefficient under staggered adoption; the effects are then combined with weights the analyst states.

Grouped-data concentration index by trapezoids for vertical equity analysis

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000372
Type formula
assumes Groups ranked by ability to pay with cumulative shares from zero, Straight-line curve within each ability to pay group
has calculator text C = 1 - sum_(t=1)^T [(p_t - p_(t-1)) * (L_t + L_(t-1))]
has common error note Entering group shares where cumulative shares are required. Using each group's own share of income as L_t, instead of the running total, gives a curve that never reaches 1. For the article's income data the result is 0.688, nearly twice the correct Gini coefficient of 0.352.
Leaving out the first trapezoid from the origin. Starting the sum at the first group point instead of the origin drops the trapezoid for the poorest group. For the article's income data the pair sums then add to 3.18 and the Gini coefficient comes out as 0.364 instead of 0.352.
has description in the module Computes a concentration index, or a Gini coefficient when the curve is a Lorenz curve, from T groups ranked from poorest to richest. The curve joins the group points with straight lines, so the area under it is a sum of trapezoids and the index is one minus twice that area. The result is the same as the grouped-data formula of Fuller and Lury given in the World Bank guide.

Growth of the relative unit cost of health care over a horizon

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000363
Type formula
assumes Constant annual productivity growth in each sector, Productivity measured on a comparable basis in both sectors
has calculator text R_T = R_0 * ((1+g_o)/(1+g_h))^T
has common error note Adding up the Baumol productivity gap instead of compounding it. Multiplying the gap in growth rates by the number of years, 1 + 0.015 × 20 = 1.30, understates the relative cost after twenty years, which compounds to about 1.3449. The shortfall grows with the horizon and with the size of the gap.
Applying the Baumol labour cost factor to full unit costs. R_T describes the labour cost of a unit of health care. Applying it to full unit costs, including medicines, equipment and buildings, assumes that those inputs follow the same path as staff costs, which the model does not claim. A projection of full costs applies the factor to the staff share and projects other inputs separately.
has description in the module Projects the relative unit labour cost of health care T years ahead when output per hour grows at a constant annual rate g_h in health care and g_o elsewhere. Each year the relative cost is multiplied by (1 + g_o)/(1 + g_h), so health care becomes relatively dearer whenever g_o exceeds g_h. The wage does not appear, so the result is the same whether pay rises with productivity in the progressive sector or not.

Harberger approximation to deadweight loss from a small ad valorem tax

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000477
Type formula
assumes Compensated elasticity and no other distorted market, Small tax on a good supplied at constant marginal cost
has calculator text DWL = 0.5 * eps * tau^2 * p * q
has common error note Applying the approximation to a large tax on curved demand. With a constant elasticity of 1 instead of linear demand, a 40 per cent tax on the same starting point gives a Marshallian loss of about 12,690 pounds, while the approximation gives 20,000 (computed here for illustration). For large wedges the area is computed from the demand curve itself.
Entering the tax per unit in place of the tax rate. Tau is a proportion of the price. Entering a tax of 10 pounds per session as tau = 10 instead of 0.2 multiplies the result by 2,500.
has description in the module Writes the triangle in terms of spending before the tax and the price elasticity of demand. With constant marginal cost the wedge is tau times p and quantity falls by about eps times tau times q, so the loss is half their product. Zero elasticity gives zero loss, and doubling the tax rate roughly quadruples it. The expression is the single-tax case of the second-order approximation that Auerbach and Hines attribute to Harberger, with the quantity response written through the elasticity.
has formalisation level catalogue record
has implementation Harberger deadweight loss from named elasticity, tax rate and spending

Amsterdam: Elsevier; 2002. p. 1347-1421 (read as NBER Working Paper 8181, 2001). Section 2.2: the second-order approximation around the undistorted point approximates the total excess burden (Harberger 1964a); for a single tax with producer prices fixed, the excess burden is minus one half of the tax change times the compensated demand response to it times the tax change, so excess burden increases with the square of a tax. Section 2.3: Harberger derived the approximation used to measure deadweight loss. https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w8181/w8181.pdf
Hines JR Jr. Three sides of Harberger triangles. Journal of Economic Perspectives. 1999;13(2):167-188 (read as NBER Working Paper 6852, 1998). Dupuit observed that the welfare loss triangle is generally a function of the square of the tax rate; Harberger's 1964 papers derived and applied the triangle method; Harberger triangles usually approximate compensated measures closely. https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w6852/w6852.pdf
has test Doubling the tax rate quadruples the Harberger loss, Elasticity of 0.2 on the less responsive curve, Harberger inputs entered with the right signs and units, Harberger loss close to the triangle from observed quantities, Twenty per cent tax at the article's full price

Hazard ratio from event counts and person-time under constant hazards

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000470
Type formula
assumes Constant hazard in each arm over follow-up for the rate ratio, Events and person-time counted on the same basis in both arms
has calculator text HR = (d_T / PT_T) / (d_C / PT_C); SE_beta = sqrt(1 / d_T + 1 / d_C)
has common error note Dividing event counts instead of event rates. With equal numbers randomised, the second example's counts give 42 / 60 = 0.70, while the rates give 0.65625, because the treatment arm has more person-time at risk (computed here for illustration). A ratio of counts or proportions ignores how long each arm was followed and is not a hazard ratio.
Zero events in one arm of a person-time hazard ratio. With no events in one arm the rate ratio is 0 or undefined and 1 divided by the zero count makes the standard error infinite. The Cochrane Handbook notes that 0.5 may be added to each count in that case, and the correction is reported.
has description in the module Estimates each arm's hazard as its number of events divided by its person-time at risk and divides the treatment rate by the comparator rate, which gives the rate ratio. Under an exponential model each hazard is constant, so the rate ratio estimates the hazard ratio, and the approximate standard error of its natural logarithm depends only on the two event counts. The time unit cancels, so person-years and person-months give the same ratio when both arms use the same unit. The interval around the estimate follows HE-FM-HR-006.

Health capital stock carried into the next period

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000258
Type formula
assumes Depreciation rate exogenous but age-dependent, Health stock and investment in common units
has calculator text H_(t+1) = H_t - delta_t * H_t + I_t
has common error note Reading a rising stock as optimal investment. The equation shows how the stock moves for given investment. Whether 12 units is the right investment depends on its cost and on the value of the healthy time it produces, which the optimality condition addresses.
Treating medical care as the health stock. Medical care is one input to gross investment I_t, not the stock itself. Higher use of care alongside a lower stock, as when depreciation rises with age, is consistent with the model.
has description in the module Grossman's equation (2-2) sets net investment, the change in the stock, equal to gross investment minus depreciation. Rearranged, the stock at the start of the next period is the current stock, less the share delta_t that depreciates during the period, plus gross investment. Holding the stock constant requires gross investment equal to delta_t × H_t.

Health care share of working hours with the output mix held fixed

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000364
Type formula
assumes Ratio of health output to other output held constant
Constant productivity growth and a common wage in the hours projection
has calculator text x_T = x_0 * ((1+g_o)/(1+g_h))^T; s_hT = x_T / (1 + x_T)
has common error note Applying the Baumol cost factor to the share of hours. Multiplying the starting share by the relative cost factor, 0.10 × 1.3449 = 0.1345, overstates health care's share after twenty years, which is about 0.1300. The factor applies to the ratio of health hours to other hours, and over long horizons the shortcut can give a share above 1.
Projecting a rising health share of hours when output is not held fixed. The rising share follows only if health output keeps its ratio to other output. Where demand falls as the relative price rises, Baumol's model predicts declining relative output in the slow sector instead, and Nordhaus found falling relative real output in stagnant United States industries, so the hours path depends on the demand assumption.
has description in the module Gives the hours needed in health care when the ratio of health output to other output is held constant, for example because a publicly financed service keeps pace with the rest of the economy. The ratio of health hours to other hours grows by the same annual factor as the relative cost, and the share of total hours follows from that ratio. With equal wages and only labour costs, the share of hours is also health care's share of total spending.

Health discount rate from the cost discount rate and growth in the consumption value of health

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000570
Type formula
assumes Health measured in QALYs whose money value grows at a constant rate
Gravelle and Smith framing with no binding health budget
has calculator text r_H = (1 + r_C) / (1 + g_v) - 1; r_H_sub = r_C - g_v
has common error note Allowing for the growing value of health twice. Attema and colleagues note that the growing value of health can also be handled through a monetary threshold that rises over time; an analysis that both lowers the health rate by g_v and raises the threshold at g_v counts the same growth twice.
Treating growth in the value of health as a reason for differential rates under a fixed budget. Claxton and colleagues show that, with a fixed budget, expecting growth in the consumption value of health does not on its own justify differential rates but implies a lower rate for both costs and health.
has description in the module When the money value of a unit of health grows at g_v a year, discounting the volume of health at r_H gives the same present value as inflating each year's QALYs at g_v and discounting them at the cost rate, provided one plus r_H equals one plus r_C divided by one plus g_v. Gravelle and Smith derive this exact form and summarise it as the cost rate minus the growth rate, the subtraction rule the Dutch guideline uses.

has implementation Exact and subtraction health discount rates from named cells

York: Centre for Health Economics, University of York; 2000 (full text read). Section 2.1, equation 6: (1 + rh)/(1 + rc) = v0/v1, and the discount rates on health and costs are the same only if the value of health is the same in both periods; with gv the growth rate of the value of health this rearranges to rh = (1 + rc)/(1 + gv) minus 1, approximately rc minus gv. Hedges' g from Cohen's d with the approximate correction factor J

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000740
Type formula
assumes Normal outcomes with a common standard deviation behind the Hedges' correction
Degrees of freedom of the standard deviation actually used in the Hedges' correction
Algebraic approximation in place of the exact gamma-function factor for Hedges' g
has calculator text m = n_1 + n_2 - 2; J = 1 - 3 / (4 * m - 1); g = J * d
has common error note Hedges' correction applied to an estimate that is already g. Multiplying a reported Hedges' g by J again, often because a paper labels g as d, gives about 0.7743 instead of 0.8048 for the article's trial (0.962025 squared times 0.8366, computed here for illustration). The article lists applying the correction twice among the frequent mistakes that make pooled results inconsistent.
Pooled degrees of freedom used with a comparator-group standard deviation. When the difference is standardised by the comparator group's standard deviation alone, Hedges sets m to the comparator group size less 1. Using the pooled value of 20 for the article's trial, whose comparator arm has 12 patients, gives a J of about 0.9620 instead of about 0.9302 for 11 degrees of freedom and leaves almost half of the bias in place, an expected overstatement of about 3.4% instead of about 7.5% with the exact factor, computed here for illustration.
Total sample size written in place of the degrees of freedom in Hedges' J. Writing 1 minus 3 over (4N minus 1), with N the total sample size, mixes the two forms of the factor. For the article's trial it gives a J of about 0.9655 instead of 0.9620 and a g of about 0.8078 instead of 0.8048, computed here for illustration, so part of the bias stays in the estimate.
has description in the module Multiplies the uncorrected standardised mean difference d of HE-FM-CD-001 by a correction factor J that depends only on the degrees of freedom m of the standard deviation used to standardise, which for the pooled standard deviation is the total sample size less 2. The factor 1 minus 3 over (4m minus 1) is Hedges' algebraic approximation to an exact factor written with gamma functions, which HE-CF-HEDG-001 computes. Substituting for m gives 1 minus 3 over (4N minus 9) with N the total sample size, the form Review Manager prints. J is below 1, so g is always nearer zero than d, and J approaches 1 as the sample grows.
has formalisation level catalogue record
has implementation Hedges' g in three cells from Cohen's d and the two group sizes
has mathematical variable Degrees of freedom for the Hedges' g correction factor, Comparator group size for Hedges' g, Approximate Hedges' correction factor J, Cohen's d entering the Hedges' correction, Intervention group size for Hedges' g, Hedges' g bias-corrected estimate
has module record identifier HE-FM-HEDG-001
has source in the module Deeks JJ, Higgins JPT, on behalf of the Cochrane Statistical Methods Group. Statistical algorithms in Review Manager. Cochrane; May 2022. Section Standardized difference in means (standardized mean difference) (page 3), which states that the version implemented in RevMan is Hedges' adjusted g, very similar to Cohen's d but with an adjustment for small sample bias, and gives the SMD as the difference in means over the pooled standard deviation times 1 minus 3/(4N minus 9), with N the sum of the two group sizes. https://documentation.cochrane.org/revman-kb/files/210600101/210600103/1/1654774257333/Statistical_methods_in_revman.pdf
Hedges LV. Distribution theory for Glass's estimator of effect size and related estimators. Journal of Educational Statistics. 1981;6(2):107-128. Theorem 1 (page 111), which for normal outcomes with a common variance gives the expectation of the uncorrected estimate as delta over c(m), with m equal to the control group size less 1 or the total of both groups less 2 depending on whether a control group or pooled standard deviation is used, and defines c(m) as Gamma(m/2) over the square root of m/2 times Gamma((m minus 1)/2) (equation 6e). Section 4, An unbiased estimator based on the standardized mean difference (pages 112 to 114), which defines the unbiased estimator as the uncorrected one times c(m) (equation 7) and gives the approximation c(m) about 1 minus 3/(4m minus 1), with a maximum error of 0.007 when m is 2, accuracy within 0.00033 when m is at least 10 and an error not above 0.000015 when m exceeds 50. Table I (page 115) tabulates c(m) to five decimals for each m up to 50. In Hedges' notation g is the uncorrected estimator and the corrected one is g with superscript U. https://doi.org/10.3102/10769986006002107
Lakens D. Calculating and reporting effect sizes to facilitate cumulative science: a practical primer for t-tests and ANOVAs. Frontiers in Psychology. 2013;4:863. Section Cohen's d in between-subjects designs, equation 4, which gives Hedges's g as Cohen's d times 1 minus 3/(4(n1 + n2) minus 9), and states that the difference between the two is very small, especially in sample sizes above 20. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2013.00863
What Works Clearinghouse. What Works Clearinghouse Procedures and Standards Handbook, Version 5.0 (WWC 2022008). US Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance; August 2022. Herd immunity threshold and critical vaccination coverage for a vaccine of effectiveness E

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000699
Type formula
assumes Homogeneous mixing and an R_0 above one for the herd immunity threshold
Lasting all-or-nothing protection given before exposure for the critical coverage
has calculator text H = 1 - 1 / R_0; V_c = H / E
has common error note Herd immunity threshold read as the share that will be infected. The threshold marks where incidence starts to fall, not where the epidemic ends. With no programme an SIR epidemic with R_0 of 3 infects about 94% of the population (the article's final size, computed as in HE-CF-ATR-001), well beyond the threshold of 66.7%, because infections continue while the epidemic declines.
Herd immunity threshold used as the coverage target for an imperfect vaccine. Vaccinating 66.7% of the population with a 90% effective vaccine immunises 60%, leaving R_t of 3 times 0.4, or 1.2, so spread continues; the article's critical coverage is 74.1%.
has description in the module Sustained spread stops once the susceptible proportion is below 1/R_0, so the proportion that must be immune is H = 1 minus 1/R_0, the herd immunity threshold of the WHO guide, which calls the matching level the critical effective immunisation level. Van den Driessche gives the same condition for a perfect vaccine, and Pitman and colleagues state that in a homogeneously mixing population coverage has to be greater than this value for herd immunity to occur. An all-or-nothing vaccine that fully protects a proportion E of those vaccinated immunises V times E of the population, so the critical coverage is V_c = H/E, the form Masterson and colleagues use, and when E is below H, V_c exceeds 1 and that vaccine alone cannot stop sustained spread. Pitman and colleagues and van den Driessche state the condition as coverage greater than the threshold, while the WHO guide writes p_c as at least 1 minus 1/R_0. At coverage exactly V_c the effective reproduction number of HE-FM-BRN-002 equals 1, the boundary that HE-CF-ATR-001 classifies as no major epidemic, since it returns a final attack rate of 0 whenever R_0 s_0 is 1 or less.

Heterotrait-monotrait ratio for two constructs with two indicators each

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000906
Type formula
assumes Reflectively measured constructs for the HTMT ratio, Indicator scores coded in one direction before the HTMT ratio, Correlations from the same respondents for the HTMT ratio, Cut-off rule and ties for the HTMT ratio
has calculator text rbar_ij = (r_i1j1 + r_i1j2 + r_i2j1 + r_i2j2) / 4; HTMT_ij = rbar_ij / sqrt(r_i1i2 * r_j1j2)
has common error note Arithmetic mean in the HTMT denominator. Eq. 6 uses the geometric mean of the two within-construct means, which for positive correlations is never larger than their arithmetic mean, so the arithmetic version understates the ratio (derived here). With the article's 0.64 and 0.52 the gap is small, 0.4914 against 0.494, but with illustrative within-construct correlations of 0.90 and 0.30 and a between-construct mean of 0.45 the ratio is 0.866, above 0.85, against 0.75 with the arithmetic mean, which misses the flag (computed here).
Passing HTMT ratio read as clean discriminant evidence. In the article's example the ratio of 0.494 passes easily, yet the questionnaire's two subscales correlate 0.45, only 0.07 below the mood validity value of 0.52, a method problem confined to the self-reports that the pooled ratio averages away. The article notes that if both subscales then enter a mapping function to EQ-5D as separate predictors, part of what each coefficient picks up is a shared reporting style, so the multitrait-multimethod table is read alongside the ratio.
Reverse-coded indicator left in the HTMT ratio. If the clinician mood rating in the article's example were scored so that higher means worse, its three correlations would change sign, the between-construct mean would fall to 0.045 and the product under the square root would be 0.64 times minus 0.52, so the ratio is undefined and Excel returns #NUM!. With both mood indicators reversed the ratio is minus 0.494, below any cut-off however much the constructs overlap (computed here).
Same-method correlations dropped from the HTMT numerator. Averaging only the different-method cells 0.18 and 0.21, the discriminant cells of the multitrait-multimethod matrix, gives 0.195 in place of 0.285 and a ratio of 0.338 in place of 0.494, 32% lower (computed here). Henseler and colleagues define the heterotrait-heteromethod part as all the correlations between the indicators of the two constructs, and in the article's example the dropped same-method value of 0.45 is where the shared method variance shows.
has description in the module With two indicators per construct each within-construct mean is a single correlation, r_i1i2 or r_j1j2, and the between-construct mean rbar_ij has four terms, so the heterotrait-monotrait ratio is rbar_ij divided by the square root of r_i1i2 times r_j1j2. This is Eq. 6 of Henseler, Ringle and Sarstedt with K_i and K_j both equal to 2, and HE-CF-DISV-001 takes any numbers of indicators. The authors describe the ratio as an estimate of the correlation between the two constructs, so a value clearly below 1 indicates constructs that differ. Used as a criterion, a value above a cut-off of 0.85 or 0.90 points to a lack of discriminant validity, a level the authors call debatable. In the article's example the questionnaire and the clinician rating serve as the two indicators of physical functioning and of mood.

Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science. 2015;43(1):115-135. doi:10.1007/s11747-014-0403-8 (open access, full text read on the publisher page). The section on the heterotrait-monotrait ratio of the correlations approach, Eq. 6, which defines the HTMT of constructs i and j with K_i and K_j indicators as the average of the heterotrait-heteromethod correlations, those between the indicators of the two constructs, divided by the geometric mean of the average monotrait-heteromethod correlations, those among the indicators within each construct. The same section states that the HTMT is an estimate of the correlation between the constructs and that the multitrait-multimethod approach requires at least two constructs from the same respondents. The two-indicator form is Eq. 6 with K_i and K_j equal to 2 (derived here). https://doi.org/10.1007/s11747-014-0403-8
Henseler J, Ringle CM, Sarstedt M. A new criterion for assessing discriminant validity in variance-based structural equation modeling. Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science. 2015;43(1):115-135. doi:10.1007/s11747-014-0403-8 (open access, full text read on the publisher page). The section on the heterotrait-monotrait ratio, which states that a value higher than a predefined threshold indicates a lack of discriminant validity, that the exact threshold is debatable, and that some authors suggest 0.85 and others 0.90. The section Key findings and recommendations calls the 0.85 criterion the most conservative and regards a more liberal criterion as warranted for constructs that are conceptually different but hard to distinguish empirically, and the section Further research and concluding remarks states that the HTMT-based criteria assume reflectively measured constructs. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11747-014-0403-8

Horizontal inequity index as a difference of concentration indices

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000377
Type formula
assumes Equal means of actual and need-expected use in the difference form
Same people and income ranking for both concentration indices
Remaining inequality in use read as horizontal inequity
has calculator text HI = C_M - C_N
has common error note Reading the concentration index of actual use as horizontal inequity. Unstandardised inequality in use mixes differences in need with inequity. In the article's example actual visits have an index of minus 0.04, which suggests that the poor are favoured, while the horizontal inequity index of 0.06 shows pro-rich inequity at equal need.
Subtracting the index of actual use from the index of need-expected use. C_N minus C_M reverses the sign of the result. The article's data would give minus 0.06 and suggest pro-poor inequity where the distribution at equal need is pro-rich.
Treating a horizontal inequity index near zero as equal treatment. An index near zero can come from a concentration curve of standardised use that crosses the line of equality, with the areas on each side cancelling out. The curve is read alongside the index before concluding that there is no inequity.
has description in the module Measures horizontal inequity in the delivery of care as the concentration index of actual use minus the concentration index of need-expected use, with people ranked by income or another living standards measure from poorest to richest. It equals the concentration index of need-standardised use and is sometimes labelled HI_WV after Wagstaff and van Doorslaer. Zero is consistent with horizontal equity, a positive value indicates pro-rich inequity and a negative value pro-poor inequity. Each concentration index is computed as in HE-FM-HINQ-005 on the Health Inequality page.

assumes I-squared inherits the degrees of freedom of Q

has common error note Reading I-squared as the size of heterogeneity. I-squared is a proportion of variation, not an amount of it. The Cochrane Handbook notes that the importance of a value depends on the magnitude and direction of effects and on the strength of evidence for heterogeneity, and that simple thresholds should be avoided when studies are few. The 70.9% in the three-trial example rests on three estimates.
has description in the module Rescales Q to the percentage of total variation across studies attributed to heterogeneity rather than chance. Negative values, which arise when Q is below its degrees of freedom, are set to zero so that the result lies between 0% and 100%.

has calculator text x_bar = sum_(i=1)^n [x_i] / n; SE_inf = sqrt(sum_(i=1)^n [(x_i - x_bar)^2]) / n
has common error note Reading the small-sample shortfall of the bootstrap as lower cost variability. With six patients the bootstrap standard error is about 9% below the usual value, 527.05 against 577.35 pounds in arm T, before skewness plays any part.
