Immortal-time bias factor in a responder rate ratio from pre-response person-time counted as responder time

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000739
Type formula
assumes Constant hazards within each response group for the bias factor, No deaths in the pre-response person-time of responders, Response time known for every responder in the person-time split
has calculator text RR_naive = (d_R / (PT_R + I)) / (d_N / PT_N); RR_split = (d_R / PT_R) / (d_N / (PT_N + I)); F = RR_naive / RR_split
has common error note Immortal time dropped instead of moved to the side without a response. Removing I from the responders without adding it to the person-time without a response gives a rate ratio of 0.458 in the illustration, still below the time-split 0.535 (computed here). Suissa names excluded as well as misclassified immortal time as a source of bias in the rate ratio.
Pre-response time counted as responder time in a rate ratio. In the article-based illustration the naive rate ratio of 0.354 suggests a death rate 65% lower for responders, against 47% lower with person-time split at the response (computed here for illustration). Suissa reports that the bias in the rate ratio from misclassified immortal time increases with the duration of immortal time.
has description in the module Compares two constant-hazard rate ratios of responders against patients without a response, each of the form of HE-FM-HR-005. The naive ratio RR_naive adds the immortal time I, the person-time responders spent before responding, to the responders' person-time, while RR_split moves it to the side without a response up to the time status changes, as the extended Cox model with a time-varying covariate does in Giobbie-Hurder, Gelber and Regan. No death can fall in I, so the event counts are the same in both ratios and F, their ratio, equals PT_R PT_N divided by (PT_R + I)(PT_N + I) (derived here), which depends on person-time alone. F is 1 when I is zero and falls further below 1 as I grows (checked over a grid in Python), so the naive ratio always flatters responders, and dividing a naive rate ratio by F recovers the time-split ratio.

has implementation Naive and time-split responder rate ratios and the bias factor from named person-time

has source in the module Anderson JR, Cain KC, Gelber RD. Analysis of survival by tumor response. Journal of Clinical Oncology. 1983;1(11):710-719. doi:10.1200/JCO.1983.1.11.710. Abstract, which states that the usual method of comparing responders and nonresponders is biased in favour of responders, that two valid methods are discussed, and that a comparison by response category should not be used for inference about treatment effectiveness. The person-time form of the bias in HE-FM-LMA-002 is derived here and is not taken from the paper. https://doi.org/10.1200/JCO.1983.1.11.710
Giobbie-Hurder A, Gelber RD, Regan MM. Challenges of guarantee-time bias. Journal of Clinical Oncology. 2013;31(23):2963-2969. doi:10.1200/JCO.2013.49.5283 (full text read in PubMed Central, PMC3732313). Analytic Methods, Extended Cox Model With Time-Varying Covariates, which states that all patient data are used, that patients who develop the classifying event are switched into its group at the time it occurs and remain there, and that the resulting hazard ratio compares patients after the event with those who had not yet or never had it. The person-time split and the closed form of F are derived here for constant hazards. https://doi.org/10.1200/JCO.2013.49.5283
Giobbie-Hurder A, Gelber RD, Regan MM. Challenges of guarantee-time bias. Journal of Clinical Oncology. 2013;31(23):2963-2969. doi:10.1200/JCO.2013.49.5283 (full text read in PubMed Central, PMC3732313). Background and Figure 1, which state that patients in the transplantation group were guaranteed to survive at least until a donor was available, that their survival reflects the total time before and after transplantation, and that the extra waiting time is guarantee time. https://doi.org/10.1200/JCO.2013.49.5283
Suissa S. Immortal time bias in pharmaco-epidemiology. American Journal of Epidemiology. 2008;167(4):492-499. doi:10.1093/aje/kwm324. Abstract, which defines immortal time as a span of cohort follow-up during which, because of exposure definition, the outcome could not occur, and states that the bias in the rate ratio from misclassified or excluded immortal time increases with the duration of immortal time. The closed form of F is derived here and is not taken from the paper. https://doi.org/10.1093/aje/kwm324

Implicit cross-subsidy per member under community rating

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000435
Type formula
assumes Premium set at the pool's mean expected cost for the cross-subsidy
Expected, not realised, costs in the community-rating cross-subsidy
has calculator text s_i = P - c_i
has common error note Measuring the community-rating cross-subsidy against a loaded premium. If loadings for administration and profit stay in the premium, every group appears to pay a positive amount and the cross-subsidies no longer sum to zero. The loadings are removed before the cross-subsidy is computed.
Treating the community-rating cross-subsidy as risk pooling. Risk pooling spreads unpredictable costs among members with similar risks. The £1,000 a year paid by each low-risk member in the article's example is predictable from the start and is a transfer between groups, which is why low-risk members have a reason to leave when buying cover is voluntary.
has description in the module The community-rated premium minus a member's expected cost. A positive value is the amount a member pays above expected cost towards others, as low-risk members do; a negative value is the amount by which a high-risk member's expected cost exceeds the premium. Weighted by the number of members, the cross-subsidies sum to zero across the pool, because the premium equals the pool's mean expected cost. Read from the insurer's side, the same quantity is the expected profit on that member in HE-FM-CSKM-001.

Implied annual discount rate for health from a TEMPUS open-ended stated choice

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000678
Type formula
assumes Constant annual rate over the delay between the two illnesses
Days of ill health weighed by their number in the TEMPUS equation
Individual implied rate used for description and not as the social rate
has calculator text r = (y / 20)^(1 / (s - 2)) - 1
has common error note Individual implied rate used as the social discount rate. Applying the respondent's long-delay rate of 5.49% would leave a weight of 0.343 on a QALY in year 20 against 0.503 at the 3.5% of the NICE reference case, as in step 3 of the article's worked example, so prevention with distant gains would be valued about a third lower.
TEMPUS delay counted from now in place of from year 2. Using s in the exponent instead of s minus 2 spreads the trade-off over years that are not part of the delay. For 24 days in year 4 the rate becomes 4.66% instead of 9.54% (computed here for illustration), about half the true value.
TEMPUS ratio inverted to 20 over y. Writing (20/y) in place of (y/20) turns positive time preference into negative. For 24 days in year 4 the rate becomes minus 8.71% instead of plus 9.54% (computed here for illustration), so the respondent would be misclassified as preferring ill health sooner.
has description in the module Converts one answer to a TEMPUS open-ended question into the constant annual rate it implies. The respondent states the largest number of days y of ill health in year s at which a one-off minor treatment, delaying 20 days of ill health expected in 2 years' time, would still be worthwhile. With b = 1/(1 + r) the answer implies 20 b^2 = y b^s, which gives equation (1) of Cairns and van der Pol (2000). An answer above 20 days gives a positive rate, exactly 20 days a zero rate and fewer than 20 a negative rate. The rate is the r of the factor in HE-FM-DR-001, and rates that fall as the delay grows point to the non-constant forms of HE-FN-HYPD-001.

Implied inequality aversion from the switching weight by inverting the Atkinson relative weight

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000669
Type formula
assumes Ordered positive health levels and a weight of at least 1, Relative inequality concept of the implied aversion, Weights taken at baseline health for the implied aversion
has calculator text epsilon_star = log(w_star) / log(h_better / h_worse)
has common error note Reading the approximate aversion as the exact switching value. The formula gives about 2.38 for the article's example, but the EDE comparison switches at about 2.35. At an aversion of 2.36 the EDE of F already exceeds that of E by about 0.0002 years, although 2.36 lies below the approximate value.
Reporting a negative aversion when no trade-off exists. A switching weight below 1 means the fairer option has at least as much total health. An illustrative weight of 0.8 with 74 and 66 years returns about minus 1.95, which is not a valid Atkinson parameter, and the case is reported as having no trade-off.
Switching weight taken from per-person gains without population shares. Entering the per-person group gains in HE-FM-WE-004, whose group QALYs are totals, gives a switching weight of 0.35 divided by 0.40, or 0.875, in place of 0.21 divided by 0.16, or 1.3125. F then appears to be preferred even with equal weights, and the implied aversion comes out at about minus 1.17 instead of 2.38.
Using mean health in place of the better-off group's health. Replacing 74 years with the population mean of 70.8 in the ratio gives about 3.87 instead of 2.38, because the weight in HE-FM-ATK-004 compares the two groups, not one group with the mean.
has description in the module Inverts the live Atkinson relative weight HE-FM-ATK-004, in which a small gain to the worse-off group counts (h_better / h_worse) to the power epsilon times a gain to the better-off group. Setting that weight equal to the switching weight w_star, the w_s of HE-FM-WE-004 for the two options, and taking natural logarithms gives the approximate inequality aversion at which the two options tie. Cookson and colleagues note that an equity parameter implies a set of weights once combined with the existing distribution of health, and this formula reads the relation backwards. It is an approximation because the weights are taken at baseline health, while the exact switch solves the comparison of equally distributed equivalent health. The function log is the natural logarithm.

Incentive and participation slacks of a two-type procurement menu

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000931
Type formula
assumes Outside option of zero for both supplier types, Observable and enforceable quantity and transfer, Two cost types with constant marginal cost in the screening check, Weak inequalities and indifferent types in the screening check
has calculator text U_L = t_L - theta_L * q_L; U_H = t_H - theta_H * q_H; IC_L = U_L - (t_H - theta_L * q_H); IC_H = U_H - (t_L - theta_H * q_L); feasible = (IC_L >= 0) and (IC_H >= 0) and (U_L >= 0) and (U_H >= 0)
has common error note Checking participation only in a screening menu. A menu that pays each type its cost, such as 120 procedures for GBP 480,000 and 100 for GBP 500,000, passes both participation constraints, yet the low-cost type takes the second contract and earns GBP 100,000 (computed here). The purchaser then buys 100 procedures for GBP 500,000 from a supplier whose cost is GBP 400,000, so a menu is checked against all four constraints.
Mimicking payoff evaluated at the wrong type's cost. The incentive constraint of the low-cost type values the high-cost contract at the low cost, t_H minus theta_L q_H. Using theta_H there turns IC_L into U_L minus U_H, which is 0 for the first-best menu of HE-EX-MECH-002, so a menu that fails by 100 (GBP 100,000) is passed as feasible (computed here).
Strict inequality used for a binding screening constraint. The purchaser's optimal menu leaves the low-cost type exactly indifferent, IC_L = 0 in HE-EX-MECH-001. Testing IC_L > 0 in place of IC_L >= 0 rejects the second-best menu, and with costs typed as 4.0 and 4.6 a binding slack can carry a floating-point residue (about 6E-14 in a Python check of the second-best menu for those costs), which the ROUND in HE-IM-MECH-001 removes.
has description in the module A purchaser offers two contracts, (t_L, q_L) intended for a low-cost supplier and (t_H, q_H) for a high-cost one, and cannot observe which type it faces. Each type's information rent is its transfer less its cost on its own contract, and each incentive slack is that rent less what the type would earn by taking the other contract at its own cost. The menu is incentive feasible when both incentive slacks and both rents are at least zero, inequalities (2.9) to (2.12) of Laffont and Martimort. These are the article's incentive compatibility and participation constraints for one participant with two types and an outside option of zero. A low-cost type that takes the high-cost contract earns the high-cost type's rent plus (theta_H minus theta_L) q_H, which is why a menu that leaves both types no rent fails. Each rent takes the form of the margin in HE-FM-CTH-001 with no reimbursed share (derived), there computed per case of hospital care; the incentive slacks, which value one type's cost on the other type's contract, have no live counterpart.

Authors' manuscript dated 6 February 2001, deposited in Toulouse Capitole Publications, record 14941 (full text read). Published as The Theory of Incentives. The Principal-Agent Model. Princeton University Press; 2002. doi:10.1515/9781400829453 (not seen). The printed book numbers the chapter 2 sections one lower than the manuscript (its section 2.3 is Incentive Feasible Menu of Contracts) and its equation numbers were not checked, so the section and equation numbers below are the manuscript's. Chapter 2, section 2.4.1 (Incentive Compatibility and Participation), Definition 2.1 and inequalities (2.9) and (2.10), the incentive constraints t minus theta q at least t-bar minus theta q-bar for the efficient type and the reverse for the inefficient type; inequalities (2.11) and (2.12), the participation constraints with a zero status quo; Definition 2.2, a menu is incentive feasible when (2.9) to (2.12) hold; footnote 8 on weak preference. Section 2.5 (Information Rents), (2.18), the efficient type's payoff from mimicking equals the inefficient type's rent plus Delta theta times the inefficient type's output. Sections 2.2.1 and 2.2.2 set the linear cost, the two types and the verifiable quantity and transfer. https://publications.ut-capitole.fr/id/eprint/14941/1/Laffont_14941.pdf
Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences. Mechanism design theory. Scientific background on the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel 2007. 2007 (full text read). Section 2.1 (Incentive compatibility and the revelation principle) states Hurwicz's definition of an incentive-compatible direct mechanism, adds a participation constraint that no agent be made worse off by participating, and states that by the revelation principle much of the literature seeks a direct mechanism that maximises the goal function subject to the incentive-compatibility constraint and, where appropriate, the participation constraint, the problem the article displays. https://www.nobelprize.org/uploads/2018/06/advanced-economicsciences2007.pdf

Incidence-based years lived with disability for one sequela without discounting

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000581
Type formula
assumes Constant weight over the whole duration of a case, Future health loss assigned to the year and age of onset
definition source the Source rows of the Functions and Formulae module record HE-FM-YLD-001
editor note The incidence-based years lived with disability without discounting, the convention of the Global Burden of Disease study of 1990. The DALY of HEMO-HOOK-05 uses the prevalence-based form HE-FM-DWT-001.
feeds DALYs for a cause as the sum of its years of life lost and years lived with disability
formalises disability weight
has calculator text YLD_inc = I * DW * L
has common error note Comparing an incidence-based YLD with a figure from GBD 2010 onwards. GBD 2010 and WHO switched to prevalence-based YLDs, so an incidence-based figure counts a different quantity; the two agree only when incidence and duration have been stable for a long time.
Placing the health loss at the age of onset when ages of experience matter. In an incidence perspective all YLDs for congenital hearing loss fall at age 0, whereas in a prevalence perspective they are spread fairly evenly across age groups, which suits what WHO notes policy-makers are often more interested in, the ages at which health loss is experienced.
Reading the fall in an incidence-based count as a fall in current burden. WHO lists as the first drawback of the incidence approach that it does not reflect the current prevalent burden of a condition whose incidence has fallen substantially; in the article's example the count halves at once while people with earlier onset still live with the condition.
has Content MathML <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><apply><csymbol cd="relation1">eq</csymbol><ci>YLD_inc</ci><apply><csymbol cd="arith1">times</csymbol><ci>I</ci><ci>DW</ci><ci>L</ci></apply></apply></math>
has description in the module Counts the new cases of a sequela in the reference year and multiplies them by the disability weight and by the average duration of a case until remission or death, so all of each case's future health loss is assigned to the year, and the age, in which it begins. This is the form used by the GBD 1990 study and WHO's updates before 2010, here without their discounting and age weighting.

assumes Mutually exclusive options with the larger option costing more, One classification for both options in an incremental ratio
has calculator text BCR_YX = (PVB_Y - PVB_X) / (PVC_Y - PVC_X)
has common error note Choosing between exclusive options by their average ratios. Picking the option with the higher ratio against doing nothing selects X in the article's base case (2.0 against 1.56 counted gross, 5.0 against 2.25 netted) and gives up £1.0 million of net present value. The choice between exclusive options rests on the incremental ratio or on net present value.
has description in the module Divides the extra present-value benefits of option Y over option X by its extra present-value costs. When Y costs more than X, an incremental ratio above one is the same condition as Y having the higher net present value, so the ratio applied incrementally gives the same choice as net present value. Average ratios of each option against doing nothing do not.

Incremental cost per QALY of a programme with two cost instalments and one later QALY gain under separate cost and health rates

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000569
Type formula
assumes Amounts fall at whole-year points with year 0 as the start of treatment
Increments over the same comparator for each programme
has calculator text C_d = C_0 + C_a / (1 + r_C)^a; Q_d = Q_b / (1 + r_H)^b; ICER = C_d / Q_d
has common error note Expecting a lower health rate to make future QALYs count more than present ones. A lower health rate raises the weight of a QALY in year 20 from about 0.50 at 3.5 per cent to about 0.74 at 1.5 per cent, relative to costs and to a QALY today, but the weight stays below one.
Reading a ratio from one pair of rates against a threshold set for another. The NICE reference case discounts costs and health effects at 3.5 per cent a year, so its threshold range applies to ratios like the 34,004 pounds of the first example, not to the 23,490 pounds the same programme shows at 3 and 1.5 per cent; a report should state both rates and the guideline behind them.
Treating the NICE 1.5 per cent option as differential discounting. PMG36 allows a non-reference-case rate of 1.5 per cent for both costs and health effects when all three of its criteria are met, which is uniform discounting at a lower rate; it gives the prevention programme 25,074 pounds per QALY, not the 23,490 of the 3 and 1.5 per cent pair.
has description in the module Discounts a cost paid at the start (year 0) and a second cost in year a at the cost rate, discounts a QALY gain that arrives in year b at the health rate, and divides the discounted cost by the discounted QALY gain. It is the article's prevention programme, whose costs fall early and whose health gain falls late, so the pair of rates can change its ratio a great deal; a treatment with all its cost in year 0 is the special case with no second instalment.

Incremental net monetary benefit written through the ICER in each quadrant of the cost-effectiveness plane

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000663
Type formula
assumes Non-zero effect difference in the quadrant identity, One subtraction direction for the ratio and the net benefit
has calculator text R = Delta_C / Delta_E; INMB = Delta_E * (lambda - R)
has common error note Effect difference near zero read through the ratio. With an extra cost of GBP 10, an effect difference of 0.001 QALYs gives R of GBP 10,000 per QALY and a difference of minus 0.001 gives minus GBP 10,000, which reverses how the ratio is read, while INMB at GBP 20,000 per QALY moves only from GBP 10 to minus GBP 30 (computed here for illustration). Stinnett and Mullahy note that ratios of near-infinite size when the effect difference is close to zero also disturb bootstrap estimates of the ratio's mean and variance.
Positive ratio below the threshold accepted in the south-west quadrant. A cheaper, less effective option with R of GBP 10,000 per QALY looks acceptable at GBP 20,000 when its quadrant is ignored, yet INMB is minus GBP 1,000 because the saving per QALY forgone is below the value of that QALY. In this quadrant the option is acceptable only when R exceeds lambda, for example a saving of GBP 3,000 for 0.10 QALYs lost, which gives R of GBP 30,000 and INMB of GBP 1,000 (computed here for illustration). HE-ER-NMB-003 describes the same error in general terms.
has description in the module Rewrites incremental net monetary benefit (HE-FM-NMB-002) as the effect difference times the gap between the threshold and the ICER (HE-FM-ICER-001), which holds whenever Delta_E is not zero. The sign of INMB is the sign of Delta_E times the sign of lambda minus R. With a health gain (north-east and south-east) a positive INMB means R below lambda, and with a health loss (south-west and north-west) it means R above lambda, so the same ratio can call for opposite decisions. This is the ambiguity between quadrants that Stinnett and Mullahy describe. Plotted against lambda, the expression is the line that Hoch and colleagues describe, with intercept minus Delta_C, slope Delta_E and a zero crossing at the ICER.

Incremental utility-cost ratio in QALYs gained per one million of net expenditure

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000605
Type formula
assumes Both increments of the utility-cost ratio from one comparison, Quadrant fixes how an incremental utility-cost ratio is read
has calculator text IUCR = Delta_Q / Delta_C * 1000000
has common error note Averaging subgroup utility-cost ratios directly. PHARMAC states that directly weighting the estimates for each subgroup is not appropriate. In an illustrative case with two equal subgroups, one with increments of 0.40 QALYs and GBP 8,400 (IUCR 47.619) and one with 0.10 QALYs and GBP 20,000 (IUCR 5.000), the mean of the two ratios is 26.310. Averaging first gives 0.25 QALYs and GBP 14,200, an IUCR of 17.606, which is the correct aggregate.
Ignoring the quadrant of a positive utility-cost ratio. An illustrative intervention that saves GBP 8,400 and loses 0.40 QALYs has the same IUCR of 47.619 as the article's example, but it counts QALYs lost per GBP 1 million saved. At GBP 25,000 per QALY its incremental net monetary benefit is minus GBP 1,600, so the same figure that supports the north-east case rejects the south-west one, as Paulden describes for the ICER.
Reading a utility-cost ratio as if lower were better. The IUCR runs in the opposite direction to the ICUR. In the article's table, at an incremental cost of GBP 8,400, an IUCR of 47.619 is the GBP 21,000 per QALY case and an IUCR of 5.952 the GBP 168,000 per QALY case, so reading the smaller IUCR as the better result inverts the conclusion. The direction of a reported figure has to be checked before figures from PHARMAC and from other agencies are compared.
has description in the module Divides the incremental QALYs by the incremental cost, both taken as the intervention minus the comparator and both discounted, and multiplies by one million. PHARMAC calls the result the incremental utility-cost ratio (IUCR) and describes the incremental cost per QALY as in effect its inverse, so 1,000,000 divided by the IUCR returns the ICUR of HE-FM-CUA-001. For a QALY gain at extra cost a higher IUCR indicates better value, the opposite direction to the ICUR.

Incurred claims and unpaid claims from a completion factor

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000345
Type formula
assumes Past payment pattern applies to the current month, Completion factor matched to the lag of the month
has calculator text I_m = P_m / c_d; U_m = I_m - P_m
has common error note Applying completion factors to paid claims inflated by large claims. When the amount paid to date includes an unusually high number or amount of large claims, dividing by the completion factor scales those claims up as if more were still to come, so incurred claims are overstated. Large claims are reviewed and adjusted before the factor is applied.
Dividing by the share paid in one month instead of the cumulative share. If 30% of a month's claims are typically paid in the second month alone, dividing £4 million by 0.30 gives about £13.33 million instead of £5 million. The completion factor is the cumulative share paid by the lag, not the increment.
Using unadjusted paid claims for recent months. Counting the £4 million paid so far as the month's cost understates it by £1 million, a fifth of the estimated £5 million. Applied to the latest months of a claims extract, unadjusted totals suggest a spurious fall in spending.
has description in the module Estimates the total claims incurred for a month of service by dividing the amount paid so far by the completion factor, the cumulative share of a month's eventual claims that past experience shows to be paid by the same lag. The difference between estimated incurred and paid claims is the unpaid claims liability for that month, covering both unreported claims and claims reported but not yet paid.

Inequity share of a decomposed health gap under stated fairness judgements

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000433
Type formula
assumes Parts that add up to the standardised gap for the inequity share, Positive standardised gap for the inequity share
has calculator text Delta = sum_(j=1)^J [Delta_j] + Delta_res; s = (sum_(j=1)^J [u_j * Delta_j] + u_res * Delta_res) / Delta
has common error note Carrying an individual-level judgement on unexplained variation over to groups without saying so. Asada and colleagues considered unexplained variation between individuals. Treating a residual gap between groups in the same way is an analogy, as the article notes, and is reported as an assumption of the analysis.
Reading the inequity share as fixed by the data. The same standardised gap gives shares of 1, 0.6875, 0.625 and 0.3125 under the four combinations of judgements in the article's table, computed here for illustration. Asada and colleagues found the same dependence in survey data, with about 60% of inequality inequitable under direct standardisation and almost all of it under indirect standardisation.
has description in the module Expresses the inequity in a decomposed gap as a share of the whole gap. The gap is first rebuilt from its explained parts and the unexplained remainder, and the inequity counts each explained part judged unfair and the remainder when it is judged unfair. An indicator of 0 for the remainder gives the direct unfairness result of HE-FM-INEQ-002 and an indicator of 1 the fairness gap result of HE-FM-INEQ-003. Asada and colleagues report results in this form for survey data, with about 60% of health inequality inequitable when unexplained variation was treated as acceptable and almost all of it when it was treated as unfair.

Abstract, which treats unexplained inequality as ethically acceptable under direct standardisation and as unfair under indirect standardisation, and reports that about 75% of the variation in the Health Utilities Index was unexplained and that about 60% of health inequality was inequitable under direct standardisation against almost all of it under indirect standardisation. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12939-015-0138-2

Infections averted in one step under a static and a dynamic force of infection

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000712
Type formula
assumes Both runs share parameters and differ only in their compartment counts
has calculator text lambda_b = beta * I_b / N; A_stat = lambda_b * (S_b - S_p) * dt; A_dyn = beta * (S_b * I_b - S_p * I_p) / N * dt; A_ind = A_dyn - A_stat
has common error note Static count of infections averted reported as the whole effect of a programme. Over the article's two days the static count averts 13.16 infections and the dynamic count 14.58, so the static figure misses 1.42, about a tenth of the dynamic total, and at the article's GBP 40 per infection treated it values averted treatment costs at GBP 526 instead of GBP 583. The gap grows over the early generations of transmission, to about 2,024.6 infections by day 29 with the article's inputs, and then narrows to about 482.6 once both epidemics have ended (HE-CF-CMPM-001, computed here for illustration), so a static count from a short run understates the indirect effect by a different share from one taken over the whole epidemic.
has description in the module Compares one step of a programme run with the same step of the no-programme run. The static count applies the no-programme force of infection lambda_b to the programme's susceptibles, so infections averted are lambda_b times the fall in susceptibles, the direct effect only. The dynamic count recalculates the force of infection from the programme's own infectious count, as the WHO guide describes for a dynamic model, and the difference A_ind is the indirect effect of fewer infectious people, which simplifies to beta S_p (I_b minus I_p) dt/N (derived). The two counts agree in a step that both runs start with the same infectious count and diverge once the programme has lowered I. Summed over the article's two days this gives the article's comparison, and HE-CF-CMPM-001 runs longer horizons with the static run keeping its own susceptible count, and Jit and Brisson explain why against no intervention the dynamic count is usually the larger, so that a static estimate is conservative.

has source in the module Jit M, Brisson M. Modelling the epidemiology of infectious diseases for decision analysis. A primer. PharmacoEconomics. 2011;29(5):371-386. Section 3.1, Types of Models, which defines the force of infection as the instantaneous rate at which susceptible people become infected, constant in a static model and a function of the proportion infected in a dynamic model; and section 3.2, When to Use Transmission Dynamic Models, which states that a dynamic model will usually show an intervention as more cost effective than an equivalent static model, because it predicts more infections prevented, including those indirectly protected through herd immunity, and a faster fall in infections, and that a static model may therefore be sufficient to obtain a conservative estimate of cost effectiveness. https://doi.org/10.2165/11539960-000000000-00000
Pitman R, Fisman D, Zaric GS, Postma M, Kretzschmar M, Edmunds J, Brisson M. Dynamic transmission modeling. A report of the ISPOR-SMDM Modeling Good Research Practices Task Force-5. Value in Health. 2012;15(6):828-834. The section on when a dynamic approach is appropriate, with best practice V-1, which calls for a dynamic model when an intervention has an impact on disease transmission in the target population, and its subsection Indirect effects of intervention programs, which states that indirect effects are not always beneficial because a higher average age at infection increases complication risk and mortality for many diseases, for example hepatitis A and varicella; and section Reporting Results and Informing Decision Making, which states that infections can be disaggregated according to whether they are directly or indirectly prevented. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jval.2012.06.011
World Health Organization. WHO guide for standardization of economic evaluations of immunization programmes, 2nd edition (WHO/IVB/19.10). Geneva, WHO, 2019. Section 6.3.1, Basic types of infectious disease models, which states that in a dynamic transmission model the force of infection can change over time, that a dynamic model recalculates it cyclically or continuously from the proportion of infectious people it projects at each point in time, that in a static model it remains constant and independent of the proportion of infectious people, and that dynamic models are typically solved as differential equations in continuous time, with discrete time intervals often applied for practical reasons. https://iris.who.int/handle/10665/329389

Type formula
assumes Deaths measure information for a survival outcome, Final number of deaths estimated while the trial runs
has calculator text t_k = d_k / D
has common error note Measuring the information fraction in calendar time. Using elapsed calendar time, for example two years of a planned four, gives t of 0.5 even when only 100 of 400 deaths have occurred. Under the Pocock type function the trial would then spend about 0.0155 instead of about 0.0089 at that look, using error that belongs to later analyses.
has description in the module Measures trial progress on the information scale that a spending function uses: the information available at analysis k divided by the information planned for the final analysis. For a survival outcome compared with the log-rank test, the fraction is approximated by the deaths observed so far divided by the deaths expected by the end of the trial. For a comparison of means it is the number of patients analysed divided by the target sample size.

Integer optimum of the 0-1 funding problem for four indivisible programmes with its gaps to a funding rule and to the divisible fill

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000922
Type formula
assumes Positive costs and QALY gains on one basis in the 0-1 funding problem
Whole programmes, one budget and independent additive gains in the 0-1 funding problem
Ties and comparison inputs for the integer optimum
has calculator text H_star = max(max(max(max(max(max(max(max(max(max(max(max(max(max((c_1 <= B) * q_1, (c_2 <= B) * q_2), (c_3 <= B) * q_3), (c_4 <= B) * q_4), (c_1 + c_2 <= B) * (q_1 + q_2)), (c_1 + c_3 <= B) * (q_1 + q_3)), (c_1 + c_4 <= B) * (q_1 + q_4)), (c_2 + c_3 <= B) * (q_2 + q_3)), (c_2 + c_4 <= B) * (q_2 + q_4)), (c_3 + c_4 <= B) * (q_3 + q_4)), (c_1 + c_2 + c_3 <= B) * (q_1 + q_2 + q_3)), (c_1 + c_2 + c_4 <= B) * (q_1 + q_2 + q_4)), (c_1 + c_3 + c_4 <= B) * (q_1 + q_3 + q_4)), (c_2 + c_3 + c_4 <= B) * (q_2 + q_3 + q_4)), (c_1 + c_2 + c_3 + c_4 <= B) * (q_1 + q_2 + q_3 + q_4)); G_rule = H_star - H_rule; L_ind = H_div - H_star
has common error note Adding the gains of programmes that serve overlapping patients. If B and C in the article's table served overlapping patients, so that funding both gained an illustrative 280 QALYs in place of 375, the additive model would still choose B plus C and report 375, while A plus D, at 290, would then be the better package by 10 QALYs (computed here for illustration). Interacting programmes need a joint cost and gain for the combination, or extra variables and constraints, before the search.
Reporting the divisible fill as the health a budget buys from whole programmes. The divisible fill of the article's table reports 392 QALYs for GBP 10 million, but no package of whole programmes buys more than 375, so 17 of the reported QALYs cannot be delivered. H_div is a ceiling on H_star for independent programmes, not an achievable total, as HE-ER-CELT-006 shows for the league table.
Rounding the divisible answer in place of solving the 0-1 funding problem. For the article's programmes the divisible answer funds A and 0.8 of B. Rounding the share of B up gives A plus B at GBP 11 million, over the GBP 10 million budget, and rounding it down gives A alone at 240 QALYs, 135 below the optimum of 375 (computed here for illustration). Crown and colleagues warn that a rounded solution may be infeasible, or feasible but not optimal.
has description in the module Each of the 15 packages that fund at least one of four programmes contributes its total QALYs when its total cost is at most the budget and zero when it is not, and H_star is the largest contribution, the optimum of the article's binary problem of maximising the sum of q_i x_i subject to the sum of c_i x_i at most B with each x_i equal to 0 or 1. Funding nothing gives zero, so H_star is zero when no programme fits. G_rule is the health that a funding rule's package, with health H_rule, leaves unbought at the same budget, the loss of benefit that Crown and colleagues say optimisation shows for the choice finally made, and with H_rule taken from HE-FM-CELT-003 it is the gain of the optimum over the league table. L_ind is the health the divisible fill of HE-FM-CELT-001, H_div, buys above the optimum, the health lost purely because programmes cannot be split (derived). The formula is written out for four programmes so that it runs as calculator text, and HE-CF-IPH-001 does the same search for any number.

has source in the module Crown W, Buyukkaramikli N, Sir MY, Thokala P, Morton A, Marshall DA, Tosh JC, Ijzerman MJ, Padula WV, Pasupathy KS. Application of constrained optimization methods in health services research: report 2 of the ISPOR Optimization Methods Emerging Good Practices Task Force. Value in Health. 2018;21(9):1019-1028. Section 2, Overview of applications of constrained optimization in health care (accepted manuscript), which describes a planner with a number of investment opportunities and a fixed budget inadequate to fund them all, states that choosing the best set to fund under a fixed budget to meet an objective such as maximising total QALYs can be addressed as an optimisation problem, citing Martello and Toth on knapsack problems, and gives vaccination leaving fewer cases to treat as an example of interactions between investments. The abstract's Conclusions state that the methods give decision makers insight into optimal target solutions and the magnitude of the loss of benefit or increased costs associated with the ultimate policy choice. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jval.2018.05.003
Crown W, Buyukkaramikli N, Thokala P, Morton A, Sir MY, Marshall DA, Tosh J, Padula WV, Ijzerman MJ, Wong PK, Pasupathy KS. Constrained optimization methods in health services research: an introduction. Report 1 of the ISPOR Optimization Methods Emerging Good Practices Task Force. Value in Health. 2017;20(3):310-319. Section A Simple Illustration of a Constrained Optimization Problem, which writes the problem of a health care centre as maximising health benefit f_R x_R + f_L x_L subject to a budget constraint c_R x_R + c_L x_L at most B and a time constraint, with the decision variables zero or above and integer, places it in linear optimisation because the objective and constraints are linear while the decision variables must be integers, and warns that rounding a linear solution can give an infeasible solution or, if feasible, one that is not optimal. Section Definition of Constrained Optimization notes that in some problems two or more different decisions may yield the same optimum, and the table of model components contrasts deterministic and stochastic problems. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jval.2017.01.013
Dakin H, Tsiachristas A. Rationing in an era of multiple tight constraints: is cost-utility analysis still fit for purpose? Applied Health Economics and Health Policy. 2024;22(3):315-329 (author manuscript read in Europe PMC, PMC7615833). Section 2.1, Constrained optimisation, which states that constrained optimisation can allocate resources across a healthcare system to maximise population health conditional on the budget and any other constraints, calls this an integer programming approach that has been adapted for healthcare, and frames the allocation as a 0-1 knapsack problem of choosing which items to pack to maximise value without exceeding a weight constraint or packing more than one of each item. Section 2.2 states that the league table, adopting interventions from the lowest ICER upwards until the budget is exhausted, is equivalent to the greedy algorithm for the knapsack problem. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40258-023-00858-w
Stinnett AA, Paltiel AD. Mathematical programming for the efficient allocation of health care resources. Journal of Health Economics. 1996;15(5):641-653. Abstract, which states that previous discussions of allocating health care resources subject to a budget constraint relied on unnecessarily restrictive assumptions, that a general mathematical programming framework can accommodate returns to scale, partial and complete indivisibility and programme interdependence, and that methods are presented for incorporating ethical constraints, including explicit identification of the cost of equity. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0167-6296(96)00493-6

Inter-arrival gap sampled by inverse transform

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000317
Type formula
assumes Constant rate until the next arrival, Fresh independent random number for each arrival gap
has calculator text X = -log(U) / lambda
has common error note Constant-rate gaps for time-varying demand. Sampling every gap at the daily average rate removes the daytime peak, so the simulation shows the congestion and cover cost of steady demand. A service with a peak needs a time-varying rate, for example generated by thinning.
Multiplying by the arrival rate instead of dividing. Writing the gap as minus log U times lambda treats the rate as a mean gap. At 3 patients per hour and U of 0.5 it gives about 2.08 hours instead of 0.231, so arrivals are generated nine times too slowly.
has description in the module Samples the gap to the next arrival in a homogeneous Poisson process by inverting the exponential distribution function. The function log is the natural logarithm. In a discrete event simulation the sampled gap is added to the current arrival time, S_n equal to S_(n-1) plus X, and the next arrival is placed on the event queue.

Inverse probability weighted ATE estimator

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000348
Type formula
assumes Ignorability given the propensity covariates, Overlap of treated and untreated patients for IPW, Correctly specified propensity score model
has calculator text ATE_IPW = (1/n) * sum_(i=1)^n (T_i * Y_i / e_i) - (1/n) * sum_(i=1)^n ((1 - T_i) * Y_i / (1 - e_i))
has common error note Comparing unweighted arm means under confounding by indication. In the 20-patient example the treated average 4.91 QALYs and the untreated 5.80, a difference of minus 0.89 QALYs, with mean costs of £7,800 against £2,300. Sicker patients are treated more often, so the raw comparison makes the treatment look harmful when the ATE is a gain of 0.22 QALYs.
Leaving extreme inverse probability weights unchecked. A treated patient with a propensity score of 0.01 receives a weight of 100 and counts as 100 patients in the treated mean. TSD 17 warns that scores close to zero make the method unstable, so the distribution of propensity scores and weights is examined before the estimate is used.
Weighting untreated patients by one over the propensity score. Using one over e_i for untreated patients, instead of one over one minus e_i, gives an untreated weighted mean of about 11.03 QALYs in the 20-patient example, far above the 6.10 QALYs of the best-off patient, and an estimate of about minus 5.61 QALYs.
has description in the module Estimates the ATE from patient-level observational data. Each treated patient is weighted by one over the propensity score and each untreated patient by one over one minus the propensity score, so that each weighted arm resembles the whole sample, and the estimate is the difference between the two weighted means. Applied with the same weights to costs and to QALYs, it gives the incremental cost and QALYs for the ICER (HE-FM-ICER-001) and the incremental net monetary benefit (HE-FM-NMB-002).

has implementation IPW ATE estimate from patient rows

Section on inverse probability of treatment weighting using the propensity score, which defines each patient's weight as the inverse of the probability of the treatment actually received and gives this estimator of the ATE. https://doi.org/10.1080/00273171.2011.568786

NICE DSU Technical Support Document 17: the use of observational data to inform estimates of treatment effectiveness in technology appraisal: methods for comparative individual patient data. Sheffield: Decision Support Unit, ScHARR; 2015. IPCW-weighted Kaplan-Meier survival through one interval with two prognostic groups

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000525
Type formula
assumes Dependent censoring explained by the measured prognostic groups, Switchers censored before deaths in the IPCW-weighted interval
has calculator text S_2 = S_1 * (1 - (w_1 * d_1 + w_2 * d_2) / (w_1 * n_1 + w_2 * n_2))
has common error note Assuming censoring at switch is conservative. The bias runs in the direction of who switches: if poorer-prognosis patients switch, as here, control survival is overstated and the benefit understated; if fitter patients switch, the bias reverses.
Censoring switchers without weighting. Because switchers came from the poorer-prognosis group, simple censoring raises two-year survival from 0.585 to 0.619; the NICE manual advises avoiding censoring or excluding patients who cross over, because these methods are very susceptible to selection bias.
has description in the module Applies one Kaplan-Meier step with weighted counts: weighted deaths divided by the weighted number at risk give the interval's hazard, and survival is carried forward by the product-limit rule (unweighted form HE-FM-ADMC-002). Weighting non-switchers rebuilds the risk set that censoring at switch removed. Written for two prognostic groups; with more groups each adds a term to both sums.

Isoelastic Atkinson health social welfare of three equal-sized groups for epsilon other than 1

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000680
Type formula
assumes Equal-sized groups each at its mean health in the isoelastic welfare
Inequality aversion as a value judgement in the isoelastic welfare
Isoelastic welfare and the NICE limits on inequality aversion functions
has calculator text W = h_1^(1 - epsilon) / (1 - epsilon) + h_2^(1 - epsilon) / (1 - epsilon) + h_3^(1 - epsilon) / (1 - epsilon)
has common error note Comparing isoelastic welfare values across epsilon values. W for option P is about 49.5993 at epsilon of 0.5 and minus 0.0442201 at epsilon of 2. The fall reflects the change of scale alone, so W is compared only between allocations at one epsilon, and a comparison across epsilon values uses EDE health from HE-FM-ATK-002, which is in years of QALE.
Dropping the divisor 1 minus epsilon from isoelastic welfare. For epsilon above 1 the divisor is negative, so leaving it out flips the sign of every term and reverses the ranking. In the article's example at epsilon of 2 the values become 0.0442201 for P, 0.0441926 for T and 0.0443603 for R, so R would appear best and T worst, the opposite of the correct order.
has description in the module Adds h_i^(1-epsilon)/(1-epsilon) over the groups, the welfare function Atkinson derived from constant relative inequality aversion with its two constants set to 0 and 1, which leaves every ranking unchanged. The line is written for the three groups of the article's example, and with n people or groups the sum has n terms. At epsilon of 0 W is total health, the utilitarian rule of maximising total QALYs; as epsilon rises the weight on a small gain to group i, h_i^(-epsilon), shifts priority to the less healthy (HE-FM-ATK-004), and the ranking approaches the maximin rule of HE-FM-SWF-003. Solving W = n h_EDE^(1-epsilon)/(1-epsilon) for h_EDE gives the EDE health of HE-FM-ATK-002, so W and EDE health rank allocations identically, and W has meaning only in comparisons made at the same epsilon.

Japanese foreign average price adjustment of a calculated new drug price

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000706
Type formula
assumes Adjustment limited to the pricing methods named by the MHLW, Foreign average price trimmed before the adjustment
has calculator text P_adj = min(max(P_calc, min(P_calc / 3 + P_fap / 2, 2 * P_calc)), P_calc / 3 + 5 * P_fap / 6)
has common error note Price cut to exactly 1.25 times the foreign average. Setting the price to the threshold gives 131.25 in place of about 134.17 for a calculated price of 140 against 105. The slide's formula keeps one third of the excess above 1.25 times the foreign average, 2.92 here (derived here).
Raise applied without the cap at twice the calculated price. Without the cap a calculated price of 20 against 105 rises to about 59.17, almost three times the calculated value, against the capped 40 (computed here for illustration).
has description in the module Moves a price calculated by cost accounting, or by similar efficacy comparison for a product without a similar pharmacological action, towards the foreign average price when it is far from it, as the 2021 MHLW slide sets out. Above 1.25 times the foreign average the price becomes P_calc/3 plus 5 P_fap/6, below 0.75 times it becomes P_calc/3 plus P_fap/2 up to twice P_calc, and between the two it is unchanged. The single line writes the slide's branches with min and max (derived here); the branches meet the unchanged price at exactly 1.25 and 0.75 times P_fap, so a tie at either threshold gives the same price whichever branch is applied. P_fap is the mean of the converted prices of the four-country basket after the slide's trimming of an outlying highest price, a mean that HE-CF-BOC-002 computes for any number of countries, and the threshold test is HE-FM-BOC-004.

Jevons elementary aggregate of three matched consumer prices

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000714
Type formula
assumes Equal weights for the prices in a Jevons elementary aggregate
Matched products with positive prices in a Jevons elementary aggregate
has calculator text J = (p1_t / p1_0 * p2_t / p2_0 * p3_t / p3_0)^(1 / 3)
has common error note Carli arithmetic mean of relatives in place of the Jevons index. The arithmetic mean of the worked example relatives is 1, no change, against a Jevons fall of about 0.33%, and an arithmetic mean is never below the geometric mean of the same relatives (computed here for illustration). The manual records that Eurostat regulations forbid the Carli index and that in certain circumstances, combined with chain-linking of the within-year indices, it introduces an upward bias known as chain drift (section 3.4).
Unmatched replacement product entered as a Jevons price change. Replacing the third product, priced 4.00 in the base month, with a different product at 3.00 and treating it as the same item gives a Jevons index of 0.937889, a spurious fall of about 6.2% (illustrative, computed here for illustration). The manual excludes such a price or makes a quality adjustment (sections 3.4 and 9).
has description in the module Combines the prices of matched products within one elementary aggregate, where no expenditure weights exist, as the geometric mean of their price relatives, the formula the ONS technical manual names as the one primarily used at this level in the UK CPI and CPIH (section 3.4). Each price carries the same weight, the reciprocal of the number of prices. The manual gives an algebraically equivalent form, the ratio of the geometric means of current and base prices. J is a ratio, and 100 times it gives the elementary index on the scale of HE-FM-CPI-001; item and higher-level indices are weighted averages of these elementary indices (section 3.5). The formula is written out for three prices so that the calculator runs.

Kakwani index of progressivity for a health financing source

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000371
Type formula
assumes Health payments attributed by economic incidence, Kakwani index read alongside the concentration and Lorenz curves, Same ability to pay ranking for both indices in the Kakwani index
has calculator text pi_K = C_P - G_X
has common error note Ranking households by the payment instead of by ability to pay. Ranking households by the size of their payment gives the Gini coefficient of payments, not their concentration index. The Gini coefficient of payments is never smaller than their concentration index, so the source looks more progressive than it is whenever households with similar ability to pay make different payments.
Subtracting the payment concentration index from the Gini coefficient. Reversing the order, G_X minus C_P, flips the sign of the index. Out-of-pocket payments in the article's example would then show a value of 0.168 and appear progressive, although they take a falling share of income as income rises.
has description in the module Measures how far one source of health finance departs from proportionality to ability to pay, as the concentration index of the payment minus the Gini coefficient of ability to pay. It equals twice the area between the Lorenz curve of ability to pay and the concentration curve of the payment. A positive value indicates a progressive source, a negative value a regressive one, and zero is consistent with proportionality.

Kaldor-Hicks aggregate net gain across groups

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000262
Type formula
assumes Equal weight on every unit of money, Hypothetical compensation, Consistent ranking
has calculator text NG = sum_(i=1)^n [N_i * CV_i]
has common error note Omitting the programme's resource cost. In applied cost-benefit analysis the opportunity cost of the resources used is a loss to someone and enters the sum. The worked example sets it aside only because every option costs the same.
Reading a positive net gain as a Pareto improvement. A net gain of 100,000 pounds leaves 1,000 people worse off unless compensation is paid. The test shows potential, not actual, improvement.
has description in the module Adds the money measure of each group's gain or loss, weighted by the number of people in the group. A change passes the Kaldor potential compensation test when the total is greater than zero, because the gainers could then compensate the losers and still be better off, whether or not compensation is paid. The sum is the welfare-economic basis of net benefit in cost-benefit analysis, where the programme's resource cost enters as a loss.

Kaplan-Meier step with a risk set restricted to people who have already entered

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000541
Type formula
assumes Entry and event times independent in the risk-set correction, Follow-up intervals open at entry and closed at exit
has calculator text n_j = N_in - N_out; S_j = S_prev * (1 - d_j / n_j)
has common error note Dropping late entrants instead of using their entry times. Restricting the analysis to patients with no delay discards most of a registry cohort and, as Brown and colleagues note, introduces other selection biases.
Numbers-at-risk tables that only fall. With late entry the number at risk can rise as well as fall; a table that only decreases suggests entry times were not used.
Starting every record at the origin. In the example the naive curve ends at 0.25 at 33 months instead of 0.1875; in Betensky and Mandel's simulation of two groups with identical survival, one entering 1.5 years after the origin, a Cox model ignoring delayed entry gave a hazard ratio of 5.01 instead of 1.
has description in the module Counts the risk set at an event time as those who have entered and not yet left. With follow-up intervals open at entry and closed at exit, a person is at risk at t_j when L_i < t_j <= X_i, so the count is the number who entered before t_j less the number who exited before t_j (anyone who left before t_j had also entered before it). The product-limit step itself is HE-FM-ADMC-002; only the risk set changes.

Kaplan-Meier survival under administrative censoring

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000424
Type formula
assumes Censoring at the cut-off unrelated to prognosis, Censored patients at risk at their own censoring time
has calculator text S_j = S_prev * (1 - d_j / n_j)
has common error note Censored patients dropped from the analysis. Excluding the four censored patients leaves four known outcomes, all deaths, which implies that no one survives. The Kaplan-Meier estimate of 0.40 instead uses each patient for as long as they were observed.
Censored patients kept in the Kaplan-Meier risk set. Removing only the deaths from the risk set treats censored patients as if they were still observed. In the article's arm the risk sets at months 14 and 20 become 6 and 5 instead of 5 and 3, and survival ends at 0.50 rather than 0.40, the same answer as counting every censored patient as a survivor. The 0.50 is computed here for illustration.
has description in the module The product-limit estimate multiplies survival before each distinct event time t_j by one minus the deaths at t_j divided by the number still at risk just before t_j. Chaining the step over all event times up to t gives the product of the factors, the Kaplan-Meier curve S(t). Patients censored at the cut-off leave the risk set at their censoring time, and because administrative censoring removes the latest recruits first, the number at risk falls steadily towards the end of follow-up.

Type formula
assumes No tied ranks in the Begg test, Enough studies of differing size for the Begg test
has calculator text S = C - D; tau = S / (K * (K - 1) / 2); Var_S = K * (K - 1) * (2 * K + 5) / 18; Z = S / sqrt(Var_S)
has common error note Reading the uncorrected normal Begg statistic with four studies. With four studies in perfect order the uncorrected Z of about 2.04 suggests significance at 5%, but the exact two-sided p-value is about 0.083, so even perfect concordance cannot reach significance on the exact test with four studies. With five it is about 0.017.
Reporting a Begg p-value without stating its version. For the article's ten trials the uncorrected normal p-value is about 0.040, the continuity-corrected one about 0.049 and the exact permutation p-value about 0.047. All lie close to 0.05, so a result reported without its version cannot be checked or compared.
Treating a non-significant Begg test as evidence of no bias. Begg and Mazumdar warned that bias cannot be ruled out when the test is not significant. In simulations by Sterne, Gavaghan and Egger with ten trials, a 20% control event rate and no treatment effect, moderate bias was detected by the rank correlation test in 14.7% of meta-analyses and severe bias in 31.1%, judging evidence at P < 0.1.
has description in the module Compares every pair of studies once. A pair is concordant when the study with the larger variance also has the larger standardised effect (HE-FM-BEGG-002), and discordant when it has the smaller one. Kendall's score S, the difference between the two counts, is divided by the number of pairs to give tau, and by the square root of its null variance without ties to give a statistic compared with the standard normal distribution. When benefit is negative, as with log hazard ratios, exaggerated benefit in the smaller studies gives a negative tau. Stata's Kendall routine, to which its meta bias command refers, uses abs(S) minus 1 in the numerator as a continuity correction, and metafor's ranktest reports an exact p-value where it can, so a report states which version it used.

O'Brien-Fleming type boundaries solved numerically

The Lan-DeMets function only approximates the original O'Brien-Fleming boundary, and less closely than the Pocock type function approximates the Pocock boundary. Using 1 minus alpha inside the O'Brien-Fleming type quantile. Writing Phi^-1(1 minus alpha) with alpha at the one-sided 0.025 makes the function reach 0.05 at t of 1, twice the planned budget, and every boundary is set too low.

Large-sample variance and standard error of Hedges' g

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000741
Type formula
assumes Large-sample approximation to the variance of Hedges' g
Independent groups with a pooled standard deviation for the variance of Hedges' g
has calculator text V_d = (n_1 + n_2) / (n_1 * n_2) + d^2 / (2 * (n_1 + n_2)); V_g = J^2 * V_d; SE_g = sqrt(V_g)
has common error note One over the total sample size in place of the group-size term for Hedges' g. Writing the first term as 1 over (n_1 + n_2) instead of (n_1 + n_2) over n_1 n_2 shrinks it about fourfold with equal arms. For the article's trial the standard error falls to about 0.2383 and the lower 95% limit rises to about 0.338, so a trial compatible with no effect appears clearly beneficial, computed here for illustration.
Variance of Cohen's d attached to Hedges' g. Using V_d as the variance of g ignores the factor J squared. For the article's trial the standard error becomes about 0.4464 instead of 0.4294 and the study's inverse-variance weight about 7.5% lower than it should be, computed here for illustration.
has description in the module Gives the large-sample variance of d as a term for the precision of the mean difference, (n_1 + n_2) over n_1 n_2, plus a term that grows with the size of the effect, d squared over twice the total sample size. Multiplying d by the constant J multiplies its variance by J squared, so the variance of g is J squared times V_d and its square root is the standard error. J comes from HE-FM-HEDG-001 and d from HE-FM-CD-001. The inverse of V_g is the study's weight in HE-FM-ADMA-001 and HE-FM-ADMA-005, and HE-FM-AN-001 with SE_g gives the confidence interval.

League-table fill of three indivisible programmes funded whole or not at all

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000719
Type formula
assumes A whole programme that does not fit is passed over, Whole programmes only in the indivisible league-table fill
has calculator text y_1 = (Delta_C_1 <= B); y_2 = (y_1 * Delta_C_1 + Delta_C_2 <= B); y_3 = (y_1 * Delta_C_1 + y_2 * Delta_C_2 + Delta_C_3 <= B); H_w = y_1 * Delta_E_1 + y_2 * Delta_E_2 + y_3 * Delta_E_3; U_w = B - (y_1 * Delta_C_1 + y_2 * Delta_C_2 + y_3 * Delta_C_3)
has common error note Part-funding an indivisible programme in the league table. Applying the divisible share of HE-FM-CELT-001 to step 3 of the article funds 0.8 of Q and reports 92 QALYs, the 60 of P plus 0.8 of Q's 40, a result that cannot be delivered when Q must be funded whole (computed here for illustration).
Reading the whole-programme fill as the best choice of whole programmes. In step 3 of the article the fill buys 60 QALYs, while funding Q and R in place of P spends the same GBP 1,000,000 for 80 QALYs, 20 more. Following the order does not guarantee the best choice of whole programmes, the case integer programming is built for, and the mathematical programming framework of Stinnett and Paltiel handles complete indivisibility directly.
has description in the module Funds whole programmes in ascending order of ICER, each only if its full incremental cost fits in the budget left after the programmes already funded, and otherwise passes over it to the next. Each y_i is 1 when programme i is funded and 0 otherwise, H_w is the health bought and U_w the budget left unspent. Dakin and Tsiachristas frame the allocation of healthcare resources as a 0-1 knapsack problem, in which each item is packed whole or not at all, and the league table as the greedy algorithm for it, and Stinnett and Paltiel show that mathematical programming handles partial and complete indivisibility. Following the order need not give the most health that whole programmes can buy (HE-ER-CELT-005). The best choice of whole programmes belongs to the Integer Programming article.

Least-cost split of an outlay between medical care and own time for Cobb-Douglas gross investment

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000735
Type formula
assumes Input prices fixed and the outlay spent on care and own time, Interior least-cost mix with both inputs used
has calculator text M = (1 - K) * C / P; TH = K * C / W; I = exp(rho_H * E) * M^(1 - K) * TH^K; MP_M = (1 - K) * I / M; MP_TH = K * I / TH; R_MP = MP_M / MP_TH
has common error note Equal quantities of care and time in place of the least-cost shares. Buying the same number of units of each input, 800 GBP over 50 GBP for 16 units of care and 16 hours in the article's example, gives 16 units of gross investment against 20, 20% less for the same outlay (computed here for illustration). The least-cost rule sets the spending shares to 1-K and K, not the quantities.
Least-cost shares swapped when the time share is not one half. With K of 0.25 the least-cost mix spends three quarters of the outlay on care. Swapping the shares buys 5 units of care and 60 hours, which gives 9.31 units of gross investment against 16.12, 42% less (computed here for illustration). With the article's K of 0.5 the swap leaves the result unchanged, so HE-VT-HPF-004 tests the split at another K.
Shortfall from a non-least-cost mix of care and time read as wasted inputs. The article's alternative mix of 15 units and 20 hours lies on the production function, so no input is wasted, yet it yields 17.32 units against 20 for the same 800 GBP. In the terms of HE-FM-EFF-002 the minimum cost of 17.32 units is 692.82 GBP, so cost efficiency and input-mix allocative efficiency are both 692.82 / 800 = 0.866 while technical efficiency is 1 (computed here for illustration). The remedy is a change of mix, not fewer inputs.
has description in the module Spends the share 1-K of the outlay on medical care and the share K on own time, the cost shares that Grossman gives for the Cobb-Douglas form of HE-FM-HPF-001, and returns the gross investment the outlay buys. The quantities follow from Grossman's least-cost condition (derived here), under which the ratio of the marginal product of care, (1-K) I / M, to that of time, K I / TH, equals the ratio of the price of care to the wage. The chain therefore also returns both marginal products and their ratio, so the condition can be checked against P / W. With the outlay fixed, a higher wage buys fewer hours and leaves the units of care unchanged, so the mix shifts towards care.

has module record identifier HE-FM-HPF-002
has source in the module Grossman M. The Demand for Health: A Theoretical and Empirical Investigation. National Bureau of Economic Research, New York; 1972. Chapter 1, A Stock Approach to the Demand for Health, pages 1 to 10. Page 5, which states that equation (1-11) shows the condition for minimising the cost of producing a given quantity of gross investment, met when the change in gross investment from spending an additional dollar on medical care equals the change from spending an additional dollar on time, and that with a function homogeneous of degree one and prices independent of the level of the inputs average cost is constant and equal to marginal cost. https://www.nber.org/system/files/chapters/c3485/c3485.pdf
Grossman M. The human capital model of the demand for health. NBER Working Paper 7078. National Bureau of Economic Research, Cambridge, MA; 1999. Published as The human capital model, in Culyer AJ, Newhouse JP, editors. Handbook of Health Economics. Vol 1A. Elsevier, Amsterdam; 2000. p. 347-408. Section 2.2, equation (2-10), which sets the marginal cost of gross investment equal to the price of medical care over the marginal product of medical care and to the wage over the marginal product of own time, and the text after it, which states that this is the condition for minimising the cost of producing a given quantity of gross investment; section 5.1, which states the least-cost equilibrium condition that the ratio of the marginal product of medical care to the marginal product of time must equal the ratio of the price of medical care to the wage rate, and gives 1-K as the share of medical care in the total cost of gross investment; section 3.2, which defines K as the fraction of the total cost accounted for by time. The quantities (1-K) C / P and K C / W are derived here from these statements and equation (5-3). https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w7078/w7078.pdf

Least-cost split gives 15 units of care and 20 hours when K is 0.25

Lee and Liu predictive probability for a single-arm trial with a binary response

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000487
Type formula
assumes Binary response observed before each interim look, Design parameters fixed in advance
has calculator text PP = sum_(i=0)^m [w_i * (B_i > theta_T)]
has common error note Plugging in the observed response rate for future patients. Treating future responses as binomial with the observed rate of 16/23 ignores uncertainty in the rate and gives about 0.581 instead of 0.5656 in the Lee and Liu example (computed here for illustration).
Using the current posterior probability as the predictive probability. In the Lee and Liu example the current posterior probability that the response rate exceeds 0.6 is about 0.836, but the probability that the trial will end with a posterior probability above 0.90 is 0.5656 (computed here for illustration).
has description in the module With x responses in n patients so far, a beta(a_0, b_0) prior and a maximum of N_max patients, the number of responses Y among the m = N_max minus n patients still to come is beta-binomial(m, a_0 + x, b_0 + n minus x), with weight w_i for Y = i. For each i, B_i is the final posterior probability that the response rate exceeds p_0, from a beta(a_0 + x + i, b_0 + N_max minus x minus i) distribution. The predictive probability sums the weights of the future results for which B_i exceeds theta_T; the trial stops for futility if it falls below theta_L and for efficacy if it exceeds theta_U.

has common error note Applying the late-entry loading for life. The loading is withdrawn after 10 years of cover in both countries, so an estimate of lifetime premiums that keeps it for life overstates what late entrants pay. The Health Insurance Authority's 2017 report described the Irish loadings as applying for life, which the 2017 amendment changed.
Counting Australian late-entry years from age 35. Ireland counts years from age 35 and Australia counts years over 30. For a person first taking out hospital cover at 41, the Commonwealth Ombudsman's example gives 11 years and 22%; counting as in Ireland would give 7 years and 14%, computed here for illustration, understating the Australian loading.

Australia's Lifetime Health Cover, introduced on 1 July 2000, adds 2% for each year a person is over 30 when taking out hospital cover after the 1 July following their 31st birthday, up to 70%, and the loading stops after 10 years of continuous cover. The function min returns the smaller of its two arguments.

Lifetime infection risk of an unvaccinated child and infections per birth in an endemic infection with vaccination at birth

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000925
Type formula
assumes Endemic SIR steady state with births balancing deaths behind the infection risk
Fully protective vaccination at birth and coverage below one for the endemic infection risk
has calculator text pi = max(0, 1 - 1 / (R_0 * (1 - v))); n = (1 - v) * pi
has common error note Epidemic final size used as the lifetime risk in an endemic infection. The final size of a closed epidemic without births, HE-CF-ATR-001, answers a different question. Applied to the article's R_0 of 5 with 0.4 of the population susceptible it returns a final attack rate of about 0.319 of the whole population, or about 0.797 of the unvaccinated, against the endemic lifetime risk of 0.5 at 60% coverage, so read as the risk of an unvaccinated child it overstates the private benefit of vaccination by about 59% and understates the external share.
Unvaccinated child's risk applied to every birth in the endemic infection count. pi is the risk of a child who is not vaccinated. Multiplying it by all births in place of the unvaccinated births gives 0.5 × 1,000 = 500 infections per 1,000 births at the article's 60% coverage in place of 200, two and a half times the true count, and inflates the loss under voluntary uptake from GBP 100,000 to GBP 250,000.
has description in the module In an endemic infection with lifelong immunity, births and deaths at rate mu and a share v of each birth cohort given a fully protective vaccine at birth, the susceptible share settles at 1/R_0 while the infection persists, so the force of infection lambda settles where the unvaccinated births mu(1 minus v) balance the outflow (lambda + mu)/R_0 from the susceptible pool. An unvaccinated child then leaves the susceptible state by infection or by death, and its lifetime chance of infection lambda/(lambda + mu), the long-horizon limit of HE-FM-TP-004 (derived), becomes pi = 1 minus 1/(R_0(1 minus v)), Eq. 15 of Bauch and Earn and equation (15) of Goodkin-Gold and colleagues, which falls as coverage rises and is zero at or above the threshold H of HE-FM-BRN-003. The same expression is 1 minus 1/R_t with R_t = R_0(1 minus v) from HE-FM-BRN-002 (derived), but HE-FM-BRN-003 is defined for the basic reproduction number and returns an immune share, not a probability of infection. Infections per birth n are the unvaccinated share times that risk, the pathway probability of HE-FM-CHN-002 with factors 1 minus v and pi, which equals (1 minus v) minus 1/R_0 below H (derived from the endemic infected share in Eq. 14 of Bauch and Earn), so each extra vaccination below H removes exactly one infection in total; the share infected in a closed epidemic without births is the final size of HE-CF-ATR-001, a different quantity.

Section Incorporation of an Epidemic Model, which uses the SIR model with births and deaths at rate mu and vaccination of a proportion p of newborns, assuming that individuals are never infected before being vaccinated, gives the critical coverage p_crit = 1 minus 1/R_0 for R_0 above 1 (Eq. 12), the endemic state S-hat = 1 minus p_crit (Eq. 13) and I-hat = f/(1 + f)(p_crit minus p) (Eq. 14), and expresses the probability that an unvaccinated individual eventually becomes infected as the proportion of susceptible individuals becoming infected versus dying in any unit time, pi_p = 1 minus 1/(R_0(1 minus p)) (Eq. 15), noting that the parameter f does not appear in it; and the Appendix, which states that pi_p decreases with p until p reaches the eradication threshold and that pi_p = 0 for p at or above p_crit. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0403823101
Goodkin-Gold M, Kremer M, Snyder CM, Williams HL. Optimal vaccine subsidies for endemic and epidemic diseases. NBER Working Paper 28085. Cambridge, MA: National Bureau of Economic Research; 2020. Section 2.1, Epidemiological Model, which adds births and deaths at rate mu and immunisation of newborns to the SIR model and gives the steady-state susceptible share as the smaller of 1 minus theta Q/mu and 1/R_0 (equation 7) and the infected share mu/(alpha + mu) times (1 minus 1/R_0 minus theta Q/mu), floored at 0 (equation 8); and section 2.2, Consumer Demand, which treats infection and natural death as competing Poisson risks and gives the probability that a susceptible consumer is infected over the lifetime as beta I/(beta I + mu) (equation 14), equal to 1 minus 1/((1 minus theta Q/mu) R_0) below the eradication quantity Q_0 and 0 at or above it (equation 15). https://www.nber.org/papers/w28085

Lifetime partitioned survival QALYs with exponential PFS and OS curves

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000590
Type formula
assumes Constant PFS and OS hazards for a lifetime, Continuous discounting of partitioned survival areas
has calculator text QALY_exp = u_PF / (lambda_PFS + rho) + u_PD * (1 / (lambda_OS + rho) - 1 / (lambda_PFS + rho))
has common error note Exponential hazards that put PFS above OS. With a PFS hazard below the OS hazard the progressed area is negative: hazards of 0.4 and 0.5 give 1 divided by 0.5 minus 1 divided by 0.4, or minus 0.5 years progressed. The formula still returns a number, so the hazards need checking before use.
Using median PFS and OS in place of means for partitioned survival QALYs. For an exponential curve the median is log(2) divided by the hazard, about 0.693 times the mean. Using medians of 0.693 and 1.386 years in the standard-care example gives about 0.936 QALYs instead of 1.35, understating QALYs by about 31%.
has description in the module Closed form of HE-FM-PSM-003 when both curves are exponential and the horizon is lifetime. The area under an exponential curve with constant hazard lambda is 1 divided by lambda, or 1 divided by (lambda + rho) when time is discounted continuously at rate rho. Setting rho to 0 gives undiscounted results; rho = log(1 + d) converts an annual rate d (HE-FM-CONT-003).

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000421
Type formula
assumes Nested models for a chi-square likelihood ratio test
Null value away from the parameter boundary for the likelihood ratio test

has calculator text LR = 2 * (ell_1 - ell_0); df = q_1 - q_0
has common error note Likelihood ratio test used to choose between non-nested survival curves. TSD 14 states that the negative 2 log likelihood is only suitable for comparing nested models and that it has been used erroneously in past NICE technology appraisals. A log-likelihood difference between a Weibull and a log-logistic curve has no chi-square reference.
Log-likelihood gain not doubled in a likelihood ratio test. Comparing the gain of 4.5 itself with chi-square on one degree of freedom gives a p-value of about 0.034 instead of 0.0027.
has description in the module The likelihood ratio statistic is twice the gain in maximised log-likelihood when the parameters fixed in the restricted model are freed. Under Wilks' theorem, in large samples, under the null model and when certain regularity conditions hold, LR is compared with chi-square on df degrees of freedom, the difference in the number of free parameters. The p-value is the right-hand tail, from the computational function below or, when df is 2, from HE-FM-CHISQ-003.
