Likelihood ratios and diagnostic odds ratio from sensitivity and specificity

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000536
Type formula
assumes No empty cells for finite likelihood ratios
Sensitivity and specificity from the same study and threshold for likelihood ratios
has calculator text LR_pos = Se / (1 - Sp); LR_neg = (1 - Se) / Sp; DOR = LR_pos / LR_neg
has common error note Pooling likelihood ratios separately across studies. Separate pooling ignores the correlation between the positive and negative ratios and can produce impossible estimates; likelihood ratios for a model are better derived from jointly pooled sensitivity and specificity.
Ranking tests by the diagnostic odds ratio. Test B's DOR of 96 beats test A's 76, yet test A gives more net monetary benefit at 5 per cent prevalence (HE-FM-DXA-005); the DOR reflects the product of false negatives and false positives, while a clinician is usually interested in their sum and a model in their separate consequences.
has description in the module The positive likelihood ratio says how many times more likely a positive result is in people with the condition than in people without it, and the negative likelihood ratio the same for a negative result. Multiplying pre-test odds by a likelihood ratio gives post-test odds. The diagnostic odds ratio is their ratio, equal to TP times TN over FP times FN.

Linear partial value score of a technology on one MCDA criterion

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000929
Type formula
assumes Linear partial value function on the MCDA criterion range, Performance inside the fixed range of the MCDA criterion, Interval meaning of a partial value score in MCDA
has calculator text v = 100 * (x - x_worst) / (x_best - x_worst)
has common error note Local range of the appraised technologies in place of a fixed MCDA scale. Scoring health gain on the range of the three technologies in hand, 0 to 0.6 QALYs, in place of the fixed 0 to 0.8 range gives A 100 and B 66.67 in place of 75 and 50, and with the article's weights A's total becomes 85 and B's 73.33 in place of 72.5 and 65 (computed here for illustration). The swing weight of 0.50 was judged for a swing of 0.8 QALYs, so it no longer matches the scores, and the scale moves whenever a new technology widens the range. The second ISPOR report keeps local scales for one-off decisions and asks for global scales where criteria are reused, as in HTA.
Reading MCDA partial value scores as ratios. In the article's example severity scores 50 for a moderate and 100 for a severe condition, which does not make treating a severe condition twice as valuable, because zero marks a mild condition, the bottom of the chosen range. The second ISPOR report makes the same point with a range of 6 to 10, on which 10 scores 100 and 8 scores 50 but 10 is not twice as good as 8.
Worst and best ends swapped on a lower-is-better MCDA criterion. Entering 5 bb as x_worst and 10 bb as x_best for the ISPOR appendix's criterion B, on which lower is better, returns 100 less the correct score, 60 in place of 40 for alternative 1 and 30 in place of 70 for alternative 2, so the alternative with the lower, better level is scored as the worse one.
has description in the module Places a technology's performance on one criterion on a 0 to 100 scale whose ends are the worst and best performance of the criterion's fixed range, so equal changes in performance earn equal changes in score. The same line serves a criterion on which lower performance is better, such as a rate of adverse events, by entering the worse, higher level as x_worst, as the first ISPOR MCDA task force appendix does for its criterion B. Zero marks the bottom of the chosen range, not an absence of value, so differences in score can be compared but ratios cannot. Where equal changes in performance are not equally valued, the score is read from an elicited nonlinear partial value function instead.
has formalisation level catalogue record
has implementation Excel linear partial value score for an MCDA criterion
has mathematical variable Best performance of the fixed range of an MCDA criterion, Partial value score on an MCDA criterion, Performance of a technology on an MCDA criterion, Worst performance of the fixed range of an MCDA criterion
has module record identifier HE-FM-MCDH-001
has source in the module Marsh K, IJzerman M, Thokala P, Baltussen R, Boysen M, Kaló Z, et al. Multiple criteria decision analysis for health care decision making: emerging good practices. Report 2 of the ISPOR MCDA Emerging Good Practices Task Force. Value in Health. 2016;19(2):125-137. Step 2b, Report and justify the criteria definitions, states that the use of criteria over multiple decisions, as in HTA, requires a range covering the best and worst performance that could realistically occur (global or fixed scales), while a one-off decision can use the best and worst performance of the alternatives evaluated (local or relative scales). Step 4a, Report and justify the methods used for scoring, notes that a 0 to 100 scale is often used and that, for a range of 6 (scored 0) to 10 (scored 100) with a linear partial value function, going from 6 to 8 is as good as going from 8 to 10, but 10 is not twice as good as 8. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jval.2015.12.016

Report 1 of the ISPOR MCDA Emerging Good Practices Task Force. Value in Health. 2016;19(1):1-13. Appendix, MCDA Modeling Example, Scoring, develops partial value functions over the feasible range of each criterion, with the score often defined on a scale of 0 to 100 points, and assumes linear functions for criterion A (65 to 90 aa, higher better) and criterion B (5 to 10 bb, lower better) in Figures A1 and A2; Table A2 gives the scores 80 and 32 on criterion A and 40 and 70 on criterion B, and the Uncertainty Analysis paragraph scores 6 bb on criterion B at 80. Criterion C has a nonlinear function (Figure A3), which the appendix says could be developed by the bisection method. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jval.2015.12.003

Log risk ratio and its variance from the two-by-two counts of one head-to-head trial

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000606
Type formula
assumes Inverse-variance use of the trial log risk ratio in a pairwise meta-analysis
Same arm order and outcome in every trial of a pairwise meta-analysis
Zero-cell rule for the log risk ratio in a pairwise meta-analysis
has calculator text RR = (a / n1) / (c / n2); y = log(RR); v = 1 / a + 1 / c - 1 / n1 - 1 / n2
has common error note Reversing the arms of one trial in a pairwise meta-analysis. If trial 3 of the article is entered with drug B as group 1, its log risk ratio becomes 0.7340 with an unchanged variance. The fixed-effect risk ratio moves from 0.813 to about 0.914, Cochran's Q rises from about 4.72 to about 8.94 and the DerSimonian and Laird random-effects risk ratio moves from 0.784 to about 0.958, so one reversed trial removes most of the pooled benefit and inflates the heterogeneity.
Using the log odds ratio variance for a trial log risk ratio in a pairwise meta-analysis. For trial 1 the log odds ratio variance, one over each of the four cells 30, 170, 45 and 155, is about 0.06789 against 0.04556 for the log risk ratio, so mixing the two cuts the trial's weight from about 21.951 to about 14.730. RevMan gives the two measures different standard errors, and the variance has to belong to the measure being pooled.
has description in the module Divides the risk of the event on drug A, a/n1, by the risk on drug B, c/n2, takes the natural log, and computes the variance of the log risk ratio as one over a plus one over c, minus one over n1 and one over n2. This is the square of the standard error of the log risk ratio in the RevMan statistical algorithms, and one over v is the trial's inverse-variance weight in HE-FM-ADMA-001. The formula is applied to each trial in turn, so the trial subscript i of the article is dropped; y and v become the y_i and v_i that the pooling records take.

Logarithmic health social welfare of three equal-sized groups at epsilon of 1

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000681
Type formula
assumes Health above zero for logarithmic social welfare
has calculator text W = log(h_1) + log(h_2) + log(h_3)
has common error note Excel LOG in place of LN for logarithmic welfare. LOG with one argument is base 10, so W for option P becomes about 5.5008 instead of 12.6661. The ranking is unchanged, but the EDE health exp(W/3) becomes about 6.26 years instead of 68.17.
General isoelastic formula applied at epsilon close to 1. At epsilon of exactly 1 the formula of HE-FM-SWF-001 divides by zero. Entering 0.999 instead gives about 3,012.6929 for option P, which ranks correctly but differs from the logarithmic 12.6661 by the constant 3/(1-epsilon), here 3,000, plus a small remainder, so the two values cannot be set side by side.
has description in the module At epsilon of 1 the isoelastic form of HE-FM-SWF-001 divides by zero, and Atkinson's welfare function becomes the natural logarithm, so W adds the logarithms of the groups' health. Once the constant n/(1-epsilon), which does not affect rankings, is taken away, HE-FM-SWF-001 tends to this form as epsilon tends to 1, so rankings change smoothly with epsilon through 1. The weight on a small gain to group i is 1/h_i, so a gain of 1% counts the same for every group. Dividing W by n and taking the exponential gives the geometric-mean EDE health of HE-FM-ATK-003. The function log is the natural logarithm.

Lowe fixed-basket consumer price index of a two-item basket

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000713
Type formula
assumes Fixed basket measuring pure price change in the consumer price index
Household spending scope of the consumer price index basket
Fixed-basket form valid within one annual link of the CPI
has calculator text E_0 = p1_0 * q1_b + p2_0 * q2_b; E_t = p1_t * q1_b + p2_t * q2_b; I_0t = 100 * E_t / E_0
has common error note Consumer price index ratio taken as the cost of NHS care. The CPI follows household payments and leaves out care free at the point of use, and PMG36 section 4.4.12 asks for inflation indices appropriate to the cost perspective. In the article's worked example, uprating GBP 2,500 in 2019/20 prices to 2023/24 prices with the CPI ratio through HE-FM-COST-002 gives GBP 3,041.25, about 3.4% more than the GBP 2,942.25 given by the NHS cost inflation index pay and prices series for NHS providers (HE-SR-CPI-010), whose 2023/24 increase is provisional.
Current quantities in the numerator of a fixed-basket CPI. Pricing the current basket at current prices against the old basket at base prices measures the change in spending, a value index, and not price change. If the quantities in the worked example double, the result is 217.1429 in place of 108.5714 (computed here for illustration), although no price rose by more than 10%.
Unweighted average of item relatives in place of CPI basket weights. Averaging the relatives of 110 and 105 without weights gives 107.5, while the basket in the worked example gives 108.5714 (computed here for illustration), because the first item accounts for 100 of the 140 of base-period spending. Above the elementary aggregate the manual combines indices as weighted averages (section 3.5).
has description in the module Prices the same basket of quantities q_b, bought in the weight reference period b, at time t prices and at base-period prices, and expresses the first cost as a percentage of the second, the Laspeyres-type index of section 3.3 of the ONS technical manual. Because the UK quantities come from a period before the base period, the manual classes the CPI and CPIH as Lowe-type indices. The same index is a weighted arithmetic average of the price relatives p_t / p_0, each weighted by its share of the basket cost at base-period prices, the route HE-CF-CPI-001 follows from expenditure data. The formula is written out for two items so that the calculator runs, and the Excel and code forms take any number of items. A ratio of two index values is the input of HE-FM-COST-002.
has formalisation level catalogue record
has implementation Lowe fixed-basket CPI from named price and quantity ranges
has mathematical variable Base-period price of the first item in a Lowe CPI basket, Base-period price of the second item in a Lowe CPI basket, Cost of the Lowe CPI basket at base-period prices, Cost of the Lowe CPI basket at time t prices, Lowe consumer price index level at time t, Time t price of the first item in a Lowe CPI basket, Time t price of the second item in a Lowe CPI basket, Weight reference quantity of the first item in a Lowe CPI basket, Weight reference quantity of the second item in a Lowe CPI basket
has module record identifier HE-FM-CPI-001
has source in the module Jones KC, Weatherly H, Birch S, Castelli A, Chalkley M, Dargan A, et al. Unit Costs of Health and Social Care 2024 Manual. Canterbury and York, Personal Social Services Research Unit (University of Kent) and Centre for Health Economics (University of York), 2025. Section 12.1.1, the NHS Cost Inflation Index (NHSCII), table 12.1.1, which gives annual increases in the NHSCII pay and prices series for NHS providers of 2.49% for 2020/2021, 2.58% for 2021/2022, 7.32% for 2022/2023 and 4.31% for 2023/2024, the last marked provisional. Their product, 1.1769, gives the GBP 2,942.25 in HE-ER-CPI-002 (computed in the article). https://doi.org/10.22024/UniKent/01.02.109563
National Institute for Health and Care Excellence. NICE technology appraisal and highly specialised technologies guidance: the manual (PMG36). Published 31 January 2022, last updated 13 October 2026. Chapter 4 economic evaluation, section 4.4.12, which states that when current costs are not available, costs from previous years should be adjusted using inflation indices appropriate to the cost perspective, such as the NHS cost inflation index and the PSS pay and prices index from the PSS Research Unit report on unit costs of health and social care, or the Office for National Statistics consumer price index. https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/economic-evaluation-2
Office for National Statistics. Consumer Prices Indices Technical Manual, 2019. Newport, Office for National Statistics, 2019, page last revised 26 March 2025. Section 2.5.5, expenditure items, which states that typically no account is taken of services free at the point of consumption, even if paid for indirectly through taxes or National Insurance contributions, and that NHS prescription and dental charges are included in the CPIH and CPI but not the full economic cost. Section 13.11, the cost of living, which defines the cost of living as the minimum cost at current prices of the base-period level of utility, states that because of the stress on minimum cost a cost of living index will usually give a lower rate of inflation than the consumer price inflation indices, and describes substitution towards goods and services that are becoming relatively cheaper. https://www.ons.gov.uk/economy/inflationandpriceindices/methodologies/consumerpricesindicestechnicalmanual2019
Office for National Statistics. Consumer Prices Indices Technical Manual, 2019. Newport, Office for National Statistics, 2019, page last revised 26 March 2025. Section 3.3, index calculation, which gives the Laspeyres-type or fixed-basket index I_0,t = 100 x sum of p_i^t q_i^b over sum of p_i^0 q_i^b, its equivalent form as a weighted arithmetic average of price relatives with weights w_i^0;b = p_i^0 q_i^b over sum of p_i^0 q_i^b, and the statement that UK consumer price indices are Lowe-type indices with quantities taken from a period before the base period and price-updated to it. Section 2.4.1.2 states that the harmonised index is not a cost of living index, section 3.5 forms higher-level indices as weighted averages, and section 12.4.2 states that a chain-linked index spanning more than one year cannot be represented as a basket ratio or a weighted average of price relatives. A notice on the page dated 25 March 2026 states that some aspects of the manual are out of date and that it has been replaced by the ONS Consumer prices indices technical guidance (last revised 28 May 2026), whose article Higher-level aggregation and weights in consumer prices (last revised 25 March 2026) still gives aggregation as a Laspeyres-type weighted average with price-updated expenditure weights (sections 3 and 4). https://www.ons.gov.uk/economy/inflationandpriceindices/methodologies/consumerpricesindicestechnicalmanual2019

Marginal expected survival and background hazard of a cohort mixing two sexes

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000696
Type formula
assumes Group shares fixed at model start, Group survival and hazard from each group's own life table
has calculator text S_star = w_f * S_f + (1 - w_f) * S_m; h_star = (w_f * S_f * h_f + (1 - w_f) * S_m * h_m) / S_star
has common error note Background hazard read at the mean starting age. Mortality rises steeply with age, so the hazard at the mean age is below the average hazard of a cohort with a spread of ages. With illustrative hazards that double every 10 years, 0.010 at 60, 0.020 at 70 and 0.040 at 80, a cohort split equally between ages 60 and 80 has an average entry hazard of 0.025, while the hazard at the mean age of 70 is 0.020 (computed here for illustration).
Fixed equal-weight blend of female and male background hazards. Averaging the two hazards with the starting shares at every time ignores that men die sooner. In the first worked example the blend gives 0.025 against 0.024667, and the gap widens as the cohort ages; TSD 21 section 6.2 weights each expected hazard by expected survival instead.
has description in the module Averages expected survival over the members of a cohort and weights each group's background hazard by its expected survival, the grouped form of equations 18 and 19 of NICE DSU TSD 21 for two groups such as women and men. Because the group with the higher hazard dies sooner, its weight in the marginal hazard shrinks over time, and the marginal background hazard falls below a fixed blend of the two hazards. The same form applies to age groups in a cohort with a spread of entry ages, where it avoids reading one hazard at the mean age. S_star is the expected survival of HE-FM-BGM-001 and h_star the background hazard of HE-FM-BTH-005 for the whole cohort.

Marginal rate of substitution and contour slope of the two-group CES health welfare

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000684
Type formula
assumes Fair innings calibration of the CES contour, Small changes at the current point for the CES marginal rate
has calculator text MRS = (alpha / (1 - alpha)) * (h_b / h_a)^(1 + r); slope = -MRS
has common error note Exponent r in place of 1 plus r in the CES marginal rate. The exponent on the health ratio is 1 + r, which is the Atkinson epsilon. Using r gives 1.2 instead of 1.44 for 60 and 72 years at r = 1, and at the English median epsilon of 10.95 (r of 9.95) it gives about 6.14 instead of the 7.36 of HE-ER-ATK-007 between the same groups.
Treating a CES equity weight as fixed while health changes. The weight depends on the current gap. With r = 1 and equal weights it is 1.44 at 60 and 72 years but about 1.19 once group a reaches 66 years, so a weight computed once and applied to large gains overstates the priority on the later gains.
has description in the module Divides the marginal welfare of health in group a by that in group b. The result is the health of group b that could be given up for one more unit to group a with W unchanged, and the social indifference curve through the point, drawn with h_a on the horizontal axis, has slope minus MRS. Dolan and Tsuchiya read the MRS as the equity weight on a marginal gain to group a relative to group b. At equal health it reduces to alpha/(1-alpha) for any r, which is how they identify alpha from survey choices, and with alpha = 0.5 it equals the Atkinson relative weight of HE-FM-ATK-004 with epsilon = 1 + r when group a is the less healthy, so the factor alpha/(1-alpha) is what this formula adds. Williams' fair innings equity weights come from these slopes at current health on the contour whose EDE is 70 QALYs.

Marginal social cost, social benefit and net benefit at one margin

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000253
Type formula
assumes Marginal values at the current level of activity, No double counting within the stated perspective, Decision-maker bears the private terms in full
has calculator text MSC = MPC + MEC; MSB = MPB + MEB; NB_S = MPB + MEB - MPC - MEC; NB_P = MPB - MPC
has common error note Counting a consumption externality on both sides. Entering the resistance cost of antibiotic use as a positive MEC and also as a negative MEB subtracts it twice. By convention an external effect of consumption is entered once, on the benefit side.
Reading a positive social return as proof that a subsidy is worth paying. A net social benefit of 15 at one margin shows that one more vaccination is worth having. Whether a subsidy programme is worthwhile also depends on its administrative cost, on how many people would have been vaccinated anyway and on how the external benefit falls as coverage rises.
Using an average external effect for a marginal decision. The total transmission benefit of a programme divided by the number vaccinated is an average. The marginal external benefit of the last person vaccinated is usually smaller at high coverage, because herd immunity already protects many of those who remain susceptible.
has description in the module Marginal social cost is the marginal private cost borne by the decision-maker plus the marginal external cost imposed on others; marginal social benefit is the marginal private benefit plus the marginal external benefit received by others. Subtracting cost from benefit with and without the external terms gives the net gain to society and to the decision-maker from one more unit. When the two net gains differ in sign, the private decision goes against the social one, and a subsidy or tax larger than the private shortfall at that margin reverses it. By convention production externalities enter the cost side and consumption externalities the benefit side, so an external cost of consumption, such as the contribution of antibiotic use to resistance, is entered as a negative MEB.

Martingale residual and survival deviance residual of one patient from a fitted cumulative hazard

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000557
Type formula
assumes One record per patient with the cumulative hazard from the fitted model
Positive cumulative hazard for the survival deviance residual
has calculator text M = delta - H; r_D = M / abs(M) * sqrt(-2 * (M + delta * log(delta - M)))
has common error note Excluding a patient because the deviance residual is large. NICE DSU TSD 14 concludes that data points should be excluded only when they can be clearly shown to be erroneous outliers, so a large residual is a reason to check the record and the model, not to drop the patient from the survival analysis.
Reading censored long survivors as poorly fitted. A censored patient's residual is minus the square root of 2H, which grows in size with follow-up by construction: the patient censored at month 5 has minus 1.225 without being an outlier, so large negative values among censored patients carry little information on their own.
Using normal cut-offs when censoring is heavy. Xue and Schifano report Therneau and colleagues' finding that the survival deviance residual is approximately normal with less than 25 per cent censoring, but that with more than 40 per cent too many points lie near 0, and Nardi and Schemper's finding that censoring often makes its distribution bimodal; a cut-off of plus or minus 1.96 is then unreliable for immature data.
has description in the module The martingale residual is the event indicator minus the fitted cumulative hazard at the patient's observed time, the Cox-Snell residual. It cannot exceed 1 and has no lower bound, so it is skewed; the deviance residual rescales it to be roughly symmetric about zero. Since delta minus M equals the fitted cumulative hazard, the log term is always defined, and for a censored patient, with delta = 0, the residual reduces to minus the square root of twice the cumulative hazard. Treating delta as a Poisson count with mean H, the quantity under the square root is the Poisson unit deviance given in Stata's glm Methods and formulas, which links the survival residual to the GLM residual of HE-FM-DEVR-001.
has formalisation level catalogue record
has implementation Martingale and survival deviance residuals from named event and hazard cells
has mathematical variable Event indicator of one patient in a survival model, Fitted cumulative hazard at one patient's observed time, Martingale residual of one patient in a survival model, Survival deviance residual of one patient
has module record identifier HE-FM-DEVR-002
has source in the module Latimer N. NICE DSU Technical Support Document 14: Survival analysis for economic evaluations alongside clinical trials, extrapolation with patient-level data. Sheffield: Decision Support Unit, ScHARR, University of Sheffield; 2011, last updated March 2013 (full text read). Section 5 (Review conclusions), conclusion 8: excluding data points should only be undertaken when it can be clearly demonstrated that certain points are erroneous outliers, and unless a very clear rationale is offered all data should be included in the survival analysis. https://doi.org/10.15131/shef.data.33745843
StataCorp. Stata Survival Analysis Reference Manual, Release 19: stcox postestimation. College Station, TX: Stata Press; 2025 (full text read). Methods and formulas: martingale residuals lie in the range from minus infinity to 1; deviance residuals are calculated as sign(r_M) times the square root of minus 2{r_M + delta log(delta minus r_M)}, are expected to be symmetric about zero and do not necessarily sum to zero. Example 6: plots against the linear predictor, survival time, rank order of survival or observation number help identify aberrant observations. https://www.stata.com/manuals/ststcoxpostestimation.pdf
StataCorp. Stata Survival Analysis Reference Manual, Release 19: streg postestimation. College Station, TX: Stata Press; 2025 (full text read). Methods and formulas: the Cox-Snell residual is the estimated cumulative hazard H(t) = minus log S(t) at the observed time; the martingale-like residual is the failure indicator minus the Cox-Snell residual, takes values from minus infinity to 1 and is not symmetric about zero; the deviance residual is sign(M) times the square root of minus 2{M + d log(d minus M)}, a scaling intended to make it symmetric about zero. https://www.stata.com/manuals/ststregpostestimation.pdf
Xue Y, Schifano ED. Diagnostics for the Cox model. Communications for Statistical Applications and Methods. 2017;24(6):583-604. doi:10.29220/CSAM.2017.24.6.583 (full text read). Section 3.3 (Outlying observations): Therneau and colleagues concluded that with less than 25 per cent censoring the deviance residual is approximately normally distributed and that with censoring above 40 per cent too many points lie near 0, although the residuals remain symmetrised; Nardi and Schemper found its empirical distribution often becomes bimodal because of censoring. https://doi.org/10.29220/CSAM.2017.24.6.583

Maxdiff model probability of a best and worst pair in one choice set

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000482
Type formula
assumes Random utility with independent extreme value errors for the pair, Best and worst chosen jointly from the same set
has calculator text P_max = exp(V_b - V_w) / (S_pos * S_neg - J)
has common error note Labelling any best-worst analysis as MaxDiff. Hollin and colleagues call the MaxDiff label a potential misnomer, because it implies the maxdiff assumption, and found that most object case studies did not state their choice model. The model behind the estimates should be named.
Leaving pairs of an item with itself in the maxdiff denominator. Reading the double sum over all j and k literally, as some statements of the model print it, adds the J pairs of an item with itself, each equal to 1, to the denominator: 21.643 instead of 17.643 in the article's set, and a probability of about 0.2071 instead of 0.2540 (computed here for illustration). One item cannot be both best and worst in a task, so the probabilities of the J(J minus 1) possible pairs then sum to less than 1.
has description in the module Gives the probability that item b is chosen best and item w worst from a set of J items when the respondent picks, from all ordered pairs of distinct items, the pair with the largest utility difference. The denominator is the sum of exp(V_j minus V_k) over all J(J minus 1) ordered pairs with j not equal to k, which equals S_pos times S_neg minus J, where S_pos sums exp(V_j) and S_neg sums exp(minus V_j) over the set; the J terms with j equal to k each equal 1. The probabilities over all ordered pairs sum to 1.

Maximin health social welfare of three groups as the Rawlsian limit

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000682
Type formula
assumes Maximin welfare compares groups at their mean health
has calculator text W = min(h_1, min(h_2, h_3))
has common error note Expecting maximin welfare to credit gains to healthier groups. Raising the third group in option P from 76.7 to 80 years leaves W at 60.3, so a programme that helps only healthier groups scores no gain under maximin even though nobody is worse off.
Reading maximin health welfare as Rawls's own theory. The maximin health form borrows Rawls's priority for the worst off, but Brouwer and colleagues note that Rawls explicitly excluded health and health care from his list of primary goods, so the health version is an analogy drawn from his work.
has description in the module Sets social welfare equal to the health of the least healthy group, the Rawlsian or maximin form. Atkinson gives it as the limit of the isoelastic family as epsilon tends to infinity (HE-FM-SWF-001), and Dolan and Tsuchiya as the limit of the two-group CES form as r approaches infinity (HE-FM-SWF-004). Two allocations with the same minimum have the same W and are ranked as tied however the other groups fare, so a gain to a healthier group alone leaves W unchanged. The nested min written here returns the smallest of the three values.

has common error note Comparing MAE across series in different units. Errors on the scale of the data cannot be used to compare series that involve different units, such as admissions and bed-days; percentage or scaled errors are needed for that comparison.
Measuring accuracy on the data used to fit the method. A method that fits the training data well will not necessarily forecast well, so accuracy is judged only on data held back from fitting.
Using the MAPE for small or zero counts. Percentage errors are infinite or undefined when an observed value is zero and extreme when it is close to zero, a real problem for rare procedures; the example's MAPE of about 71 per cent rests on one month with a single procedure.
has description in the module Summarises forecast errors, observed minus forecast, over periods held back from fitting. The MAE is in the units of the data; the MAPE expresses each error as a percentage of the observed value, so it is unit-free but undefined when an observed value is zero and extreme when values are close to zero. The general forms average over any number of test periods; three are written out here so that the calculator can run. Evaluating Stockholm's forecasts of annual growth in drug expenditure, Linnér and colleagues reported a mean absolute error of 1.9 percentage points.

Mean and median of a log-normal cost

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000601
Type formula
assumes Log cost normally distributed with no zero costs, Log-normal parameters treated as known
has calculator text E_C = exp(mu + sigma^2 / 2); M_C = exp(mu)
has common error note Reporting the exponentiated mean log cost as the expected cost. For 5,000 patients the median or back-transformed mean log cost gives a budget of £10.0 million against an expected £16.49 million, a shortfall of about £6.49 million or 39.3 per cent of the true total, as in the article.
Treating a log-normal mean cost as secure when it rests on the modelled tail. Raising the standard deviation of log cost from 1.0 to 1.2 with the same median moves the expected cost from about £3,297 to about £4,109. Thompson and Nixon found cost-effectiveness conclusions sensitive to how the upper tail of the cost distribution beyond the observed data is modelled.
Using the log-normal mean when costs are not log-normal. Briggs and colleagues found in simulations that the sample mean is always unbiased, while the log-normal mean estimator can perform very poorly when the true distribution is not log-normal; where the distribution is unknown the sample mean generally remains the estimator of choice.
has description in the module When the natural log of cost is normally distributed with mean mu and standard deviation sigma, the median cost and the geometric mean cost both equal exp(mu), and the expected cost is the median multiplied by exp(sigma squared over 2). The factor is Jensen's inequality for the convex exponential: exponentiating the mean log cost returns the median, not the mean. The expected cost is the figure that, multiplied by the number of patients, gives the total budget.

Mean and variance of specific stop-loss reimbursement over a three-level claims distribution

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000737
Type formula
assumes Remaining claims probability below every specific attachment point compared
Cap at or above the specific attachment point and full reimbursement entered as 1
One covered person and one contract year on the specific contract's own basis
has calculator text E_R = c * (p_1 * max(min(C_1, U) - A, 0) + p_2 * max(min(C_2, U) - A, 0) + p_3 * max(min(C_3, U) - A, 0)); M2_R = c^2 * (p_1 * max(min(C_1, U) - A, 0)^2 + p_2 * max(min(C_2, U) - A, 0)^2 + p_3 * max(min(C_3, U) - A, 0)^2); V_R = M2_R - E_R^2; SD_R = sqrt(V_R)
has common error note Assuming the spread of transferred claims falls in step with expected reimbursement. Raising the attachment point from USD 50,000 to USD 200,000 cuts the expected reimbursement of 1,000 members by two thirds, from USD 900,000 to USD 300,000. Scaling the standard deviation down in the same proportion would put it at about USD 161,741, but the variance formula gives about USD 299,850, because the rare USD 500,000 claim carries most of the variance. Treating a higher attachment point as giving up mainly predictable spending, as the article does, rests on this difference.
Mean specific reimbursement per claimant used as the mean per member. At a USD 100,000 attachment point the members who reach the layer, 0.4% of the group, receive on average USD 137,500 each, but the expected reimbursement per member is USD 550. Pricing the layer at the per-claimant mean overstates its expected cost 250-fold; the probability of claims above A has to stay in the expectation, as it does in E_R.
Whole claim reimbursed once it passes the specific attachment point. Paying the full claim of a person whose claims exceed A, instead of the excess over A, turns the excess layer into a franchise. At USD 100,000 it gives 0.003 times 150,000 plus 0.001 times 500,000, USD 950 per member, about 73% more than the USD 550 of the excess rule of 45 CFR 153.230(c) and HE-FM-ASL-001.
has description in the module Gives the expected reimbursement per covered person, its second moment, variance and standard deviation when the person's annual eligible claims take one of three levels C_1 to C_3 with probabilities p_1 to p_3, and the remaining probability sits at claims that never reach the attachment point. Each level's payment is the specific layer rule of HE-FM-ASL-001 with a layer limit of U minus A, times the coinsurance rate c, and E_R is the probability-weighted mean of HE-FN-EV-001 over those payments, the net premium per person for the layer before any loading, carried here because the variance needs it. V_R is the second moment less the squared mean, following the expected value and second moment of the excess of loss cost function in Miccolis 1977. The record works from the discrete distribution of the article's worked example; the normal closed form for an aggregate total is the separate record HE-FM-ASL-005. For a group of n independent members the expected total is n times E_R and its standard deviation SD_R times the square root of n, the rule of HE-FM-ASL-003, which the computational function below applies. Raising A by an amount that passes no claim level and stays below the cap lowers E_R by c times that amount times the probability that claims exceed the old attachment point (derived), so expected reimbursement falls steeply while, as the worked examples show, the standard deviation falls more slowly.

Mean cost of an algorithm-flagged cohort weighted by the positive predictive value

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000552
Type formula
assumes Cost depends only on true disease status, Predictive value of the population costed
has calculator text C_flag = PPV * C_1 + (1 - PPV) * C_0; Bias = C_flag - C_1
has common error note Carrying the validation sample's predictive value into routine data. Benchimol and colleagues found that in 65.9 per cent of validation studies reporting predictive values the validation cohort had a higher prevalence than the administrative data, potentially inflating those values; in the article's example the PPV falls from 0.82 to 0.27 and the flagged mean cost from 5,091 to 2,343 pounds.
Correcting the mean but not the number of patients. The flagged cohort is 3.35 times the true number of cases, so its total cost of 15.7 million pounds per 100,000 people is about 31 per cent above the 12 million spent on true cases, even though its mean cost is too low; both the count and the mean need correcting.
Treating the cost bias as a fixed property of the algorithm. With sensitivity and specificity unchanged, the bias is minus 909 pounds in the validation sample and minus 3,657 pounds in the database, because PPV moves with prevalence; it has to be recomputed for each population costed.
has description in the module When cost depends only on true disease status, the flagged cohort is a mix of true cases, in proportion PPV, and false positives, in proportion 1 minus PPV, so its mean cost is the PPV-weighted average of the two group costs. The bias against the true mean cost of cases is minus (1 minus PPV) times the cost gap. The PPV to use is the one in the population the cohort is drawn from (HE-FM-DXA-003), not the validation sample's (HE-FM-DXA-001).

Mean overall survival as a cure-fraction weighted average of group means

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000596
Type formula
assumes Cured and uncured patients share the same background mortality, Lifetime areas under the cure model survival curves
has calculator text T_bar = pi * E_B + (1 - pi) * E_U
has common error note Cure-fraction mean survival over a horizon that ends too soon. A 40-year horizon leaves cured patients alive at its end. With the article's inputs the restricted mean at pi = 0.25 is about 6.49 years against a lifetime mean of 7.75, so about 1.26 years of the benefit of cure is cut off (computed here for illustration).
Uncured mean survival from the excess hazard alone. E_U must include background mortality. With an excess hazard of 0.46 a year, one over 0.46 gives about 2.17 years instead of one over 0.50, or 2 years, and T_bar at pi = 0.25 becomes about 7.88 years instead of 7.75.
has description in the module Mean survival of a population with a cure fraction is the weighted average of the mean survival of cured and uncured patients, weighted by their proportions. E_B is the area under background survival S_star(t) and E_U the area under S_star(t) times S_u(t). Because T_bar is linear in pi, each unit of cure fraction adds E_B minus E_U years.

Mean stay of a discrete-cycle Markov state against the exponential mean at the same constant exit rate

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000673
Type formula
assumes One constant exit rate behind both Markov mean stays, Discrete Markov mean stay counted from the cycle of entry
has calculator text p_ii = exp(-lambda * Delta); D_mean = Delta / (1 - p_ii); T_mean = 1 / lambda; gap_c = (D_mean - T_mean) / Delta
has common error note Counting gap read as a structural effect of the Markov assumption. The 0.508-year difference between the article's 10.653 discrete post-event years and the continuous 10.145 comes from whole-cycle counting at one constant rate, whereas the difference between 16 years with the tunnel and 10.653 without it comes from the missing time since entry. A half-cycle correction changes the first and leaves the second untouched, as the article notes.
has description in the module Compares the mean stay in a cycle model whose stay probability comes from a constant exit rate with the mean time in the state of the continuous process it represents. Here p_ii is 1 minus the exit probability of HE-FM-TP-001, D_mean turns the mean cycles of HE-FM-MKCH-002 into time by multiplying by the cycle length, and T_mean is the exponential mean of HE-FM-CONT-002. The geometric count credits a whole cycle for the cycle of entry and for every cycle begun in the state, so D_mean exceeds T_mean, and the excess gap_c, in cycles, is above one half and below one, and approaches one half as lambda times Delta shrinks. This is the overestimate from counting membership at the start of each cycle that Sonnenberg and Beck describe, a matter of counting that a half-cycle correction addresses, not of memory.

Using one minus a survival probability as the hazard. Taking each hazard as 1 minus the survival probability, 0.25 and 0.22, gives 1.0 plus 3.41, about 4.41 years, instead of 3.89; hazards are minus the log of survival.

Fed with a q_2 biased by dependent censoring, it shows how a small gap at two years becomes a large gap in life expectancy.

Mean survival under a bathtub hazard with an open final interval

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000351
Type formula
assumes Final bathtub hazard held constant without limit, Undiscounted mean survival from a bathtub schedule
has calculator text E_T = A_closed + S_c / h_K
has common error note Bathtub mean survival stopped at the last cut point. Summing only the closed intervals gives a restricted mean. In the article's example it returns 8.9753 years instead of 10.5784, leaving out the 1.6031 life-years lived after year fifteen.
Stable post-peak hazard extrapolated without the late rise. Carrying the middle hazard of a bathtub forward for life omits the age-related rise. In the article's example mean survival becomes 18.33 years instead of 10.58, and every arm of a cost-effectiveness model is credited with too many life-years and QALYs.
has description in the module Adds the life-years from the closed intervals to the life-years in the open final interval, where a constant hazard h_K applies for ever. The open interval contributes survival at the last cut point divided by h_K, the area under an exponential tail. The result is the undiscounted mean survival per person entering the cohort.

Mean, standard deviation and coefficient of variation of a group's total net claims

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000335
Type formula
assumes Independent members' claims in the pooled group, Common mean and standard deviation for every member
has calculator text E_S = n * mu; SD_S = sigma * sqrt(n); CV_S = sigma / (mu * sqrt(n))
has common error note Assuming independence when claims share common shocks. Real pools are finite and members' claims can move together, for example in an epidemic or a high-utilisation year. The square-root rule then overstates how much pooling narrows the distribution, so a large group's protection from aggregate stop-loss looks less valuable than it is.
Scaling the standard deviation of total claims with group size. Multiplying the per-member standard deviation by the number of members gives 15,000 × 200 = 3,000,000 dollars for Employer 1 instead of about $212,132. The attachment point would then lie only 0.125 standard deviations above expected claims, and a normal approximation would put the chance of reaching it near 0.45 rather than 0.0385.
has description in the module Gives the expected value, standard deviation and coefficient of variation of a group's total net claims when members' claims are independent with a common mean and standard deviation. Total claims grow in proportion to n but their spread only with the square root of n, so the relative spread falls as the group grows. The function sqrt is the square root.

Mean, variance and skewness of a chi-square distribution

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000417
Type formula
assumes Chi-square moments describe the null reference distribution
has calculator text E_X = k; V_X = 2 * k; g_X = sqrt(8 / k)
has common error note Treating a chi-square statistic near its degrees of freedom as evidence of misfit. A statistic close to k is what the null hypothesis predicts. The generalised gamma against Weibull statistic of 0.8 on one degree of freedom is below its mean of 1 and has a p-value of about 0.37, so it gives no evidence that the extra parameter improves the fit.
has description in the module A statistic that follows chi-square on k degrees of freedom under the null hypothesis has expected value k, so only values well above k give small p-values. The skewness falls towards zero as k grows, and because the variable is a sum of k independent terms the central limit theorem makes it close to a normal distribution with the same mean and variance. The function sqrt is the square root.

Mean, variance and standard deviation of a binomial event count

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000411
Type formula
assumes Binomial conditions for the moments of an event count
Fixed probability behind the chance variation of a simulated binomial count
has calculator text E_R = n * p; V_R = n * p * (1 - p); SD_R = sqrt(V_R)
has common error note Simulated binomial count variance used as parameter uncertainty. The variance n p (1 minus p) of a simulated count describes chance variation among patients, not how well p is known. For 1,000 simulated patients at 0.15 it implies about 128 to 172 events, whereas the Beta(7, 35) distribution from the 40-patient study implies about 72 to 292 events per 1,000. Using the narrower range as parameter uncertainty understates the uncertainty carried through to costs and QALYs.
has description in the module Gives the expected number of patients with the event and the variance and standard deviation of that count. In a cohort model the number moving is the mean n p, with no chance variation. In a microsimulation of n patients with a fixed probability, the count varies around that mean with variance n p (1 minus p), the stochastic or first-order uncertainty of the ISPOR-SMDM task force. The variance is largest when p is one half. The function sqrt is the square root.

Mean, variance and standard error of a beta-distributed probability

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000389
Type formula
assumes Positive beta shape parameters, Beta variance read as parameter uncertainty
has calculator text E_p = alpha / (alpha + beta); V_p = alpha * beta / ((alpha + beta)^2 * (alpha + beta + 1)); SE_p = sqrt(V_p)
has common error note Treating beta fits with the same mean as interchangeable. Two beta distributions with the same mean can carry very different uncertainty. Beta(24, 96) and Beta(12.6, 50.4) both have mean 0.20 but standard errors of about 0.036 and 0.050, because the second behaves like evidence from about 63 patients rather than 120. Reporting only the mean hides this, which is why the ISPOR-SMDM task force asks for each distribution and its parameters to be disclosed.
has description in the module Gives the expected value and the variance of a probability that follows Beta(alpha, beta), and its standard error as the square root of the variance. The mean depends only on the ratio of the two parameters, while their sum acts like a sample size: the larger alpha + beta, the narrower the distribution. The function sqrt is the square root.

Mean, variance, covariance and correlation of two components of a three-destination Dirichlet row

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000573
Type formula
assumes Positive parameters and components that add to one, One precision parameter for the whole row
has calculator text alpha_0 = alpha_1 + alpha_2 + alpha_3; E_2 = alpha_2 / alpha_0; V_2 = alpha_2 * (alpha_0 - alpha_2) / (alpha_0^2 * (alpha_0 + 1)); V_1 = alpha_1 * (alpha_0 - alpha_1) / (alpha_0^2 * (alpha_0 + 1)); C_12 = -alpha_1 * alpha_2 / (alpha_0^2 * (alpha_0 + 1)); R_12 = C_12 / sqrt(V_1 * V_2)
has common error note Rescaling independent beta draws to force a row total of one. Dividing each independent draw by the row total conserves the cohort but not the distribution: in the article's simulation of 400,000 iterations the rescaled progression probability had a central 95 per cent range of about 0.136 to 0.267, narrower than the 0.128 to 0.283 of the correct beta marginal, so uncertainty is understated.
Sampling each exit from its own independent beta. Independent draws from Beta(70, 30), Beta(20, 80) and Beta(10, 90) are each correct on their own, but the row total then has variance 0.002079 + 0.001584 + 0.000891 = 0.004554, a standard deviation of about 0.067, and about 30 per cent of iterations in the article's illustration fall below 0.93 or above 1.07.
Treating the components of a sampled row as independent in later analysis. The components are negatively correlated, so an expected value of partial perfect information for one component would need the others drawn from their conditional distribution given it; the row is usually treated as one group of parameters.
has description in the module For a row with parameters alpha_1, alpha_2 and alpha_3, the mean of each component is its parameter over the sum alpha_0, the variances and covariances shrink as alpha_0 grows, and every covariance is negative, so a sampled row that sends more of the cohort to one destination sends less to the others. The correlation depends only on the means, while alpha_0 sets the precision.

Median and central 95% range of a log-normal heterogeneity prior

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000382
Type formula
assumes Log-normal heterogeneity prior stated for tau2 on a named effect scale
Prior parameters on the log scale of the between-study variance
has calculator text tau2_med = exp(m_LN); tau2_low = exp(m_LN - 1.96 * s_LN); tau2_high = exp(m_LN + 1.96 * s_LN)
has common error note Borrowing a heterogeneity prior from another effect scale or setting. A prior derived for log odds ratios is not automatically suitable for another measure, and the general healthcare prior is far wider than the one tailored to all-cause mortality. The NICE manual (PMG36, 2022, updated 2026) recommends distributions tailored to particular outcomes and disease areas, with the source noted and justified and a sensitivity analysis of candidate priors.
Placing a published tau2 prior on tau. The Turner priors are for tau2. Placing LN(-3.95, 1.34^2) on tau instead gives a prior median for tau of about 0.0193 rather than about 0.139, and with the article's four trials it pulls the posterior median of tau down to about 0.020 instead of 0.133.
Reading the squared log-scale parameter as the standard deviation. In LN(-3.95, 1.34^2) the standard deviation of the logarithm of tau2 is 1.34. Reading 1.34^2, about 1.80, as the standard deviation raises the upper 95% limit of tau2 from about 0.266 to about 0.650 and lowers the lower limit from about 0.0014 to about 0.0006.
has description in the module Summarises a log-normal prior for the between-study variance tau2, the form of the empirical priors published by Turner and colleagues, by its median and central 95% range. LN(m_LN, s_LN^2) means that the logarithm of tau2 is normal with mean m_LN and standard deviation s_LN, so the median and limits follow by exponentiating m_LN and m_LN plus or minus 1.96 s_LN. Square roots of the three values give the same summaries for tau.

has common error note Adding the percentage changes. Adding 0.49, 0.75 and 2.50 per cent to the 2025 factor gives 33.5563 for qualifying participants instead of 33.5675 (computed here for illustration); the components compound.

Medication possession ratio capped at 1

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000461
Type formula
assumes Cap applied to each patient's ratio before averaging
has calculator text MPR_capped = min(MPR, 1)
has common error note Averaging uncapped MPRs. Among adults with asthma using inhaled corticosteroids, Vollmer and colleagues found means of 0.61 and 0.63 for two uncapped measures often called the MPR, with maxima of 50 and 100, against 0.55 and 0.52 once each was capped at 1. A few extreme values pull the uncapped mean upwards.
Capping the mean MPR instead of each patient's MPR. Capping a group mean of 0.61 leaves it at 0.61, while capping each patient's ratio first gave a mean of 0.55 in the same data, so the skew from oversupply stays in the result (computed here for illustration).
has description in the module Truncates any of the MPR variants at 1, so supply beyond the days in the denominator no longer raises the ratio. Sikka and colleagues note that early refilling takes the MPR above 1.0 and that it is often truncated there; Vollmer and colleagues define their capped measures as the minimum of the uncapped ratio and 1. Capping limits the upward skew of averages but still credits surplus supply against days without medicine.

Memoryless residual stay and constant per-cycle exit probability of a geometric Markov sojourn

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000671
Type formula
assumes One homogeneous group followed from entry for a Markov memorylessness check
Residual stay measured on the clock that starts at entry to the Markov state
has calculator text R_ab = p_ii^(a + b) / p_ii^a; h_d = p_ii^(d - 1) * (1 - p_ii) / p_ii^(d - 1)
has common error note Model-time probabilities used for time since entry to a Markov state. Applying the article's post-event death probabilities by model cycle, 0.25 in the first cycle and 0.05 after, gives someone who has the event in model year three a first post-event probability of 0.05 instead of 0.25. A model-time curve treats everyone as having entered at the start, which is right only if all enter together.
Survival matched at one duration taken as proof of memorylessness. The article's single post-event state with a death probability of 0.09387 reproduces five-year survival of 0.61088 exactly, yet gives one-year post-event survival of about 0.906 against 0.75 and 10.653 post-event years per event against 16, a third less. In the article this overstates the life-years gained by about 0.64, or 15.7%, so agreement at one horizon does not show that time since entry can be ignored.
has description in the module Gives the probability that a stay already longer than a cycles lasts more than a + b cycles, and the probability of leaving in cycle d of the stay among those still in the state in that cycle. Neither depends on the time already spent, since R_ab equals p_ii to the power b whatever a is and h_d equals 1 minus p_ii at every d, which is the memoryless property that Grinstead and Snell derive for the geometric distribution. The first part is the conditional survival ratio of HE-FM-LTR-001 applied to the geometric stay, and the second divides f_d by G_d of HE-FM-MKA-001. Applied to a survival curve for time since entry, the same ratios test the assumption, since only a memoryless curve has the same per-cycle exit probability at every duration; HE-CF-MKA-001 carries out that check, and HE-FM-CUMH-002 gives the per-cycle probabilities of a fitted curve.

Chapter 5, section 5.1, Example 5.1, page 186, which computes P(T > r + s | T > r) = q^(r+s)/q^r = q^s for a geometric waiting time, independent of the time r already served, and states that this property is called the memoryless property and is also obeyed by the exponential distribution. https://math.dartmouth.edu/~prob/prob/prob.pdf

Minimal important difference as a multiple of the baseline standard deviation

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000558
Type formula
assumes Half a standard deviation summarises earlier published MIDs in chronic disease
Baseline standard deviation from the population of interest
has calculator text MID_SD = k_SD * SD_0
has common error note Quoting half a standard deviation as a fixed property of an instrument. Revicki and colleagues note that the MID for a patient-reported outcome instrument is not an immutable characteristic and may vary by population and context; the half standard deviation value moves with every sample's spread.
Setting utility gains below the MID to zero in a cost-utility analysis. The NICE manual multiplies the time in each health state by its utility with no importance threshold; in the article a gain of 0.03 for two years at 1,200 pounds is 20,000 pounds per QALY although 0.03 is below every group-level yardstick.
Treating half a standard deviation as minimally important change. De Vet and colleagues argue that half a standard deviation corresponds more to minimally detectable than to minimally important change; in the article's example it is 0.10, twice the anchor-based estimate of 0.05.
has description in the module Multiplies the baseline standard deviation of scores by a chosen multiple: 0.5 for the half standard deviation rule of Norman, Sloan and Wyrwich, or 0.2 for Cohen's small effect size benchmark. The result is in the instrument's own units and grows with the heterogeneity of the sample.

Abstract: 38 studies gave 62 effect sizes; for all but 6 studies the MID estimates were close to one half a standard deviation (mean 0.495, SD 0.155); population-based estimation and brief follow-up were associated with smaller effect sizes and acute conditions with larger ones; for chronic diseases the threshold appears to be about half a standard deviation. https://doi.org/10.1097/01.MLR.0000062554.74615.4C

Minimally detectable change and reliable change index from the standard error of measurement

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000560
Type formula
assumes Independent equal measurement errors for the MDC and reliable change index
has calculator text S_diff = sqrt(2) * SEM; MDC = 1.96 * S_diff; RC = (x_2 - x_1) / S_diff
has common error note Applying the minimally detectable change to a difference between trial arms. The MDC and RC describe change in one person beyond measurement error; in the article's example the MDC of 0.247 is about five times the anchor-based estimate of 0.05, so using it as a threshold for a difference in arm means would dismiss changes patients notice.
Leaving out the square root of 2 for a change score. De Vet and colleagues include the square root of 2 because two measurements are involved in measuring change; without it the MDC in the article's example falls from 0.247 to 0.174 (1.96 x 0.089, computed here for illustration) and more patients are classed as changed.
Using distribution-based change as the sole basis for a responder definition. The FDA's 2009 guidance on patient-reported outcome measures says the empirical evidence for any responder definition is derived using anchor-based methods, and that distribution-based methods are supportive and not appropriate as the sole basis for one.
has description in the module A change score involves two measurements, so its standard error is the square root of 2 times the SEM. The minimally detectable change (MDC) is 1.96 of these standard errors, the 95 per cent limit for no change, and the reliable change index (RC) of Jacobson and Truax divides one person's change by the same standard error; a value beyond 1.96 in either direction would arise from measurement error alone with probability of 5 per cent or less. Both thresholds apply to one person's change, not to a difference in group means.

Mixed-strategy equilibrium probabilities of a 2 x 2 game from the indifference conditions

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000947
Type formula
assumes Expected payoffs and independent mixing in the 2 x 2 mixed equilibrium
No payoff ties against a fixed choice of the other player
Each player mixes over both of its strategies
has calculator text a_1 = u_11 - u_21; a_2 = u_22 - u_12; q_star = a_2 / (a_1 + a_2); b_1 = v_11 - v_12; b_2 = v_22 - v_21; p_star = b_2 / (b_1 + b_2); interior = (q_star > 0) and (q_star < 1) and (p_star > 0) and (p_star < 1)
has common error note Missing a continuum of equilibria when payoffs tie. In the break-even angioplasty game of HE-EX-NASH-002, a_1 is 0, the formula gives q_star = 1 and interior = 0, and it would be easy to conclude that only pure equilibria exist. With hospital B investing for sure, hospital A earns 0 whatever it does and investing stays a best reply for B against any mix by A, so every probability with which A invests is part of an equilibrium (computed here).
Reporting a value outside the unit interval as a mixing probability. The formula returns a number for any game whose gap sums are not zero, and when investing is dominant it gives 1.3333 (HE-EX-NASH-008), which is not a probability. The game then has no completely mixed equilibrium and its single equilibrium is the pure cell (Invest, Invest), so q_star and p_star are read only when interior is 1.
Setting a player's mixing probability from its own payoffs. The row player's probability keeps the column player indifferent, so it comes from v_jk. In the battle of the sexes of HE-EX-NASH-006, solving each player's own indifference for its own probability gives the row player 1/3 and the column player 2/3 in place of 2/3 and 1/3. At a column probability of two thirds the row player earns 1.3333 from its first strategy and 0.3333 from its second (computed here), so it would switch and the pair is not an equilibrium. In a symmetric game such as the angioplasty game the two values coincide and the error goes unseen.
has description in the module In a mixed equilibrium of a game in which each player has two strategies, each player randomises over both, which it is willing to do only if both give it the same expected payoff, so each player's mixing probability is set by the other player's payoffs. Equating the row player's expected payoffs from its two strategies, q u_11 + (1 minus q) u_12 = q u_21 + (1 minus q) u_22, gives the probability q_star that the column player chooses its first strategy, and the column player's indifference gives the probability p_star that the row player chooses its first strategy. Slantchev states this condition for 2 x 2 games and solves it for the equilibrium probabilities; the closed forms are that equation solved (derived). The pair is a mixed equilibrium when both values are above 0 and below 1, which is what Proposition 1 of Slantchev requires when each player mixes over two strategies (derived); when q_star is not, the row player has a strictly dominant strategy (derived, for games without the ties of HE-AS-NASH-005), and likewise p_star for the column player. The algebra is that of the decision curve threshold HE-FM-DCA-004, p_t = L / (G + L), and of the blend weight in HE-FM-EXD-002, with a_1 and a_2 in place of G and L, but HE-VR-DCA-013 to HE-VR-DCA-015 define p_t as a patient's risk and G and L as a patient's benefit and harm, while here the probability is the other player's equilibrium choice, set by the payoffs of the player it leaves indifferent and an equilibrium only as a pair with p_star. When a_1 and a_2 are both negative, as in the angioplasty game, listing the row player's strategies in the other order makes both positive and leaves q_star unchanged (derived). Each player's expected payoff at the equilibrium is HE-FM-CHN-001 applied to its payoffs against the other's mix.

Mixed strategies are probability distributions over the pure strategies and the payoff functions are the expectations of the players; Nash proves, with Kakutani's fixed point theorem, that every such game has an equilibrium point. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.36.1.48
Slantchev BL. Game theory: dominance, Nash equilibrium, symmetry. Lecture notes, Department of Political Science, University of California, San Diego; 23 May 2008 (full text read). Section 2.3 (Mixed Strategy Nash Equilibrium), matching pennies, each player's expected payoffs from its pure strategies against the other's mix and the unique equilibrium with both probabilities one half; section 2.3.1 (Battle of the Sexes), the row player's payoffs 2q and 1 minus q equal at q = 1/3 and the column player's equal at p = 2/3, the mixed equilibrium (2/3, 1/3) for the row player and (1/3, 2/3) for the column player, and outcome probabilities found by multiplying the two players' equilibrium probabilities. Section 2.4 (Computing Nash Equilibria), Proposition 1, a mixed profile is an equilibrium only if each player's pure strategies in its support give the same payoff and no other strategy gives more, and the statement that a randomising player must be indifferent among the pure strategies in its support. Section 2.4.1 (Myerson's Card Game), the simplified 2 x 2 game, in which any mixture uses both strategies and the equilibrium probabilities are found by equating the payoffs, and the statement that each player's mixed strategy makes the other indifferent. https://slantchev.ucsd.edu/courses/gt/04-strategic-form.pdf

Mixture cure model all-cause survival in the relative survival form

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000594
Type formula
assumes Population-level cure with zero excess hazard in the mixture cure model
Expected survival from matched life tables in the mixture cure model
Mature data and a justified uncured distribution for a mixture cure fit
has calculator text S = S_star * (pi + (1 - pi) * S_u)
has common error note Fitting a mixture cure model to all-cause survival with no background mortality. Without S_star the cured group never dies, so all-cause survival stays at pi for ever and mean survival grows with the model horizon. TSD 21 notes that the event cannot be all-cause mortality because the survival function must reach zero; the model belongs in a relative or cause-specific survival framework.
Reading the cure fraction off the all-cause survival curve. In the relative survival form the cure fraction is higher than all-cause survival at the cure time, because some patients die of other causes first. In the illustrative example all-cause survival at 20 years is about 0.112 while the cure fraction is 0.25, so taking the level at which the all-cause curve flattens as pi understates the cure.
has description in the module Writes all-cause survival at time t as the expected survival of the matched general population multiplied by relative survival, which is the cure fraction plus the uncured share times the survival of the uncured from the excess hazard. As the uncured die out, relative survival falls to pi and all-cause survival to S_star times pi. This is equation 11 of NICE DSU TSD 21.

Type formula
assumes Refilling between first and last dispensing describes adherence

has description in the module Divides the days' supply of every fill except the last by the days between the first and last dispensing. Raebel and colleagues list it as MPR modified (MPRm). Because the last fill's supply and the time it would cover are both left out, the ratio describes refilling between the first and last dispensing and ignores any stop after the last refill.

Monte Carlo bootstrap standard error from B replicates

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000402
Type formula
assumes Bootstrap samples copy the trial design, Sample stands in for the population of costs, Statistic with a finite variance that behaves like an average
has calculator text theta_bar = sum_(b=1)^B [theta_b] / B; SE_B = sqrt(sum_(b=1)^B [(theta_b - theta_bar)^2] / (B - 1))
has common error note Dividing the replicate standard deviation by the square root of B. Dividing by the square root of B gives the simulation error of the replicate mean, which shrinks towards zero as replicates are added. With the five illustrative replicates it gives about 651.92 pounds instead of 1,457.74.
Using STDEV.P for the replicate standard deviation. STDEV.P divides by B rather than B minus 1. With the five illustrative replicates it gives about 1,303.84 pounds instead of 1,457.74; the gap shrinks as B grows, but only STDEV.S matches the definition.
has description in the module Estimates the bootstrap standard error as the standard deviation, with divisor B minus 1, of the statistic recalculated on B bootstrap samples. As B grows the estimate approaches the ideal bootstrap standard error over every possible resample. The replicate standard deviation is itself the standard error and is not divided by the square root of B.

Monte Carlo runs needed for a target standard error of a mean agent-based model outcome

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000692
Type formula
assumes Independent runs with separate random number seeds, Pilot standard deviation taken as a conservative estimate, Paired runs with common random numbers for an incremental outcome
has calculator text R_req = (s_run / e_target)^2
has common error note Counting agents rather than runs as the replications. Dividing the spread of outcomes across the agents of one run by the square root of the number of agents, for example 5,000, treats the agents as independent when interaction makes their outcomes correlated, so the standard error is understated and too few runs are chosen. The standard error of a mean over runs comes from the spread across independent runs.
Doubling runs to halve the Monte Carlo standard error. Doubling the illustrative 900 runs to 1,800 gives a standard error of about GBP 7.07, not GBP 5. Halving the standard error needs 3,600 runs.
has description in the module Inverts the Monte Carlo standard error of a mean over independent runs, s_run divided by the square root of the number of runs (the form of HE-FM-ANTV-002 with one observation per run, with the standard deviation taken with divisor R minus 1 as in HE-FM-BSE-001), to give the number of runs R_req whose standard error equals a chosen target e_target. s_run is the standard deviation of the outcome across a pilot set of runs, for example of mean cost per person or, for an increment, of the paired difference between strategies run with common random numbers. The result is rounded up to a whole number of runs. Halving the target multiplies the runs by four.

Section 5.4 and Table 1 report 5,000 runs of each scenario in the case study. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40273-015-0254-2
Morris TP, White IR, Crowther MJ. Using simulation studies to evaluate statistical methods. Statistics in Medicine. 2019;38(11):2074-2102. The checklist in Table 1 advises setting the random number seed once per repetition and using separate streams when running chunks in parallel. https://doi.org/10.1002/sim.8086

Monte Carlo runs needed for a target standard error of a share of agent-based model runs

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000693
Type formula
assumes Expected share set before the agent-based model runs, Binary run result with independent runs for a share
has calculator text R_prop = P_exp * (1 - P_exp) / e_share^2
has common error note Reading the share of first-order runs as the probability of cost-effectiveness. The share of runs at fixed inputs in which a strategy comes out cost-effective measures chance between simulated histories, first-order uncertainty. The probability that a strategy is cost-effective for a decision comes from draws of uncertain inputs, second-order uncertainty, which Chhatwal and He treat separately under probabilistic sensitivity analysis.
Share and target standard error in different units. Entering the target of 0.5% as 0.5 while the share is entered as 0.95 gives 0.19, rounded up to 1 run, instead of 1,900. The share and the target are entered in the same units, both as proportions or both as percentages.

Putting in the expected share and rearranging gives the number of runs R_prop for a target standard error e_share, equation 1 of Morris and colleagues. The product P_exp(1 minus P_exp) is largest at a share of 0.5, so 0.25 divided by the squared target is a worst-case count when the share is unknown.

assumes Every option evaluated in the same simulations, Complete set of options

has common error note Building a multi-option curve from pairwise comparisons. Comparing each option separately with one common baseline and plotting the pairwise probabilities gives values that can sum to more than 1 and do not answer which option is best. Each draw is credited to the single option with the highest net monetary benefit.
has description in the module Counts the simulations in which option j has the highest net monetary benefit among all included options at threshold lambda, and divides the count by the number of simulations. Each option's net monetary benefit in a draw is lambda times its simulated effect minus its simulated cost. With mutually exclusive options and consistent tie handling, the values for all options sum to 1 at each threshold. Because no option can exceed the maximum, the indicator 1(NMB_ij >= NMBmax_i) equals 1 exactly when option j attains the highest net monetary benefit in draw i.

Murphy partition of the Brier score into reliability, resolution and uncertainty

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000407
Type formula
assumes Patients grouped by identical predicted values, Uncertainty term shared by models validated in the same patients
has calculator text REL = sum_(k=1)^K [n_k * (f_k - o_k)^2] / N; RES = sum_(k=1)^K [n_k * (o_k - o_bar)^2] / N; UNC = o_bar * (1 - o_bar); REF = UNC - RES; BS = REL - RES + UNC
has common error note Reporting partition terms without the binning used. With continuous predictions the partition is computed after grouping into bins, and the reliability and resolution terms change with the number and width of the bins. Terms reported without the binning cannot be reproduced or compared.
Taking a shared AUC as evidence of equal calibration. Models A and B rank the patients identically, so they share an AUC of about 0.788, yet model B's reliability term is 0.01845 against 0.0007 because it overpredicts admissions in every group. Only the reliability term exposes the difference.
has description in the module When predictions take a limited set of K distinct values, the Brier score splits exactly into a reliability term, which measures miscalibration, minus a resolution term, which measures how far the group event rates spread from the overall rate, plus an uncertainty term, the score of the non-informative model. Refinement, uncertainty minus resolution, is the average uncertainty left within the groups, and the score also equals reliability plus refinement.

Nash bargaining price between a reservation price and a payer's maximum price

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000355
Type formula
assumes Money payoffs that move one for one with the negotiated price, Complete information and a non-empty bargaining range, Bargaining weight fixed by the negotiating setting
has calculator text p_star = c + beta * (p_bar - c)
has common error note Estimating the bargaining weight from list prices. A weight backed out as the price minus c, divided by p_bar minus c, needs the price actually paid. Where confidential discounts apply, the list price is higher than the price paid, so the estimate overstates the manufacturer's share.
Reading the threshold price as the expected negotiated price. The payer's maximum price of £8,000 is the predicted outcome only when the manufacturer holds all the bargaining power. Under symmetric weights the price is £4,500 and the cost per QALY £13,000 rather than £20,000, and the payer keeps £3,500 per patient of net monetary benefit that pricing at the threshold would pass to the manufacturer.
Reversing the manufacturer's and payer's bargaining weights. Using beta as the payer's weight hands each side the other's share. With a manufacturer weight of five sevenths the price is £6,000 per patient; with the weights reversed it becomes £3,000.
has description in the module Gives the negotiated price when both parties' payoffs are in money and move one for one with the price: the manufacturer gains the price minus its reservation price c, and the payer gains its maximum price p_bar minus the price paid. Maximising the weighted Nash product of the two gains gives a weighted average of the two limits, so the manufacturer receives the share beta of the surplus p_bar minus c and the payer the share 1 minus beta. Berdud, Ferraro and Towse state the same weighted average in cost-effectiveness ratio units, from the developer's reserve ratio to the payer's maximum.

Need-expected use of health care by indirect standardisation

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000375
Type formula
assumes Observed need indicators capture need in the need regression, Average relation between need and use taken as the vertical norm, Linear need regression for indirect standardisation
has calculator text yX_i = alpha_hat + sum_(j=1)^J [beta_hat_j * x_ji] + sum_(k=1)^K [gamma_hat_k * z_bar_k]
has common error note Leaving non-need controls out of the need regression. If a correlate of use that is not need, such as more generous insurance cover for people in poor health, is left out of the regression, the coefficient on poor health picks up part of its effect. The appropriate need difference is then overstated, and part of a non-need effect is removed from the measured inequity as if it were need.
Predicting need-expected use with each person's own control values. Using individual values of the controls puts their effects into need-expected use, so the part of the inequality carried by income or insurance is standardised away. In the illustrative regression an insured person in poor health would be given 7.5 visits instead of 7.0, and need-expected use would vary with insurance status as well as need.
has description in the module Predicts the use of care each person would be expected to have given their need, from a linear regression of use on need variables and non-need control variables. Each person's own need values enter the prediction, while every control is set to its sample mean, so the controls protect the need coefficients from omitted-variable bias without being standardised for. This is the first step of indirect standardisation; the second is HE-FM-HEQ-002.
