Negative likelihood ratio of a negative result on both of two tests with conditional covariances

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000749
Type formula
assumes Both tests read on every person under the either-positive rule, Conditional covariances inside their valid limits, Accuracy and covariances from people who had both tests
has calculator text Se_par = 1 - (1 - Se_1) * (1 - Se_2) - C_pos; Sp_par = Sp_1 * Sp_2 + C_neg; LR_neg_12 = (1 - Se_par) / Sp_par
has common error note Multiplying the negative likelihood ratios of two dependent tests. With the second worked example's covariance of 0.02 among people with the condition, multiplying 0.10 by 0.125 gives 0.0125 against a joint ratio of 0.0625. At a 30% pre-test probability the product suggests a residual risk of about 0.53% when it is about 2.61%, close to the article's 2.73% discharge threshold.
Setting the covariances to zero without data on both tests. Taking each test's sensitivity and specificity from a different study leaves C_pos and C_neg unknown, and a zero then assumes conditional independence. Gardner and colleagues state that dependence between the sensitivities or specificities of two tests changes their accuracy in combination, so the assumption needs a scenario analysis with plausible covariances.
Using the both-negative ratio for a pathway that retests only positives. If the second test is given only to people positive on the first and a person is discharged when either result is negative, the negative result is at least one negative, with ratio (1 minus Se_1 Se_2 minus C_pos) / (1 minus (1 minus Sp_1)(1 minus Sp_2) minus C_neg). For the independent worked example that is 0.145 / 0.90, about 0.161, against 0.0125 (derived from the joint probabilities of Wang, Lin and Nelson).
has description in the module When two tests are combined so that a person is called negative only if both are negative, the combined sensitivity Se_par and specificity Sp_par follow from the single-test values and the conditional covariances, C_pos among people with the condition and C_neg among people without it, in the joint probabilities that Wang, Lin and Nelson give. The combined ratio LR_neg_12 is then the LR_neg of HE-FM-DXA-002 applied to Se_par and Sp_par. With both covariances zero, the conditional independence that the article warns about, LR_neg_12 equals the product of the two single-test ratios (derived). A positive C_pos raises the ratio above that product, so multiplying the ratios overstates the rule-out, while a positive C_neg on its own lowers it below the product (derived).

Negotiated price when the payer holds a binding outside option

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000358
Type formula
assumes Outside option available only by leaving the negotiation, Outside option that still leaves a deal the manufacturer accepts
has calculator text p_neg = min(p_star, p_bar - v_P)
has common error note Applying the rule when the outside option leaves no bargaining range. A competing therapy worth £7,500 per patient gives a formula price of £500, below the £1,000 reservation price. The manufacturer would not sell at that price, so no agreement is reached and the payer funds the alternative.
Treating the outside option as the payer's disagreement payoff. Subtracting v_P from the payer's gain inside the Nash product and then splitting what is left overstates the payer's power. Under symmetric weights a £4,000 alternative would give a price of £2,500 rather than £4,000, and a £3,000 alternative, which should leave the price at £4,500, would cut it to £3,000.
has description in the module Applies the outside option principle to the payer. An outside option, the net monetary benefit per patient v_P available by walking away for good, for example to a competing therapy, changes the price only if it is worth more than the payer's gain from the bargain without it, p_bar minus p_star. In that case the price falls until the payer's gain just equals the outside option; otherwise the threat is empty and the Nash price stands. The function min returns the smaller of its arguments.

Net benefit of a risk model at one threshold probability

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000498
Type formula
assumes Decision curve net benefit from validation data separate from model development
Threshold reflects the harm of a missed case against an unnecessary intervention
Same expected benefit for every case and harm for every non-case in net benefit
has calculator text NB = TP / n - FP / n * p_t / (1 - p_t)
has common error note Ignoring the test harm of obtaining a risk model's inputs in net benefit. If the inputs need an invasive or costly test, a test harm in units of true positives is subtracted at every threshold, for example 1/30, about 0.033, when clinicians would scan at most about 30 men to find one high-grade cancer.
Reading net benefit as money or QALYs. Decision curve net benefit is in units of true positives per patient. Converting it to money needs an explicit value per case found (HE-FM-DCA-005), and it is not the economic net monetary benefit of an option.
Weighting false positives by the threshold instead of its odds. Charging each false positive p_t instead of p_t / (1 minus p_t) understates the penalty; for model A at 40 per cent it gives 0.13 minus 0.07 x 0.40, or 0.102, instead of 0.0833.
has description in the module Counts patients whose predicted risk is at or above the threshold as positive. True positives per patient are credited in full and false positives per patient are charged at the odds of the threshold, p_t / (1 minus p_t), the exchange rate between an unnecessary intervention and a case found. A net benefit of 0.07 equals intervening in 7 patients per 100, all of whom have the event, and in no one else. The maximum is the prevalence and there is no lower limit.

BMC Medical Informatics and Decision Making. 2008;8:53. doi:10.1186/1472-6947-8-53. Abstract (Results): simulation studies showed that repeated 10-fold cross-validation provided the best method for correcting a decision curve for overfit. https://doi.org/10.1186/1472-6947-8-53
Vickers AJ, Elkin EB. Decision curve analysis: a novel method for evaluating prediction models. Medical Decision Making. 2006;26(6):565-574. doi:10.1177/0272989X06295361. Introductory theory, Equation 1 and the application section: positive if predicted probability is equal to or higher than p_t; Net Benefit = TruePositiveCount/n minus FalsePositiveCount/n times p_t/(1 minus p_t); worked example 65 true and 225 false positives among 902 at 10 per cent giving 0.0443; range from negative infinity to the incidence of disease; a version subtracting TestHarm. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2577036/
Vickers AJ, Van Calster B, Steyerberg EW. Net benefit approaches to the evaluation of prediction models, molecular markers, and diagnostic tests. BMJ. 2016;352:i6. doi:10.1136/bmj.i6. Extensions to net benefit methods: investigators who would do no more than about 30 scans to find one high grade cancer would set a test harm of 0.033 (1/30), subtracted from the net benefit of the prediction model across all thresholds. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4724785/
Vickers AJ, van Calster B, Steyerberg EW. A simple, step-by-step guide to interpreting decision curve analysis. Diagnostic and Prognostic Research. 2019;3:18. doi:10.1186/s41512-019-0064-7. Step 4: the unit of net benefit is true positives; a net benefit of 0.07 means 7 true positives for every 100 patients in the target population. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6777022/

Net benefit of intervening in every patient at a threshold probability

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000499
Type formula
assumes Intervene-in-all prevalence taken from the same validation sample
Intervening in everyone uses the threshold only as an exchange rate
has calculator text NB_all = pi - (1 - pi) * p_t / (1 - p_t)
has common error note Comparing a model only with intervening in no one. A positive net benefit shows only that a model beats no intervention. At 15 per cent model B's 0.1294 is positive but adds nothing over intervening in everyone.
Using a prevalence from another population for the intervene-in-all line. The defaults must use the validation sample's prevalence; a population figure moves the crossing point and can make a model appear to beat a default it does not beat.
has description in the module Classes every patient as positive, so true positives per patient equal the prevalence and false positives per patient its complement. The line falls as the threshold rises and crosses zero, the net benefit of intervening in no one, where the threshold equals the prevalence. A model is of value at a threshold only if it beats both defaults.

Journal of Clinical Oncology. 2016;34(21):2534-2540. doi:10.1200/JCO.2015.65.5654. Section on decision curves: under the treat-all policy TPR = FPR = 1, so NB = P minus R/(1 minus R) times (1 minus P); equating it with the treat-none NB of 0 shows the two curves cross at R = P; treat all and treat none use no individual risks but R still values the relative size of benefit and cost. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4962736/

Net days in accounts receivable from net receivables and average daily net patient revenue

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000905
Type formula
assumes Net receivables and net revenue on the same basis in days in accounts receivable
Most recent three months and actual calendar days in the days in accounts receivable denominator
Revenue earned claim by claim for days in accounts receivable
Steady daily revenue when days in accounts receivable are read as a collection period
has calculator text r_bar = R / D; DAR = AR / r_bar
has common error note A fixed 90-day denominator in place of calendar days in days in accounts receivable. For the quarter ending 30 June, dividing the USD 91.0 million of revenue by 90 days in place of the 91 calendar days gives r_bar of 1.0111 and 54.40 days in place of 55.0. HFMA counts the actual days of the three months, which differ between quarters and in leap years.
Comparing days in accounts receivable of an NHS trust with hospitals paid per claim. Under the NHS Standard Contract each commissioner pays an NHS trust one twelfth of the expected annual contract value on the fifteenth day of each month, unless another day or proportion is agreed, payments on account that do not wait for claims. A trust's receivables from its main commissioners therefore reflect contract timing and in-year adjustments, and comparing its figure with that of a US hospital paid claim by claim says nothing about collection performance.
Net receivables divided by gross daily charges in days in accounts receivable. Dividing the article's USD 55.0 million of net receivables by illustrative gross daily charges of USD 2.5 million gives 22.0 days, 40% of the 55.0 net days, because list charges are far above what payers pay. Gross receivables go over gross revenue and net over net.
Reading a payer-mix shift as slower collection in days in accounts receivable. In the article's example the overall figure rises to 61.25 days against 55.0, 6.25 days or about 11.4% higher, when the public payer's share of revenue falls by ten points to 40%, although no payer group collects any more slowly. Comparing the group days, or their revenue-weighted mean at fixed revenue shares (the weighted-mean algebra of HE-FM-CRAT-001, there with member numbers as weights), separates the mix effect from the performance of the billing office.
Taking a fall in net days from write-offs or allowances as faster collection. Raising the allowance for uncollectible accounts, or netting growing credit balances against debit balances, shrinks net receivables without any cash coming in. In the article's quarter an extra USD 5.0 million of allowance would take net days from 55.0 to 50.0 with nothing collected (computed here for illustration). HFMA's AR-1 ageing of billed receivables shows whether the fall came from collecting old accounts or from removing them, and its AR-9 net days in credit balance shows whether the credit balances netted off have grown.
has description in the module Divides the net patient receivables on the balance sheet at the end of a period by the average daily net patient service revenue of the same period, the HFMA MAP Key FM-1 net days in accounts receivable, so that receivables of providers of any size read on one scale of days. The measure applies to providers paid claim by claim, where each episode of care has to be coded, billed, adjudicated and collected before it turns into cash. Applied to one payer group the same formula gives that group's own days figure, and the overall figure is the revenue-weighted mean of the group figures by the weighted-mean identity of HE-FM-CRAT-001. Multiplying DAR by r_bar returns the receivables balance, the input to the carrying cost and the cash released that HE-FN-DAR-001 describes.

has source in the module Healthcare Financial Management Association. MAP Keys, industry-standard revenue cycle KPIs. HFMA MAP Initiative web page, accessed 18 October 2026. FM-1, Average Daily Net Patient Service Revenue, defined as the most recent three-month daily average of total net patient service revenue, with net patient service revenue equal to gross patient service revenue minus contractual allowances, minus charity care provision, then minus the provision for doubtful accounts. The definition counts the days in the three months including the last month reported, so the three months ending June 30 use April (30 days), May (31 days) and June (30 days), 91 days in all, and the FM-1 exclusions for both net A/R and revenue include capitation and premium revenue related to value-based or risk-based payer contracts. https://www.hfma.org/data-and-insights/map-initiative/map-keys/
Healthcare Financial Management Association. MAP Keys, industry-standard revenue cycle KPIs. HFMA MAP Initiative web page, accessed 18 October 2026. Financial Management group, Net Days in Accounts Receivable (A/R) (FM-1), whose equation divides net A/R from the balance sheet by average daily net patient service revenue from the income statement, describes the measure as a trending indicator of overall A/R performance, and defines net A/R as the net patient receivable on the balance sheet, net of credit balances, allowances for uncollectible accounts, discounts for charity care and contractual allowances for third-party payers. https://www.hfma.org/data-and-insights/map-initiative/map-keys/
NHS England. 2026/27 NHS Standard Contract, Service Conditions (Full Length) (PRN02123). Version 1. London, NHS England; November 2025. SC36.12, under which each commissioner that has agreed an Expected Annual Contract Value must make payments on account to the provider, and SC36.13, under which, for an NHS Trust or NHS Foundation Trust, each commissioner pays on the fifteenth day of each month (or another day agreed in writing) one twelfth, or another proportion specified in Schedule 3D, of its Expected Annual Contract Value. https://www.england.nhs.uk/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/03-nhssc-26-27-full-length-service-conditions.pdf

Net monetary benefit a strategy gives up against the frontier strategy chosen at a threshold

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000666
Type formula
assumes Chosen strategy found among the complete set of strategies, Stated value per QALY for the net monetary benefit given up
has calculator text NMB_s = lambda * Q_s - C_s; NMB_k = lambda * Q_k - C_k; L_k = NMB_s - NMB_k
has common error note Measuring the net monetary benefit given up against usual care. At GBP 35,000 per QALY R3 and usual care R0 both have a net monetary benefit of GBP 173,000, so the incremental net monetary benefit of R3 over R0 is zero and R3 can look acceptable. Against the frontier choice R4 it gives up GBP 2,500 per person.
Reading the switching-value gap as the loss at every threshold. The GBP 2,000 gap for R3 at GBP 30,000 per QALY is its smallest loss. At GBP 25,000 and at GBP 35,000 it gives up GBP 2,500 per person, so the gap is recomputed at each value reported.
has description in the module Measures how far a strategy falls below the frontier at a value λ in net monetary benefit terms, as the net monetary benefit of the strategy s chosen at λ, the one with the highest value (HE-FM-NMB-003, the same strategy as HE-FM-CEF-001 picks), less that of strategy k, each from HE-FM-NMB-001. It is the incremental net monetary benefit of HE-FM-NMB-002 with s as the intervention and k as the comparator, so it is zero for the chosen strategy and not negative for any other. For a dominated or extendedly dominated strategy it is positive at every positive λ, since such strategies never have the highest net monetary benefit. When Q_k lies within the QALY range of the frontier, its smallest value arises at the slope of the frontier segment beneath Q_k, where it equals the saving of the blend of the two frontier neighbours in HE-FM-EXD-002, the vertical distance of k above the frontier.

Published 31 January 2022, last updated 13 October 2026. Section 4.2.16, which asks for expected net health benefits as well as ICERs, particularly informative when there are several technologies or comparators, using values placed on a QALY gain of GBP 25,000 and GBP 35,000, and notes that net monetary benefits can also be shown, and section 4.10.8 on the same two values. https://www.nice.org.uk/process/pmg36/chapter/economic-evaluation-2
Suen S, Goldhaber-Fiebert JD. An efficient, non-iterative method of identifying the cost-effectiveness frontier. Medical Decision Making. 2016;36(1) 132-136. Introduction, which defines net monetary benefit as benefits converted to money at a given willingness to pay minus costs, and section III of the proof, which shows that strategies that are strictly dominated or dominated by extended dominance never have the highest net monetary benefit for any positive willingness to pay, and section II, equation 10, which shows a frontier strategy has the largest net monetary benefit at the slope between the strategies either side of it. https://doi.org/10.1177/0272989X15583496

Net monetary benefit per person of a triage test against no testing

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000539
Type formula
assumes Missed cases and true negatives fare as without testing, Gain and loss valued per person at a stated value of health, Every positive triage result confirmed by a perfect test
has calculator text NMB = p * Se * G - (1 - p) * (1 - Sp) * L - c
has common error note Assuming extra cases found by a more sensitive test benefit as much. Lord, Irwig and Simes warn that a more sensitive test detects extra cases to which results from trials enrolling only cases found by the old test may not apply; the net gain G may be smaller for them.
Choosing the test with the better accuracy summaries. Test B leads on proportion correct, PPV, the positive likelihood ratio and DOR, but at 5 per cent prevalence test A's 8 extra cases per 1,000 are worth 172,800 pounds against 76,000 pounds for its 190 extra false positives, a gain of 96.80 pounds per person.
Holding the preferred test fixed across settings. At 2 per cent prevalence test B is preferred (289.92 against 280.64 pounds); the ranking reverses at about 2.3 per cent (HE-CF-DXA-001), so the comparison must be made at the prevalence of the population modelled.
has description in the module Values each true positive at its net gain G and each false positive at its cost L, both in money at a stated value of health, and subtracts the cost of the test. False negatives and true negatives fare as they would without testing, so they add nothing. Divided by G and with the test cost removed, the expression is decision-curve net benefit (HE-FM-DCA-001) at the threshold L / (G + L) (HE-FM-DCA-004).
has formalisation level catalogue record
has implementation Net monetary benefit of a triage test from named cells
has mathematical variable Cost of a false positive triage result, Cost of the triage test per person tested, Net monetary benefit per person tested with a triage test, Net value of a true positive triage result, Prevalence of the condition among people offered the triage test, Sensitivity of the triage test in the net benefit formula, Specificity of the triage test in the net benefit formula
has module record identifier HE-FM-DXA-005
has source in the module Lord SJ, Irwig L, Simes RJ. Annals of Internal Medicine. 2006;144(11):850-855. doi:10.7326/0003-4819-144-11-200606060-00011 (abstract read). Net present value recovered from a benefit-cost ratio

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000394
Type formula
assumes Positive costs in the denominator of a reported ratio, Ratio and costs taken from the same classification
has calculator text NPV = (BCR - 1) * PVC
has common error note Ranking options by ratio without their costs. Two options with the same ratio can differ in net present value by any factor: the pilot and the national programme above both have a ratio of 3, with net present values of £20,000 and £200 million. Ratios reported without costs cannot rank options by the value they create.
Reading a reported return on investment as a benefit-cost ratio. A return on investment is the ratio minus one, but some studies label a benefit-cost ratio as a return on investment. A reported return of 4 to 1 can therefore mean a ratio of 4 or a ratio of 5; on costs of £1 million the implied net present value is £3 million or £4 million.
has description in the module Recovers net present value from a benefit-cost ratio and the present value of costs it was built on. It rearranges the identity that the ratio minus one equals net present value per unit of cost, so a ratio above one and a positive net present value are the same finding whenever costs are positive. The ratio minus one is also the return on investment as defined in public health reviews, so a reported return converts to a ratio by adding one.

Net value of waiting for a larger-later outcome judged today and one period ahead

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000634
Type formula
assumes All reversal-check weights from one function seen from today, Reversal-check amounts in common units and fixed over time
has calculator text M_0 = b * w_1 - a * w_0; M_1 = b * w_2 - a * w_1
has common error note Reversal taken as proof of hyperbolic preferences. A plan that unravels fits hyperbolic weights but does not establish them. Frederick and colleagues report Read's argument that rates falling with horizon could reflect subadditive discounting, and in their own review the link between horizon and discount factor disappears once studies with horizons of a year or less are excluded.
Steep constant discounting mistaken for present bias. An impatient exponential discounter with delta = 0.75 has M_0 = minus 0.25 and M_1 = minus 0.1875, so the person never plans to wait. A reversal needs a rate that declines with delay, not a high rate, which is the article's second misreading.
has description in the module Compares a smaller-sooner amount a with a larger-later amount b that arrives one period after it, using the weights w_0, w_1 and w_2 of any discount function at delays 0, 1 and 2 seen from today. M_0 is the advantage of waiting when the choice is immediate and M_1 the advantage, judged today, of waiting when the same choice comes one period later. A negative M_0 with a positive M_1 is a preference reversal, a plan to wait that is dropped when the time comes. Under constant-rate weights M_1 equals delta times M_0, so the two share a sign and no reversal occurs.

Net welfare change of a uniform or targeted Pigouvian subsidy with costly public funds

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000745
Type formula
assumes Linear curves and full pass-through of the subsidy, One marginal excess burden on every pound of the bill, Targeting that is exact and costless for the targeted net welfare
has calculator text Q_p = (a - c) / b; d_0 = m - g * Q_p; dQ = s / b; S_g = d_0 * dQ - 0.5 * (b + g) * dQ^2; W = S_g - lambda * s * (Q_p + dQ); W_T = S_g - lambda * s * dQ
has common error note Excess burden charged only on the induced units of a uniform subsidy. A uniform subsidy is paid to inframarginal users too, so its excess burden falls on the whole bill. Charging it only on the induced courses in the article's example reports a net gain of GBP 61,200 when the uniform subsidy of GBP 12 loses GBP 82,800, a gap of GBP 144,000 equal to the excess burden on the GBP 720,000 transfer (computed here for illustration).
Uptake response to a Pigouvian subsidy taken as the rate itself. Uptake rises by s / b, not by s. In the steeper-demand example, with b of 2, writing dQ as 12 in place of 6 gives a welfare gain of zero in place of GBP 45,000 and a net change of minus GBP 100,800 in place of minus GBP 41,400 (computed here for illustration). The two coincide only when b is 1, as in the article's curves.
has description in the module Measures the welfare gained as a per-unit subsidy s raises uptake from the private quantity Q_p of HE-FM-EXT-002 by s / b, the area between marginal social benefit and marginal cost over the induced units, and subtracts the excess burden of raising the bill, lambda times the bill of HE-FM-PIGS-001. W charges the excess burden on the whole bill of a uniform subsidy and W_T on a subsidy confined to the induced units. With the article's curves W reduces to the article's 15s minus 0.625s squared minus 0.2s(60 + s). At any rate S_g equals the deadweight loss of HE-FM-EXT-002 less the triangle of HE-FM-DWL-001 left between Q_p plus dQ and the efficient quantity, so at the Pigouvian rate it equals that deadweight loss and at a rate of d_0 it falls short by the overshoot loss (derived here and checked on a grid of curves). The general form in a, b, c, m and g is derived here from the article's example.

Net-benefit regression coefficient on a treatment indicator

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000664
Type formula
assumes One threshold per net-benefit regression, Treatment indicator coded 1 for the new option, Unadjusted coefficient equals the difference in arm means
has calculator text NB_1 = lambda * E_1 - C_1; NB_0 = lambda * E_0 - C_0; alpha = NB_0; beta = NB_1 - NB_0
has common error note Intercept read as incremental net benefit. The intercept is the comparator's mean net benefit, GBP 9,500 in the illustrative trial at GBP 20,000 per QALY, a level that depends on which costs and effects are counted. The incremental value is the treatment coefficient, GBP 500.
Treatment indicator coded in reverse in a net-benefit regression. Coding 1 for the comparator returns a coefficient of minus GBP 500 for the illustrative trial at GBP 20,000 per QALY instead of GBP 500, and the intercept becomes the new arm's mean of GBP 10,000 (computed here for illustration).
has description in the module Each patient's net benefit at threshold lambda, lambda times the patient's effect minus the patient's cost, is regressed on a treatment indicator T_i, 1 for the new option and 0 for the comparator, in the model NB_i = alpha + beta T_i + epsilon_i. With no other regressors the fitted intercept is the comparator arm's mean net benefit and the coefficient is the difference in arm means, which equals incremental net monetary benefit (HE-FM-NMB-002), so the confidence interval for beta is the interval for incremental net benefit. The calculator works from the arm means. Covariates added to the regression give an adjusted estimate of beta, which Hoch, Briggs and Willan proposed for imperfect randomisation and for subgroups.

Type formula
assumes Approximately normal change among patients not importantly changed
has calculator text c_95 = d_S + 1.645 * s_S
has common error note Choosing the stricter limit without saying so. The same data support thresholds of 6.0, 8.0 and 10.2 points; a model that gives responders and non-responders different utilities changes its responder shares, and so its QALYs, when the 10.2-point limit replaces the 6-point ROC threshold.
Using the whole reference group of the ROC analysis for the 95 per cent limit. The limit is built on the patients the anchor classes as not importantly changed; in the article's example that is the 70 rating themselves about the same, not all 110 patients outside the improved group, which include patients who got worse.
has description in the module Places the threshold for improvement at the mean change of the patients the anchor classes as not importantly changed plus 1.645 standard deviations of their change scores, the one-sided 95 per cent point of a normal distribution. De Vet and colleagues note that it corresponds to 95 per cent specificity on the ROC curve, so it is stricter than the ROC cut-off.

Non-inferiority and superiority readings of a risk difference against a margin

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000957
Type formula
assumes Margin fixed in the protocol and not greater than the control effect
Favourable outcome and test minus control orientation
Independent randomised arms large enough for the Wald interval
Two-sided 95% interval and a strict inequality at the margin
has calculator text d = p_T - p_C; SE_d = sqrt(p_T * (1 - p_T) / n_T + p_C * (1 - p_C) / n_C); L_d = d - z * SE_d; U_d = d + z * SE_d; NI = (L_d > -M); SUP = (L_d > 0)
has common error note Concluding non-inferiority from a non-significant difference. ICH E9 section 3.3.2 calls it inappropriate to conclude non-inferiority from a non-significant test of no difference. In the second worked example the interval of minus 0.0642 to plus 0.0242 contains zero, so the difference is not significant, yet with a 5-point margin the lower limit lies 1.42 points beyond minus 0.05 and non-inferiority is not shown.
Reading an adverse outcome in the favourable outcome orientation. If the outcome is failure, with failure in 16% on T and 14% on C from 500 per arm, and d is entered as test minus control (plus 0.02), the lower limit is minus 0.0242 and a 5-point margin appears to be met. Entered in the orientation of HE-AS-ACTR-002, control minus test (minus 0.02), the lower limit is minus 0.0642 and non-inferiority is not shown (illustrative, derived). The reversed sign turns a failed non-inferiority result into a pass whenever M is above 0.024246 and at most 0.064246, the two unrounded lower limits (derived).
Reading non-inferior as no worse than the control. NI equal to 1 rules out a loss larger than M and nothing more. In the third worked example the 10-point margin is met while the whole interval lies below zero, so T is statistically worse than C by between 0.6 and 3.4 points, a result the FDA guidance section III.A (Figure 2, result 6) and Schumi and Wittes (2011) both describe as non-inferior and inferior at once. A model should carry d and SE_d, not a zero difference.
Using a 90% interval for a clinical non-inferiority trial. Two-sided 90% intervals are the norm for bioequivalence (CPMP/EWP/482/99 section II.4; HE-FM-ANDA-001), not for clinical non-inferiority, where the two-sided interval is 95%. With z of 1.645 the first worked example gives a lower limit of minus 0.0571 instead of minus 0.0642, so an illustrative 6-point margin appears to be met when the 95% interval does not meet it (derived). The 90% interval corresponds to a one-sided level of 0.05, twice the 0.025 the FDA guidance ties to the 95% interval.
has description in the module Forms the difference in the proportion of patients with a favourable outcome, test minus active control, and its two-sided Wald interval, then reads the lower limit against minus the non-inferiority margin M and against zero. The chained steps are live records, d as HE-FM-ARR-001 with the subtraction reversed for a favourable outcome, as HE-AS-ARR-002 states, SE_d as the sum of the two arm variances of HE-FM-BINOM-004 (the rule of HE-VR-AN-002 and HE-FM-NMA-001), and L_d and U_d as HE-FM-AN-001. The new step is the decision, which ICH E9 section 3.3.2 and CPMP/EWP/482/99 section II.3 state as the interval lying wholly above minus the margin, and which the FDA guidance writes as the upper bound for control minus test lying below M. NI and SUP equal 1 when the reading is shown and 0 otherwise, so a trial can show non-inferiority without superiority, and when both are shown the superiority claim is allowed by CPMP/EWP/482/99 section IV.1.

has source in the module Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use. Guideline on the choice of the non-inferiority margin (EMEA/CPMP/EWP/2158/99). London, EMEA; adopted July 2005, in effect January 2006. Section 2 (General Considerations) asks for the choice of margin to be justified in the study protocol and states that defining the margin as a proportion of the difference between active comparator and placebo is not appropriate. Section 3 (Demonstrating Efficacy) asks for a conservative approach to the margin when constancy of effect cannot be assured. https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/documents/scientific-guideline/guideline-choice-non-inferiority-margin_en.pdf
Committee for Proprietary Medicinal Products. Points to consider on switching between superiority and non-inferiority (CPMP/EWP/482/99). London, EMEA; 27 July 2000. Section II.1 treats a two-sided 95% interval for the difference that excludes zero as usually equivalent to a significant difference at the 5% level and takes values to the right of zero as better on the new treatment. Section II.3 states that for non-inferiority the two-sided 95% interval should lie entirely to the right of minus the margin. Section II.4 assumes two-sided 95% intervals for all clinical trials, one-sided intervals at 97.5% and 90% intervals for bioequivalence. Section III requires the margin to be set down in the protocol, and section IV.1 accepts superiority when the interval also lies above zero. https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/documents/scientific-guideline/points-consider-switching-between-superiority-and-non-inferiority_en.pdf
International Conference on Harmonisation. ICH E10 Choice of control group and related issues in clinical trials. Step 4 guideline, 20 July 2000. Section 1.5.1.1 (Historical Evidence of Sensitivity to Drugs Effects and Choosing the Non-inferiority Margin) states that the margin cannot be greater than the smallest effect size the active drug would reliably be expected to have compared with placebo in the setting of the planned trial. Section 1.5 (Assay Sensitivity) states that a successful non-inferiority trial generally does not contain direct evidence of assay sensitivity. https://database.ich.org/sites/default/files/E10_Guideline.pdf
International Conference on Harmonisation. ICH E9 Statistical principles for clinical trials. Step 4 guideline, 5 February 1998. Section 3.3.2 (Trials to Show Equivalence or Non-inferiority) states that only the lower margin is needed for the active control non-inferiority trial, that a one-sided interval should be used, that the interval approach has a one-sided test counterpart for the treatment difference (investigational product minus control) against the lower margin, and that concluding non-inferiority from a non-significant test of no difference is inappropriate. Section 5.5 (Estimation, Confidence Intervals and Hypothesis Testing) prefers one-sided type I errors at half the conventional two-sided level in regulatory settings. https://database.ich.org/sites/default/files/E9_Guideline.pdf
Newcombe RG. Interval estimation for the difference between independent proportions: comparison of eleven methods. Statistics in Medicine. 1998;17(8):873-890. The study evaluates unconditional interval methods for the difference between binomial proportions, finds computationally simpler methods prone to aberrations and poor coverage, and reports that the methods of Mee and of Miettinen and Nurminen and a method combining Wilson score intervals for the two proportions perform well. https://doi.org/10.1002/(SICI)1097-0258(19980430)17:8%3C873::AID-SIM779%3E3.0.CO;2-I
Schumi J, Wittes JT. Through the looking glass: understanding non-inferiority. Trials. 2011;12:106. The section Superiority, equivalence, and non-inferiority states that non-inferiority is judged on the lower bound of the interval for the difference against minus the margin, and that a narrow interval can show a new treatment non-inferior and inferior at once. The section Choosing the margin, conceptually describes the 95-95 method, with M1 the lower limit of the interval for the control effect against placebo and M2 a smaller margin that preserves a set fraction of it. https://doi.org/10.1186/1745-6215-12-106
US Food and Drug Administration. Non-inferiority clinical trials to establish effectiveness. Guidance for industry. Silver Spring, MD, FDA; November 2016. Section III.A (The Non-Inferiority Hypothesis) states the null hypothesis C minus T at least M and establishes non-inferiority when the upper bound of the two-sided interval for C minus T is less than M; its Figure 2, result 6, shows a study that meets M1 while T is inferior to C. Section III.C states that the 95% two-sided interval corresponds to a one-sided test size of 0.025. Section IV.C.1 (The Fixed Margin Approach) defines the 95%-95% method, with M1 the lower bound of the historical interval and the trial interval used to rule out C minus T above M2, and notes 10 to 15% margins on the risk difference scale for antibiotics. https://www.fda.gov/media/78504/download

Non-mixture cure model all-cause survival in the relative survival form

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000595
Type formula
assumes No separate cured and uncured groups in the non-mixture cure model
Cure time fixed by the final boundary knot in a flexible non-mixture model
has calculator text S = S_star * pi^F
has common error note Putting a survival function in the exponent of the non-mixture cure model. F_z(t) must be a cumulative distribution function. Its complement, a survival function, makes relative survival start at pi and rise to 1: with pi = 0.25 the model would give relative survival of 0.25 at time zero instead of 1.
Setting the non-mixture cure time earlier than the data support. Fixing the final boundary knot early forces the excess hazard down too soon. Latimer and Rutherford report that a 5-year boundary knot gave hazards that fell steeply at around 2 years, so the knot position needs clinical justification and a check of the fitted hazard.
has description in the module Bounds the excess cumulative hazard instead of splitting the cohort: relative survival is the cure fraction raised to the power F_z(t), a cumulative distribution function that is 0 at the start and approaches 1 as time tends to infinity, so relative survival falls from 1 towards pi. Multiplying by expected survival gives all-cause survival. TSD 21 gives pi to the power F_z(t) as equation 12 and notes that the model extends to the relative survival setting in the same way as the mixture model.

Normal prior to posterior update of a treatment effect at an interim analysis

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000484
Type formula
assumes Normal likelihood with known standard error and a normal prior, Prior fixed before the interim data
has calculator text v_1 = 1 / (1 / v_0 + 1 / s^2); m_1 = v_1 * (m_0 / v_0 + y / s^2); z_1 = (m_1 - a) / sqrt(v_1)
has common error note Reading the probability of positive net benefit as the probability that the treatment works. The posterior probability that incremental net monetary benefit is positive is the probability of cost-effectiveness at the stated threshold. It depends on the threshold, costs and time horizon and differs from the probability that the clinical effect exceeds zero.
Weighting by standard deviations instead of precisions. Weighting the estimate by the ratio of standard deviations, 2.5, instead of the ratio of variances, 6.25, gives a posterior mean of about 857 pounds instead of 1,034 in the article's example (computed here for illustration).
has description in the module Combines a normal prior for the treatment effect with a normally distributed interim estimate of known standard error. The posterior precision is the prior precision plus the data precision, and the posterior mean is the precision-weighted average of the prior mean and the estimate. Dividing the posterior mean minus the minimum effect a by the posterior standard deviation gives z_1, and the posterior probability that the effect exceeds a is Phi(z_1), the standard normal distribution function, which a success criterion of the form Pr(d > a | y) > c compares with c.

Normal-approximation interval and probability for incremental net benefit

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000291
Type formula
assumes Normal approximation for a linear combination of mean differences, Fixed, stated threshold for the net benefit interval
has calculator text INB = lambda * Delta_E - Delta_C; SE_INB = sqrt(lambda^2 * SE_E^2 + SE_C^2 - 2 * lambda * Cov_CE); INB_L = INB - z * SE_INB; INB_U = INB + z * SE_INB; z_INB = INB / SE_INB
has common error note Omitting the covariance term from the net benefit variance. When the cost and effect differences are correlated, dropping the covariance term misstates the standard error: with positively correlated differences the variance is overstated, and with negatively correlated differences it is understated, which shifts both the interval and the probability.
Using one minus the two-sided p-value as the probability of positive net benefit. At £30,000 per QALY in the article's example the two-sided p-value for INB is about 0.456, and one minus it, about 0.544, understates the probability that net benefit is positive, which is about 0.772. The two-sided p-value has to be converted to a one-sided value first.
has description in the module Incremental net benefit at a threshold lambda is linear in the two differences, so its variance follows directly and no ratio is involved. A Wald interval follows, and z_INB, the estimate divided by its standard error, gives the normal-approximation probability that net benefit is positive as the standard normal cumulative distribution function evaluated at z_INB. That probability is one point on the cost-effectiveness acceptability curve. The calculator returns z_INB; Excel NORM.S.DIST and R pnorm convert it to the probability.

Number needed to treat and its confidence limits from the ARR

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000233
Type formula
assumes Benefit direction and an interval that excludes zero, Period and comparator risk attached to the NNT
has calculator text NNT = 1 / ARR; NNT_L = 1 / ARR_U; NNT_U = 1 / ARR_L
has common error note Reporting an incomplete interval when the ARR interval spans zero. Altman cites a reported NNT of minus 12.5 (minus 3.7 to infinity) for an ARR of minus 0.08 (minus 0.27 to 0.11). The complete interval is NNTH 12.5 (NNTH 3.7 to infinity to NNTB 9.1).
Rounding the NNT down or to the nearest whole number. A risk difference of minus 0.12 gives 8.33, which the Cochrane convention reports as 9. Reporting 8 overstates the benefit per person treated. An ARR entered as a percentage, 5 rather than 0.05, gives an NNT of 0.2.
has description in the module Takes the reciprocal of the ARR and of its confidence limits, which reverses their order. The NNT is the expected number of people who must receive the intervention rather than the comparator, over the stated period, for one additional person to avoid the event. By convention it is rounded up to the next whole number when reported.

Reading every EQ-5D-5L value as directly observed. In the England study 86 states were valued by time trade-off, so the values of the other 3,039 states are model predictions. The choice of model therefore shapes most of a five-level value set, and a dispute about the model is a dispute about most of the values.

The same counts give 243 states and 10 level decrements for the EQ-5D-3L, whose UK tariff in HE-FM-EQ3L-002 adds a constant and N3 to them. The share valued shows how much of a value set rests on model prediction.

Number of states in a cohort model after splitting one state into a tunnel

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000585
Type formula
assumes One state expanded into a tunnel, Tunnel length set by the cycle length
has calculator text n_S_tunnels = n_S + n_tunnels - 1
has common error note Keeping the number of tunnel states when the cycle is shortened. Three tunnel states represent three years with annual cycles but only three months with monthly ones. A model moved to a shorter cycle needs the tunnel recounted, and the growth in states is the state explosion that the ISPOR-SMDM report warns about.
Leaving the long-term state out of the tunnel count. Counting only the three one-cycle tunnel states as n_tunnels gives five states for the article's model in place of six. The missing state is the long-term state, so the survivors of T3 have nowhere to go unless T3 is given a non-zero diagonal, which breaks the tunnel.

Following Alarid-Escudero and colleagues, n_tunnels counts every state the original state is split into, including the long-term state, so with K one-cycle tunnel states n_tunnels is K+1. One is subtracted because the tunnel replaces the original state. The expanded transition matrix has n_S_tunnels rows and columns.

One Euler step of the closed SIR model with frequency-dependent transmission

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000711
Type formula
assumes Closed population with lasting immunity and an exponential infectious period in the SIR step
Both SIR flows computed from start-of-step counts before any compartment is updated
has calculator text F = beta * S * I / N * dt; G = gamma * I * dt; S_next = S - F; I_next = I + F - G; R_next = R + G
has common error note Euler step too long for the speed of the epidemic. Euler steps lag the true solution while infections grow. With one-day steps the article's epidemic has 570.0 infectious people on day 10, about 13% fewer than the 653.9 given by steps of 0.0001 day, which is close to the exact solution, and two five-day steps give 389.6 (computed here for illustration). The error builds over the run and feeds every count and cost taken from it.
Infections for the infectious compartment taken from already updated susceptibles. Updating S first and then computing the inflow to I from the new S mixes two time points. On the article's day 1 it moves 29.6109 people into I but 29.7 out of S, leaving 9,999.9109 people in the population, and the loss repeats at every step (computed here for illustration).
has description in the module Applies the compartment balance HE-FM-CMPM-001 to the susceptible, infectious and recovered compartments of Hethcote's classic SIR epidemic model, with new infections F from the force of infection of HE-FM-CMPM-002 and recoveries G at rate gamma, both computed from the counts at the start of the step. F leaves S and enters I, and G leaves I and enters R, so S_next plus I_next plus R_next equals S plus I plus R and the population is conserved at every step. Written as a cohort update the step has an S to I entry of beta I dt/N that changes with the infectious count, so the transition matrix differs at every step and the update is nonlinear in the state, whereas HE-FM-MM-001 applies one fixed matrix to a cohort that does not interact. Pitman and colleagues note that spreadsheet models often use this Euler method and that it is less accurate than other numerical techniques, so the step is kept short against the mean infectious period 1/gamma.

One-stage expected gain of continuing over stopping at an interim look with a switching cost

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000689
Type formula
assumes Normal interim posterior with known variance and outcomes observed at once
Online and offline learning in the interim reward
One-stage look-ahead as a check on the optimal sequential rule
has calculator text a = mu_t - I / P; s_m = sigma_X * sqrt(m / (n_t * (n_t + m))); z = abs(a) / s_m; phi_z = exp(-z * z / 2) / sqrt(2 * 3.14159265); EVSI_I = s_m * (phi_z - z * Q_z); Delta = P * EVSI_I - m * c + d_on * m * mu_t
has common error note Design-stage prior mean used at the interim look. Keeping the prior mean of GBP 500 when the interim posterior mean has fallen to minus GBP 1,500 gives a one-stage gain of about GBP 0.94 million, a signal to continue, where the interim evidence gives about minus GBP 377,228, a signal to stop (computed here for illustration).
Negative one-stage gain read as proof that stopping is optimal. A one-stage check looks only at plans that stop after m more pairs, so it can stop a trial too early. Flight and colleagues note that updating the EVSI with the interim data does not take account of all possible future interim analyses, and Chick and colleagues report the optimal sequential policy outperforming the one-stage policy in net gain where the prior mean lies in the sequential region.
Prior effective sample size used in place of the interim effective sample size. Computing s_m with the prior n0 of 25 in place of n_t of 125 treats the 100 pairs already observed as if they had not been, so the remaining 100 pairs are credited with about GBP 618.11 per patient instead of GBP 151.14, and the gain of continuing with about GBP 11.96 million instead of GBP 2.62 million (computed here for illustration).
has description in the module Compares two expected rewards at an interim look in the model of Chick, Forster and Pertile, with outcomes observed at once and no discounting. Stopping now adopts the new technology only if P times the posterior mean exceeds the switching cost I, which is worth P times max(a, 0), with a the posterior mean less I divided by P. Continuing with m more pairs and then choosing is worth P times the expected positive part of a after updating, less the cost c of each pair, plus the participants' expected reward d_on times m times mu_t under online learning. The difference Delta is P times EVSI_I less the sampling cost plus that online term, where s_m is the preposterior standard deviation of HE-FM-EVSI-002 with n_t and m, and EVSI_I is the closed-form EVSI of HE-FM-EVSI-003 taken about the threshold I/P in place of zero. A positive Delta for some feasible m means that a one-stage plan beats stopping, the continuation condition of the KG* rule, which Chick and colleagues set out for unknown sampling variance (their section 4) and which here takes the normal distribution of their equation 6 as in their equation 14.

One-step infection update of a susceptible agent from its own uniform random number

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000691
Type formula
assumes Agent's own random stream kept across strategies, Strict inequality in the agent uniform draw comparison, Synchronous update of all agents from start-of-step states
has calculator text P_inf = 1 - (1 - p)^k; X_next = (U < P_inf)
has common error note Fresh random numbers for each strategy in the agent update. If each strategy draws new uniform numbers, the per-agent difference in infection between three and two contacts has a variance of 0.271 × 0.729 + 0.19 × 0.81, about 0.351, against 0.081 × 0.919, about 0.074, when each agent keeps its draw. About 4.7 times as many runs are then needed for the same standard error of the infections averted.
Updating agents in sequence within a step without stating the order. If agent B, a contact of an infectious agent A, is updated before agent C, whose only contact is B, then C can be infected in the same step with probability 0.10 × 0.10, or 0.01, for a per-contact probability of 0.10, while with start-of-step states that probability is zero. The order changes the speed of spread and is part of the model specification.
has description in the module Turns the per-step infection probability of HE-FM-ABM-001 into the agent's next state by comparing it with a uniform random number U drawn for that agent. The agent becomes infected, X_next equal to 1, when U is below P_inf, and otherwise stays susceptible with X_next equal to 0, so over many draws the share infected approaches P_inf. Drawing U from a stream reserved for the agent, the per-agent seed that Chhatwal and He describe for common random numbers, gives the same agent the same U under each strategy, so a strategy that lowers P_inf can avert that agent's infection and cannot cause it. A single draw against P_inf has the same distribution as one draw per contact against p, which the computational function under HE-FM-ABM-001 uses as an independent check.

Over- or under-compensation and predictive ratio for a risk group

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000440
Type formula
assumes Groups defined by the actions plans can take, Payments and costs for the same members and period, Positive average cost for the predictive ratio
has calculator text OC_g = R_g - C_g; PR_g = R_g / C_g
has common error note Comparing a predictive ratio with a compensation difference from another study. A ratio of 0.59 and a difference of minus £3,500 describe the same group in the article but are on different scales. The same undercompensation of £3,500 against an average cost of £5,000 would give a ratio of 0.30, computed here for illustration, so results are converted to one measure before they are compared.
Judging selection incentives from a broad group only. The article's 70-year-olds as a whole show a ratio of 1 while the subgroups without and with a chronic condition show 1.43 and 0.59. A measure for a broad group can hide the incentive within it, which is why Layton and colleagues recommend defining groups by the actions plans can take.
has description in the module Two group-level measures of the selection incentive a payment system leaves. Over- or undercompensation is the average payment minus the average cost for the group, in money, and is the usual European measure; the predictive ratio is payment divided by cost, without units, and is the usual US measure. A positive difference or a ratio above 1 indicates overcompensation, and a negative difference or a ratio below 1 undercompensation, so a group with a ratio well below 1 is a likely target for selection. Both are computed over the same members, so the ratio of total payment to total cost equals the ratio of the averages.

Overall attack rate from new cases and the population at risk

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000325
Type formula
assumes Attack rate denominator limited to the population at risk, Attack rate tied to a stated period and case definition
has calculator text AR = A / N
has common error note Leaving immune people in the attack rate denominator. Illustrative figures: 18 cases in a population of 1,000 of whom 400 are known to be immune give an attack rate of 0.03 among the 600 at risk, not 0.018. Leaving immune people in N makes the infection look less transmissible among susceptible people than it is.
Spreading a seasonal attack rate evenly across model cycles. Rescaling a seasonal attack rate to equal monthly probabilities with the standard probability to rate conversion assumes a constant underlying rate. Outbreak risk rises and falls with the epidemic curve, so the model places cases and costs in the wrong cycles.
Treating an attack rate as a rate per unit of time. An attack rate has no time unit and carries time only through its stated period. Comparing an outbreak attack rate directly with an incidence rate in cases per 1,000 person-years, or reading it as a weekly or annual rate, mixes a risk with a rate.
has description in the module Divides the number of new cases meeting the case definition during a stated period by the number of people at risk at the start of that period. The result is an incidence proportion, usually reported as a percentage. A food-specific attack rate uses the same formula with the people who ate a given food as the denominator.

Overlap shifting rule, start day of an early same-drug refill in the proportion of days covered

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000455
Type formula
assumes Earlier supply finished before a refill is started, Shift applied to the same drug only, not across a class
has calculator text a_i = max(f_i, a_prev + S_prev)
has common error note Shifting from the unshifted end of the previous fill. Comparing fill 3 (day 45) with the original end of fill 2 (day 51) instead of its shifted end (day 60) starts fill 3 on day 52, so days 52 to 60 are covered twice and fills 1 to 3 cover only days 1 to 81. The PDC falls from about 0.833 to 141 / 180, about 0.783, below 80% (computed here for illustration).
Shifting overlaps between different drugs in a PDC class measure. Two different drugs in a class, each dispensed for 30 days on day 1 and taken together, cover days 1 to 30. Shifting the second to start on day 31 credits 60 covered days where the patient had medicine on 30, which overstates the PDC for the class (computed here for illustration).
has description in the module Moves the start of a refill of the same drug, collected before the previous supply has run out, to the day after that supply ends, on the PQA premise that the patient finishes the old supply before starting the new one. Fills are taken in date order and the rule is applied in sequence, so each start is compared with the end of the previous fill as already shifted. The first fill starts on its dispensing day, and a refill collected after the previous supply has ended keeps its own date. CMS defines the same drug by the active ingredient at generic name level.

Pairwise dominance rule including ties

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000198
Type formula
assumes Inclusive treatment of ties, Consistent subtraction direction for dominance, Expected values on a common basis
definition source Drummond et al. 2015; Briggs et al. 2006; the Source rows of the Functions and Formulae module record HE-FM-DOM-001
editor note HEMO states the tie tolerances tau_C and tau_E as inputs, because modelled costs and QALYs are rarely exactly equal in floating point, so a difference no larger than its tolerance counts as equal. With both tolerances 0 this is the module's formula.
The one HEMO dominance rule, weak or Pareto dominance (decision 14, confirmed by the curators on 19 October 2026). An option dominates when it costs no more and is no less effective and is strictly better on one of the two, with equality read within the stated tolerances. Its mirror is HEMO-FM-DOMD-001, strict dominance is HEMO-FM-DOMS-001 and the four-way classification is HEMO-FM-DOMC-001. Extended dominance stays a separate rule, HE-FM-EXD-001, applied after this screen. RHEO competency query cq38 differs in two cases, equal QALYs at a lower cost, which HEMO calls dominant and cq38 calls less effective and less costly, and identical cost and QALYs, which HEMO calls a duplicate and cq38 calls dominated.
has calculator text DOM = (Delta_C <= tau_C) and (Delta_E >= -tau_E) and (Delta_C < -tau_C or Delta_E > tau_E)
has calculator text in the module DOM = (Delta_C <= 0) and (Delta_E >= 0) and (Delta_C < 0 or Delta_E > 0)
has common error note Forgetting ties. Requiring both differences to be non-zero leaves equal-cost or equal-effect results unclassified, so an inferior tied option can remain in the analysis.
Reading a negative ICER as dominance. A negative ratio arises both when the intervention dominates and when it is dominated. Only the signs of Delta_C and Delta_E show which.

Type formula
assumes Ratings treated as an interval scale in a ratings-based conjoint study
Balanced orthogonal design for the mean-difference part-worth
Additive part-worths without interactions
has calculator text b_k = Rbar_1 - Rbar_0
has common error note Comparing part-worths across attributes without their reference levels. A part-worth is relative to its attribute's reference level; the nurse-led value of minus 1.00 says a consultant lead is worth 1.00 more, not that nurse-led care has negative value.
Using mean differences when profiles are missing. If profile 8 is dropped, the mean difference for a local clinic becomes 2.00 while least squares on the seven profiles gives 1.25 (computed here for illustration); unbalanced designs need the regression.
has description in the module In a balanced orthogonal design with dummy coding, the least-squares part-worth of a two-level attribute equals the mean rating of the profiles showing the coded level minus the mean rating of those showing the reference level. Any design can be fitted by multiple regression on the dummy codes (HE-CF-CJA-001); the difference of means is a shortcut that holds only in a balanced orthogonal design, where every pair of levels of any two attributes appears equally often, as in a full factorial or an orthogonal fraction of it.

Partially pooled basket response under a normal approximation

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000359
Type formula
assumes Common mean and between-basket variance treated as known
Exchangeable baskets in a basket trial
Normal approximation for basket proportions on the probability scale
has calculator text p_hat_j = y_j / n_j; s2_j = mu * (1 - mu) / n_j; w_j = tau2 / (tau2 + s2_j); p_tilde_j = w_j * p_hat_j + (1 - w_j) * mu
has common error note Basket's own proportion used in the basket sampling variance. Evaluating the sampling variance at p_hat_j rather than mu makes extreme baskets look precise. Basket C's variance falls from 0.025 to 0.009, its weight rises to about 0.714 and its estimate falls to about 0.214 rather than 0.3105. A basket with no responders would have zero variance, a weight of 1 and no borrowing at all.
Between-basket standard deviation entered as the variance. Entering the standard deviation of 0.15 where tau2 belongs raises basket C's weight from about 0.474 to about 0.857 and gives a partially pooled response of about 0.157 instead of 0.3105, so far less borrowing occurs than intended. The variance is the square of the standard deviation, 0.0225.
Reading a borrowed basket estimate as that basket's own evidence. Basket C rises from 0.10 to about 0.31 purely because of the other baskets. If basket C truly differs, the borrowed estimate overstates its response. In simulations, Berry and colleagues found that when a treatment was promising in only one group, borrowing cut the power for that group to 65%, and that borrowing could inflate the type I error rate when the drug was promising in some groups and not others.
has description in the module Shrinks the observed response proportion of basket j towards a common mean mu. The weight w_j on the basket's own data is the between-basket variance tau2 divided by the sum of tau2 and the sampling variance s2_j of a proportion near the common mean in a basket of n_j patients. Because s2_j uses the common mean rather than the basket's own proportion, the weight depends only on basket size, so small baskets receive low weight and move furthest towards the mean. This is the simplified approximation in the article; a full hierarchical model estimates mu and tau2 jointly on the log-odds scale.

has implementation Basket weight and partially pooled response in two cells

Partitioned survival QALYs as utility-weighted areas under PFS and OS

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000589
Type formula
assumes One utility for all time in each partitioned survival state, PFS and OS areas from the same curves and horizon
has calculator text QALY = u_PF * A_PF + u_PD * (A_OS - A_PF)
has common error note Post-progression survival gain created by extrapolated OS alone. When extrapolated OS curves separate more than PFS curves, the model credits treatment with longer survival after progression whether or not evidence supports it. In the example, an OS hazard of 0.3 instead of 0.4 for the new treatment would raise its progressed time from 1.0 to about 1.83 years and its QALYs from 1.725 to 2.225. TSD 19 reports that reviewers criticised such differences in five appraisals for lack of supporting evidence.
Valuing the whole OS area at the progressed utility. Adding u_PD times the whole area under OS to u_PF times the PFS area counts progression-free time twice. In the standard-care example it gives 0.75 × 1.0 + 0.60 × 2.0 = 1.95 QALYs instead of 1.35.
has description in the module Values mean progression-free time at the progression-free utility and mean progressed time, the area between the OS and PFS curves, at the progressed utility; death carries zero. A_PF and A_OS are the areas under the PFS and OS curves up to the time horizon, which equal mean progression-free and overall survival when the horizon is lifetime. Within follow-up an area can come from a Kaplan-Meier curve (HE-FM-ADMC-003) and beyond it from a fitted parametric curve. Costs follow the same pattern, and discounting weights each part of the curves before the areas are taken (HE-FM-DR-002).

Partitioned survival QALYs with utilities by time to death

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000591
Type formula
assumes Lifetime horizon so every final window lies inside the model, Utility depends on time to death alone
has calculator text W = (1 - exp(-lambda_OS * a)) / lambda_OS; QALY_TTD = u_far * (1 / lambda_OS - W) + u_near * W
has common error note Adding a progression decrement to time-to-death utilities from separate curves. Combining progression and time-to-death utilities needs the joint timing of progression and death, for example how much progressed time falls inside the final window. Separate PFS and OS curves do not provide it, so a combined structure needs patient-level data or extra assumptions.
Applying the lifetime window formula over a truncated horizon. Over a five-year horizon in the standard-care example, about 8.2% of the cohort is still alive at the end and has not reached its final window within the model. Taking the area under OS to five years with the lifetime W gives about 1.2245 QALYs, against about 1.2325 when only the part of each final window inside the horizon is counted. The difference comes only from people still alive at the horizon.
has description in the module Values time alive by closeness to death instead of by progression status, using only the OS curve. Over a lifetime horizon each person's time in the final window of length a before death is the smaller of a and their survival time, and its mean W is the area under the OS curve from 0 to a. For an exponential OS curve W is (1 minus exp(minus lambda_OS a)) divided by lambda_OS, and the remaining 1 divided by lambda_OS minus W years are valued at the utility for time further from death.

Patient time cost per visit and per year from travel, waiting and care hours

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000727
Type formula
assumes Average hours per use and one hourly value for every patient hour
One period and one price year for service counts and the value of time
Service-based hours leave out preparation, home recovery and administrative time
has calculator text h_v = t_trav + t_wait + t_care; c_v = w * h_v; C_T = n * c_v
has common error note Patient time cost counting only the time in care. Counting only the chair or consultation time leaves out travel and waiting. For the article's infusion the hours fall to 78 against 117 and the time cost at GBP 15 an hour to GBP 1,170 against GBP 1,755, a third lower, and for the oral treatment, whose 0.5 hour consultation is a quarter of a 2.0 hour visit, the cost falls by three quarters, to GBP 90 (computed here for illustration).
Same hours counted as patient time and as productivity cost. When the hours in care are taken from paid work and the analysis also values them as absence with HE-FM-ABSN-002, the same hour is counted twice. If all 117 infusion hours came out of paid work and were valued at GBP 15 under both headings, the time would add GBP 3,510 to costs in place of GBP 1,755 (computed here for illustration). The article treats this as a boundary rule, and each hour is counted under one heading only.
Visit times in minutes entered as hours in the patient time cost. Entering 60, 30 and 180 minutes as hours makes each infusion visit 270 hours and the yearly time cost GBP 105,300 in place of GBP 1,755, 60 times too large (computed here for illustration). HE-VT-PTC-002 catches this.
has description in the module Adds the hours that one use of a service takes in round-trip travel, waiting and care, values them at the hourly value of time to give a time cost per visit, and multiplies by the number of uses in the period. With n counted over a year the result is the time cost per patient-year. The article's formula sums the same product over K service types; this formula is the term for one service type, and HE-CF-PTC-001 adds the terms for several types with published time estimates. It is HE-FM-COST-001 with a single resource, patient hours, whose unit cost is w.

Patient time cost with time valued by employment status

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000729
Type formula
assumes Employment status held fixed over the costing period, Wage as the proxy for the value a patient places on time
has calculator text v_i = E_i * w_i + (1 - E_i) * w_hp; C_T_i = h_i * v_i
has common error note Group means of hours and value of time multiplied in place of person-level costs. Multiplying mean hours by a mean value of time ignores that hours and employment go together. In an illustrative group where 30% are employed, with 20 hours a year at USD 15, and 70% are not, with 50 hours at USD 5.32, the person-level mean is USD 276.20, while 41 mean hours times a mean value of USD 8.224 gives USD 337.18, 22% too high (computed here for illustration).
Valuation by employment status treated as neutral between groups. The same 55.1 hours are worth USD 293.13 at the home production value and USD 913.01 at the median wage, 68% less for a person not employed (computed here for illustration). Yabroff and colleagues warn that methods which value time differently for different populations may lead to inequities, particularly for low-income and other vulnerable groups, and kept a single median wage for their base case.
has description in the module Values a person's hours in care at the person's own hourly wage when employed for wages and at an hourly value of home production otherwise, the approach Yabroff and colleagues used in a sensitivity analysis, and multiplies by the person's hours from HE-FM-PTC-001 or HE-CF-PTC-001. The base case of the same study used one median wage for everyone, the w of HE-FM-PTC-001, so that each person's time counted equally. In that study the choice cut annual time costs for cancer survivors aged 65 and over to USD 359, against USD 913 in the base case. The value differs from the human capital value of HE-FM-ABSN-002, which values absence from paid work as lost output, usually at gross earnings including employer-paid costs.

Patients per arm for a two-arm trial with a continuous outcome and a minimal important difference as the target

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000579
Type formula
assumes Two equal arms, a continuous outcome and a two-sided test, Target difference important to a stakeholder group
has calculator text n = 2 * (z_a + z_b)^2 * sigma^2 / delta^2
has common error note Setting the target difference from a distribution-based value. DELTA2 favours anchor and opinion-seeking methods and says the distribution method should not be used; a half standard deviation target of 6 points would coincide with the MID here only by chance.
Using a within-person threshold as the target difference between arms. Taking the 8.0-point mean change of the minimally improved group as delta would give 47.3, or 48 per arm (computed here for illustration), against 85 for the between-group MID of 6.0, so the trial would be underpowered for the difference that matters between arms.
has description in the module The usual normal approximation for two equal arms and a two-sided test sets the number per arm to twice the squared sum of the two standard normal quantiles, times the outcome variance, over the squared target difference. Because the target is a difference between arms, a between-group estimate such as MID_between is the relevant MCID; halving it quadruples the trial.

Payer's maximum price per patient from a cost-effectiveness threshold

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000356
Type formula
assumes One course per patient priced as a unit, Threshold that reflects the health displaced by spending
has calculator text p_bar = k * Delta_E - Delta_C_o
has common error note Applying the maximum price per patient to each pack. When a course is supplied in several packs, setting each pack at p_bar multiplies the cost per patient. With four packs per course and a maximum of £8,000 per patient, the maximum price per pack is £2,000.
Leaving other incremental costs out of the maximum price. Multiplying the threshold by the QALY gain alone gives £10,000 rather than £8,000 per patient. At £10,000 the ratio is £24,000 per QALY, above the £20,000 threshold, so the payer would not fund the product at that price.
has description in the module Gives the highest price per patient at which a payer that funds technologies with an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio at or below the threshold k still funds the product. At this price the ratio equals k and the incremental net monetary benefit (HE-FM-NMB-002) is zero. In bargaining terms it is the payer's walk-away price, the top of the range over which the price is negotiated.

Pearson chi-square score for model calibration targets with its degrees of freedom

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000422
Type formula
assumes Expected counts of at least 5 for a Pearson chi-square reference
Parameters tuned to the same targets make a Pearson p-value descriptive
has calculator text X2 = sum_(j=1)^m [(O_j - E_j)^2 / E_j]; df = m - c - 1
has common error note Pearson gaps divided by the observed instead of the predicted counts. Dividing each squared gap by the observed count gives about 2.740 for the first parameter set instead of 2.827. It is a different statistic, and mixing the two across candidate sets distorts the ranking.
Pearson p-value quoted without its degrees of freedom rule. The first set's score of 2.827 gives a p-value of about 0.59 when the four counts are treated as independent with expectations fixed in advance, and about 0.09 under the NIST/SEMATECH rule with two calibrated parameters. Both are defensible counts of degrees of freedom, so a p-value quoted without its rule is misleading; the score is better used to rank candidate parameter sets than as a formal test.
has description in the module Scores a candidate parameter set by scaling each squared gap between an observed count and the model's predicted count by the predicted count, so a gap of 7 cases matters more for a target of 45 than for one of 450. When the score is read against chi-square, the NIST/SEMATECH rule subtracts the number of parameters estimated from the same counts, plus one, from the number of targets, which gives df. The one is subtracted because the predicted counts are constrained to add to the observed total, as in the article's example where both parameter sets total 350, the same as the observed counts. Treating the counts as independent with expectations fixed in advance gives m degrees of freedom instead, and the article's example shows how far the two readings can differ.

has implementation Pearson calibration score and degrees of freedom from two ranges

Karnon J, Vanni T. Calibrating models in economic evaluation: a comparison of alternative measures of goodness of fit, parameter search strategies and convergence criteria. PharmacoEconomics. 2011;29(1):51-62. Abstract, which reports that the chi-squared measure differentiated between parameter sets by accuracy to a far greater degree than the likelihood measure. https://doi.org/10.2165/11584610-000000000-00000
NIST/SEMATECH. e-Handbook of Statistical Methods. Section 1.3.5.15, Chi-Square Goodness-of-Fit Test. National Institute of Standards and Technology; accessed 2 October 2026. Test statistic: the sum of (O minus E) squared over E across bins; critical region: chi-square with degrees of freedom equal to the number of non-empty bins minus the number of estimated parameters plus one, written in this package's notation as m minus (c + 1); and the requirement that the expected frequency be at least 5. https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/eda/section3/eda35f.htm

assumes Constant adverse event rate across the trial period, Event-free patients as the adverse event risk pool, Adverse event as the single exit during the trial period
has calculator text r = -log(1 - P) / T; p_t = 1 - exp(-r * t)
has common error note Dividing a 24-week adverse event proportion by six cycles. Dividing 0.18 by six gives 0.03 per four-week cycle. Over six cycles that implies a cumulative risk of about 0.167, not the 0.18 observed. In a model that tracks event-free patients the shortcut understates the new drug's cumulative risk by 1.3 percentage points and its adverse event cost by about £23 per patient at £1,800 an episode.
Using a per patient-year adverse event rate with a cycle in weeks. The rate of about 0.00827 per patient-week is about 0.430 per patient-year, taking 52 weeks to a year. Entering 0.430 with a cycle length of 4 gives a cycle probability of about 0.821 instead of 0.0325. The cycle length has to be 4/52 of a year when the rate is per year.
has description in the module Turns the proportion of patients with an adverse event over the trial follow-up period T into the probability of a first episode within a model cycle of length t in two steps: it recovers the implied constant rate r, then converts that rate to the cycle probability with the constant-rate conversion HE-FM-TP-001 on the Transition Probability page. The second step also applies to a rate per person-time from HE-FM-AER-002. The two steps together equal the single-step form 1 minus (1 minus P) raised to the power t/T, the rescaling formula HE-FM-TP-003 applied to trial safety data. Dividing P by the number of cycles is not equivalent, because probabilities do not add over time in the way rates do. The function log is the natural logarithm and exp is the exponential function.

Type formula
assumes Per-period rate defined from adjacent hyperbolic weights, Rate re-measured from each new present
has calculator text rho_t = alpha / (1 + alpha * t)
has common error note First-period hyperbolic rate quoted as the rate at every delay. Treating alpha = 0.4 a month as a constant rate puts a weight of about 0.0126 on an outcome 13 months ahead, 1.4 to the power minus 13, against about 0.161 under the simple hyperbola (computed here for illustration). Alpha is the rate for the first period only.
has description in the module The per-period rate between delays t and t + 1 is the ratio of the two weights minus 1, D_H(t)/D_H(t + 1) minus 1, which simplifies to alpha/(1 + alpha t). It equals alpha for the first period and falls steadily as the delay grows, whereas the same calculation on the constant-rate factor of HE-FM-DR-001 returns r at every delay. A declining per-period rate is what Frederick and colleagues mean by hyperbolic discounting.
