has calculator text L_s = NBmax_s - NBcur_s; EVPI = sum_(s=1)^S [L_s] / S
has common error note Computing EVPI from a single deterministic run. With one set of inputs there is one best option and no loss, so an EVPI computed from a base case is zero by construction, whatever the true uncertainty. EVPI needs the full set of probabilistic draws.
Holding an option other than the highest-mean option fixed in the loss. If standard care is held fixed in the article's example although the drug has the higher mean, the mean loss is 0.65 / 5 = 0.13 QALYs, which is the EVPI of 0.06 plus the 0.07 QALYs of expected net benefit given up by the wrong current choice. The fixed option must be the one with the highest mean over the same draws.

has description in the module In each draw s the opportunity loss L_s is the highest net benefit available in that draw less the net benefit, in the same draw, of the option d* chosen on current evidence. EVPI is the mean of L_s over the S equally weighted draws. Because d* is the option with the highest mean net benefit, the result equals the mean of the maxima less the maximum of the means in HE-FM-VOI-001, and it also shows which draws carry the loss. L_s is zero in every draw where d* is also the best option.

Per-step infection probability of a susceptible agent from k infectious contacts

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000690
Type formula
assumes Independent transmission across the contacts of one agent in a step
Per-contact probability defined for the model step length
Agent susceptible at the start of the infection step
has calculator text P_inf = 1 - (1 - p)^k
has common error note Adding contact risks instead of combining escape probabilities. Summing the risks gives 3 times 0.10, or 0.30, for the article's agent instead of 0.271, about 11% too high, and for 20 such contacts gives 2.0, an impossible probability, where the formula gives about 0.878.
Counting every contact rather than infectious contacts in k. If an agent meets 10 people of whom 3 are infectious and k is set to 10, the probability with p of 0.10 is about 0.651 instead of 0.271. k counts only contacts with agents who are infectious at the start of the step.
has description in the module A susceptible agent with k contacts with infectious agents in one step, each transmitting independently with probability p, escapes infection only if every contact fails, which happens with probability (1 minus p) to the power k, the binomial probability of no events in HE-FM-BINOM-002 with k in place of n. The probability of at least one transmission, P_inf, is the complement; the article writes it P. It rises with k but less than in proportion, because a second transmission to an agent already infected adds nothing, so the sum k times p overstates it and can exceed 1. With one contact the formula returns p and with no contacts it returns zero.

Per-unit fee that brings N users of a shared resource to the joint optimum, with use and revenue under the fee

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000949
Type formula
assumes Uniform per-unit fee passed in full to every user's cost, Revenue not returned in proportion to each user's own use, Users, values and loss of value as in the equilibrium formula
has calculator text t_s = (a - c) * (N - 1) / (2 * N); q_t = (a - c - t_s) / (k * (N + 1)); Q_t = N * q_t; R_t = t_s * Q_t
has common error note Charging the whole marginal external cost when users are few. Setting the fee at k Q_s, the t_star of HE-FM-PIGT-001 with b and g equal to k and m equal to zero, ignores the share of the loss each user already bears. In the article's example a fee of 40 pounds for four prescribers cuts use to 800 courses each, 3,200 in all, below the optimum, and the rent to 153,600 pounds instead of 160,000 (derived). The whole external cost is the right fee only as N grows.
Counting the fee revenue as a loss of value. The 120,000 pounds raised in the article's example is paid by the prescribers to the authority, and the group's net value at the optimum is still 160,000 pounds. Subtracting the revenue would show 40,000 pounds and make the fee look worse than leaving the four prescribers alone at 102,400 pounds. Delaney and Jacobson likewise treat their subsidy as a transfer with no efficiency cost in itself, apart from the cost of raising the funds.
Setting the fee at the external cost observed before the fee. Valuing the loss on the other users at the untaxed equilibrium, k (N less 1) q_E, gives 48 pounds per course in the article's example, the external loss of its step 3. Each prescriber then chooses 640 courses, 2,560 in all, and the rent is 139,264 pounds, below the 160,000 pounds of the optimum (derived). The fee is the external cost at the optimum, as HE-FN-PIGT-001 sets it and as HE-FM-PIGT-003 shows for a tax set at the pre-tax external cost.
has description in the module A fee t_s on each unit raises every user's cost to c plus t_s, so use under the fee is the equilibrium of HE-FM-TOTC-001 with that cost. Setting the resulting total equal to the joint optimum (a less c) / (2k) gives t_s, the optimal Pigouvian amount Delaney and Jacobson state for their common pool resource game. It equals the loss one more unit imposes on the other N less 1 users at the optimum, k (N less 1) Q_s / N, the marginal external cost of HE-FM-EXT-001 valued at the efficient quantity as in HE-FN-PIGT-001 (derived). The user already bears their own share, so the fee is below the whole marginal external cost k Q_s, the t_star of HE-FM-PIGT-001 with b and g equal to k and m equal to zero, and tends to it, (a less c) / 2, as N grows (derived). Revenue R_t is paid by the users to the authority as a transfer and does not reduce the group's net value. A quota of Q_s / N units per user reaches the same use.

Section 2.1 states the optimal (Pigouvian) subsidy delta = (beta less alpha)(n less 1) / (2n), and section 2.2 adds delta per token to the return of the outside option and cites Pigou (1920) for the optimal subsidy as the difference between marginal private and marginal social cost at the optimal quantity. The Reviewers' Appendix gives the equilibrium with the subsidy, (beta less alpha less delta) / ((n + 1) gamma), and finds delta by setting it equal to the social optimum. Section 3 sets beta of 0.36, alpha of zero, gamma of 0.01 and n of 3, and section 3.1 sets delta at 0.12 dollars, with a symmetric Nash equilibrium of 6 tokens that yields the social optimum, and footnote 8 treats the subsidy as a transfer. https://web.williams.edu/Economics/wp/DelaneyJacobson_PaymentsOrPersuasion.pdf

Phelps optimal coinsurance rate from risk aversion, spending variance and price elasticity

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000921
Type formula
assumes Interior minimum of the Phelps welfare loss, Same approximations as the Phelps welfare loss, Risk aversion measured in the units of the spending figures
has calculator text C_star = eps * mu / (eps * mu + r * sigma^2)
has common error note Applying one coinsurance rate to all types of care. The optimal rate is service-specific. Charging the outpatient optimum of 150 / 175 = 0.857 on the illustrative hospital care raises its expected loss in HE-FM-MHHI-001 to 919.39 against 48.08 at its own optimum, and charging the hospital optimum of 100 / 2,600 = 0.038 on the outpatient visits raises theirs to 69.36 against 10.71.
Entering the elasticity as a negative number in the optimal rate. Phelps writes the elasticity as negative and the formula here takes its absolute value. Typing minus 0.1 for the illustrative hospital care gives minus 0.042, and minus 0.3 for the outpatient visits gives 1.2, both outside the range above 0 and below 1 that Phelps shows the optimum must lie in.
Risk aversion and spending in different currency units. r = 0.0001 is per dollar. Entering the illustrative hospital spending in thousands of dollars (mu = 1, sigma = 5) with the same r gives 0.1 / 0.1025 = 0.976 instead of 0.038.
Using the standard deviation of spending in place of its variance in the optimal rate. For the illustrative hospital care, r times sigma is 0.5 where r times sigma squared is 2,500, so the rate comes out at 0.995 instead of 0.038 and recommends almost no cover for the risk that most needs it.
has description in the module Gives the coinsurance rate that minimises the expected welfare loss of HE-FM-MHHI-001, found by setting its derivative with respect to C to zero. The rate is eps mu over eps mu plus r sigma squared, which Phelps puts in words as the moral hazard loss over the sum of the moral hazard loss and the risk premium. It rises with the price elasticity and falls with risk aversion and with the variance of spending, so a large, barely price-sensitive risk such as hospital care calls for near-complete cover and small, predictable, price-sensitive spending for a high rate. Phelps also gives it in relative terms with the coefficient of variation and the share of income at risk (his equation (7)), the same rule divided through by mu (derived).

Phelps second-order expected welfare loss at a coinsurance rate

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000920
Type formula
assumes Fair premium, a single coinsurance rate and no income effect of the premium in the Phelps loss
Induced care valued by the demand curve in the Phelps loss
Second-order approximation of the risk premium in the Phelps loss
Straight-line demand with one elasticity at the full price in the Phelps loss
has calculator text RP = 0.5 * r * sigma^2 * C^2; MH = 0.5 * (1 - C)^2 * eps * mu; WL = RP + MH
has common error note Entering the price elasticity with its negative sign in the Phelps loss. Phelps writes the elasticity as a negative number and subtracts its term, while the formula here takes the absolute value. Typing minus 0.1 for the illustrative hospital care turns the full-insurance loss of 50 into minus 50, a gain from induced use that the model cannot produce.
Reading the second-order risk premium as exact for hospital spending. The risk term ignores skewness. Phelps finds that for hospital care in the RAND data the third and fourth order terms are of the same order of magnitude as the variance term, so the second-order risk premium for heavily skewed hospital spending is an approximation to report with that caveat, even though the optimal rate he computes changes little between the second and fourth order.
Using the standard deviation of spending in place of its variance. The risk term needs sigma squared. With the illustrative hospital standard deviation of 5,000 used unsquared, the no-insurance risk premium is 0.25 instead of 1,250, and the loss at the optimal rate is 46.23 instead of 48.08, so the value of cover almost disappears.
has description in the module Adds two losses that move in opposite directions as cover changes. The first is the risk premium of the spending the patient still bears, one half of r times the variance of that spending, which is sigma squared times C squared when insurance pays the share 1 minus C of every bill. The second is the welfare-loss triangle of insurance-induced care, one half of (1 minus C) squared times eps times mu, which is HE-FM-MH-002 with the demand slope written as eps mu over the square of the full price (derived, for a straight-line demand curve with elasticity eps at the full price). Lowering C cuts the first term and raises the second, both quadratically, so the expected loss has a single minimum at the rate given by HE-FM-MHHI-002. Phelps prints the sum as his equation (4), with the elasticity entered as a negative number and subtracted.

Pigouvian subsidy and deadweight loss for vaccination with linear curves

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000254
Type formula
assumes Linear curves over the relevant range, Interior solution below full coverage, Subsidy passed through to the price faced
has calculator text Q_p = (a - c) / b; Q_s = (a + m - c) / (b + g); s = m - g * (a + m - c) / (b + g); DWL = 0.5 * ((a + m - c) / (b + g) - (a - c) / b) * (m - g * (a - c) / b)
has common error note Setting the subsidy at the external benefit at the private quantity. In the first example the marginal external benefit at 40 thousand is 21. A subsidy of 21 moves take-up to 61 thousand, beyond the efficient 57.5 thousand, because the external benefit has fallen to 17.5 by then. The Pigouvian rate is the marginal external benefit at the efficient quantity.
Treating the deadweight triangle as the value of the whole programme. The 183.75 thousand is the welfare gain from moving from private to efficient take-up. It does not represent the total net benefit of the vaccination programme and excludes the benefits already generated by vaccinations undertaken privately. The calculation also abstracts from any distortionary cost of financing the subsidy, since the subsidy payment itself is a transfer rather than a social cost.
has description in the module Takes a linear marginal private benefit (demand) curve a minus b × Q, a constant marginal cost c with no external cost, and a marginal external benefit m minus g × Q that falls as coverage rises, as herd immunity would suggest. The private quantity Q_p sets marginal private benefit equal to c; the efficient quantity Q_s sets marginal social benefit equal to c. The Pigouvian subsidy s is the marginal external benefit at Q_s, and the deadweight loss of leaving the market alone is the triangle between marginal social benefit and cost from Q_p to Q_s. The tax on a negative externality mirrors this: t equals the marginal external cost at the efficient quantity.

Pigouvian subsidy bill, transfer to inframarginal users and bill per induced unit

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000744
Type formula
assumes One rate paid on every unit with no displacement of private uptake
Uptake under the subsidy taken from the demand response
has calculator text B = s * Q_u; T = s * Q_p; B_n = s * (Q_u - Q_p); c_n = B / (Q_u - Q_p)
has common error note Pigouvian subsidy bill counted as a cost to society. Subtracting the whole bill from the welfare gain treats a transfer as a resource cost. In the article's example the GBP 864,000 bill against the GBP 90,000 gain gives a net loss of GBP 774,000, when the social cost of raising the bill at the illustrative 20p excess burden is GBP 172,800 and the net loss GBP 82,800 (computed here for illustration). OMB Circular A-94 excludes pure transfers from net present value and asks for their distributional effects to be discussed.
Subsidy rate read as the budget cost of each extra unit. The rate understates what the budget pays for each unit the subsidy brings about whenever most users are inframarginal. In the article's example GBP 12 a course buys 12 thousand extra courses for GBP 864,000, which is GBP 72 per extra course, six times the rate, because 60 of every 72 subsidised courses would have been taken up anyway (computed here for illustration).
has description in the module Multiplies the per-unit subsidy by the uptake it produces to give the bill to the public budget, and by the uptake there would have been without it to give the transfer to inframarginal users, people paid for doing what they would have done anyway. The rest of the bill is paid on the induced units, and dividing the whole bill by the induced units gives the public money paid out for each extra unit the subsidy brings about. The bill is a transfer and not a cost to society in itself; the social cost of raising it is the excess burden of HE-FM-DWL-004 with the bill as G, which HE-FM-PIGS-002 carries into the net welfare change. With linear demand the uptake under the subsidy is the private quantity of HE-FM-EXT-002 plus s / b.

Pigouvian tax and efficient quantity with linear demand and rising marginal external cost

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000427
Type formula
assumes Demand measures the true benefit to consumers, Linear curves and an interior efficient quantity, Tax passed through in full to the price consumers face
has calculator text Q_0 = (a - c) / b; Q_star = (a - c - m) / (b + g); t_star = m + g * Q_star
has common error note Average external cost used instead of marginal. Dividing the total external cost at the efficient quantity by the number of units gives an average of 1.60 pounds per unit in the article's example, half the marginal 3.20 pounds, because the external cost rises with consumption. A tax of 1.60 pounds leaves consumption at 144 thousand units, well above the efficient 128 thousand. These figures are computed here for illustration.
Pigouvian tax revenue counted as a cost to society. The 409,600 pounds raised in the article's example is a transfer from consumers to the government and cancels out at the level of society. Counting it as a cost, or as part of the welfare gain, misstates the case for the tax, which comes from the change in consumption.
has description in the module With marginal private benefit (the demand curve) a minus b × Q, a constant marginal private cost c and a marginal external cost m plus g × Q, consumers left alone choose Q_0, where marginal private benefit equals c. The efficient quantity Q_star sets marginal private benefit equal to marginal social cost, c plus the marginal external cost. The Pigouvian tax t_star is the marginal external cost at Q_star, and adding it to the private cost moves the private choice to Q_star.

Plant capacity utilisation from output efficiency with fixed inputs and with all inputs

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000923
Type formula
assumes Both plant capacity scores from one sample under constant returns to scale
Fixed and variable inputs classified before the plant capacity analysis
Proportional output expansion against best observed practice
has calculator text PI = E_F / E_V
has common error note Inverting the plant capacity utilisation ratio. Dividing E_V by E_F gives the factor by which output on the frontier could rise if the unused plant were brought into use, not the share of capacity in use. In the first worked example it returns 1.0526, which read as utilisation would claim that the hospital works above its capacity output (derived).
Reading the fixed-input score alone as capacity utilisation. E_F on its own is observed output over capacity output and equals PI times E_V (derived), so it mixes technical inefficiency with unused plant. Valdmanis and colleagues factor out inefficiency first because they measure plant capacity and not inefficient production. In the first worked example E_F of 0.76 would suggest that 24% of capacity output is unused, when 5% is due to idle plant and the rest of the gap to technical inefficiency (derived).
Taking the all-input score from a variable returns frontier. Both scores must come from constant returns frontiers. If E_F is from the constant returns programme but E_V is taken from a variable returns frontier, the ratio also carries scale efficiency (HE-FM-EFF-003). With E_F 0.76 and constant and variable returns scores for E_V of 0.80 and 0.90, PI falls from 0.95 to 0.844, and the scale effect is reported as idle plant (illustrative, derived).
Treating a bed occupancy ratio as plant capacity utilisation. An occupancy ratio such as HE-VR-ALOS-006 sets one used input against its capacity and says nothing about what was produced, as the article notes. A hospital can show high bed occupancy while its fixed inputs could support more output with the same variable spending, and a ratio of used to available beds cannot reveal that. PI compares outputs with what the fixed inputs could produce on the frontier.
has description in the module Divides the output efficiency score of a hospital or other unit measured with only its fixed inputs, such as beds and rostered staff, constraining output and its variable inputs unrestricted, by its output efficiency score with all inputs constraining output, both from one data envelopment analysis under constant returns to scale. The all-input score E_V carries the technical inefficiency of the unit, so dividing by it leaves the part of the shortfall from capacity output that is due to unused plant, the Johansen definition of plant capacity that Valdmanis and colleagues adopt. A value of 1 means that the unit, once on the frontier, could not raise its outputs in proportion without more fixed inputs, and a value below 1 shows unused plant capacity that could treat proportionately more patients. In 68 Thai public hospitals in 1999 the mean was 0.954. Unlike a bed occupancy ratio, the measure sets outputs against what the fixed inputs could produce.

Health Services Research. 2004;39(6 Pt 2):2117-2134. doi:10.1111/j.1475-6773.2004.00335.x (full text read in PubMed Central, PMC1361115). The Model subsection on capacity to provide increased services, the plant capacity approach, adopts the Johansen definition of plant capacity, states that the plant capacity measure PI is the ratio of the output efficiency where some inputs are variable and others fixed (E_F) to the output efficiency where all inputs are treated as variable (E_V), that a value below 1 indicates unused or underutilised plant capacity, that inefficiencies are factored out first and that the analysis is restricted to constant returns to scale, citing the methods of Färe, Grosskopf and Kokkelenberg (1989) and others. The Appendix gives the two output-based programmes, the second with the fixed inputs restricted and the variable inputs unrestricted. The Data section classes beds, doctors, nurses and other staff as fixed inputs and the three expenditure inputs as variable, and Table 4 reports a sample mean of 0.954 for 1999. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1475-6773.2004.00335.x

Poisson probability of n arrivals in a window

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000315
Type formula
assumes Constant arrival rate across the counting window, Independent arrivals unaffected by the queue
has calculator text P_n = (lambda * t)^n * exp(-lambda * t) / factorial(n)
has common error note Arrival rate and window in different time units. Entering the unit's demand of 48 patients a day as lambda with a window of 1 hour gives an expected 48 arrivals in the hour instead of 2. The probability of 4 or fewer arrivals then falls from about 0.947 to almost zero, and every hour appears to overflow.
Poisson counts for linked or booked arrivals. The Poisson model fits unscheduled, independent arrivals. Several casualties from one incident arrive together, and booked outpatient or elective arrivals cluster close to the booked times, so a Poisson count misstates the bunching in both cases. Booked arrivals are better generated from the booking pattern, with non-attenders removed.
has description in the module Gives the probability that exactly n arrivals occur in a window of length t when arrivals follow a homogeneous Poisson process with rate lambda. The expected number of arrivals is lambda times t. The function exp is the exponential function and factorial(n) is n!, the product of the whole numbers from 1 to n, with factorial(0) equal to 1.

has implementation Poisson arrival probability in one cell

Population attributable fraction of prevalent cases from a prevalence ratio

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000611
Type formula
assumes Exposure share and prevalence ratio from the costed population, Unconfounded prevalence ratio in the attributable fraction
has calculator text PAF = e * (PR - 1) / (1 + e * (PR - 1))
has common error note Entering the prevalence odds ratio in a prevalence attributable fraction. With 40% exposed, the POR of 2.4286 (214,200 / 88,200, used unrounded) gives a PAF of about 0.3636 instead of 0.2857. Applied to the article's 105,000 prevalent cases at GBP 1,200 each, attributable cases rise from 30,000 to about 38,182 and the annual cost from GBP 36.0 million to GBP 45.8 million, 27% more.
Treating a prevalence-based attributable cost as avoidable. Removing the exposure would lower prevalence only as existing cases resolve or die, and only to the extent that the association is causal. The attributable annual cost is therefore not the saving expected in the year after the exposure is removed.
has description in the module Applies the attributable-risk formula that Jo describes for top-down cost-of-illness studies, with the crude prevalence ratio in place of the relative risk. With cross-sectional evidence the result equals (P minus P_0) / P, the share of prevalent cases in excess of the unexposed prevalence, so it refers to prevalent cases and their annual costs, not to new cases and lifetime costs. Multiplying it by aggregate annual costs gives the top-down attributable burden HE-FM-COI-002.

If S1 takes two years to report, only the last three of the five annual cohorts can benefit, and population EVSI at 3.5% is about GBP 395,207 instead of GBP 682,270. Counting every cohort from year 0 overstates the value of a slow study.
Per-patient EVSI compared with the total cost of a study. Setting S1's GBP 73 per patient against an illustrative study cost of GBP 0.4 million makes the study look far too expensive, while its population EVSI over 10,000 future patients is about GBP 0.73 million undiscounted. Per-person values are scaled to the beneficiary population before any comparison with study cost.

Population mortality from attack rate and case fatality rate

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000453
Type formula
assumes All disease deaths occur among the counted cases, Same cases, period and population in both measures
has calculator text M = AR * CFR
has common error note Pairing an infection fatality ratio with a confirmed-case attack rate. With five infections per confirmed case, as in the article's example, a confirmed-case attack rate of 0.20 multiplied by an infection fatality ratio of 0.006 gives 0.0012, one fifth of the 0.006 obtained with the matching case fatality rate of 0.03 (computed here for illustration). Applying an infection fatality ratio to confirmed cases understates deaths.
has description in the module Links the case fatality rate to the proportion of a closed population that dies of the disease over an outbreak. Deaths over the population equal cases over the population multiplied by deaths over cases, so the identity holds only when both measures share the case definition, the period and the population. The result is a cumulative incidence of death for the period, not a rate per person-year. The attack rate is computed with HE-FM-ATR-001.

Lesson 3: Measures of Risk, Section 2, Morbidity frequency measures. The attack rate, or incidence proportion, divides new cases during a specified interval by the population at the start of the interval. https://archive.cdc.gov/www_cdc_gov/csels/dsepd/ss1978/lesson3/section2.html
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Principles of Epidemiology in Public Health Practice, 3rd ed. Atlanta: CDC; 2006, page last reviewed 2012. Lesson 3: Measures of Risk, Section 3, Mortality frequency measures. The mortality rate divides deaths by the size of the population among which they occurred, while the case-fatality rate divides deaths by cases. The product identity M = AR × CFR is derived here from these two definitions, for the same cases and population; the CDC text does not state it. https://archive.cdc.gov/www_cdc_gov/csels/dsepd/ss1978/lesson3/section3.html

Positive and negative predictive values at a given prevalence by Bayes' theorem

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000537
Type formula
assumes Prevalence of the people actually tested, Sensitivity and specificity transfer to the target population
has calculator text PPV = Se * p / (Se * p + (1 - Sp) * (1 - p)); NPV = Sp * (1 - p) / (Sp * (1 - p) + (1 - Se) * p)
has common error note Carrying a predictive value from an enriched validation sample. An algorithm with sensitivity 0.90 and specificity 0.95 has a PPV of about 0.82 in the Criterion Validity page's validation sample, where 20 per cent are cases, but about 0.27 at 2 per cent prevalence, so most flagged people in routine data would not have the condition.
Reading a high negative predictive value as evidence of a good test. At 2 per cent prevalence even a test with sensitivity and specificity of 0.5 has an NPV of 0.98, because almost everyone tested is free of the condition (computed here for illustration).
has description in the module Recomputes the predictive values for the population where the test will be used from sensitivity, specificity and the prevalence (pre-test probability) there. As prevalence falls, false positives from the larger disease-free group make up more of the positive results, so PPV falls and NPV rises. The odds form, post-test odds equal pre-test odds times the likelihood ratio (HE-FM-DXA-002), gives the same result.

Posterior probability of latent class membership with two classes

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000513
Type formula
assumes Class shares and class distributions taken from the fitted mixture model
Each unit belongs to exactly one latent class
has calculator text post_1 = pi_1 * f_1 / (pi_1 * f_1 + pi_2 * f_2)
has common error note Reading class shares as individual membership probabilities. The 20 per cent share is the prior; a patient's own probability depends on the data and ranges from about 0.02 to 0.99 across the three examples.
Treating the most probable class as certain. The patient with 3 attendances is allocated to the low-use class with probability of only about 0.64; carrying modal classes into a model as if known hides the allocation uncertainty, which adds parameter uncertainty to any class-specific analysis.
has description in the module Applies Bayes' rule to give the probability that a unit belongs to a class, given its observed data: the class share times the likelihood of the data under that class, divided by the same quantity summed over classes. Units are commonly allocated to their most probable class, but the probability shows how uncertain the allocation is. With K classes the denominator has K terms.

Potential years of life lost before a cut-off age for deaths in one age group

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000603
Type formula
assumes All deaths in an age group placed at its midpoint, No potential years counted at or above the cut-off age
has calculator text PYLL_a = N_a * max(C - m_a, 0)
has common error note Comparing potential years of life lost computed with different cut-off ages. The same 100 deaths at ages 75 to 79 count nothing with a cut-off of 70 and 750 years with 85, so totals and rankings change with the cut-off. WHO records that GBD 1990 chose not to use an arbitrary cut-off such as 70 years.
Reading potential years of life lost as years of life lost. In the article's example potential years of life lost before 70 total 2,715 against 5,169.1 YLLs under GBD 2010, because the cut-off drops the older deaths and no life table is used. The two measures answer different questions, and only YLLs enter the DALY.
Using the lower bound of the age group in place of its midpoint. Placing the 20 deaths at ages 1 to 4 at age 1 in place of 3 gives 1,380 potential years before 70 in place of 1,340 (computed here for illustration), and the bias grows with wider age groups.
has description in the module Counts, for each death before a cut-off age, the years between the midpoint of its age group and the cut-off, and nothing for deaths at or above the cut-off, following the method described by the US Centers for Disease Control (CDC). Unlike HE-FM-YLL-001 it uses no life table, so deaths in old age drop out of the total. The function max returns the larger of its arguments.

The measure reflects deaths before a conventional cut-off, usually 65 years, and is calculated by multiplying the deaths in an age category by the difference between the cut-off age and the mid-year of the age category, then adding the products. https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/00016649.htm

Predictive draw of a new-setting effect and the resulting treated mortality risk

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000383
Type formula
assumes Mean effect and between-study standard deviation from the same iteration
Effect additive on the log odds scale with a separate baseline risk
Predictive spread limited to true between-population variation
has calculator text theta_new = mu + tau * z; o_0 = p_0 / (1 - p_0); p_1 = o_0 * exp(theta_new) / (1 + o_0 * exp(theta_new))
has common error note Building the predictive range from posterior medians alone. Holding mu and tau at their posterior medians and taking mu plus or minus 1.96 tau gives odds ratios of about 0.607 to 1.023 under the Turner prior and 0.452 to 1.355 under the vague prior, against the article's predictive intervals of 0.489 to 1.239 and 0.225 to 2.592. The shortcut omits the uncertainty in mu and tau, which with four trials is large.
Sampling the mean effect where the predictive effect is needed. Sampling mu alone describes the average effect across trial settings. Under the Turner prior the 95% credible interval for mu gives odds ratios of 0.593 to 1.032 and treated risks of about 0.062 to 0.103, while the predictive draws give 0.489 to 1.239 and risks of about 0.052 to 0.121. TSD 3 argues that the predictive distribution may in many cases be more relevant to decision making than the distribution of the mean.
has description in the module Draws the true effect in a new setting at one iteration of a posterior sample and converts it to an annual mortality risk on treatment for a decision model. At each iteration theta_new is drawn from N(mu, tau^2) using that iteration's mu and tau, and the odds ratio exp(theta_new) is applied to the baseline odds o_0. The conversion is the baseline and odds ratio relation of HE-FM-NMA-004, applied here to a predictive draw. The 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of p_1 across iterations give the 95% predictive range of the treated risk.

Predictive probability of final success for a normal two-stage Bayesian design

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000485
Type formula
assumes Final analysis pools the prior and both stages
Second-stage estimate normal and independent of the first given the effect
has calculator text v_1 = 1 / (1 / v_0 + 1 / s_1^2); m_1 = v_1 * (m_0 / v_0 + y_1 / s_1^2); v_f = 1 / (1 / v_0 + 1 / s_1^2 + 1 / s_2^2); y2_crit = s_2^2 * (z_c / sqrt(v_f) - m_0 / v_0 - y_1 / s_1^2); z_pp = (y2_crit - m_1) / sqrt(v_1 + s_2^2)
has common error note Conditional power at the observed estimate in place of the predictive probability. Treating the interim estimate of 1,200 pounds as the true effect and ignoring posterior uncertainty gives a probability of about 0.548 that the second stage clears the boundary, against a predictive probability of about 0.474 in the article's example (computed here for illustration).
Confusing the predictive probability with the posterior probability. In the article's example the posterior probability of positive net benefit is about 0.918 while the predictive probability of meeting the final 0.975 rule is about 0.474. A high posterior probability now does not mean the final analysis is likely to succeed.
has description in the module Projects an interim look forward to the final analysis. Final success is a final posterior probability of a positive effect above Phi(z_c), so the final posterior mean must exceed z_c final standard deviations. Solving for the second-stage estimate gives y2_crit, and given the interim posterior that estimate is predicted to be normal with mean m_1 and variance v_1 plus s_2 squared. The predictive probability of success is 1 minus Phi(z_pp). Unlike the posterior probability it asks how likely the trial is to succeed, not how strong the evidence is now.

Preposterior variance of incremental net benefit for a study of size n

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000636
Type formula
assumes Normal prior and normal study estimate of incremental net benefit, Study that informs incremental net benefit directly, Sampling variance of a two-arm trial with equal arms
has calculator text n0 = sigma2 / v0; nu = n / (n + n0); s2 = nu * v0
has common error note Posterior variance used in place of the preposterior variance. After 100 per arm the posterior variance is about 666,667, the uncertainty that remains, and the preposterior variance about 333,333, the uncertainty the study resolves. Entering the posterior variance in HE-FM-EVSI-003 gives an EVSI of about GBP 134.97 per patient instead of GBP 61.68 for the illustrative prior, more than twice the correct value.
Variance of one arm used for a two-arm comparison. Setting sigma2 to the variance of one arm, 100,000,000, halves n0 to 100 and raises the fraction resolved by 100 per arm to a half instead of a third, which overstates EVSI at about GBP 99.82 per patient instead of GBP 61.68.
has description in the module Gives the variance, across the results a proposed study could produce, of the posterior mean of incremental net benefit, the preposterior variance, when the prior and the study estimate are both normal. The prior variance v0 is written as the per-patient sampling variance sigma2 divided by a prior effective sample size n0, and a study of n patients then resolves the fraction nu, n divided by n plus n0, of the prior variance. The preposterior variance is zero when n is zero, rises with n and tends to the prior variance as n grows without limit. It also equals the prior variance less the posterior variance, the known reduction in variance on which the analytic EVSI depends.

Present value of a fixed annuity payment schedule at the evaluation discount rate

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000286
Type formula
assumes Every fixed annuity instalment is paid, Yearly discounting of instalments from the date of treatment
has calculator text PV = A * (1 - (1+r)^(-n)) * (1+r) / r
has common error note Instalment schedule discounted at the financing rate. Discounting the instalments at the financing rate always returns the upfront price, so the financing charge disappears from the model. The schedule has to be valued at the evaluation's own rate, which in the £1 million example gives about £1,027,965 rather than £1,000,000.
Nominal instalment total entered as the therapy cost. Entering the nominal total of £1,099,880 in the £1 million example instead of the present value of about £1,027,965 overstates the cost by about 7%, and the gap grows with the length of the schedule and the discount rate.
has description in the module Values n equal instalments A, the first at treatment, at the discount rate r used in the economic evaluation. It equals the sum of A divided by (1 + r) to the power t for t from 0 to n minus 1, written here in closed form. This present value, not the list price or the nominal total, is the cost of the therapy in the model. When r equals the financing rate, the result equals the upfront price.

Prevalence odds ratio from a prevalence ratio and the unexposed prevalence

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000610
Type formula
assumes Crude ratios from one table in the odds ratio conversion, Implied exposed prevalence below one in the odds ratio conversion
has calculator text P_1 = PR * P_0; POR = PR * (1 - P_0) / (1 - P_1)
has common error note Falling back to logistic regression when a prevalence ratio model fails. Log-binomial models that estimate an adjusted PR may fail to converge, most often with a continuous covariate, several categorical covariates or a high prevalence. Switching silently to logistic regression changes the reported measure from a PR to a POR. Poisson regression with a robust sandwich variance estimates the PR directly.
Reporting a prevalence odds ratio as a prevalence ratio. With the survey prevalences of 0.30 and 0.15, the POR of 2.43 is about 21% above the PR of 2.00. Read as a relative prevalence, or as a relative risk beside true relative risks when priorities are set, it exaggerates the association, as Barros and Hirakata warn for frequent outcomes in cross-sectional studies.
has description in the module Converts a prevalence ratio into the prevalence odds ratio that logistic regression reports for the same cross-sectional data, given the prevalence among the unexposed. The cross-product a d / (b c) of the two-by-two table gives the same value. The factor (1 minus P_0) / (1 minus P_1) exceeds 1 whenever P_1 exceeds P_0 and falls below 1 whenever P_1 is lower, so the POR lies further from 1 than the PR whenever the two prevalences differ.

Prevalence ratio from a cross-sectional two-by-two table

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000609
Type formula
assumes Prevalence ratio reflects onset and duration together, Same case definition and timing in both prevalence ratio groups
has calculator text P_1 = a / (a + b); P_0 = c / (c + d); PR = P_1 / P_0
has common error note Inverting a prevalence ratio for the complement of the condition. The PR for being free of the condition is (1 minus P_1) divided by (1 minus P_0), not the reciprocal of the PR. In the article's survey it is 0.70 / 0.85 = 0.82, whereas 1 / 2.00 = 0.50. A model that needs the complement computes it from the two prevalences.
Using a prevalence ratio as the risk ratio for new cases. A PR used as the effect of an exposure on new cases treats differences in duration as differences in onset. An exposure that improves survival with a condition raises its prevalence without raising its incidence, so a prevention model built on the PR can misstate the cases avoided.
has description in the module Divides the proportion of exposed people who have the condition by the proportion of unexposed people who have it, using the four cells of a cross-sectional two-by-two table with exposure in rows. A value of 1 means the condition is equally common in both groups, above 1 more common among the exposed and below 1 less common. Because P_1 cannot exceed 1, the ratio cannot exceed 1 / P_0.

Reading YLDs per person as the share of people with a disability. GBD 2010's YLDs per person of 28.6 per cent at age 80 are average health loss per person, not the proportion of people aged 80 who have a disability.
Reading the change in annual burden as the effect of a programme. Neither annual count is the programme's effect: a model credits each year of the programme with 50 cases prevented, or 100 YLDs averted over the 10 years each case would have lasted (86.4 discounted at 3 per cent), whatever the burden figure shows in that year.
has description in the module For a condition that lasts exactly L years, the people living with it in the reference year are the last L annual cohorts. If incidence changed from I_old to I_new k years ago, with this year counted as one of the k, then k cohorts are of the new size and L minus k of the old, and the prevalence-based count is their person-years times the weight. It reaches the new incidence-based count only when the last of the old cohorts has recovered, L years after the change.

has calculator text u_prev = (I_1 * D_1 * u_1 + I_2 * D_2 * u_2) / (I_1 * D_1 + I_2 * D_2); u_inc = (I_1 * u_1 + I_2 * u_2) / (I_1 + I_2)
has common error note Expecting survey weights to remove the prevalent-case gap. Survey weights correct how the sample was drawn, not who is alive and ill on the survey date, so the weighted prevalent mean is still 0.75; the gap is removed by reweighting each form by the inverse of its mean duration.
Taking a prevalent-case survey mean as the baseline of an incident cohort. The survey over-represents long-lasting forms, which Simon described as length-biased sampling of living patients; in the article's example it overstates the utility of newly diagnosed patients by 0.10 and shows one severe case in six instead of one in two.
has description in the module In a steady state the prevalent pool holds each form of a condition in proportion to its incidence times its mean duration, so a survey of everyone currently living with the condition averages utility with those weights. A model of newly diagnosed patients needs the mean at onset, weighted by incidence alone. The prevalent shares are exact under the steady state even without the small-prevalence approximation, because the common factor (1 minus P) cancels. Two forms are written out so that the calculator can run; SUMPRODUCT in Excel takes any number.

Private and external benefit of one vaccination at a given coverage in an endemic infection

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000926
Type formula
assumes Marginal benefits read at one steady-state coverage of a fully protective vaccine
Same loss per infection for the family and for society in the vaccination benefit split
has calculator text pi = max(0, 1 - 1 / (R_0 * (1 - v))); MPB = L * pi; MEB = (v < 1 - 1 / R_0) * L / (R_0 * (1 - v))
has common error note External benefit counted as L times 1 minus pi at or above the threshold. Above the threshold pi is 0, so L times 1 minus pi returns the whole GBP 500 as external benefit, when one more vaccination prevents no infection and the marginal externality is zero, as Goodkin-Gold and colleagues state. Applied to the 200 vaccinations above the threshold in the article's universal requirement it credits GBP 100,000 of external benefit that does not exist.
External benefit of a vaccination treated as a fixed amount per dose. Carrying the GBP 250 external benefit found at the article's 60% coverage to the move at 75% coverage understates it by GBP 150, since it is GBP 400 there, and understates the subsidy that the marginal external benefit would justify. The external benefit per vaccination depends on the coverage at which it is read, as the article's misreadings list says.
has description in the module Splits the value of one more vaccination at coverage v, with a loss L per infection valued the same by the family and by society, into the marginal private benefit to the vaccinated child, L times the lifetime risk pi it avoids (the expected value of HE-FM-CHN-001 with branch values L and 0), and the marginal external benefit to unvaccinated children, L/(R_0(1 minus v)), which is L times 1 minus pi below the threshold H and zero at or above it. Below H the two add to L, because each extra vaccination there removes exactly one infection in total (HE-FM-VEXT-001), so the marginal social benefit of HE-FM-EXT-001 stays at L while its split moves towards the external side as coverage rises (derived). Goodkin-Gold and colleagues derive the same split, the marginal private benefit theta H Phi_I, the marginal social benefit theta H and the marginal externality theta H/((1 minus theta Q/mu) R_0) below the eradication quantity and zero above it, with theta of 1 and Q/mu equal to v for a fully protective vaccine. The external share is 0.5 at the article's 60% coverage and 0.8 at 75%, so a subsidy set at the marginal external benefit, as in HE-FM-EXT-002 with linear curves, depends on the coverage at which that benefit is read.

Proportion of between-study variance accounted for by meta-regression covariates

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000627
Type formula

has calculator text R2_het = (tau2_RE - tau2_MR) / tau2_RE
has common error note Comparing tau2 from different sets of studies. When studies without a value for the covariate drop out of the meta-regression, comparing its residual tau2 with the tau2 from the full meta-analysis mixes the effect of the covariate with the effect of removing studies. The reference model is refitted to the studies used in the meta-regression.
Reading the explained share as a share of all variation in the estimates. The ratio describes the between-study variance only. A covariate that accounts for 67% of tau2 has not explained 67% of the spread in the observed estimates, part of which is sampling error. Both tau2 values are also uncertain with few studies, as the standard error of 0.0845 for the residual estimate of 0.1108 in the BCG example shows.
has description in the module Compares the between-study variance of a random-effects meta-analysis without covariates with the residual between-study variance of the meta-regression, and expresses the fall as a share of the first. It describes heterogeneity among true effects only, not the sampling error in the observed estimates.

has common error note Quoting a proportion correct without its prevalence. Test A's proportion correct is 0.770 at 5 per cent prevalence and 0.764 at 2 per cent, and it tends to specificity as prevalence falls, so the figure cannot be transferred between settings (computed here for illustration).
Ranking tests by the proportion correct. Test B's 0.952 barely beats the 0.950 of calling everyone negative, and test A, with 0.770, gives the higher net monetary benefit at 5 per cent prevalence; NICE's 2011 diagnostics manual set this definition of accuracy aside because a test can be wrong in more than one way and the measure depends on prevalence.
has description in the module The share of results that are correct, often reported simply as accuracy, weights sensitivity by prevalence and specificity by its complement. At low prevalence it is dominated by specificity, and it counts a missed case and an unnecessary referral as equally bad.

has common error note Ending the PDC period at the last fill instead of the fixed end date. If the patient in the article's example had stopped after fill 3, the PQA period would still run to day 180 and the PDC would be 90 / 180, or 0.5. Ending the period when the supply ran out on day 90 gives 90 / 90, or 1, and hides the discontinuation (computed here for illustration).
Reporting a PDC without stating the overlap rule. The same five fills give a PDC of about 0.833 with early refills shifted and about 0.744 with overlaps merged, so the patient is adherent at 80% under one rule and non-adherent under the other. A 2022 scoping review of 76 articles found that early refills were carried over in 45% and not reported in 37%.
has description in the module Divides the number of days in the observation period on which at least one fill provides medicine, after shifting overlapping supply of the same drug, by the number of days in the period, counted from the index date (the first fill) to the end date inclusive. Each day counts once however many fills cover it, and only days inside the period count, so the PDC cannot exceed 1. It is reported as a proportion or multiplied by 100 as a percentage, and is often dichotomised at 0.8.

Proportional rise in expected reimbursement of an uncapped specific excess layer under uniform claims inflation

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000738
Type formula
assumes Claims below the three levels stay below the specific attachment point after inflation
Uniform claims inflation with the specific attachment point fixed in money
Uncapped layer, positive inflation and a layer that pays before inflation
has calculator text E_0 = p_1 * max(C_1 - A, 0) + p_2 * max(C_2 - A, 0) + p_3 * max(C_3 - A, 0); E_g = p_1 * max((1 + g) * C_1 - A, 0) + p_2 * max((1 + g) * C_2 - A, 0) + p_3 * max((1 + g) * C_3 - A, 0); rise_E = E_g / E_0 - 1; mult_E = rise_E / g
has common error note Holding a money attachment point or regulatory floor constant across years of claims inflation. A multi-year model in constant prices that keeps a money threshold, such as the USD 20,000 minimum annual attachment point per individual of the NAIC Stop Loss Insurance Model Act, at its face value treats it as if it rose in step with claims. With illustrative claims inflation of 5% a year and the threshold unchanged in money, after five years USD 20,000 corresponds to about USD 15,671 of current claims (derived), and the uncapped layer above it grows faster than claims each year (derived). The model act lets the commissioner amend its dollar amounts upon consideration of the medical components of the Consumer Price Index, and its drafting note says a state may wish to adjust them to reflect medical costs in that state.
Projecting a fixed specific attachment point layer at the general claims inflation rate. Projecting the USD 550 expected reimbursement at a USD 100,000 attachment point forward at the 10% claims inflation rate gives USD 605 per member, USD 40 below the USD 645 that the inflated distribution gives, about USD 40,000 too little for 1,000 members in one year. The gap widens with each further year at a fixed attachment point, to about USD 84 per member after two years of 10% inflation (derived, USD 749.50 against USD 665.50).
has description in the module Gives the expected reimbursement per member of an uncapped excess layer with full reimbursement before and after every claim level rises by the same inflation rate g while the attachment point stays fixed in money, the proportional rise rise_E in that expected reimbursement, and its ratio mult_E to g. Lee 1988 states that with the retention fixed the expected excess loss payment rises proportionally much more than the general rate of inflation. Miccolis 1977 shows that under a uniform inflation factor the expected loss limited at k equals the factor times the earlier expected loss limited at k divided by the factor (equation 17), from which E_g equals (1 + g) times the expected excess of current claims over A / (1 + g) (derived), so inflating claims has the same effect as lowering the attachment point in real terms, and without a cap mult_E is at least 1 (derived, checked over a grid of inputs). A coinsurance rate multiplies E_0 and E_g alike and cancels from rise_E; with a cap the top of the layer can already be used up and the rise can fall below g. The general price-year adjustment of a single cost is HE-FM-COST-002.

The uncapped excess form used here follows from equation 17 and the scaling of the mean (derived). https://www.casact.org/sites/default/files/database/proceed_proceed77_77027.pdf

Pure investment condition for the optimal health stock

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000259
Type formula
assumes Pure investment model, Constant returns in producing gross investment, Interior solution with positive gross investment
has calculator text gamma_t = W_t * G_t / pi_(t-1); UC_t = r - pi_tilde_(t-1) + delta_t
has common error note Omitting depreciation from the cost of capital. Equating the return on health to the interest rate alone, 0.03 in the first example, sets the cost of holding health capital far too low. Depreciation is part of its user cost and is the channel through which age lowers the optimal stock.
Using the price of medical care as the marginal cost of investment. pi_(t-1) is the marginal cost of producing health investment from medical care and own time. It depends on the wage and on education as well as on the price of care.
has description in the module In the pure investment version of the Grossman model, health yields no direct utility and is valued only for the healthy time it adds to earnings. The marginal monetary return on health capital, gamma_t, is the wage multiplied by the marginal product of health capital in healthy time, divided by the marginal cost of gross investment. At the optimal stock it equals the opportunity cost of health capital, the real-own rate of interest r minus pi_tilde_(t-1) plus the rate of depreciation. The formula returns both sides so that the condition can be checked.

Pure-strategy best-reply check of each cell of a 2 x 2 game with strict and weak equilibria

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000946
Type formula
assumes One-shot simultaneous game with two players and two strategies each
Each player's payoffs compared only with that player's own payoffs
Ties count as best replies in the weak equilibrium test
has calculator text NE_11 = (u_11 >= u_21) and (v_11 >= v_12); NE_12 = (u_12 >= u_22) and (v_12 >= v_11); NE_21 = (u_21 >= u_11) and (v_21 >= v_22); NE_22 = (u_22 >= u_12) and (v_22 >= v_21); S_11 = (u_11 > u_21) and (v_11 > v_12); S_12 = (u_12 > u_22) and (v_12 > v_11); S_21 = (u_21 > u_11) and (v_21 > v_22); S_22 = (u_22 > u_12) and (v_22 > v_21)
has common error note Checking only one player's best reply in a 2 x 2 game. A cell is an equilibrium only when both players are playing a best reply. Testing the row player alone in matching pennies marks the two matched cells as equilibria, although in each of them the column player moves from minus 1 to 1 by switching (computed here), and the game has no pure equilibrium.
Reading an equilibrium cell as the best outcome. The check finds stable cells, not efficient ones, and Tadelis states that Nash equilibrium does not guarantee Pareto optimality. In the Hi-lo game of HE-EX-NASH-004 the second matched cell passes both the weak and the strict test although each player earns 1 there against 10 in the other equilibrium.
Strict inequality used in the weak best-reply test. Writing the weak test with > in place of >= drops every equilibrium that rests on a tie. In the break-even angioplasty game of HE-EX-NASH-002 it finds no pure equilibrium where there are three (computed here), and the article's selection of (Invest, Invest) by removing the weakly dominated choice then has nothing to select from.
has description in the module Tests each of the four strategy pairs of a two-player game in which each player has two strategies. A cell is a pure-strategy Nash equilibrium when the row player's payoff in it is at least its payoff from switching rows against the same column, and the column player's payoff in it is at least its payoff from switching columns against the same row, which is Definition 5.1 of Tadelis applied cell by cell as in his section 5.1.1. The cell is a strict equilibrium when both comparisons hold with a strict inequality, Definition 7 of Slantchev, and a cell that passes the weak test but fails the strict one is a weak equilibrium, because some player has an alternative that does exactly as well. Each output is 1 for a pass and 0 for a fail. A game in which no cell passes, such as matching pennies, still has an equilibrium in mixed strategies (HE-FM-NASH-002).

has module record identifier HE-FM-NASH-001
has source in the module Nash JF. Equilibrium points in n-person games. Proc Natl Acad Sci USA. 1950;36(1):48-49 (full text read from the original page scan). Defines a game with a finite set of pure strategies for each player and a payment to each player for each combination, one combination countering another when each player's strategy in it yields the highest obtainable expectation against the other players' strategies in the second, and an equilibrium point as a self-countering combination. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.36.1.48
Slantchev BL. Game theory: dominance, Nash equilibrium, symmetry. Lecture notes, Department of Political Science, University of California, San Diego; 23 May 2008 (full text read). Section 2.1 (Pure-Strategy Nash Equilibrium), Definition 4, a best response as a strategy with a payoff at least that of every alternative given the others' strategies. Section 2.2 (Strict Nash Equilibrium), Definition 7, a strict Nash equilibrium requires a strictly higher payoff than every other strategy, with the Battle of the Bismarck Sea as an equilibrium that is not strict because one player is indifferent. Section 2.3 (Mixed Strategy Nash Equilibrium), Figure 18, matching pennies has no Nash equilibrium in pure strategies. https://slantchev.ucsd.edu/courses/gt/04-strategic-form.pdf
Tadelis S. Pinning down beliefs: Nash equilibrium. Chapter 5 in Game Theory: An Introduction. Princeton: Princeton University Press; 2013 (publisher's sample chapter, full text read). Section 5.1 (Nash Equilibrium in Pure Strategies), Definition 5.1, a pure-strategy profile is a Nash equilibrium when each player's strategy is a best response to the others', v_i(s_i*, s_-i*) at least v_i(s_i', s_-i*) for every alternative s_i' and every player i. Section 5.1.1 (Pure-Strategy Nash Equilibrium in a Matrix), the three-step method that marks the row player's best reply in each column and the column player's best reply in each row, a cell marked twice being a pure-strategy Nash equilibrium. Section 5.1.2 (Evaluating the Nash Equilibria Solution) states that Nash equilibrium does not guarantee Pareto optimality. https://assets.press.princeton.edu/chapters/s5-10001.pdf

Quantity and remaining welfare loss when the tax is set at the pre-tax marginal external cost

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000429
Type formula
assumes Marginal external cost rising or constant, Positive quantity under the overshooting tax
has calculator text Q_0 = (a - c) / b; Q_star = (a - c - m) / (b + g); t_0 = m + g * Q_0; Q_t = (a - c - t_0) / b; L_t = 0.5 * (Q_star - Q_t) * ((a - b * Q_t) - (c + m + g * Q_t))
has common error note Damage observed before the tax taken as the Pigouvian rate. Setting the tax at the marginal external cost observed at current consumption, 4 pounds in the article's example, overshoots the Pigouvian 3.20 pounds whenever the external cost rises with consumption. The overshoot cuts consumption 8 thousand units below the efficient level, and each of those units was worth up to 1 pound more than its social cost.
Overshooting tax judged only against the untaxed market. A loss of 4,000 pounds against 64,000 pounds with no tax shows that the overshooting tax is better than none, not that it is efficient. The comparison that identifies the error is with the Pigouvian tax, which leaves no loss.
has description in the module Sets the tax t_0 at the marginal external cost observed before the tax, at Q_0, rather than at Q_star. When marginal external cost rises with consumption, t_0 exceeds the Pigouvian rate and consumers cut back to Q_t, below the efficient quantity. The remaining loss L_t is the triangle between Q_t and Q_star, with height equal to marginal private benefit less marginal social cost at Q_t.

has common error note Leaving the cross term out of a price policy model. Modelling only the own-price response to a tax on one product misses switching to its substitutes; the IARC handbook warns that taxing substitutable products at a much lower rate can make tobacco taxation ineffective.
Using a cross-tax elasticity as a cross-price elasticity. A cross-tax elasticity equals eps_ij times the elasticity of P_j with respect to the tax; with a specific tax passed through one for one that factor is T_j / P_j, below 1, so the two differ unless a 1 per cent tax rise raises the price by 1 per cent.

For small changes this equals the article's approximation, proportional change in Q_i about equal to the sum of eps_ij times the proportional change in P_j.

Quasi-hyperbolic beta-delta discount weight with its short-run and long-run per-period rates

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000633
Type formula
assumes Immediate outcome carries a quasi-hyperbolic weight of one, Period length chosen with the one-period conflict in mind
has calculator text D_Q = beta * delta^t; r_0 = (1 - beta * delta) / (beta * delta); r_L = (1 - delta) / delta
has common error note Present-bias factor applied to the immediate outcome. Weighting the present period by beta as well removes the bias. In the article's example smoking today would be worth 7 against 9.009 for quitting, so the smoker would quit at once instead of postponing (computed here for illustration).
Present-bias factor compounded with delay. Writing (beta delta)^t applies beta once per period instead of once in total. With beta = 0.7 and delta = 0.99 the weight two periods ahead becomes about 0.480 instead of 0.686 (computed here for illustration), which is steep exponential discounting at the factor 0.693 and gives no preference reversal.
has description in the module For a delay of one period or more the weight is beta times delta to the power t, while an outcome now keeps a weight of 1, so beta is a one-off discount on everything that is not immediate. The per-period rate is r_0 between now and the next period and r_L between any two later periods, as Frederick and colleagues give them. Setting beta = 1 returns exponential discounting with the factor delta, the HE-FM-DR-001 factor with r equal to (1 minus delta)/delta, and Wang and Sloan read beta below 1 as present bias.

RAND arc elasticity of medical spending

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000257
Type formula
assumes A single price summarises each plan, Two arrangements that differ in price only
has calculator text eta_arc = ((q_2 - q_1) / (q_2 + q_1)) / ((p_2 - p_1) / (p_2 + p_1))
has common error note Comparing plans with free care alone. When p_1 is zero the price term equals 1 whatever the coinsurance rate of the other plan, so an arc elasticity against free care reflects only the change in spending. The 25% and 95% plans are then treated as the same change in price.
Treating minus 0.2 as a constant of nature. The RAND figure rests on an episode-based model and on assumptions about how people respond to non-linear contracts. Aron-Dine and colleagues obtain estimates from about minus 0.04 to minus 0.6 from simple alternative summaries of the same experiment.
has description in the module Divides the change in spending, as a proportion of the average of the two spending levels, by the change in price, as a proportion of the average of the two prices. The RAND investigators used arc elasticities because the free care plan had a price of zero, from which an ordinary percentage change cannot be computed. The widely quoted RAND elasticity of about minus 0.2 comes from arc elasticities of this kind computed from an episode-based model; Aron-Dine and colleagues identify Keeler and Rolph 1988 as its underlying source.
has formalisation level catalogue record
has implementation Arc elasticity from two plans

has module record identifier HE-FM-MH-003

Random-effects inverse-variance pooled mean and standard error

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000303
Type formula
assumes Different but related true effects across studies, Between-study variance plugged in as known
has calculator text theta_R = sum_(i=1)^k [y_i / (v_i + tau2)] / sum_(i=1)^k [1 / (v_i + tau2)]; SE_R = sqrt(1 / sum_(i=1)^k [1 / (v_i + tau2)])
has common error note Taking the random-effects mean as automatically the better model input. Random-effects pooling gives relatively more weight to smaller studies. In the three-trial example the largest trial falls from 70.9% of the weight to 42.3%, and the mean moves towards the larger effects of the two smaller trials. If small studies report larger effects because of small-study bias, the shift reflects bias rather than true variation, so the choice between the two estimates belongs in a scenario analysis.
has description in the module Pools the study estimates with weights 1/(v_i + tau2), so that the between-study variance is added to each study's own variance. The result estimates the mean of a distribution of true effects rather than one common effect. Larger tau2 makes the weights more equal and the standard error larger.

Random-effects meta-regression model with one study-level covariate

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000625
Type formula
assumes Known within-study variances on an approximately normal effect scale
Linear covariate relation with normal residual heterogeneity
Enough studies and pre-specified covariates for a meta-regression
has calculator text y_i = beta_0 + beta_1 * x_i + u_i + e_i
has common error note Fitting a fixed-effect meta-regression by default. Omitting u_i treats all variation around the line as sampling error. The Cochrane Handbook generally prefers a random-effects model for comparing groups of studies because a fixed-effect comparison carries a high risk of false-positive results, and in the TSD 3 example on BCG vaccine trials and latitude the fixed-effect model fitted very poorly, with a posterior mean residual deviance of 40 against 26 data points.
Reading a trial-level slope as a patient-level relationship. When a patient characteristic such as age enters only as a study mean, a strong relationship within each trial can be invisible across trials with similar mean ages, and the direction across studies can even be the opposite of the direction within them. Geissbühler and colleagues found 53 of 81 aggregate-data meta-regressions (65%) susceptible to this ecological fallacy.
Regressing effects on the observed comparator group risk. The observed risk in each study's comparator group is part of its effect estimate, so a risk that is high by chance tends to come with a larger effect. The Cochrane Handbook calls the result a false correlation from regression to the mean, and TSD 3 instead uses the true baseline, estimated with its uncertainty in a Bayesian model, as the covariate.
has description in the module Writes the effect estimate of study i as a point on a regression line in the covariate x_i plus two error terms, the study's deviation u_i from the line, with u_i ~ N(0, tau2), and its sampling error e_i, with e_i ~ N(0, v_i) and v_i treated as known. The slope beta_1 is the change in the expected effect per unit increase in x_i, and tau2 is the residual between-study variance not accounted for by the covariate. A fixed-effect meta-regression omits u_i, so sampling error is the only random variation. Further covariates enter as further terms, with a categorical characteristic of J groups coded as J minus 1 dummy variables.
has formalisation level catalogue record
has implementation Weighted least squares slope and intercept of a meta-regression from three ranges

Random-effects precision weight of a study in a meta-regression

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000626
Type formula
assumes Residual variance taken from the fitted meta-regression
has calculator text w_i = 1 / (v_i + tau2)
has common error note Adding tau instead of tau2 to a meta-regression weight. Adding the between-study standard deviation to a variance mixes scales. With a variance of 0.01 and a residual tau2 of 0.03, tau is about 0.173 and the weight falls to about 5.46 instead of 25.
Weighting a meta-regression with the tau2 from the meta-analysis without covariates. Using the between-study variance before the covariate is added, 0.09 in the article's example, instead of the residual 0.03 gives the larger trial a weight of 10 instead of 25 and the smaller one about 7.69 instead of 14.29. The weights become too equal and the analysis ignores the heterogeneity the covariate has explained.
has description in the module Weight given to study i when the regression coefficients are estimated by weighted least squares. The weight is the inverse of the study's within-study variance plus the residual between-study variance, so larger studies have more influence on the slope, but less than in a fixed-effect meta-regression, where tau2 is zero and the weight is 1/v_i.

Random-effects prediction interval for the effect in a new setting

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000304
Type formula
assumes Normally distributed true effects for the prediction interval
has calculator text PI_low = theta_R - t_crit * sqrt(tau2 + SE_R^2); PI_high = theta_R + t_crit * sqrt(tau2 + SE_R^2)
has common error note Using 1.96 in place of the t quantile with few studies. With three studies the normal value of 1.96 gives limits of about -0.973 and 0.343, hazard ratios of about 0.378 to 1.410, much narrower than the 0.17 to 3.10 obtained with the t value of 4.303.
Using the interval of the mean as the range of effects in a new setting. The confidence interval describes uncertainty in the mean only. In the three-trial example it runs from hazard ratios of 0.502 to 1.062, while the prediction interval runs from about 0.17 to 3.10. Sampling the pooled log hazard ratio with the standard error of the mean, 0.191, in a probabilistic analysis instead of the predictive standard deviation, 0.336, ignores the between-study variation.
has description in the module Gives an approximate 95% range for the true effect in a new study or setting, combining the between-study variance with the squared standard error of the random-effects mean and using the 97.5th percentile of a t distribution with k-1 degrees of freedom. The square root term is also the standard deviation of the predictive distribution that NICE DSU TSD 3 suggests may be more relevant to decision making than the distribution of the mean.

has common error note Treating the annualisation gap as small for buildings. The 11% gap for a five-year device at 3.5% does not carry over to long-lived assets. For a 60-year building the economic charge is about 2.4 times the straight-line charge, so straight-line depreciation understates building costs far more than equipment costs.
has description in the module With no resale value, the annualised charge, K divided by A, and the straight-line charge, K divided by n, differ by the ratio n divided by A, which depends only on the useful life and the rate. Because A is smaller than n at any positive rate, the ratio exceeds 1 and rises with the useful life, and it tends to 1 as r approaches zero.

Refill-interval medication possession ratio including the last fill

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000459
Type formula
assumes At least two fills on different days for the refill interval, Treatment ends when the last supply runs out
has calculator text MPR_refill = sum_(i=1)^n [S_i] / (f_n - f_1 + S_n)
has common error note Using a refill-interval MPR where discontinuation matters. A patient who stops after the third fill of the article's history scores about 1.216 on the refill interval and 0.5 on the fixed interval (computed here for illustration). Where the question includes stopping treatment, the refill interval overstates adherence.
has description in the module Divides the total days' supply from the first to the last dispensing by the days between the first and last dispensing plus the days' supply of the last fill. Sikka and colleagues describe it as an often-used definition; Raebel and colleagues list it as less common and note that it has also been called MPRm. The clock stops when the last fill's supply ends, so the ratio does not account for discontinuation, and early refilling takes it above 1.

Regression-based EVPPI estimator from fitted incremental net benefits

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000657
Type formula
assumes Regression captures the conditional mean of net benefit given theta_i
One probabilistic sample from the joint distribution for regression EVPPI
formalises regression-based EVPPI method
has calculator text EVPPI_R = sum_(n=1)^N [max(0, g_2n, g_3n)] / N - max(0, sum_(n=1)^N [g_2n] / N, sum_(n=1)^N [g_3n] / N)
has common error note Additive regression that omits an interaction between parameters of interest. In the article's example the incremental net benefits of GBP 2,000, 1,000, 200 and -2,400 depend on A and B jointly. A least squares regression on indicators of A and B without an interaction term fits GBP 2,400, 600, -200 and -2,000 and returns GBP 550 for the pair, although the EVPPI for A and B together equals the EVPI of GBP 600 (computed here for illustration). Strong, Oakley and Brennan replace the additive formula INB ~ s(x5)+s(x14) with the tensor product INB ~ te(x5,x14) when the parameters interact.
Generalised additive model with many interacting parameters of interest. Strong, Oakley and Brennan warn that with more than about six parameters of interest that interact in the model, the number of GAM parameters is likely to exceed the number of runs, so the method fails. They recommend Gaussian process regression in that case.
Regressing on every model parameter for a group EVPPI. Including parameters outside theta_i as regressors lets the fit follow the model outputs more closely, so the estimate moves towards the EVPI. In the illustrative table a fit that reproduces every output returns GBP 575, the EVPI, in place of GBP 325 for theta_i.
has description in the module Regresses the incremental net benefit of each option against a baseline on the parameters of interest across the N runs of one probabilistic sample and treats the fitted values as the conditional expected net benefits, so no inner loop or extra model runs are needed. The estimate is the mean over runs of the largest fitted value, with zero for the baseline, less the largest mean fitted value. This is Equation 9 of Strong, Oakley and Brennan written for three options as incremental net benefits, which they note leaves the result unchanged and needs one regression fewer. Using the fitted values in both terms exploits the positive correlation between them and improves precision. Strong, Oakley and Brennan fit a generalised additive model or a Gaussian process, and Algorithm 4 of the second ISPOR report sets out the same scheme.

Relative change in a QALY gain and in the ICER when an analysis is rescored with another value set

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000722
Type formula
assumes Only the value set differs between the two QALY gains, Both QALY gains positive for the ICER change
has calculator text r_Q = dQ_B / dQ_A - 1; r_I = dQ_A / dQ_B - 1
has common error note Computing an ICER change after the value set reverses the gain. Gerlinger and colleagues report that a change of EQ-5D-5L state 44444 into 55511 is an improvement of 0.679 under the Dutch set and a worsening of 0.169 under the Uruguayan one. Held for one year these are QALY changes of 0.679 and minus 0.169, so r_Q is minus 1.2489 and r_I is minus 5.0178, a number with no meaning as a change in cost per QALY gained (computed here). An r_Q below minus 1 signals the reversal, and the result is then read by dominance or net health benefit.
Reading a mean ICER change from a mean QALY change. The reciprocal identity holds for one decision, not for averages across decisions. Navega Biz and colleagues report a mean fall of 37.5% in incremental QALYs and a mean rise of 61.4% in ICERs for 11 non-oncology decisions without a survival gain, while the identity applied to a single 37.5% fall gives a rise of 60.0% (derived). Each decision's ICER change has to be computed from its own pair of gains before averaging.
Taking the ICER change as minus the QALY change. A fall in the QALY gain raises the ICER by more than the fall. In the article's example the QALY gain falls 13.3% and the ICER rises 15.4%, not 13.3%, and for the UK and Zimbabwe comparison a fall of 46.3% raises the ICER by 86.3%, not 46.3% (computed here). The gap matters most near a threshold, where the article's two sets put the same treatment on opposite sides of GBP 25,000 per QALY.
has description in the module Compares the QALY gain of the same treatment scored with two value sets, each the HE-FM-EQ3L-003 gain or any other QALY gain, and expresses the second as a share of the first. r_Q is the share of the QALY gain that changes with the value set, and with the incremental cost unchanged the ICER of HE-FM-CUA-001 changes by r_I, the reciprocal ratio less 1 (derived). The two changes are not mirror images, since (1 + r_Q) times (1 + r_I) equals 1, so a fall of 13% in the QALY gain raises the ICER by more than 13%. The gap in incremental net health benefit (HE-FM-CET-002) between the two sets is dQ_A minus dQ_B, since the cost term is the same under both (derived).
