has common error note Comparing case weights across systems or years. A weight is scaled to the average case of its own costing sample. One NWAU, one Medicare weight unit and an implicit HRG weight refer to different averages, so their values are not comparable, and a weight from one year is not paired with a base rate set for another.
Scaling case weights by the unweighted mean of group means. Taking the simple average of £2,000, £5,000 and £13,000 gives about £6,667 instead of the case-weighted £4,000, and weights of 0.30, 0.75 and 1.95 (computed here for illustration). has description in the module Divides the mean cost per case in one group by the mean cost per case across all groups of the costing sample, the calculation that the European Observatory study of DRG systems describes in greatly simplified terms. Real systems refine the ratio, for example with IHACPA's inlier and outlier cost model for each AR-DRG, but keep the same scaling to a reference cost.

has common error note Adding intermediate levels changes importance. Relative importance rises with the number of levels defining an attribute even with the minimum and maximum fixed; in one study price's importance rose by seven percentage points when two intermediate levels were added to three.
Comparing importances across studies with different level ranges. An importance holds only over the levels in its own study; a 26-week maximum wait gives waiting time 0.77 instead of 0.55 with the same per-week preference.
Using signed part-worths in place of ranges. Dividing minus 3.00 by the sum of the signed part-worths, minus 2.50, gives 1.2, a share above 1; ranges are differences between the best and worst levels and cannot be negative.
has description in the module Takes the range of an attribute's part-worths, the difference between its most and least preferred levels over the levels in the study, and divides it by the sum of the ranges of all attributes. Written here for three attributes; with K attributes the denominator has K ranges. The share depends on the levels chosen, so it describes the study's design as much as the respondent.

A value above 1 shows higher health in the advantaged groups.

Relative survival as all-cause survival over expected background survival

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000694
Type formula
assumes Expected survival based on fixed life-table rates matched to the patients
Common time origin and attained age for the two survival curves
has calculator text R_t = S_t / S_star_t
has common error note Expected survival divided by all-cause survival. Inverting the ratio returns 2.2259 in place of 0.4493 at 10 years in the article's example (computed here for illustration). A relative survival above 1 for a group with excess mortality is the sign of the inversion.
Relative survival used in place of all-cause survival. Leaving out expected survival treats relative survival as the survival of the patients, so cured patients never die, which TSD 21 section 4.3.5 warns against. In the article's illustrative cure model life years to 30 years rise from 11.93 to 14.40, an overstatement of 2.47 years, or 21%.
has description in the module Divides the all-cause survival of the patient group at time t by the survival expected at the same time in a comparable group of the general population, matched on age, sex and calendar year. This is equation 14 of NICE DSU TSD 21, the survival-scale form of the additive hazard HE-FM-BTH-005. Because all-cause survival is the product of expected survival and survival from the excess hazard, relative survival equals exp of minus the cumulative excess hazard (HE-FN-CUMH-001), so it falls only while the excess hazard is above zero and levels off at the cure fraction in a mixture cure model (HE-FM-CRM-001). A value above 1 means that cumulative modelled mortality up to t is below that of the general population.

Relative unit labour cost of health care from output per hour

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000362
Type formula
assumes Common hourly wage in health care and other sectors, Labour as the only cost in the Baumol ratio
has calculator text R = a_o / a_h
has common error note Inverting the output per hour ratio in the Baumol relative cost. Dividing health care output per hour by output per hour elsewhere gives about 0.7436 instead of 1.3449 in the twenty-year example, which reads as health care becoming cheaper relative to other output when it has become dearer.
Reading a rising Baumol relative cost as falling health productivity. A rising relative cost does not mean that health care output per hour has fallen or that services are run inefficiently. In the twenty-year example output per hour in health care rises by about 10.5 per cent, yet its relative unit cost rises by about 34.5 per cent, because productivity grows faster elsewhere. Baumol argued that such cost rises arise for reasons largely beyond the control of those running the services.
has description in the module Gives the labour cost of one unit of health care relative to one unit of other output. Labour cost per unit is the hourly wage divided by output per hour, w/a_h in health care and w/a_o elsewhere, and with the same wage w in both sectors the ratio of the two reduces to the ratio of output per hour. Health care is therefore relatively dearer whenever output per hour is lower there, whatever the level of pay.

Quoting the Atkinson weight without its health levels. The same epsilon implies different weights at different health gaps. At epsilon of 10.95 the weight is about 6.94 between QALE of 62 and 74 years but about 7.36 between 60 and 72 years, so a statement such as seven times describes epsilon only at the stated levels.

It follows from the EDE formula, in which the weight on a small gain to person i is proportional to h_i raised to the power minus epsilon. It turns epsilon into a statement a decision committee can read: how many times a QALY to the less healthy group counts.

has calculator text T_c = T_E + T_I; R_exp = 1 + r * T_c; R_seir = (1 + r * T_E) * (1 + r * T_I); R_delta = exp(r * T_c)
has common error note Infectious period used as the generation interval when there is a latent stage. Ignoring the 4-day latent stage of the illustrative example and using R = 1 plus r T_I with the 6-day infectious period gives 2.2 instead of 3.96 at a growth rate of 0.2 per day, which would put the herd immunity threshold at about 0.545 instead of 0.747 (computed here for illustration).
has description in the module In the early phase of an outbreak new infections grow as exp(r t), and Wallinga and Lipsitch show that the reproduction number implied by a growth rate r depends only on the generation interval distribution, through R = 1/M(minus r) with M its moment generating function. An exponential generation interval with mean T_c gives R = 1 plus r T_c; a latent stage and an infectious stage, each exponentially distributed with means T_E and T_I, give (1 plus r T_E)(1 plus r T_I); and a fixed interval gives exp(r T_c), the upper bound for a given growth rate and mean. In the SIR model T_c is the mean infectious period 1/gamma, so the exponential form is van den Driessche's R_0 = 1 plus r/gamma, the inverse of r = gamma(R_0 minus 1). A growth rate taken from an epidemic doubling time T_d, as used in HE-FM-CFR-003, is log(2)/T_d.

has calculator text RMST_tau = sum_(k=1)^K [S_k * L_k]
has common error note Restricted mean read as lifetime mean survival. The 21.7 months covers only the first 34 months. With 40% still alive at month 34, the lifetime mean also includes the area of the tail, between about a third and a half of the total under the article's tail assumptions, so using the restricted mean in a lifetime model understates survival in both arms.
Survival at the end of each interval used as its height. Multiplying each width by the survival reached at the end of the interval places every drop too early. For the article's curve it gives 18.65 months instead of 21.7. The 18.65 is computed here for illustration.
has description in the module The restricted mean survival time is the area under the Kaplan-Meier curve from time 0 to a restriction time tau no later than the last observed follow-up. Because the curve is a step function, the area is the sum over the K intervals between 0, the successive event times and tau of the survival in each interval multiplied by its length.

has common error note Comparing returns on public sector cost across different objectives. The Green Book restricts summary metrics of social value, including this ratio, to options that meet the same objectives. A higher return does not show that a proposal is better than another proposal serving a different objective.
Ranking by the benefit-cost ratio when only public money is constrained. When part of the cost of an option falls outside the public sector, the benefit-cost ratio divides by costs that the budget does not pay. In the illustrative split above, option X returns about 2.33 per pound of public cost but 2.0 per pound of total cost, so ranking by the benefit-cost ratio understates its return to the budget.
has description in the module Divides present-value benefits net of costs borne outside the public sector by present-value public sector costs, as set out in the Green Book (2026). Costs that fall on patients, families or other sectors move from the denominator to the numerator, so the ratio measures social value per pound of public spending. It suits ranking options when the public sector budget is the binding constraint.

Returns to scale of a Cobb-Douglas hospital production function with free output elasticities

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000907
Type formula
assumes Constant output elasticities in the Cobb-Douglas hospital production function
Positive inputs and elasticities with technology held fixed in the hospital scale formula
Returns to scale measured over the inputs included in the estimated hospital function
has calculator text Q = A * L^alpha * K^beta; RTS = alpha + beta; Q_s = A * (s * L)^alpha * (s * K)^beta; g_s = Q_s / Q
has common error note Diminishing marginal returns to staff read as decreasing returns to scale. Diminishing returns concern one input rising with the others fixed, returns to scale all inputs rising together. With elasticities of 0.5 each, 40 units of capital and A of 1, raising labour from 10 to 20 lowers its marginal product alpha Q / L (HE-FM-HPF-002) from 1 to 0.7071, yet doubling both inputs doubles output because RTS is 1 (computed here for illustration). A falling marginal product of nurses in a fixed building says nothing on its own about the returns to expanding the whole hospital.
Linear reading of returns to scale for a large change in hospital inputs. RTS is the percentage response to a small proportional change. For a large change the exact ratio is s to the power RTS. Doubling both inputs with RTS of 0.68 raises output by 60.2%, while multiplying the 100% rise by 0.68 gives 68% (computed here for illustration).
Output elasticities multiplied instead of added for hospital returns to scale. The degree of returns to scale is the sum of the output elasticities. Multiplying Sielska and Nojszewska's 0.2 and 0.48 gives 0.096 and implies that a 1% rise in nurses and electricity raises patient-days by about 0.096%, about a seventh of the 0.68% that the sum gives (computed here for illustration).
Returns to scale of two included inputs read as the returns of the whole hospital. If an illustrative hospital's full function also had doctors with an elasticity of 0.32, its returns to scale would be 1, while the elasticities of nurses and electricity in that function, 0.2 and 0.48, sum to 0.68. A 1% rise in nurses and electricity alone, with doctors fixed, then raises output by 0.68%, and a 1% rise in all three by 1% (derived, computed here for illustration). A sum below 1 from a function that leaves out inputs does not by itself show decreasing returns to scale for the hospital.
has description in the module Gives a provider's activity from labour and capital in the Cobb-Douglas form that hospital studies estimate, with the output elasticities alpha and beta left free, and returns the degree of returns to scale RTS, their sum, with the output Q_s and the ratio g_s when every input is multiplied by s. Sielska and Nojszewska define economies of scale as the sum of the output elasticities, the percentage change in output when all inputs rise by 1%, and g_s equals s to the power RTS for any s (derived), so returns to scale are decreasing when RTS is below 1 and increasing when it is above 1. With alpha + beta = 1 the function is the constant-returns HE-FM-HPF-001, under which g_s always equals s. The marginal products alpha Q / L and beta Q / K have the form of those in HE-FM-HPF-002, each exponent times output over the input, a form that holds at any RTS (derived), although HE-FM-HPF-002 computes them only for exponents summing to one. RTS is a property of the estimated function and is the same at every size, unlike scale efficiency HE-FM-EFF-003, a ratio of frontier scores for one unit.

has source in the module Cylus J, Papanicolas I, Smith PC, editors. Health system efficiency: how to make measurement matter for policy and management. Copenhagen: European Observatory on Health Systems and Policies; 2016. The Glossary, page xvi, defines decreasing returns to scale as a proportionate increase in all inputs leading to a lower proportionate increase in outputs, increasing returns to scale as one leading to a greater proportionate increase in outputs, and constant returns to scale as a given increase in inputs always giving the same increase in outputs, regardless of the scale of operations. https://iris.who.int/items/5e2a6617-4313-4c47-bb14-1e3ddcc3890f
Sielska A, Nojszewska E. Production function for modeling hospital activities. The case of Polish county hospitals. PLoS One. 2022;17(5):e0268350. The Methods section defines economies of scale as the sum of the elasticities of production with respect to each factor, showing by how many percent production changes when the employment of all factors rises by 1%, in an unnumbered expression before equation (5), which gives this elasticity of scale as a limit. Equations (8) to (10) give the Cobb-Douglas function as alpha_0 times the product of each factor raised to its power alpha_i, its logarithmic form and the elasticity of production of each factor, equal to alpha_i and not dependent on the employment of factors, and the section states that the functions were estimated by least squares in R. The Discussion reports, for the two-factor Cobb-Douglas function with electricity and nurses, that a 1% rise in electricity costs raises patient-days by 0.48% and a 1% rise in nurse FTEs by 0.2%, and that economies of scale do not exceed 1, so a 1% rise in both inputs gives less than 1% more patient service capacity. The text after equation (11) describes Cobb-Douglas economies of scale as the sum of the elasticities but prints the expression with a product sign; the records follow the sum. The sum 0.68 and the ratio s to the power RTS are computed here and are not printed in the paper. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0268350

Revenue and provider margin per case under an Ellis and McGuire mixed payment

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000544
Type formula
assumes Linear cost of care in the mixed payment model, Payment based only on verifiable cost and case counts
has calculator text R = P + r * c * q; M = P - (1 - r) * c * q
has common error note Cutting the case price to remove the margin. Lowering the pure case price from 3,200 to 1,600 pounds removes the margin on a four-day stay but leaves the hospital bearing every extra bed-day, so stays remain at four days; Ellis and McGuire note that recalibrating the prospective amount keeps the marginal incentive to reduce services and transfers the net gain to the payer and patients.
Reading r as the provider's share of cost. r is the share the payer reimburses; the provider's supply-side cost share is 1 minus r, which Ellis and McGuire set equal to the index of agency at the optimum (HE-FM-CTH-003). Swapping them is harmless only when r is 0.5; at r of 0.2 the provider bears 80 per cent of the cost of each extra day, not 20 per cent.
has description in the module A mixed payment pays a fixed prospective amount per case plus a share r of the cost of the care given, so revenue rises by r times c for each extra unit and the provider bears the rest, (1 minus r) times c. Pure case payment is r = 0 and full cost reimbursement is P = 0 with r = 1. The margin is revenue minus cost, written in Ellis and McGuire's equation (12) as P + (r minus 1) c q.

has source in the module Ellis RP, McGuire TG. Journal of Health Economics. 1986;5(2):129-151. doi:10.1016/0167-6296(86)90002-0 (full text read). Section 2.2: revenue R(q) depends on the payment system, total cost is a constant c times quantity in the simple linear case. Section 4: the mixed system combines a prospective amount with a partial cost-based payment, R(q) = a + rC(q), the fraction of costs paid r; with linear cost, net revenue is a + (r minus 1)cq (eq. 12). Section 3.1: reducing the prospective payment to the new level maintains the marginal incentives to reduce supply but transfers the net gains to the payer and patients. Section 4: the optimal cost sharing on the supply side (1 minus r) equals the index of agency. (The paper's symbol for the prospective amount is written P here.) https://doi.org/10.1016/0167-6296(86)90002-0

Review Manager standard error of Hedges' adjusted g

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000742
Type formula
assumes Hedges' adjusted g as the standardised mean difference of Cochrane reviews
Inverse-variance weights from the Review Manager standard error
has calculator text N = n_1 + n_2; SE_RM = sqrt(N / (n_1 * n_2) + g^2 / (2 * (N - 3.94)))
has common error note Correction factor applied again to the Review Manager standard error. Multiplying SE_RM by J, as the What Works Clearinghouse form does for its own expression, mixes two conventions and shrinks the Review Manager value. For the article's trial it gives about 0.4316 instead of 0.4486, computed here for illustration.
Two standard error formulas for Hedges' g mixed in one meta-analysis. Taking SE_RM for some studies and SE_g of HE-FM-HEDG-002 for others weights like studies unequally. For a trial the size of the article's, the Review Manager form gives a weight about 8% lower (0.4294 squared over 0.4486 squared, about 0.916), computed here for illustration.
has description in the module Review Manager, the software Cochrane reviews use, gives the standard error of Hedges' adjusted g from the total sample size N, the two group sizes and the corrected estimate g, with N less 3.94 in the denominator of the effect term. It differs from SE_g of HE-FM-HEDG-002 because J is not applied as a multiplier and the effect term is g squared over twice (N less 3.94) in place of d squared over twice N, and it is slightly larger in small trials. Reproducing the weights of a Cochrane forest plot needs this form, while the article's interval uses HE-FM-HEDG-002. g comes from HE-FM-HEDG-001.

Rise in the ICER when incremental patient time cost is added to health service costs

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000728
Type formula
assumes QALY gain unchanged when patient time is costed, Perspective that counts patient time in the incremental cost
has calculator text dC_T = C_T_new - C_T_comp; ICER_S = ICER_H + dC_T / dE; g_ICER = (ICER_S - ICER_H) / ICER_H
has common error note Patient time ICER reported as the NICE reference-case result. Reporting ICER_S, GBP 28,950 per QALY in the article's example, as the NICE reference-case result mixes perspectives, since PMG36 section 4.2.9 sets the reference-case perspective on costs as the NHS and PSS, which gives GBP 15,000. PMG36 section 4.4.23 allows costs paid by patients and not reimbursed by the NHS and PSS to be presented separately; showing patient time separately in the same way is an inference, since the manual's chapter on economic evaluation does not mention patients' time.
Total patient time cost of the new option added to the incremental cost. Adding the new option's whole time cost rather than the difference from the comparator counts the comparator's patient time as if it were extra. In the article's example the ICER becomes GBP 32,550 per QALY in place of GBP 28,950, GBP 3,600 or 12% too high (computed here for illustration).
has description in the module Takes the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio from the health service view, computed with HE-FM-ICER-001, and adds the incremental patient time cost divided by the same QALY gain, which gives the ratio from a limited societal perspective that counts patient time. Because the QALY gain is unchanged, the rise in the ICER is the incremental time cost over the QALY gain, and the rise as a share of the health service ICER equals the incremental time cost over the incremental health service cost (both derived here from HE-FM-ICER-001). The time cost of each option comes from HE-FM-PTC-001 or HE-CF-PTC-001. In net benefit terms the same step lowers the incremental net monetary benefit of HE-FM-NMB-002 by the incremental time cost, which also covers a QALY gain of zero or below.

Risk equalisation transfer that offsets community-rating cross-subsidies

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000436
Type formula
assumes Fund risk groups match the insurer's information on expected cost
Risk equalisation based on predicted, not incurred, costs
has calculator text T_i = c_i - P
has common error note Assuming risk equalisation removes every selection incentive. In the article's example the transfers remove the incentive only because the fund's two risk groups are the same as the insurer's. Van de Ven and colleagues found that even with the best risk adjustment formulas, insurers in European markets retain substantial incentives to select.
Paying risk equalisation on the costs an insurer incurs. Setting transfers from each insurer's actual costs rather than the expected cost of its members' risk groups turns risk equalisation into risk sharing. That reduces the gain from avoiding expensive members but also weakens the incentive to control costs, a trade-off set out on the Cream Skimming page.
has description in the module A payment from a central fund to an insurer for each member of risk group i, or from the insurer to the fund when negative, equal to the group's expected cost minus the community-rated premium. After the transfer each member brings the insurer an expected result of zero, because premium plus transfer equals expected cost. When the transfers use the same members and premium as the pool they sum to zero, so the fund balances. Van de Ven and colleagues report a consensus that removing the predictable over- and undercompensation of subgroups that community rating creates is part of the goal of risk equalisation.

Rogan-Gladen corrected prevalence from the share flagged by an imperfect algorithm

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000551
Type formula
assumes Informative algorithm with Se + Sp above 1, Sensitivity and specificity transfer from the validation sample
has calculator text p = min(1, max(0, (a + Sp - 1) / (Se + Sp - 1)))
has common error note Correcting with accuracy estimated in another population. Lewis and Torgerson note that the Rogan-Gladen estimator requires sensitivity and specificity to be known and constant, and that estimates above one or below zero mean the values are wrong for the population at hand; accuracy from an enriched validation sample may not hold in routine data.
Reporting a negative corrected prevalence. Flor and colleagues note that the estimate is a valid proportion only if the false positive rate is below sensitivity and the flagged share lies between them, and that it is truncated to the range 0 to 1 in practice; a negative value signals a mismatch, not a usable estimate.
Using the flagged share as the prevalence. The algorithm flags 6.7 per cent of the database against a true 2 per cent, so counting flagged patients as cases inflates the cohort 3.35 times even though sensitivity and specificity look high.
has description in the module The share flagged, the apparent prevalence, mixes true positives and false positives: a = Se p + (1 minus Sp)(1 minus p). Solving for p gives the Rogan-Gladen estimator, which removes the false positive rate from the flagged share and divides by Youden's index, Se + Sp minus 1. Values outside the range 0 to 1 are truncated, the usual convention, and arise when the flagged share lies below the false positive rate or above the sensitivity.
has formalisation level catalogue record
has implementation Corrected prevalence from the flagged share and named accuracy
has mathematical variable Apparent prevalence flagged by a claims algorithm, Sensitivity of a claims algorithm against medical records, Specificity of a claims algorithm against medical records, True prevalence recovered by the Rogan-Gladen correction
has module record identifier HE-FM-CRV-001
has source in the module Flor M, Weiß M, Selhorst T, Müller-Graf C, Greiner M. Comparison of Bayesian and frequentist methods for prevalence estimation under misclassification. BMC Public Health. 2020;20:1135. doi:10.1186/s12889-020-09177-4 (full text read). Background: the apparent prevalence is AP = Se times pi + (1 minus Sp)(1 minus pi) (eq. 1); solving for the prevalence gives the Rogan-Gladen estimate (AP minus (1 minus Sp)) / (Se minus (1 minus Sp)) (eq. 2), truncated in practice to the interval from 0 to 1 (eq. 3); a valid proportion needs 1 minus Sp below Se, 1 minus Sp no greater than AP and AP no greater than Se (eqs. 4a to 4c). https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7370479/
Lewis FI, Torgerson PR. A tutorial in estimating the prevalence of disease in humans and animals in the absence of a gold standard diagnostic. Emerging Themes in Epidemiology. 2012;9:9. doi:10.1186/1742-7622-9-9 (full text read). Section on the simple model: the classic Rogan-Gladen estimator of true prevalence requires that Se and Sp are both known and constant, which may be unrealistic, and it can produce estimates of prevalence that exceed one or are negative, in which case Se and Sp must be incorrect for the population of interest. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3558341/
Rogan WJ, Gladen B. Estimating prevalence from the results of a screening test. American Journal of Epidemiology. 1978;107(1):71-76. doi:10.1093/oxfordjournals.aje.a112510 (abstract read). Abstract: a common use of tests is to estimate the prevalence of disease; the frequency of positive tests is shown to be a bad estimate, and the necessary adjustments are given. https://doi.org/10.1093/oxfordjournals.aje.a112510

Corrected prevalence no higher than the flagged share divided by sensitivity

Rubinstein first proposer's share of the surplus under alternating offers

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000357
Type formula
assumes Alternating offers with fixed per-round discounting
Complete information and no outside options in Rubinstein bargaining
has calculator text s_1 = (1 - delta_2) / (1 - delta_1 * delta_2)
has common error note Ignoring which party makes the first offer. The share s_1 includes the advantage of moving first. Using the manufacturer's opening share of five sevenths when the payer actually opens overstates the manufacturer's weight, which is nine fourteenths, and raises the price from £5,500 to £6,000 per patient.
Swapping the proposer's and responder's discount factors. Putting the first proposer's own discount factor in the numerator gives the share the responder would obtain if it opened. With the manufacturer opening at 0.9 against 0.8 the swap gives about 0.357 instead of 0.714, and a price of £3,500 rather than £6,000 per patient.
has description in the module Gives the share of a surplus of size one obtained by the party that makes the first offer in the unique perfect equilibrium of Rubinstein's alternating-offers model, in which each party discounts agreement by a fixed factor per round of delay. The more patient a party, the larger its share, and the responder receives 1 minus s_1. Multiplied by the surplus p_bar minus c it gives the first proposer's gain, so s_1 can serve as the weight beta in HE-FM-BARG-001 for the party that opens.

Type formula
assumes Linear marginal value of output in the second-best menu

has calculator text q_L = (a - theta_L) / b; theta_v = theta_H + nu / (1 - nu) * (theta_H - theta_L); q_H = max(0, (a - theta_v) / b); U_L = (theta_H - theta_L) * q_H; t_L = theta_L * q_L + U_L; t_H = theta_H * q_H
has common error note Distorting the low-cost type's output as well. Laffont and Martimort's solution leaves the low-cost type's output at first best, since its rent depends only on q_H (2.26). Setting q_L where marginal value equals theta_L plus the same distortion term, 4 + 1 = 5, gives 100 procedures in place of 120 and lowers the commissioner's expected payoff from 260 to 255 (GBP thousand) with no saving in rent (computed here).
Low-cost transfer that leaves out the information rent. Paying the low-cost type only its cost, t_L = 4 x 120 = 480, with the high-cost contract of 80 procedures for GBP 400,000 makes the low-cost type better off on the high-cost contract by GBP 80,000, so it mimics and the menu fails HE-FM-MECH-001 (IC_L of minus 80, computed here).
Prior probability used in place of the odds in the virtual cost. The distortion term is nu / (1 minus nu) times the cost gap, the odds of the low-cost type. Writing nu alone gives a virtual cost of 5.5 in place of 6 with equal priors, a high-cost output of 90 in place of 80 and a rent of GBP 90,000 in place of GBP 80,000 (computed here); with nu = 0.9 it gives 5.9 and an output of 82 where the correct menu shuts the high-cost type out.
has description in the module The purchaser values output at S(q) and, knowing only that the supplier is low-cost with probability nu, chooses the menu that maximises expected S(q) less the transfer subject to the constraints of HE-FM-MECH-001. In Laffont and Martimort's solution the low-cost type produces its first-best output, the high-cost type's output is set where the marginal value equals the virtual cost theta_H + nu / (1 minus nu) (theta_H minus theta_L), and the low-cost type receives the information rent (theta_H minus theta_L) q_H while the high-cost type receives none. With a linear marginal value S'(q) = a minus b q, an illustrative form chosen here, both outputs solve in closed form (derived). The output step takes the form of HE-FM-CTH-002 and the first-best output that of HE-FM-CTH-003, which compute stays of hospital care; here the cost fed in is the virtual cost of (2.28). The max function sets q_H to zero when (2.28) has no positive solution, the authors' shut-down case.

Second-order approximation to the expected value of a curved model output

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000599
Type formula
assumes Smooth output and a concentrated parameter distribution, Single uncertain parameter in the second-order expansion
has calculator text E_g = g_mu + 0.5 * d2g * Var_theta
has common error note Leaving out the factor of one half in the second-order correction. Without the half, the approximate fracture probability becomes about 0.318, further from the exact 0.36 than the deterministic 0.3935 is.
Reporting the second-order approximation as the expected value. The expansion is a guide to sign and rough size. For the log-normal cost it gives £3,000 against the exact £3,297; where no closed form exists the simulated mean of a probabilistic analysis is the estimate, as the article states.
Using the standard deviation of the parameter in place of its variance. Multiplying by the standard deviation of the hazard, about 0.0707, rather than its variance of 0.005 gives a correction of about minus 0.536 and an approximate five-year probability of about minus 0.14, which is impossible.
has description in the module Approximates the expected value of an output g(theta) that depends on one uncertain parameter by its value at the parameter mean plus half its second derivative at the mean times the parameter variance. The correction shows the direction of Jensen's inequality: it is negative for a concave output, positive for a convex one and zero for a linear one. With several parameters the article's double sum adds a term for each pair, weighted by their covariance; for the product N times U the only second derivative is the cross term, equal to 1, so the expansion is exact and gives HE-FM-EV-001. The approximation indicates sign and rough size; the simulated mean (HE-FM-ENB-001) or a closed form is the estimate.

Sensitivity, specificity and misclassification of one candidate change-score cut-off against an anchor

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000576
Type formula
assumes Anchor as reference standard with a fixed split of the cohort, Share of improved patients near one half
has calculator text Se_c = a_c / N_I; Sp_c = (N_N - b_c) / N_N; M_c = (1 - Se_c) + (1 - Sp_c); J_c = Se_c + Sp_c - 1
has common error note Comparing ROC thresholds from cohorts with very different shares improved. The ROC estimate is biased when the share of improved patients is not 50 per cent, so thresholds from a cohort where most patients improved and one where few did are not directly comparable; Terwee and colleagues recommend predictive modelling, which can be corrected for this bias.
Reporting the mean change of the minimally improved group as if it were the ROC estimate. Terwee and colleagues note that in theory the mean change method overestimates the minimal important change; in the article's example it gives 8.0 points against the ROC threshold of 6, so a report should name its estimator.
has description in the module Treats the change score as a diagnostic test and the anchor as the reference standard. At a candidate cut-off, sensitivity is the share of anchor-improved patients whose change reaches it and specificity the share of all other patients whose change falls below it; the ROC cut-off is the candidate with the smallest sum of the two misclassification proportions, the same as the largest Youden index.

Sensitivity, specificity and predictive values from a diagnostic two-by-two table

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000535
Type formula
assumes Reference standard taken as correct in the accuracy table, One threshold and one population behind the four cells, Predictive values tied to the study sample's prevalence
has calculator text Se = TP / (TP + FN); Sp = TN / (TN + FP); PPV = TP / (TP + FP); NPV = TN / (TN + FN)
has common error note Pooling predictive values across studies. Predictive values depend on prevalence, so the Cochrane Handbook does not recommend pooling them across studies: between-study differences in prevalence add heterogeneity, and the pooled value refers to an average but unknown prevalence.
Reading sensitivity as the chance that a positive result is a case. Test A detects 96 per cent of cases, but at 5 per cent prevalence only about 17 per cent of its positive results are cases; using 0.96 as the probability of disease after a positive result overstates confirmed cases more than fivefold.
Treating sensitivity and specificity as fixed test properties. STARD 2015 states that they are not fixed test properties: the relative numbers of false positive and false negative results vary with how patients present and which tests they have already had, so model inputs should come from the population and pathway position modelled.
has description in the module Sensitivity and specificity are proportions of the people with and without the target condition who receive the correct index test result, so they are conditional on disease status (the columns of the table). The predictive values are proportions of the positive and negative results that are correct, so they are conditional on the test result (the rows) and carry the prevalence of the study sample. Likelihood ratios are HE-FM-DXA-002 and predictive values at another prevalence HE-FM-DXA-003.

Sequential best-then-worst model probability in one choice set

Type formula

has calculator text P_seq = exp(V_b) / S_pos * exp(-V_w) / (S_neg - exp(-V_b))
has common error note Appending worst choices without reversing the explanatory variables. When worst data are stacked under best data for a conditional logit, every explanatory variable in the worst rows is multiplied by minus one. Without that step the worst choices pull utilities the wrong way.
Keeping the best item in the worst-choice set. Dividing exp(minus V_w) by S_neg instead of S_neg minus exp(minus V_b) gives 0.455 x 0.455, about 0.2071 instead of 0.2305 in the article's set (computed here for illustration).
has description in the module Treats the best choice as a logit choice from the whole set and the worst choice as a logit choice on minus the utilities from the items left once the best is removed, and multiplies the two. S_neg minus exp(minus V_b) is the sum of exp(minus V_k) over the set without item b. From the same utilities it gives different probabilities from the maxdiff model (HE-FM-BWS-003), so a study should state which it assumed.

Share of mean survival from an exponential tail beyond the last observed follow-up

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000426
Type formula
assumes Constant hazard for life after the last follow-up, Tail starts at the last observed follow-up
has calculator text A_tail = S_tau / h; P_tail = A_tail / (RMST_tau + A_tail)
has common error note Share censored read as the share extrapolated. Half of the article's patients were censored, but survival at month 34 is 0.40 and the tail supplies between about 32% and 48% of the mean depending on the hazard. Maturity is judged from survival at the end of follow-up and the hazard assumed after it, not from the proportion censored.
Tail hazard taken from the earliest recruits alone. After month 24 the article's curve rests on one of the earliest recruits. If prognosis improved during recruitment, a tail hazard fitted to that part of the curve describes the earliest cohort and misstates the share of mean survival for the arm as a whole.
has description in the module When survival at the last observed follow-up tau is S_tau and a constant hazard h is assumed afterwards, the area under the tail is S_tau divided by h. The share of mean survival that comes from that tail is the tail area divided by the restricted mean plus the tail area. The denominator is the mean survival of HE-FM-BTH-002 with the restricted mean in place of the closed-interval life-years, and a trial estimate of h is events divided by person-time, HE-FM-AER-002.

Share of the life years gained over the model horizon observed within trial follow-up

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000733
Type formula
assumes Model horizon means from extrapolations that follow the trial data
Restricted means of both arms taken at one follow-up time
Within-trial share of life years gained read as a share only for a positive gain
has calculator text dRMST = RMST_1 - RMST_0; dLY_life = LY_1 - LY_0; phi = dRMST / dLY_life; dLY_beyond = dLY_life - dRMST
has common error note Restricted means of the two arms taken at different follow-up times. Setting the new treatment's restricted mean at two years, 1.55, against the comparator's at three years, 1.45, gives a within-trial gain of 0.10 and a share of 15.4% instead of 0.30 and 46.2% for the article's curves (computed here). Both restricted means are taken at the same tau.
Within-trial life years gained used as the effect in a cost per life year. Holding the article's GBP 12,000 fixed for illustration, the within-trial gain of 0.30 gives GBP 40,000 per life year against GBP 18,462 on the undiscounted gain of 0.65 over the horizon (computed here), more than double. TSD 14 warns that a survival benefit restricted to what the trial observed is likely to underestimate the true survival gain.
Within-trial share of life years gained read from one arm's tail share. Taking the new treatment's restricted mean as a share of its own mean, 1.55 over 2.15, suggests that 72.1% of the benefit is observed in the trial, while the share of the gain is 46.2% for the article's figures (computed here). The tail share of HE-FM-ADMC-004 describes one arm's survival; the share of a gain needs both arms.
has description in the module Takes the restricted mean survival times of the two arms at a follow-up time tau and their mean survival over the model horizon, and returns the within-trial gain, the gain over the horizon, the share of that gain lying within follow-up and the gain lying after it. The restricted means come from HE-FM-ADMC-003 for a Kaplan-Meier curve or from the modelled curves, as in the article's step 6, and the horizon means from an extrapolation such as HE-FM-BTH-002 or HE-FN-CRM-001. The difference of two restricted means is the measure of Royston and Parmar and is not new here; the share phi and the gain after follow-up are derived here. HE-FM-ADMC-004 gives the share of one arm's mean survival that comes from its tail, whereas 1 minus phi is the difference between the arms in the area after tau divided by the gain over the horizon, which depends on both arms' means as well as their tail shares (derived here).

BMC Medical Research Methodology. 2013;13:152. Background, which recalls the authors' earlier proposal to express the treatment effect as the difference in restricted mean survival time between the randomised arms at a suitable follow-up time t*, and Methods, section Definition of RMST, which reads the restricted mean of equation 1 as the t*-year life expectancy and gives the difference between arms as the area between the survival curves, in the unnumbered expression that follows equation 1. https://doi.org/10.1186/1471-2288-13-152

Share of total scatter removed by a K-cluster k-means solution

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000512
Type formula
assumes Within-cluster sum of squares from the best of several k-means starts
Same units, variables and scaling for every number of clusters
has calculator text R_K = 1 - W_K / W_1
has common error note Choosing the number of clusters by minimising the within-cluster sum of squares. W(K) generally falls as clusters are added, even when evaluated on new data, and reaches 0 with one unit per cluster, so neither its minimum nor cross-validation picks K; analysts look for the kink or use a criterion such as the gap statistic.
Reading the share removed as cost or outcome variation explained. The 86 per cent refers to scatter in the clustering variables only; in the example it says nothing about how much variation in annual cost, which was kept out of the clustering, the clusters explain.
has description in the module Compares the within-cluster sum of squares W(K), the squared distances of units from their own cluster mean that k-means minimises, with its value for one cluster, the total sum of squares about the overall mean. The share removed rises as clusters are added, so the number of clusters is judged by where the gains flatten (the kink or elbow), not by maximising it.

Shared losses of a two-sided BASIC accountable care organisation with the minimum loss rate and loss recoupment limit

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000953
Type formula
assumes Adjustments to shared losses outside the formula, Two-sided BASIC levels for performance years from 2024
has calculator text g_L = (E - B) / B; L_raw = r_L * N * (E - B); LRL = min(rho_R * Rev, rho_B * N * B); SL = (g_L >= MLR) * min(L_raw, LRL)
has common error note Treating the minimum loss rate as a deductible on losses. The 30% loss rate applies to the whole excess once the MLR is reached. Applying it only to the excess above the MLR gives 0.3 times 120 per beneficiary in the first Level D example, USD 720,000 instead of USD 2.16 million, a third of the amount owed.
Using the revenue-based loss recoupment limit without its benchmark ceiling. The revenue-based limit applies only while it is below the benchmark-based limit (42 CFR 425.605(d)(1)(iii)(D)(2)). In the Level C example the revenue-based figure alone would let CMS recoup USD 4 million when the limit is USD 2.4 million, 1% of the benchmark.
has description in the module Computes what an ACO in BASIC Level C, D or E repays CMS when its per capita spending E exceeds the updated benchmark B. The loss ratio g_L must reach the minimum loss rate MLR, which mirrors the MSR, and the fixed 30% shared loss rate r_L then applies to the whole excess, the loss counterpart of HE-FM-ACO-001. The amount may not exceed the loss recoupment limit LRL, a share rho_R of the ACO participants' Medicare fee-for-service revenue, never more than a share rho_B of total benchmark expenditure, as 42 CFR 425.605(d)(1)(iii) to (v) and (i)(2) set out. The final min step is the cap form of HE-FM-ASL-001 with no attachment point. With the article's case 3 figures a 3% overspend gives USD 2.16 million, the article's result, whenever the limit is at least that amount.

The preamble section Generally Applicable Nominal Amount Standard, under Advanced APM Criteria (87 FR 70117), finalises as proposed the removal of the 2024 end date from 414.1415(c)(3)(i)(A), so that the 8 percent revenue-based nominal amount standard applies to all QP performance periods beginning on or after 1 January 2023; the amendment to 414.1415 in the same rule gives the paragraph its current wording, "For QP Performance Periods beginning in 2023, 8 percent". https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2022-11-18/pdf/2022-23873.pdf
Code of Federal Regulations, Title 42, section 414.1415, Advanced APM criteria. eCFR text up to date as of 15 October 2026. Paragraph (c)(3)(i)(B) sets the generally applicable nominal amount standard at 3 percent of the expected expenditures for which an APM entity is responsible, so the Level E benchmark-based loss recoupment limit of 425.605(d)(1)(v)(D)(2) is 4% of the updated benchmark. Paragraph (c)(3)(i)(A) gives the revenue-based standard as 8 percent of revenue for QP performance periods beginning in 2023, the Level E revenue-based limit of 425.605(d)(1)(v)(D)(1); HE-SR-ACO-008 records that this applies to every QP performance period from 2023 on. https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/section-414.1415
Code of Federal Regulations, Title 42, section 425.605, Calculation of shared savings and losses under the BASIC track. eCFR text up to date as of 15 October 2026. Paragraph (b)(2) has a two-sided ACO choose a zero, symmetrical 0.5 to 2.0% or size-based MSR/MLR, and (b)(4) makes it share losses when spending is above the benchmark by at least the MLR. Paragraphs (d)(1)(iii), (iv) and (v), sub-paragraph (C), fix the shared loss rate at 30% for Levels C, D and E. Sub-paragraph (D) limits losses to 2% of ACO participant revenue but not above 1% of the benchmark in Level C, 4% of revenue but not above 2% of the benchmark in Level D, and in Level E the percentage of 414.1415(c)(3)(i)(A) of revenue but not above one point more than the 414.1415(c)(3)(i)(B) percentage of the benchmark. Paragraph (f) reduces losses for extreme and uncontrollable circumstances after the rate and limit, and (i)(2) defines the revenue-based and benchmark-based limits. https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/section-425.605

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000954
Type formula
assumes ENHANCED loss rate rule for performance years from 2024
ENHANCED loss recoupment limit and adjustments outside the formula
has calculator text r_E = min(max(1 - 0.75 * Q, 0.4), 0.75); g_L = (E - B) / B; SL_E = (g_L >= MLR) * min(r_E * N * (E - B), 0.15 * N * B)
has common error note Leaving out the 40% floor on the ENHANCED loss rate. Without the floor a quality score of 90% gives a rate of 0.325 and losses of USD 2.34 million in the article's population, against the USD 2.88 million the 40% floor requires. The floor binds for every score of 0.8 or more (derived).
Taking the ENHANCED loss rate as 1 minus the 75% sharing rate. The rule multiplies 75% by the quality score before subtracting from 1. Using 1 minus 0.75, or 0.25, for every ACO ignores both the quality score and the 40% floor; with a 70% score it would collect USD 1.8 million instead of USD 3.42 million.
has description in the module Computes what an ACO in the ENHANCED track repays CMS when per capita spending E exceeds the benchmark B by at least the MLR. The shared loss rate r_E is 1 minus 75% of the quality score Q, held to at least 40% and at most 75%, and is 75% when the ACO meets neither quality standard, as 42 CFR 425.610(f)(4) sets for performance years from 2024. Entering Q = 0 for an ACO that meets neither standard returns the same 75%, since the ceiling binds for every score up to one third, and the floor of 40% binds for every score of 0.8 or more (derived, checked on a grid of 1,001 scores). Losses apply to the whole excess and may not exceed 15% of total benchmark expenditure under 425.610(g), the cap form of HE-FM-ASL-001 with no attachment point; there is no revenue-based limit in this track.

Shared savings payment of an accountable care organisation with the minimum savings rate gate and payment limit

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000952
Type formula
assumes Benchmark and spending on one assigned population and basis
Qualification at the minimum savings rate and the low revenue route
Track rates for performance years from 2024 in the shared savings payment
has calculator text g_S = (B - E) / B; S_raw = s * q * N * (B - E); PPL = c_P * N * B; P = (g_S >= MSR) * min(S_raw, PPL)
has common error note Applying the performance payment limit to savings before sharing. The limit caps the amount of shared savings the ACO receives, not the savings that are shared (42 CFR 425.610(e)(2), 425.605(d)(1)(v)(B)(2)). In the ENHANCED example, capping savings at 20% of the benchmark and then taking three quarters gives USD 36 million instead of the USD 48 million limit that binds on the payment.
Multiplying by the quality score when the quality standard is met. The quality score scales the sharing rate only for an ACO that meets the alternative quality performance standard; an ACO that meets the standard itself is paid the full rate. Applying a 70% score in the first worked example would pay USD 2.52 million instead of USD 3.6 million.
Treating the minimum savings rate as a deductible. Once the MSR is met the sharing rate applies to all savings on a first dollar basis (42 CFR 425.605(d)(1)(v)(B)(1)). Sharing only the savings above the MSR pays 0.5 times 120 per beneficiary in the first worked example, USD 1.2 million instead of USD 3.6 million, two thirds too little, and removes the jump at the MSR.
has description in the module Computes the payment CMS makes to an accountable care organisation for a performance year in which its assigned beneficiaries' average per capita spending E falls below the updated benchmark B. The savings ratio g_S must reach the minimum savings rate MSR, and once it does the final sharing rate, s times the quality factor q, applies to all the savings on a first dollar basis, as 42 CFR 425.605(d) and 425.610(e) state. The payment may not exceed the performance payment limit PPL, a share c_P of total benchmark expenditure, 10% in the BASIC track and 20% in ENHANCED; that last step is the cap form of HE-FM-ASL-001 with no attachment point. Because the gate is a test and not a deductible, the payment jumps from zero to s q MSR N B at the MSR when the cap does not bind (derived), USD 2.4 million for the article's Level E ACO. A low revenue BASIC ACO that beats its benchmark but not its MSR is paid under 425.605(h) at half the sharing rate, entered as s halved with MSR set to 0.

has source in the module Code of Federal Regulations, Title 42, section 425.512, Determining the ACO quality performance standard for performance years beginning on or after January 1, 2021. eCFR text up to date as of 15 October 2026. Paragraph (a)(5) sets for performance years from 2024 the standard of a quality score at or above the 40th percentile of MIPS Quality performance category scores and, in (a)(5)(ii), an alternative standard of a score at or above the 10th percentile of the performance benchmark on at least one outcome measure of the APP Plus set from 2025. Paragraph (b)(3) states that for 2025 the quality score with bonus points may not exceed 100 percent. https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/section-425.512
Code of Federal Regulations, Title 42, section 425.605, Calculation of shared savings and losses under the BASIC track. eCFR text up to date as of 15 October 2026, last amended 5 November 2025 (90 FR 50018). Paragraph (a) compares per capita Parts A and B spending with the updated benchmark and requires it to be below by at least the minimum savings rate. Paragraph (b) sets the MSR options, a sliding scale for one-sided levels and a zero, 0.5 to 2.0% or size-based MSR/MLR for two-sided levels. Paragraph (d)(1)(i) to (v), sub-paragraph (A)(4), gives sharing rates of 40% for Levels A and B and 50% for Levels C to E from 2024, multiplied by the quality score for the alternative standard; sub-paragraph (B) applies the rate on a first dollar basis once the MSR is met and limits shared savings to 10% of the updated benchmark. Paragraph (h) allows a low revenue ACO below its benchmark to be paid at one half of the applicable rate, and (i)(1) computes the limit on total benchmark expenditure as per capita benchmark times assigned beneficiary person years. Section 425.20 (same eCFR date) defines a low revenue ACO as one whose participants' Parts A and B fee-for-service revenue is less than 35 percent of its assigned beneficiaries' Parts A and B fee-for-service expenditure. https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/section-425.605
Code of Federal Regulations, Title 42, section 425.610, Calculation of shared savings and losses under the ENHANCED track. eCFR text up to date as of 15 October 2026. Paragraph (b)(2) requires spending below the benchmark by at least the MSR; (d)(4) sets the sharing rate at 75% for performance years from 2024, multiplied by the quality score for an ACO meeting the alternative quality performance standard; (e)(1) applies it on a first dollar basis and (e)(2) caps shared savings at 20% of the updated benchmark; (l)(2) computes the limit from per capita benchmark times assigned beneficiary person years. https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/section-425.610
Social Security Act, section 1899 (42 U.S.C. 1395jjj), Shared savings program, as amended, text read on the Cornell Legal Information Institute page on 18 October 2026. Subsection (d)(1)(B)(i) requires spending to be at least a percent specified by the Secretary below the benchmark, set to account for normal variation in expenditures and based on the number of assigned beneficiaries. Subsection (d)(2) allows a percent of the difference between spending and the benchmark to be paid to the ACO as shared savings, subject to the quality performance standards, leaves the remainder with Medicare and requires limits on the total amount of shared savings. https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/1395jjj

Shares of each trial arm reaching a responder threshold when changes are normal with a common standard deviation

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000578
Type formula
assumes Normal changes with a common standard deviation in both arms
has calculator text z_C = (c - mu_C) / sigma; z_T = (c - mu_T) / sigma; P_C = 1 - Phi_C; P_T = 1 - Phi_T; RD = P_T - P_C
has common error note Replacing the comparison of means by a responder analysis. Under the normal model of Snapinn and Jiang a responder analysis needed about 60 per cent more participants than a comparison of means even with the threshold midway between the arm means, and with a large enough sample any small difference in responder rates becomes statistically significant.
Treating a mean difference below the MCID as no benefit. The Cochrane Handbook warns that a difference smaller than the MID may be read as trivial when a substantial proportion of patients achieved an important benefit; in the article's example a 4-point mean difference comes with about 13 percentage points more treated patients reaching the threshold.
has description in the module If changes in each arm are normally distributed with a common standard deviation, the share of an arm reaching a threshold is one minus the standard normal distribution function at the threshold's distance from the arm's mean in standard deviations, and the responder difference is the treated share minus the control share. The site's calculator has no normal distribution function, so Phi_C and Phi_T, its values at z_C and z_T, are entered as inputs (NORM.S.DIST(z, TRUE) in Excel, pnorm(z) in R).

Abstract: the first step establishes the smallest change in score that patients consider, on average, to be important; the second estimates the proportion of patients who have achieved that minimum important difference. https://doi.org/10.4065/77.4.371
Schunemann HJ, Vist GE, Higgins JPT, Santesso N, Deeks JJ, Glasziou P, Akl EA, Guyatt GH. Chapter 15: Interpreting results and drawing conclusions. In: Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions version 6.5. Cochrane; 2024 (full text of the chapter read). Section 15.5.3.5: expressing results in MID units is risky in that a difference less than the MID may be interpreted as trivial when a substantial proportion of patients may have achieved an important benefit. https://www.cochrane.org/authors/handbooks-and-manuals/handbook/current/chapter-15
Snapinn SM, Jiang Q. Responder analyses and the assessment of a clinically relevant treatment effect. Trials. 2007;8:31. doi:10.1186/1745-6215-8-31 (full text read). Methods: with the measurement normally distributed with known variance and response defined as reaching a threshold x_0, power and sample size for a responder comparison depend on the mean difference and on x_0; even with the threshold midway between the group means the responder analysis needed approximately 60% more participants; with a large enough sample size any arbitrarily small difference in response rates can be statistically significant. https://doi.org/10.1186/1745-6215-8-31

Silver Spring, MD: FDA; December 2009 (full text read). Section IV.E: the empiric evidence for any responder definition is derived using anchor-based methods; a display of the cumulative distribution of responses in each arm may be preferable to attempting to provide categorical definitions of responders. https://www.fda.gov/media/77832/download

Shrinkage factor and shrunken trial estimate in a Bayesian meta-analysis

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000381
Type formula
assumes Mean effect and between-study variance held fixed for trial shrinkage
Normal random effects and known within-trial variance for trial shrinkage
has calculator text B_i = s_i^2 / (s_i^2 + tau2); theta_post_i = B_i * mu + (1 - B_i) * y_i
has common error note Treating plug-in shrunken trial estimates as fully Bayesian. Plugging point estimates of mu and tau2 into the formula treats them as known. Higgins and colleagues note that these empirical Bayes expressions can be improved to account for uncertainty in the estimates, while fully Bayesian shrunken estimates come from the posterior distributions of the trial effects. With four trials a single plug-in tau2 can understate or overstate the shrinkage.
Using tau in place of tau2 in the shrinkage factor. Using tau, about 0.139, in place of tau2 = 0.0193 in the denominator gives a shrinkage factor of about 0.393 for trial 3 and a shrunken estimate of about -0.458 instead of -0.303, so the small trial keeps most of its extreme effect.
has description in the module Gives the posterior mean of one trial's true effect theta_i given the mean effect mu and the between-study variance tau2. The trial estimate y_i is pulled towards mu by the shrinkage factor B_i, the share of the trial's total variance that comes from sampling error. Small trials, with large s_i, are pulled further, and every trial is pulled further when tau2 is small.

has source in the module Higgins JPT, Thompson SG, Spiegelhalter DJ. A re-evaluation of random-effects meta-analysis. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series A. 2009;172(1):137-159. Section 5.3, which gives the conditional distribution of the effect in study i as normal with mean lambda_i mu plus one minus lambda_i times the study estimate, with lambda_i equal to sigma_i^2 divided by sigma_i^2 plus tau^2, and describes fully Bayesian shrunken estimates as borrowing strength from the other studies. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-985X.2008.00552.x

Silhouette of one unit in a cluster solution

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000514
Type formula
assumes Nearest other cluster chosen by mean distance, Silhouette distances measured as in the clustering
has calculator text s_i = (b_i - a_i) / max(a_i, b_i)
has common error note Computing the silhouette from squared distances. Squared distances for P2 give a mean of 3.5 to its own cluster and 26.3 to cluster B, a silhouette of about 0.87 against 0.64 from Euclidean distances (computed here for illustration); values are not comparable with published silhouettes.
Using the mean distance to all other units as b. With more than two clusters, b_i is the mean distance to the nearest other cluster only; averaging over every unit outside the cluster inflates b and the silhouette.
has description in the module Compares a unit's mean distance to the other members of its own cluster, a_i, with its mean distance to the members of the nearest other cluster, b_i. Values run from minus 1 to 1: near 1 the unit sits well inside a dense, well-separated cluster, around 0 the clusters overlap and below 0 the unit is closer to another cluster than to its own. The mean over all units summarises a solution.

has implementation Silhouette from named mean distances

has source in the module scikit-learn developers. Clustering. scikit-learn User Guide, section 2.3, version 1.9.1. Accessed 3 October 2026. Section 2.3.11.5, Silhouette Coefficient: a is the mean distance between a sample and all other points in the same class, b the mean distance between a sample and all other points in the next nearest cluster, and s = (b minus a) / max(a, b); the score for a set of samples is the mean; it is bounded between minus 1 for incorrect clustering and plus 1 for highly dense clustering, and scores around zero indicate overlapping clusters. https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/clustering.html

Simple exponential smoothing forecast for the next period

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000533
Type formula
assumes No clear trend or seasonal pattern in the smoothed series
Smoothing parameter and starting level estimated from training data
has calculator text yhat_next = alpha * y_t + (1 - alpha) * yhat_t
has common error note Extrapolating through a structural break. Smoothing uses only the series' own past; in Stockholm, Linnér and colleagues found forecast accuracy was affected by the timing of new medicines and generics, the uptake of new medicines and sudden changes in reimbursement policy, which no extrapolation anticipates.
Smoothing a series with a trend or seasonal pattern. The forecast is flat, so a series that is rising, or that peaks every winter, is forecast too low in growth periods and in winter; Holt or seasonal methods are needed.
has description in the module Forecasts the next period as a weighted average of the latest observation and the forecast that had been made for it, or equivalently the previous forecast corrected by a share alpha of its error. Unrolled, the weights on past observations decline exponentially with age. The method suits series with no clear trend or seasonal pattern; Holt's method adds a trend and seasonal versions add a seasonal component.
has formalisation level catalogue record
has implementation Simple exponential smoothing update from named cells
has mathematical variable Forecast that had been made for the latest period, Next-period forecast produced by simple exponential smoothing, Latest observed value in the smoothed series, Smoothing parameter of simple exponential smoothing
has module record identifier HE-FM-DFC-002
has source in the module Hyndman RJ, Athanasopoulos G. Forecasting: Principles and Practice. 3rd ed. Melbourne: OTexts; 2021. Section 8.1, simple exponential smoothing: suitable for forecasting data with no clear trend or seasonal pattern; the forecast at T + 1 is a weighted average of the most recent observation and the previous forecast; if alpha is close to 1 more weight is given to recent observations; the smoothing parameter and initial level can be estimated by minimising the SSE. https://otexts.com/fpp3/ses.html
Linnér L, Eriksson I, Persson M, Wettermark B. Forecasting drug utilization and expenditure: ten years of experience in Stockholm. BMC Health Services Research. 2020;20:410. doi:10.1186/s12913-020-05170-0 (abstract read). Abstract: accuracy was affected by the timing of the introduction of both new medicines and generics, the rate of uptake of new medicines and sudden changes in reimbursement policies; forecasts should be updated as close as possible prior to the decision date. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7212573/

Single-loop EVPPI shortcut for a model linear in the remaining parameters

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000656
Type formula
assumes Net benefit linear in the remaining parameters given theta_i
Remaining parameters independent of the parameters of interest for the shortcut
has calculator text ibar_k = alpha_k + beta_k * mu_c; EVPPI_1L = sum_(k=1)^K [max(ibar_k, 0)] / K - max(sum_(k=1)^K [ibar_k] / K, 0)
has common error note Marginal mean used for a remaining parameter correlated with theta_i. When theta_c is correlated with theta_i, the mean that applies at draw k is the mean of theta_c given theta_i at that draw, and a single marginal mean for every draw misstates each conditional expected net benefit. Brennan and colleagues report that even relatively small correlation can make the shortcut substantially inaccurate.
Single-loop shortcut applied to a model curved in the remaining parameter. Suppose, for illustration, that a remaining parameter takes the values 0 or 2 with equal probability, so its mean is 1, and enters squared, with incremental net benefit GBP 1,000 plus GBP 250 times its square given high A and GBP -1,600 plus GBP 250 times its square given low A. The true conditional means are GBP 1,500 and GBP -1,100 and the EVPPI for A is GBP 550. Plugging in the mean gives GBP 1,250 and GBP -1,350, a current decision that wrongly rejects the new treatment and an EVPPI of GBP 625 (computed here for illustration).
has description in the module Replaces the inner loop by one model run for each draw of theta_i with the remaining parameters theta_c set at their mean. The second ISPOR report allows this when the model is linear or multilinear in theta_c, with no correlation between complementary parameters that are multiplied together, and prefers single-loop methods where they apply because they reduce Monte Carlo error. Here the incremental net benefit at draw k is alpha_k plus beta_k times theta_c, with alpha_k and beta_k depending on theta_i only, so its expectation over theta_c is that line evaluated at the mean mu_c. Brennan and colleagues show that the shortcut can be substantially inaccurate when even relatively small correlation or nonlinearity is present.

Six-month matrix as the square root of a progressive three-state annual transition matrix

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000580
Type formula
assumes Progressive structure with an absorbing death state, Annual matrix with a valid root, Same six-month matrix in both halves of the year
has calculator text r_11 = sqrt(p_11); r_22 = sqrt(p_22); r_12 = p_12 / (r_11 + r_22); r_13 = 1 - r_11 - r_12; r_23 = 1 - r_22
has common error note Converting each annual probability to six months separately. Applying 1 minus (1 minus p) to the power one half to each cell gives 0.105573 for progression and 0.051317 for death from progression-free; every row still sums to one, but two cycles leave about 711 progression-free, 171 progressed and 118 dead per 1,000 after a year, against 700, 200 and 100 in the evidence, because annual deaths after progression are counted as direct deaths.
Splitting the progression-free exits in proportion to the annual exits. A proportional split under constant competing hazards (HE-FM-TP-004) gets the progression-free entry right but treats the progressed state as absorbing, giving 0.175 progressed and 0.125 dead after one year in the article's example in place of 0.200 and 0.100.
Taking the root once for the mean matrix in a probabilistic analysis. The root is a non-linear function of the matrix and whether it is valid depends on the probability values, so it has to be taken, and checked, for each sampled annual matrix rather than once for the mean.
has description in the module For a progressive model with states progression-free (1), progressed (2) and dead (3), no return from 2 to 1 and death absorbing, the annual matrix is upper triangular, so its eigenvalues are its diagonal entries and the square root has diagonal entries equal to their square roots. The progression entry follows from requiring the root squared to return the annual progression probability, the death entries are the row remainders, and two six-month cycles then reproduce every entry of the annual matrix.

Medical Decision Making. 2016;36(8):952-964. doi:10.1177/0272989X16656165 (full text of the author manuscript read). Background: the traditional approach is relevant to only two-state progressive models. Error with the traditional approach: with the lifetime horizon, the total error in the cumulative incidence of hepatocellular carcinoma, costs and QALYs was minus 42%, minus 19% and 0.9%; the success of the eigendecomposition approach depends not only on the structure of a model but also on the transition probability values. https://doi.org/10.1177/0272989X16656165
Chhatwal J, Jayasuriya S, Elbasha EH. Changing cycle lengths in state-transition models: challenges and solutions. Medical Decision Making. 2016;36(8):952-964. doi:10.1177/0272989X16656165 (full text of the author manuscript read). Conditions for the existence of stochastic roots: necessary conditions for embeddability include a positive determinant no greater than the product of the diagonal entries and no states i and j such that j is accessible from i but p_ij = 0; these may also be necessary for the eigendecomposition approach to work. Limitations: not all matrices are diagonalisable, and the root may include complex entries or not be stochastic. https://doi.org/10.1177/0272989X16656165
Chhatwal J, Jayasuriya S, Elbasha EH. Changing cycle lengths in state-transition models: challenges and solutions. Medical Decision Making. 2016;36(8):952-964. doi:10.1177/0272989X16656165 (full text of the author manuscript read). Eigendecomposition approach: converting an annual cycle length to a cycle one n-th of a year requires the n-th root of the annual transition probability matrix, P = V D V^-1 and P^(1/n) = V D^(1/n) V^-1; because the example matrix is upper triangular, its eigenvalues are given by the diagonal elements. Issues with the traditional approach: the traditional formula introduced a different Markov chain. https://doi.org/10.1177/0272989X16656165
Jones E, Epstein D, Garcia-Mochon L. A procedure for deriving formulas to convert transition rates to probabilities for multistate Markov models. Medical Decision Making. 2017;37(7):779-789. doi:10.1177/0272989X17696997 (full text read). Introduction: a person can experience more than one type of event in a single cycle, for example healthy to ill and ill to dead, and the simple formula 1 minus exp(minus rt) is always wrong if there are competing risks. https://doi.org/10.1177/0272989X17696997
Siebert U, Alagoz O, Bayoumi AM, Jahn B, Owens DK, Cohen DJ, Kuntz KM. State-transition modeling: a report of the ISPOR-SMDM Modeling Good Research Practices Task Force-3. Value in Health. 2012;15(6):812-820. doi:10.1016/j.jval.2012.06.014 (full text read). Slope index of inequality for grouped health data

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000367
Type formula
assumes Naturally ordered groups for the slope index of inequality
Between-group inequality only in the grouped slope index
Straight line fitted by population-weighted least squares for the slope index
has calculator text SII = cov_hr / var_r
has common error note Fitting an unweighted line for the slope index with unequal group sizes. An unweighted fit, for example with Excel SLOPE, gives every group the same weight whatever its size. In the unequal-shares example the unweighted slope is about 12.66 years against 13.0 years with population weights.
Reading the slope index of inequality as the gap between extreme groups. The slope index compares predicted health at ranks 0 and 1, the ends of the population distribution, not the means of the first and last groups. In the article's example it is 12.5 years against a simple gap of 10 years, so the two numbers are not interchangeable in a report.
has description in the module Gives the slope of the line fitted by population-weighted least squares to group mean health against the midpoint rank of each group, with the population ranked from the most disadvantaged (rank 0) to the most advantaged (rank 1). The slope equals predicted health at rank 1 minus predicted health at rank 0, so the index is in the units of the health variable. From group values, cov_hr is the sum over groups of f_j times (h_j minus mu) times (r_j minus 0.5), and var_r is the sum of f_j times (r_j minus 0.5) squared, because the population-weighted mean rank is 0.5. The computational function HE-CF-HINQ-001 carries out the full procedure from group means and population shares.

Small-sample corrected Akaike information criterion (AICc)

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000279
Type formula
assumes Sample size exceeds the parameter count plus one
has calculator text AICc = 2 * k - 2 * lnL + 2 * k * (k + 1) / (n - k - 1)
has common error note Using AIC in a small arm where AICc is needed. Burnham and Anderson call the use of AIC where AICc is needed a pervasive mistake. In an arm of 30 patients the correction is about 0.14 for a one-parameter model and about 0.92 for a three-parameter model, so plain AIC understates the extra penalty on the three-parameter model by about 0.78 units.
has description in the module Adds a second-order correction to AIC that matters when the number of parameters is large relative to the sample size. The correction shrinks towards 0 as n grows, so AICc converges to AIC. Burnham and Anderson recommend AICc unless the ratio of sample size to parameters exceeds about 40, which makes it relevant for small trial arms.

Smallest effort bonus, expected payment and limited liability rent for a binary effort choice

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000945
Type formula
assumes One task and an indicator the agent cannot move without the effort
Two effort levels and an indicator linked to effort only through its probability
Risk-neutral parties and a floor on payments to the agent
Weak incentive constraint and an indifferent agent at the smallest bonus
has calculator text b_star = c / (p_H - p_L); F = min(ell, p_L * b_star); E_pay = p_H * b_star - F; R = E_pay - c
has common error note Bonus set so that the expected payment just covers the cost. Setting the bonus to c / p_H, so that a practice making the review is paid its cost on average, ignores that the indicator is also met without the review. With the weak indicator of HE-EX-PAP-001 the bonus is 42.86 pounds, the practice earns nothing above cost from the thorough review and 19.29 pounds per patient without it, so it skips the review and the purchaser pays 19.29 pounds per patient for indicators met by chance (derived).
Cutting the bonus below the smallest bonus to save the rent. The rent cannot be reduced by paying less than b_star when no fee can be charged. With the weak indicator a bonus of 100 pounds raises the practice's expected bonus by 25 pounds for a review costing 30, so it skips the review and the purchaser pays 45 pounds per patient for indicators met by chance and buys no reviews (derived). Only a fee or an indicator that separates the two efforts better lowers the rent.
Judging whether to buy the effort against its cost alone. For an agent that cannot be charged a fee, condition (4.23) of Laffont and Martimort induces effort only when the gain in expected benefit is at least the second-best cost, E_pay here, which exceeds the first-best cost c by the rent, so with limited liability some effort worth more than its cost is not worth buying (their Figure 4.3 and Proposition 4.3). With the weak indicator of HE-EX-PAP-001 a review worth at least 30 and less than 84 pounds per patient to the purchaser would be bought if effort were observed but not through the bonus; with the sharper indicator of HE-EX-PAP-002 that band narrows to at least 30 and less than about 38.57 pounds (derived).
Probabilities typed as percentages. Entering p_H and p_L as 70 and 45 makes the difference 25 and the bonus 1.20 pounds. The practice's real chances are still 0.70 and 0.45, so the review raises its expected bonus by 0.30 pounds against a cost of 30 pounds, it skips the review, and the purchaser pays 0.54 pounds per patient for indicators met by chance (derived).
has description in the module A risk-neutral agent, such as a general practice, chooses a high effort that costs it c per patient or a low effort that costs nothing, and is paid a bonus for each patient whose recorded indicator is met, which happens with probability p_H after high effort and p_L otherwise. The smallest bonus that satisfies the incentive constraint, p_H b minus c at least p_L b, is b_star = c / (p_H minus p_L), the gap between the transfers (4.20) and (4.19) of Laffont and Martimort, and the principal also charges a fixed fee F per patient, the smaller of the liability limit ell and p_L b_star, which combines the two cases of their Proposition 4.2 (derived). The expected payment, the two-branch expected value of HE-FM-CHN-001 with branches b_star minus F and minus F, is the second-best cost of inducing effort, and the rent R is that payment less c, the form of the HE-FM-CTH-001 margin with no reimbursed share. With ell = 0 the rent is c p_L / (p_H minus p_L), which equals what the agent would earn without the effort and, for p_L above 0, c / (p_H / p_L minus 1) (derived), the limited liability rent (4.21) that the authors describe as the extra payment caused by moral hazard combined with limited liability. At ell equal to p_L b_star the rent (4.21) of the second case of their Proposition 4.2 falls to zero, and for a larger ell the first case applies, with no rent.

has implementation Excel bonus, fee, expected payment and rent for a binary effort choice
