has module record identifier HE-FM-PAP-001
has source in the module Laffont JJ, Martimort D. The Theory of Incentives I. The Principal-Agent Model. Authors' manuscript dated 6 February 2001, deposited in Toulouse Capitole Publications, record 14941 (full text read). Published as The Theory of Incentives. The Principal-Agent Model. Princeton University Press; 2002. doi:10.1515/9781400829453 (not seen), so the section, equation and page numbers below are the manuscript's. Chapter 4, on moral hazard. Section 4.2.2 (Incentive Feasible Contracts), pages 151 and 152, writes the incentive constraint (4.3) as a weak inequality with the participation constraint (4.4) and Definition 4.1. Section 4.3 (Risk Neutrality and First-Best Implementation), pages 154 and 155, gives the transfers (4.12) and (4.13) with an expected payment equal to the disutility of effort psi, and Remark 2 notes that they make the incentive constraint exactly binding. Section 4.4 (The Trade-Off between Limited Liability Rent Extraction and Efficiency), pages 156 to 159, adds the limited liability constraints (4.17) and (4.18), and Proposition 4.2 gives, for a liability limit l at most pi_0 psi / Delta pi, the transfers (4.19) t SB = minus l and (4.20) t-bar SB = minus l plus psi / Delta pi and the expected limited liability rent (4.21) EU SB = minus l plus pi_0 psi / Delta pi, with no rent for a larger l. The text calls this rent the additional payment the principal incurs because of moral hazard combined with limited liability, and with l = 0 gives (4.22), the condition (4.23) for inducing effort, the second-best cost C SB = pi_1 psi / Delta pi, Figure 4.3 and Proposition 4.3. The records map c to psi, p_H to pi_1, p_L to pi_0 and ell to l. https://publications.ut-capitole.fr/id/eprint/14941/1/Laffont_14941.pdf

Scientific background on the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel 2016. 10 October 2016 (full text read). Section 2.1 (Optimal Incentive Contracts), page 5, notes that payments between principal and agent are constrained by their financial resources, a constraint first set aside. On page 6, in the paragraph on hidden action and the classic moral-hazard model, a risk-neutral agent with sufficient financial resources is given a franchise contract, paying a fixed fee and receiving all of the realised benefit, so that it chooses the first-best action, and footnote 11 adds that managerial wealth constraints may be binding. The records follow this in letting a fee up to ell remove the rent (HE-EX-PAP-003). https://www.nobelprize.org/uploads/2018/06/advanced-economicsciences2016.pdf

Adding total contacts, the sum of the two counts, as a third variable counts the same care use twice: the squared distance from P2 rises from 5 to 6 for P3 but from 20 to 56 for P4 (computed here for illustration), so the shared dimension gains weight without any new information.
Clustering on raw cost alongside counts of care. Stabilised IPCW weight updated over one interval

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000524
Type formula
assumes Numerator model uses baseline covariates only, Same switching data for numerator and denominator models
has calculator text sw_t = sw_prev * p_num / p_den
has common error note Leaving baseline covariates in the numerator out of the outcome model. Stabilised weights leave the baseline part of the censoring mechanism to the outcome model, so any prognostic baseline variables in the numerator must also be included in the weighted outcome model.
Putting time-dependent covariates in the numerator. If the numerator also conditions on progression it equals the denominator, every weight becomes 1 and the analysis is simple censoring of switchers, 0.619 instead of 0.585 at two years in the example.
has description in the module Multiplies the previous stabilised weight by the probability of remaining uncensored given baseline covariates only, divided by the same probability given baseline and time-dependent covariates. The numerator shrinks the weights towards 1, which makes the weighted analysis more efficient; when the time-dependent covariates do not affect censoring every stabilised weight is 1.

Standard error of measurement from the score standard deviation and reliability

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000559
Type formula
assumes Reliability for the SEM estimated in a stable population
has calculator text SEM = SD * sqrt(1 - R)
has common error note Computing the SEM with Cronbach's alpha for change over time. Alpha comes from one measurement and describes internal consistency; de Vet and colleagues regard test-retest reliability in a stable population as more appropriate for change between two time points, and a higher alpha gives a smaller SEM that can understate the error in a change score.
Using one SEM as the minimal important change in every setting. De Vet and colleagues summarise studies in which one SEM matched anchor-based standards and a set of musculoskeletal studies using ROC methods in which the important change was 2.3 or 2.6 SEM, and conclude that one SEM equalling the minimally important change is not a universal truth.
has description in the module The standard error of measurement (SEM) is the standard deviation of scores times the square root of one minus a reliability coefficient, and estimates in the instrument's units how far an observed score is likely to stray from a person's true score. Test-retest reliability in a stable population suits change between two time points better than Cronbach's alpha. One SEM equals half a standard deviation when reliability is 0.75.

Standard error of the antithetic estimate from pair means

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000321
Type formula
assumes Pairs as independent observations for the antithetic standard error
Enough pairs for a stable antithetic standard error
has calculator text SE_anti = s_anti / sqrt(m)
has common error note Dividing the antithetic pair-mean standard deviation by the root of n. The divisor is the root of the number of pairs, not of the number of evaluations. In the survival example, 4.2137 divided by the root of 1,000 gives about 0.133 years instead of 0.188, understating the standard error by about 29%.
Treating antithetic runs as independent for the standard error. Computing the standard error from all 1,000 runs as if they were independent gives about 10 divided by the root of 1,000, or 0.316 years, in the survival example instead of 0.188, hiding the gain. When the within-pair correlation is positive the same mistake gives a standard error that is too small, which is falsely reassuring.
has description in the module Gives the Monte Carlo standard error of the antithetic estimate by treating each pair as one observation. Each pair mean is the average of the two outputs in a pair, s_anti is the sample standard deviation of the m pair means and m equals n/2. The same rule applies to mean costs and QALYs, the probability that a strategy is cost-effective and each point on the cost-effectiveness acceptability curve estimated from paired PSA iterations.

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000481
Type formula
assumes Every respondent completes the same design, Scores read as an ordering summary
has calculator text S_i = (B_i - W_i) / (N * r_i)
has common error note Reading best-minus-worst scores as ratios. Scores can be negative and sum to zero across items, so a statement that one item is twice as important as another has no meaning on this scale. The square root of best over worst counts is undefined for items never chosen worst, as for A, B, C and D in the article's example.
Trusting one respondent's counts for middle-ranked items. In the article's example C scores 0 and D 0.25 although the respondent prefers C, because every set with C also held A or B. Middle items get less information than extreme ones, so a sample, a model or both are needed.
has description in the module Divides the difference between the number of times an item was chosen best and the number of times it was chosen worst by the number of times it could have been chosen: the number of respondents times its appearances in each respondent's design. Scores run from minus 1, always worst, to plus 1, always best, and across all items the differences sum to zero.

Standardised distance from expected claims to the aggregate attachment point

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000336
Type formula
assumes Normal approximation to a group's total net claims
has calculator text z = (A - E_S) / SD_S
has common error note Reading the normal tail probability as reliable for a small group. For 20 members the claims distribution is strongly skewed, and a few very costly members or a shared shock can push claims far above the attachment point more often than the normal curve implies. The 0.2881 figure for Employer 2 is a lower guide, not an estimate to price on.
Reversing the sign of the standardised distance. Computing z as expected claims minus the attachment point gives minus 1.7678 for Employer 1, and 1-NORM.S.DIST then returns about 0.9615 instead of 0.0385, so the carrier appears to pay in almost every year.
has description in the module Expresses the gap between the aggregate attachment point and expected net claims in standard deviations of total claims. Under a normal approximation to total claims, the probability that claims exceed the attachment point is 1 minus Phi(z), where Phi is the standard normal cumulative distribution function; Excel returns it as 1-NORM.S.DIST(z,TRUE). The calculator on this page returns z, since it has no normal distribution function.

Standardised effect of one study for the Begg test

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000463
Type formula
assumes Effect estimates on an approximately normal scale for the Begg test
Common-effect pooled estimate in the Begg standardisation
has calculator text t_j = (theta_j - theta_IV) / sqrt(v_j - 1 / W)
has common error note Correlating raw effects instead of standardised effects with the variances. Ranking the raw log hazard ratios of the article's trials against their variances gives 10 concordant and 35 discordant pairs, S of -25 and Z of about -2.24 (p about 0.025), a stronger result than the standardised test's -2.06 (computed here for illustration). The raw estimates do not have equal variance, so their ranks mix precision with any small-study effect.
Standardising against a random-effects pooled estimate. The variance of the difference, v_j less 1/W, is derived for the inverse-variance common-effect estimate. Subtracting a random-effects mean, which gives small studies more weight, breaks that variance and the zero sum of weighted deviations, so the standardised values no longer follow the test's definition.
has description in the module Subtracts the inverse-variance pooled estimate from a study's effect estimate and divides by the standard deviation of that difference. The variance of the difference is the study's own variance less the variance of the pooled estimate, one over the sum of the weights, which allows for the study's own contribution to the pooled value. Without small-study effects the standardised values show no trend with study variance.

Static value of targeting treatment by subgroup

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000349
Type formula
assumes Treatment against one comparator in each subgroup, Subgroup membership known at the point of decision, Subgroup estimates under current information
has calculator text V_strat = sum_(x=1)^K (P_x * max(0, INMB_x)) - max(0, sum_(x=1)^K (P_x * INMB_x))
has common error note Comparing a subgroup INMB with the population INMB. The high-risk INMB of £6,000 is per high-risk patient. Set against the population INMB of £2,100 it suggests a gain of £3,900 from targeting, when the high-risk-only policy yields £2,400 per member of the population and the gain is £300.
Deciding on the population INMB when targeting is possible. The positive population INMB of £2,100 suggests treating everyone, yet each low-risk patient treated loses £500. Treating everyone gives up £300 per member of the population against treating only high-risk patients. Subgroup estimates are less precise than the population average, so the subgroups are preferably specified in advance.
has description in the module Measures the expected net monetary benefit per member of the population gained by treating only the subgroups with a positive incremental net monetary benefit, rather than making one decision for everyone on the population average. Each INMB_x comes from HE-FM-NMB-002 with the subgroup's effects on QALYs and cost, and the population value is their share-weighted sum, as in HE-FM-ATE-001. Espinoza and colleagues call this gain the static value of heterogeneity, separate from the value of further research on subgroups.

Steady-state point prevalence from incidence and mean duration

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000554
Type formula
assumes Consistent time units for incidence and duration, Steady-state population for the prevalence relation
has calculator text P = I * D / (1 + I * D); P_approx = I * D
has common error note Back-calculating incidence when a factor changes duration. Dividing prevalence by a common duration assumes every group has the same mean duration; Hill and colleagues show that an association seen among prevalent cases can be spurious when a risk factor influences mortality from the disease studied, and so the duration of prevalent cases.
Using P equal to I times D for a common condition. HealthKnowledge states the approximation for prevalence below about 0.11; at I times D of 0.25 (illustrative) it overstates prevalence by a quarter, so for common conditions the odds form should be used.
has description in the module In a steady state, where incidence, duration and population size are stable and there is no net migration of cases, the prevalence odds equal the incidence rate in the population at risk times the mean duration, P / (1 minus P) = I times D. Solved for P this is I D / (1 + I D). When prevalence is small, (1 minus P) is close to 1 and P is approximately I times D, the form used in the article's worked example; the approximation overstates P by the factor 1 / (1 minus P).
has formalisation level catalogue record
has implementation Steady-state prevalence and its approximation from named cells
has mathematical variable Incidence rate in the population at risk of the condition, Mean duration of the condition from diagnosis, Steady-state point prevalence of a condition, Point prevalence by the incidence times duration approximation
has module record identifier HE-FM-XSD-002
has source in the module Faculty of Public Health. Measures of disease frequency and disease burden. HealthKnowledge epidemiology resource, section 5. Accessed 3 October 2026 (full text read). A population in which the numbers with and without the disease remain stable is a steady-state population; there the point prevalence is approximately equal to the product of the incidence rate and the mean duration of disease (from diagnosis to recovery or death), providing that prevalence is less than about 0.11. https://www.healthknowledge.org.uk/e-learning/epidemiology/practitioners/measures-disease-frequency-burden
Freeman J, Hutchison GB. Prevalence, incidence and duration. American Journal of Epidemiology. 1980;112(5):707-723. doi:10.1093/oxfordjournals.aje.a113043 (abstract read). Abstract: prevalence, incidence and duration of a condition in a steady-state population are interrelated so that two of these quantities may be used to obtain the third. https://doi.org/10.1093/oxfordjournals.aje.a113043
Hill G, Connelly J, Hébert R, Lindsay J, Millar W. Neyman's bias re-visited. Journal of Clinical Epidemiology. 2003;56(4):293-296. doi:10.1016/s0895-4356(02)00571-1 (abstract read). Abstract: in case-control studies using prevalent cases an apparent association may be spurious if the risk factor affects survival; a compartment model shows it can explain the association only if the risk factor influences mortality from the disease being studied. https://doi.org/10.1016/s0895-4356(02)00571-1
Reichenheim ME, Coutinho ESF. Measures and models for causal inference in cross-sectional studies: arguments for the appropriateness of the prevalence odds ratio and related logistic regression. BMC Medical Research Methodology. 2010;10:66. doi:10.1186/1471-2288-10-66 (full text read). Formal relations between measures, equation (3): P_i = ID_i T_i / (ID_i T_i + 1), with ID_i the incidence density and T_i the mean duration of the outcome, equivalent to P / (1 minus P) = ID times T (equation 8 rearranged); Structuring conditions: the population must be in steady state over the study period, with no selective survival and equal mean duration across exposure groups. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2919549/

Stinnett and Mullahy confidence interval for incremental net health benefit from two trial arms

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000662
Type formula
assumes Independent samples for the two arms of a net health benefit interval
Normal approximation for the net health benefit estimator
Threshold fixed for each net health benefit interval
has calculator text INHB = E_1 - E_0 - (C_1 - C_0) / lambda; Var_INHB = (s_E1^2 + s_C1^2 / lambda^2 - 2 * r_1 * s_E1 * s_C1 / lambda) / n_1 + (s_E0^2 + s_C0^2 / lambda^2 - 2 * r_0 * s_E0 * s_C0 / lambda) / n_0; SE_INHB = sqrt(Var_INHB); L_INHB = INHB - z * SE_INHB; U_INHB = INHB + z * SE_INHB; z_INHB = INHB / SE_INHB
has common error note Patient standard deviations not divided by the arm sizes. Leaving out the division by n_1 and n_0 treats patient-level standard deviations as standard errors. In the illustrative trial at GBP 25,000 per QALY the standard error becomes about 0.348 instead of 0.0284, about 12.2 times larger (the square root of 150), and the interval spans about minus 0.643 to 0.723 QALYs (computed here for illustration).
Within-arm correlation left out of the net health benefit variance. Setting r_1 and r_0 to zero in the illustrative trial at GBP 25,000 per QALY raises the standard error from about 0.0284 to 0.0316 QALYs and widens the interval to about minus 0.0219 to 0.1019 (computed here for illustration). With positive correlations, as here, dropping them overstates the standard error, and with negative correlations it understates it.
has description in the module Estimates incremental net health benefit with the analogy estimator, the difference in arm mean effects less the difference in arm mean costs divided by lambda, and estimates its variance from each arm's sample variances of effect and cost, their within-arm correlation and the arm size (Stinnett and Mullahy, equations 6 and 7). The estimator is linear in the four sample means, so its variance is a direct sum of sample terms with no Taylor series approximation, and the interval is a normal (Wald) interval as in HE-FM-AN-001 (their equation 8). The statistic z_INHB, the estimate divided by its standard error, converts to the probability that net health benefit is positive through the standard normal cumulative distribution function, which the calculator lacks, so Excel NORM.S.DIST or R pnorm does that step. Multiplying every term by lambda gives the money-scale result of HE-FM-AN-004.

Subgroup prevalences from an overall prevalence, an exposed share and a prevalence ratio

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000612
Type formula
assumes Prevalence ratio transportable to the target population
Overall prevalence and exposed share from one population and period
has calculator text P_0 = P / (1 + e * (PR - 1)); P_1 = PR * P_0; n_1 = N * e * P_1
has common error note Multiplying the overall prevalence by the prevalence ratio. Treating the overall prevalence as the unexposed baseline overstates the exposed prevalence. In the article's neighbouring area it gives 0.435 instead of 0.30 and an illustrative 39,150 eligible exposed cases instead of 27,000.
has description in the module Recovers the prevalence among the unexposed and among the exposed when local records give only the overall prevalence and the exposure mix, and a published PR gives the relative prevalence. It rearranges P = e P_1 + (1 minus e) P_0 with P_1 = PR x P_0, and multiplies the exposed prevalence by the exposed population to size an eligible population for a budget impact analysis.

Sullivan active life expectancy over three age bands with life expectancy and dependent years

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000958
Type formula
assumes Bands cover all remaining life on one life table
Prevalence is the share of the band dependent at the time of the survey
Dependency treated as a single yes or no state
Stationary mortality and dependency prevalence behind a period figure
has calculator text e_x = (L_1 + L_2 + L_3) / l_x; ALE_x = ((1 - pi_1) * L_1 + (1 - pi_2) * L_2 + (1 - pi_3) * L_3) / l_x; DLE_x = e_x - ALE_x; s_A = ALE_x / e_x
has common error note Applying an unweighted mean prevalence to life expectancy. Averaging the band prevalences without weights and applying the mean to e_x ignores that the oldest band, where dependency is highest, holds the fewest person-years. On the baseline the mean of 0.2833 gives 13.2583 years, 1.2167 years below the Sullivan value of 14.475 (derived). The person-years of each band are the weights.
Leaving a prevalence cell blank. In Excel a blank cell in DependentShareByBand counts as 0, so that band is read as wholly active and no error appears. A blank prevalence for 85 and over on the baseline raises ActiveLifeExpectancy to 15.975 years against 14.475 (derived). A band with no survey estimate needs a value or an explicit flag before the result is used.
Prevalence from a household survey that leaves out care homes. A survey of people living at home, like the non-institutionalised sample of Katz and colleagues, misses many of the most dependent people. If the measured prevalence at 85 and over were 0.40 in place of a whole-population 0.50, active life expectancy on the baseline would be 14.775 years, 0.3 years too high (illustrative, derived).
Reading the active share without the years of dependence. A rising active life expectancy can come with more years of dependence. In the article's Scenario B active life expectancy rises by 0.5 years, yet the active share falls to 76.8% against 78.2% at baseline and dependent years rise by 0.5, which adds GBP 15,000 of expected care cost per person at GBP 30,000 a year (HE-FM-COST-001). Both levels, ALE_x and DLE_x, are reported with s_A.
Weighting person-years by the dependency prevalence in place of its complement. Multiplying each L_i by pi_i in place of 1 minus pi_i gives the expected years lived dependent, not the active years. On the article's baseline it returns 4.025 years in place of 14.475, and the error is hard to spot when prevalence is near one half in most bands.
has description in the module Weights the person-years that a period life table assigns to each age band after the starting age x by the share of the band free of dependency, adds them and divides by the survivors at x, as Sullivan's method does. The article's three bands (65 to 74, 75 to 84, and 85 and over) are written term by term; more bands add terms in the same way, and the last band is open-ended so that all remaining life is counted. Setting every pi_i to 0 returns life expectancy e_x, person-years over survivors (Imai and Soneji equation 7). That first part is HE-FM-ASF-002 with U_t of 1 and r of 0, its single-year L_t summed within each band to give L_i over l_x (derived), and is cited, not restated. DLE_x, the expected years lived dependent, is the difference and s_A is the share of remaining life lived active. The sum has the form of HE-FM-ASF-002 with r of 0 and U_t replaced by 1 minus pi_i, a use that record does not cover because its U_t is a utility norm (HE-VR-ASF-007); here the weight is a prevalence share with dependent time counting zero.

Type formula

has common error note Dividing the whole budget by all QALYs produced. The average cost per QALY across the whole budget is not k. The threshold concerns the health produced by the marginal pound, which is the health lost when spending is displaced.
Presenting a willingness-to-pay value as opportunity cost. A demand-side value of a QALY, estimated from willingness-to-pay studies, answers a different question from k. Such values are generally larger than supply-side estimates, so using one as k can approve spending that reduces population health under a fixed budget.

Survey-weighted prevalence from a cross-sectional health survey with three weighting classes

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000553
Type formula
assumes One measurement occasion and valid answers only, Weights supplied by the survey and used as given
has calculator text P_w = (w_1 * d_1 + w_2 * d_2 + w_3 * d_3) / (w_1 * n_1 + w_2 * n_2 + w_3 * n_3)
has common error note Analysing a complex survey as a simple random sample. STROBE asks cross-sectional studies to describe analytical methods that take account of the sampling strategy; ignoring the weights gives 0.075 instead of 0.0735 in the illustrative example, and ignoring clustering and stratification also misstates the standard error.
Quoting a simple random sample standard error for a weighted estimate. The Health Survey for England methods report notes that standard errors and confidence intervals for its estimates are generally larger than those of an unweighted simple random sample of the same size, and expresses this through the design factor, the ratio of the two standard errors.
has description in the module Each respondent counts in proportion to the survey weight, which corrects for unequal selection, non-response and the population profile, so the prevalence is the weighted share of respondents with the condition, the sum over respondents i of w_i y_i divided by the sum of w_i, with y_i equal to 1 for a respondent with the condition and 0 otherwise. When respondents in a weighting class share one weight, the sum reduces to the class form below; three classes are written out so that the calculator can run, and SUMPRODUCT in Excel takes any number. The formula gives the point estimate only: its standard error needs the strata and primary sampling units of the design.

Survival and life-years in one interval of a piecewise bathtub hazard

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000350
Type formula
assumes Hazard constant between bathtub cut points, One clock from the procedure for every bathtub interval
has calculator text S_j = S_prev * exp(-h_j * L_j); A_j = S_prev * (1 - exp(-h_j * L_j)) / h_j
has common error note Bathtub interval life-years taken as length times starting survival. Multiplying the interval length by survival at its start ignores the deaths during the interval. For three months to five years, 4.75 × 0.904837 = 4.297976 life-years against 3.825707, an overstatement of about 0.47 life-years in a single interval.
Hazard times interval length used as a bathtub interval probability. Treating h_j L_j as the probability of dying in the interval fails for long intervals or high hazards. From five to fifteen years, 0.08 × 10 = 0.8 would leave only a fifth of the survivors alive, whereas the exponential factor exp(-0.8) leaves about 0.4493. The conversion on the Transition Probability page (HE-FM-TP-001) applies.
has description in the module For an interval of length L_j with constant hazard h_j, survival at the end of the interval is survival at its start multiplied by exp(-h_j L_j), and the expected life-years lived in the interval per person entering the cohort are the area under the survival curve across the interval. Chaining intervals with a high early hazard, a low middle hazard and higher late hazards reproduces a bathtub shape exactly, without fitting a single distribution. The function exp is the exponential function.

has calculator text R_j = abs(Y_jU - Y_jL)
has common error note Ranking ICER bars when effects approach zero. When incremental effects approach zero or change sign at an endpoint, the ICER becomes unstable or changes meaning, and its swing misranks inputs. Incremental net monetary benefit keeps a consistent meaning across endpoints.
Reading bar width as precision of the estimate. A wide bar does not show that a parameter is poorly estimated, and a narrow bar does not show that it is known precisely, because the width combines the model's sensitivity with the chosen range.
Treating one-way results as joint uncertainty. One-way analysis holds every other input fixed, so it ignores correlation and interaction and gives no probability of cost-effectiveness. In the Quintavel model, setting baseline risk and relative risk to their unfavourable endpoints together gives an ICER of £66,000 per QALY, which no single bar shows.
has description in the module Takes the absolute difference between the model outputs at the lower and upper values of input j, each run with all other inputs at their base-case values. The swing is the width of the input's bar in a tornado diagram, and bars are ordered with the widest at the top.

Swing-weighted additive value of a technology on three MCDA criteria

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000930
Type formula
assumes Preference independence of criteria in the additive MCDA value, Positive total of swing points in the MCDA weights, Non-overlapping MCDA criteria without double counting, Swing points judged over the ranges of the partial value scores
has calculator text w_1 = p_1 / (p_1 + p_2 + p_3); w_2 = p_2 / (p_1 + p_2 + p_3); w_3 = p_3 / (p_1 + p_2 + p_3); V = w_1 * v_1 + w_2 * v_2 + w_3 * v_3
has common error note Additive MCDA value for a technology with no health gain. Technology C in the article has no health gain and still scores 50, because severity and strength of evidence earn value on their own, and it ranks first whenever the health gain weight is below 2/7, scoring 75 against A's 71.25 at a weight of 0.25. The second ISPOR report describes this counterintuitive result as the effect of an additive model when health gain and severity interact.
Changing an MCDA criterion range without new swing points. Widening the health gain range to 0 to 1.6 QALYs halves the health gain scores to 37.5 for A and 25 for B. Kept at 0.50, the old weight then gives A 53.75, B 52.5 and C 50 in place of 72.5, 65 and 50 (computed here for illustration), although a swing of 1.6 QALYs would be judged worth more points than a swing of 0.8. The second ISPOR report ties weights that act as scaling constants to elicitation over the range of performance, so a new range needs new points.
Cost per MCDA value point read as relative efficiency. Dividing cost by overall value, GBP 18,000 by 72.5 for A and GBP 8,000 by 65 for B, gives about GBP 248 and GBP 123 per point, the ratio form of HE-FM-ACER-001. The totals are on an interval scale. Adding 20 to every partial value, as if the bottom of each range scored 20, adds 20 to every total because the weights sum to one (derived), and gives GBP 194.59 and GBP 94.12 per point, so the ratio of the two figures becomes 2.07 in place of 2.02 with no change in either technology (computed here for illustration). The second ISPOR report states that a cost-benefit ratio needs benefits measured on a ratio scale.
has description in the module Divides each criterion's swing points by the total points to give weights that sum to one, then multiplies each partial value score by its criterion's weight and adds the three products, the additive (weighted-sum) model that both ISPOR MCDA task force reports describe as the usual aggregation in health care. With partial values on a 0 to 100 scale the overall value is on the same scale. The weights act as scaling constants for the ranges over which the swings were judged, so a change of range calls for new points. The formula is written for three criteria, the article's health gain, severity and strength of evidence; more criteria add terms in the same way, and HE-CF-MCDH-001 applies it to several technologies.

Symmetric first-price equilibrium bid and expected winning bid in a reverse auction with uniform costs

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000951
Type formula
assumes Procurement bid derived from the printed selling bid by mirroring the cost range
Symmetric risk-neutral equilibrium in a first-price tender with uniform costs
Single winner paid its own bid with at least two bidders and no binding ceiling
has calculator text b = c + (c_high - c) / N; E_c1 = c_low + (c_high - c_low) / (N + 1); E_b = E_c1 + (c_high - E_c1) / N
has common error note Bid shading spread over the whole cost range. The margin a supplier adds depends on how far its own cost lies below c_high, (c_high minus c) / N, not on the full range. Adding (c_high minus c_low) / N gives the 2.60 supplier a bid of 3.60 in place of 3.40 and an expected winning bid of 3.75 in place of 3.50, breaking revenue equivalence (computed here).
First-price bids assumed equal to suppliers' costs. Bidding cost is dominant only under the second-price rule. Assuming that a pay-as-bid tender attracts bids at cost puts the expected price at the expected lowest cost, 2.75 per pack in the article's example, in place of 3.50, the same understatement of GBP 750,000 on 1,000,000 packs as HE-ER-AUCT-002 (computed here).
One tender's winning bid read as a test of revenue equivalence. Revenue equivalence concerns expected prices. In the article's draw the first-price rule pays 3.40 and the second-price rule 3.20, a gap of 0.20 in one tender, while both expected prices are 3.50, so a single tender, or a few, cannot show which rule is cheaper (computed here).
has description in the module Under the first-price rule the lowest bidder wins and is paid its own bid, so a supplier bids above its cost, trading a higher price on winning against a lower chance of winning. With N suppliers whose costs are independent and uniform on the interval [c_low, c_high], the symmetric equilibrium bid adds to the supplier's cost c the expected gap to the lowest of the other N minus 1 costs, given that they all exceed c, which is (c_high minus c) / N. Klemperer prints the selling form, a bid of v_low + ((n minus 1) / n) (v minus v_low); the procurement form is derived by mirroring each cost to the value c_low + c_high minus c on the same range and checked here by a best-response search and by simulation. Because the bid is linear in cost, the expected winning bid is the bid at the expected lowest cost E_c1 of HE-FM-AUCT-001 (derived), and it equals that formula's expected price E_p, revenue equivalence for this case.

Section 5 (Risk Aversion) states that risk aversion makes bidders bid more aggressively in first-price auctions. Symmetric Nash equilibrium use of a shared resource by N users and the share of its rent dissipated

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000948
Type formula
assumes Identical users whose use lowers the value of every unit by the same amount
Independent one-shot choices by selfish users with an interior equilibrium
One period with no benefit of use to non-users
has calculator text q_E = (a - c) / (k * (N + 1)); Q_E = N * q_E; v_E = a - c - k * Q_E; V_E = Q_E * v_E; Q_s = (a - c) / (2 * k); V_s = Q_s * (a - c - k * Q_s); d_E = 1 - V_E / V_s
has common error note Dropping each user's own share of the loss from the first-order condition. A user who takes the value of a course as fixed sets a less c less k Q to zero, the average-return behaviour of the rent dissipation literature, and the total becomes (a less c) / k for every N, the open-access limit Q_0 of HE-FM-PIGT-001 with b equal to k. In the article's example it gives 8,000 courses and a rent of zero for four prescribers instead of 6,400 courses and 102,400 pounds (derived). The full open-access loss holds only as N grows.
Measuring dissipation on gross yield rather than net value. Delaney and Jacobson define gross efficiency on the yield of the resource, which leaves out the opportunity cost of use, and note that it equals net efficiency in their experiment because the outside return is set to zero. With the article's values the gross yield is 240,000 pounds at the optimum and 230,400 pounds at the equilibrium, a loss of 4%, while the net rent falls by 36% (derived). The share d_E uses net values, as the article does.
Reading every rise in antibiotic use as a loss to society. The formula counts only the loss of effectiveness from use and no benefit to anyone but the patient. Where treatment stops transmission, use protects others, and Porco and colleagues found that more antibiotic use benefits society in some circumstances, so the predicted overuse and dissipated share hold only when the external effect of use is a cost, as assumed in HE-AS-TOTC-003.
has description in the module Each of N identical users chooses q_i to maximise q_i (a less c less k Q), where Q is the use of all users together. Setting the derivative to zero gives a less c less k Q less k q_i equal to zero, and with identical users the unique equilibrium gives each user (a less c) / (k (N + 1)), the result Falk, Fehr and Fischbacher state as Proposition 1. The chain then gives total use, the net value of each unit at that use and the rent V_E, the net value to the group. Q_s is the joint optimum, the efficient quantity of HE-FM-PIGT-001 with b and g equal to k and m equal to zero (also the equilibrium at N = 1), V_s the rent it yields, (a less c) squared / (4k), which equals the open-access deadweight loss of HE-FM-PIGT-002 with the same b, g and m (derived), and d_E the share of V_s lost at the equilibrium, which equals ((N less 1) / (N + 1)) squared (derived, checked on a grid). Use rises and the rent falls as users are added, and the rent tends to zero as N grows, the open-access outcome.

Working paper, March 2015 (read in full); published as Environmental and Resource Economics. 2016;65(4):747-772. doi:10.1007/s10640-015-9923-z (published version not seen). Section 2.1, A common pool resource appropriation game, sets each agent's payoff as alpha times unused tokens plus (beta less gamma times total extraction) times own extraction, states that it is mathematically identical to the payoff of Ostrom and colleagues (1994), and gives the symmetric Nash equilibrium (beta less alpha) / ((n + 1) gamma) and social optimum (beta less alpha) / (2 n gamma) per agent, equal only for n = 1 or beta at or below alpha. The Reviewers' Appendix derives both from the first-order conditions. https://web.williams.edu/Economics/wp/DelaneyJacobson_PaymentsOrPersuasion.pdf
Falk A, Fehr E, Fischbacher U. Appropriating the Commons: A Theoretical Explanation. Chapter 5 in National Research Council. The Drama of the Commons. Washington, DC, The National Academies Press; 2002. doi:10.17226/10287 (chapter read in the publisher's online edition). The section The Standard Common-Pool Resource Game (pages 164 and 165) states Proposition 1 (Selfish Nash Equilibrium), that with purely selfish preferences the unique Nash equilibrium is symmetric with individual appropriation a / (b (n + 1)), for payoffs written e plus a x_i less b x_i times total appropriation after the unit cost is netted out, and gives 8 per player, a total of 64 and a social optimum of 36 for eight players with the Walker and colleagues revenue 23 times total tokens less 0.25 times its square and a cost of 5. The Appendix to Chapter 5 (pages 185 and 186) derives the best reply, the total n a / (b (n + 1)) and the social optimum a / (2b). The records write their a as a less c. https://www.nationalacademies.org/read/10287/chapter/7

Workshop in Political Theory and Policy Analysis working paper W88-7, Indiana University, September 1988 (read in full in the Digital Library of the Commons). Its introduction traces the rent dissipation hypothesis to Gordon (1954). Section III, Theoretical Predictions, contrasts group optimality (maximum rents, where marginal revenue product equals marginal cost), the Nash equilibrium and complete rent dissipation (where average revenue product equals marginal cost), and prints the payoff of eight players with a revenue of 25 times total tokens less 0.3 times its square and an outside return of 5. Its pure-strategy Nash equilibria total 59 tokens and earn approximately 41% of the rents possible, against 33 tokens for maximum rents and 67 for zero rents. The continuous equilibrium of HE-FM-TOTC-001 gives 59.3 tokens and keeps 39.5% (derived). https://dlc.dlib.indiana.edu/dlc/items/a2bc4d30-01b6-4646-b673-4c405465dbac

Thall and Wathen response-adaptive allocation probability

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000486
Type formula
assumes Two arms with outcomes observed quickly, Stable patient population and standard of care over recruitment
has calculator text pi_E = P^c / (P^c + (1 - P)^c)
has common error note Reading the allocation probability as the probability that the treatment is better. An allocation probability of 0.770 comes from a posterior probability of 0.918 shrunk towards one half by c. It is a design choice, not an estimate of benefit, and unequal arms leave fewer control patients for the costs and utilities an economic model needs.
Using Thompson sampling without regard to allocation variability. With c of 1 allocation follows every swing in the posterior. In the simulations reported by Robertson and colleagues, Thompson sampling with 200 patients had about a 14% chance of a sample size imbalance of more than 10% of the total in the wrong direction, and the Thall and Wathen rule reduced it.
has description in the module Sets the probability that the next patient is allocated to the experimental arm from the current posterior probability that the experimental arm has the higher success rate. The tuning constant c controls how hard allocation follows the posterior: c of 0 gives equal randomisation, c of 1 gives Thompson sampling, and one half, or a value rising with the number enrolled such as i / (2n), has been suggested to reduce the variability of allocation.

Three-state occupancy from PFS and OS curves in a partitioned survival model

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000587
Type formula
assumes PFS and OS from the same arm and time origin, Forward-only movement through the partitioned states
has calculator text P_PF = S_PFS; P_PD = S_OS - S_PFS; P_D = 1 - S_OS
has common error note Separately extrapolated PFS curve crossing above OS. Because PFS and OS are fitted and extrapolated independently, the PFS curve can rise above OS, implying more people progression-free than alive. With an extrapolated PFS hazard of 0.4 and an OS hazard of 0.5 a year, PFS at one year is about 0.670 against OS of about 0.607, and the progressed share is about minus 0.064. TSD 19 reports that the adjustment used to avoid this in TA295 was criticised by the ERG and not accepted by the committee.
Setting OS equal to PFS in probabilistic draws where the curves cross. Most appraisals reviewed in TSD 19 sampled PFS and OS independently in probabilistic sensitivity analysis, so some draws can cross even when the base case does not. In TA285 the company set OS equal to PFS in those simulations, an approach the ERG considered inappropriate. Doing so hides the inconsistency and does not model the correlation between endpoints.
has description in the module Gives the proportions progression-free, progressed and dead at time t from the PFS and OS survival functions of one treatment arm. The PFS curve gives the progression-free share directly, the dead share is 1 minus OS, and the progressed share is the gap between the two curves. Each arm has its own pair of curves.

Threshold range in which a frontier strategy has the highest net monetary benefit

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000665
Type formula
assumes Neighbours taken from the finished cost-effectiveness frontier, End strategies of the cost-effectiveness frontier, Expected values for one population on the frontier
has calculator text lambda_in = (C_k - C_i) / (Q_k - Q_i); lambda_out = (C_j - C_k) / (Q_j - Q_k); best = (lambda >= lambda_in) and (lambda <= lambda_out)
has common error note Applying the largest-ICER rule before extended dominance is removed. With R2 removed but R3 still in the list, the ratios in cost order are GBP 20,000, 50,000, 10,000 and 60,000 per QALY. At GBP 35,000 the largest ratio not above the value is R1's GBP 20,000, so the rule picks R1 instead of R4 and gives up GBP 1,000 per person (computed here for illustration from the article's table). The rule holds only on a finished frontier whose ratios rise.
Reading the frontier choice from ratios against usual care. Against usual care alone R3 has a ratio of GBP 35,000 per QALY, which could look acceptable at GBP 35,000, yet its range is empty and the choice at that value is R4. Choosing R3 there gives up GBP 2,500 per person of net monetary benefit, GBP 173,000 against GBP 175,500.
has description in the module For a frontier strategy k whose neighbours on the frontier are i, the next less effective, and j, the next more effective, k has the highest net monetary benefit for every λ at or above lambda_in, the slope of the segment entering it, and at or below lambda_out, the slope of the segment leaving it. Both slopes are sequential ICERs (HE-FM-CEA-001), so the strategy chosen at λ is the frontier strategy with the largest ICER not above λ, the decision rule stated by Suen and Goldhaber-Fiebert, and it is the same strategy that HE-FM-NMB-003 selects. The slopes are the switching values at which two neighbours tie. For a middle strategy that is not on the frontier the range is empty, because lambda_in exceeds lambda_out exactly when D_M of HE-FM-EXD-001 is positive.

Some sources define the acceleration factor as the reciprocal of the time ratio, writing S(t) as S_0 of the factor times t. A published value of 1.5 on one definition is about 0.667 on the other, so the definition is checked before the estimate is used.
Reading a time ratio as a hazard ratio. A time ratio of 1.50 means longer survival times, whereas a hazard ratio of 1.50 means a higher hazard and shorter survival. The two are linked only through a fitted distribution, and for log-logistic and log-normal models no single hazard ratio exists.

Time trade-off utility of a chronic state under the linear QALY model

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000908
Type formula
assumes Linear QALY model behind the time trade-off rule
Chronic state judged at least as good as immediate death
One respondent's value and the public valuation in the NICE reference case
has calculator text U_TTO = T_y / T_x
has common error note Applying the time trade-off ratio to a state judged worse than dead. A respondent who prefers immediate death to T_x years in the state has no T_y of zero or more that makes the two sides equal, so T_y over T_x cannot fall below 0 and the ratio stops at 0 (derived). Values below 0, which the live HE-VR-QALY-001 allows for states worse than dead, need a task framed for states worse than death, whose use Torrance describes, and no formula for that case is given here.
Mixing standard gamble and time trade-off utilities in one comparison. Morimoto and Fukui report a strong tendency for the standard gamble to give the highest values of the three methods they review. In the review of 32 studies by Arnold and colleagues the mean values were 0.81 across the cases valued by standard gamble and 0.77 across those valued by time trade-off, and PMG36 section 4.3.5 states that results from different methods or instruments cannot always be compared. Valuing the same state at 0.81 for one option and 0.77 for its comparator over 5 years creates a difference of 0.20 QALYs that no treatment produced (illustrative, derived).
Recording the share of time given up as the time trade-off utility. The share of life given up, T_x minus T_y over T_x, is one minus U_TTO. In the first worked example it is 0.25, so recording it as the utility values a state the respondent rated at 0.75 at a third of that value (derived).
has description in the module The time trade-off utility is the ratio of the years in full health T_y to the years in the state T_x that the respondent judges equal. The rule follows from the indifference once full health is valued at 1, immediate death at 0 and utility of life duration is linear in years, as Lipman, Brouwer and Attema set out, and it gives one respondent's value for one state judged at least as good as immediate death. The standard gamble asked about the same state gives the indifference probability itself as the utility (HE-FN-UTIL-001), and the two methods tend to give different values (HE-ER-UTIL-001).

Tipping-point shift for QALYs lost to follow-up at a cost-effectiveness threshold

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000747
Type formula
assumes Additive shift on imputed QALYs of those lost to follow-up
Incremental cost unchanged by the loss to follow-up shift
Positive denominator and the tie at the loss to follow-up tipping point
has calculator text H_d = Delta_C / lambda; delta_star = (H_d - Delta_E_obs) / (p_T - r * p_C)
has common error note Agreement of complete case and multiple imputation read as robustness to loss to follow-up. Running complete case analysis as the base case and multiple imputation as a sensitivity analysis, or the reverse, and finding the same conclusion does not show that the result holds under loss to follow-up that is missing not at random. Leurent, Gomes and Carpenter call this misleading because both methods rely on missingness being independent of the unobserved data. In the article's example, where the missing QALYs are taken to resemble the observed ones, both give a gain of 0.10, while the conclusion at GBP 20,000 per QALY changes once those lost from the new treatment arm are worse off by more than 0.125 QALYs.
Common-shift tipping point quoted for loss to follow-up confined to one arm. With 20% lost from the new treatment arm and 10% from usual care, a shift common to both arms moves the gain by only 0.1 times the shift, so its tipping point is -0.25, twice as far from zero as the -0.125 for a shift confined to the new treatment arm. Quoting -0.25 when those who leave the new treatment arm may be worse off because of side effects overstates how far the conclusion can be trusted. With equal shares lost a common shift has no tipping point, which says nothing about a shift in one arm. Leurent and colleagues found that departures assumed the same in both arms had little effect on incremental QALYs, which they expect when the missing data pattern is broadly similar across arms, so that the bias applies roughly equally to each arm and cancels out in the comparison, while arm-specific departures changed the conclusion.
QALY gain shortfall reported as the tipping-point shift for those lost to follow-up. In the article's example the gain must fall from 0.10 to 0.075 for the ICER to reach GBP 20,000 per QALY, a shortfall of 0.025, but only the 20% of the new treatment arm lost to follow-up are shifted, so those lost must be worse off by 0.025 / 0.2 = 0.125 QALYs. Reporting 0.025 as the tipping point understates the shift the conclusion withstands by a factor of 1 / p_T, five here. The shift is a difference in mean QALYs for the people lost, while the shortfall is a difference in the arm mean over everyone randomised.
has description in the module Sets the delta-adjusted QALY gain equal to the gain needed at threshold lambda, H_d = Delta_C / lambda (HE-FM-CET-002), and solves for the shift. With a shift delta for those lost from the new treatment arm and r times delta for those lost from usual care, the gain is Delta_E_obs plus (p_T minus r times p_C) times delta (HE-FM-LOCF-002 read as in HE-FN-LTFU-001), so the tipping-point shift is H_d minus Delta_E_obs, divided by p_T minus r times p_C (derived). Setting r = 0 confines the shift to the new treatment arm and gives the article's delta_star = (Delta_C / lambda minus Delta_E_obs) / p_T, and r = 1 applies the same shift to both arms, when only the difference in the proportions lost moves the gain. A negative delta_star is a QALY shortfall for those lost that the base case can absorb. When the denominator is positive the base-case conclusion holds for every shift that lies on the same side of delta_star as zero.

has module record identifier HE-FM-LTFU-001
has source in the module Faria R, Gomes M, Epstein D, White IR. A guide to handling missing data in cost-effectiveness analysis conducted within randomised controlled trials. PharmacoEconomics. 2014;32(12):1157-1170. Section 5, Stage 3, Sensitivity Analysis to the Missing at Random (MAR) Assumption, states that under the pattern mixture approach data are first imputed under MAR, the imputed values are shifted by a sensitivity parameter, the analysis is repeated for a range of plausible values, and either a range of results or the value of the sensitivity parameter required to change the results is reported. Section 6.3 applies the approach to the REFLUX study and finds that the probability of cost-effectiveness changes considerably only when the QALYs of those with missing data in the surgery arm alone are reduced. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40273-014-0193-3
Leurent B, Gomes M, Carpenter JR. Missing data in trial-based cost-effectiveness analysis: an incomplete journey. Health Economics. 2018;27(6):1024-1040. Section 4.3, Recommendations, states that many reviewed studies used complete case analysis for the primary analysis and multiple imputation as a sensitivity analysis, or the reverse, and concluded that the results were robust to missing data, and calls this misleading because both methods rely on the assumption that the missingness is independent of the unobserved data. Section 4.1, Summary of findings, reports that only two studies (4%) assessed whether conclusions were sensitive to departures from missing at random. https://doi.org/10.1002/hec.3654
Leurent B, Gomes M, Faria R, Morris S, Grieve R, Carpenter JR. Sensitivity analysis for not-at-random missing data in trial-based cost-effectiveness analysis: a tutorial. PharmacoEconomics. 2018;36(8):889-901. Section 2.3, Sensitivity Analysis with Pattern-Mixture Models, describes an offset parameter delta as the average difference between the missing and observed values, Y_miss = Y_obs + delta, and the steps of imputing under missing at random, modifying the imputed values by adding delta or multiplying by a scale parameter, and combining the analyses with Rubin's rules. Section 4.3, Choosing the MNAR Parameters, describes the tipping-point or threshold analysis as changing the MNAR parameter until a different conclusion is reached, such as being or not being cost-effective. Section 4.1, Missing Cost, extends the shifts to missing costs. The Results of the illustrative application state that departures assumed the same in both arms had little effect on incremental QALYs, which will usually be the case when the missing data pattern is broadly similar across arms, as the bias applies roughly equally to each arm and cancels out in the comparison. The closed form for the tipping-point shift is derived from these statements, not printed in the paper. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40273-018-0650-5

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000242
Type formula
assumes Quantities and unit costs on the same basis, Resources identified within the stated perspective, Unit costs reflect opportunity cost
definition source the Source rows of the Functions and Formulae module record HE-FM-COST-001
formalises resource valuation, unit cost valuation process, cost aggregation process
has calculator text C = sum_(i=1)^n [q_i * p_i]
has common error note Charges or list prices used as unit costs. A charge, tariff or list price reflects negotiation and cross-subsidy and can sit well above or below the resources used. The NICE manual asks for prices that reflect as closely as possible those paid in the NHS.
Overheads counted twice. Adding a separate overhead line to a unit cost that already includes overheads, such as a national average cost per healthcare resource group, counts the same resources twice.
Staff time and unit cost in different units. Multiplying 90 minutes of nurse time by an hourly cost of 60 pounds gives 5,400 pounds instead of 90. Quantities and unit costs are converted to the same unit before they are multiplied.

Total health forgone for equity between a health-maximising and a fairer option

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000668
Type formula
assumes Net gains after the displaced health in each group
Population shares sum to one and gains are per person
Two options of equal cost from one budget in the health forgone for equity
has calculator text H_max = s_worse * g_worse_max + s_better * g_better_max; H_fair = s_worse * g_worse_fair + s_better * g_better_fair; H_forgone = H_max - H_fair; f_forgone = H_forgone / H_max
has common error note Averaging group gains without population shares. Taking the simple average of the two groups' gains gives 0.35 years for E and 0.375 for F, so F appears to gain 0.025 years more and the trade-off disappears. With the 40% and 60% shares E leads by 0.05 years per person.
Reading the switching weight as removing the health forgone. A weight on the worse-off group above the switching weight of 1.3125 from HE-FM-WE-004 changes the ranking but not the health outcome. Choosing F still gives up 0.05 years per person of total health, which is why the article recommends reporting weighted results beside the unweighted ones.
Stating the share forgone on gross gains. Using gains before the 0.10 years of displaced health gives mean gains of 0.50 and 0.45 years. The difference is still 0.05 because both options displace the same health, but the share forgone falls to one-tenth instead of one-eighth, understating the cost of equity relative to what E delivers.
has description in the module Gives the mean net health gain per person of each option as the population-share weighted sum of the two groups' net gains, and the health forgone for equity as the gain of the health-maximising option less the gain of the fairer option. Asaria and colleagues call this difference in total health the health opportunity cost of choosing the option that reduces inequality, and Cookson and colleagues describe counting it as equity constraint analysis. The share f_forgone expresses the same loss as a fraction of the health-maximising option's net gain. A positive H_forgone means a trade-off exists, and a value of zero or below means the fairer option costs no health.

Transition probability rescaled to a new cycle length

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000216
Type formula
assumes Constant hazard across both intervals, Two-state transition only
definition source Fleurence and Hollenbeak 2007; the Source rows of the Functions and Formulae module record HE-FM-TP-003
formalises probability estimate
has calculator text p_new = 1 - (1 - p_old)^(Delta_new / Delta_old)
has common error note Dividing an annual probability by 12. Dividing 0.20 by 12 gives a monthly probability of about 0.01667. Applied for 12 months it implies an annual probability of about 0.1826 rather than 0.20, so the model understates the event. The error grows with the size of the probability.
Rescaling each exit of a multi-exit state separately. In a state with more than one exit, rescaling each destination probability separately with this formula gives a row that no longer reproduces the source data. In the article's example with annual exit probabilities of about 0.10876 and 0.07251, separate rescaling to three months keeps about 0.8248 of the cohort in the starting state after four cycles rather than 0.8187.

Treatment effect at a chosen covariate value from a centred meta-regression

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000629
Type formula
assumes Covariate centred on the scale of the linear predictor
Decision population inside the covariate range of the trials
One interaction term common to all treatments in a network meta-regression
has calculator text theta_z = d + b * (z - x_bar)
has common error note Adopting an adjusted effect as the base case without a pre-specified interaction. With few trials and one covariate, an effect adjusted by meta-regression would normally be a scenario unless the interaction was pre-specified, plausible and precise. NICE asks whether the relative effect is constant over baseline risks when the model's comparator event rate differs greatly from those in the meta-analysis.
Entering the baseline risk instead of its log-odds. Using z as 0.05 rather than the log-odds of -2.944 gives an adjusted log odds ratio of 0.125, an odds ratio of about 1.13, which reverses the direction of the effect. The covariate value has to be on the scale on which the model was fitted.
Using the centred effect with an uncentred covariate value. Adding b times z to d without subtracting x_bar gives a log odds ratio of about -1.283 for a 5% risk, an odds ratio of about 0.277 instead of 0.462, which overstates the benefit in the decision model.
has description in the module TSD 3 centres the covariate at its mean, so the fitted effect d applies at the mean covariate value x_bar, and the effect at any other value z is recovered by un-centring. A decision model uses it to take the relative effect for its own population, for example its baseline risk, instead of the average over the trials.

Treatment survival from a baseline curve under proportional hazards

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000220
Type formula
assumes Proportional hazards from the origin to t, Same population, time origin and event
has calculator text S_T = S_C^HR
has common error note Applying one hazard ratio after proportional hazards has failed. When hazards cross, or the treatment effect wanes or is delayed, a single ratio applied over a lifetime horizon can misstate both the size and the timing of benefit. TSD 14 advises testing the assumption and, if it fails, fitting separate parametric models of the same type to each arm or allowing the hazard ratio to vary over time.
Multiplying the survival probability by the hazard ratio. Multiplying 0.81873 by 0.70 gives about 0.5731, which would imply that treatment lowers survival. The ratio acts on the cumulative hazard, so it enters as a power of the survival probability.
has description in the module Applies a constant hazard ratio to the comparator survival probability at time t to give the treatment survival probability at the same time. It follows because the cumulative hazard of the treatment group is HR times that of the comparator. The comparator curve supplies the absolute level; the ratio alone cannot.

has calculator text ibar_1 = (INB_11 + INB_12) / J; ibar_2 = (INB_21 + INB_22) / J; EVPPI_2L = (max(ibar_1, 0) + max(ibar_2, 0)) / K - max((ibar_1 + ibar_2) / K, 0)
has common error note Inner draws from the marginal distribution when parameters are correlated. When theta_c is correlated with theta_i, drawing the inner values from the marginal distribution of theta_c ignores what each value of theta_i implies for them, so the inner means and the estimate are wrong. Strong, Oakley and Brennan describe this conditional sampling as a limitation of the two-level method, and the regression estimator HE-FM-EVPP-003 needs only the joint sample.
Inner loop too small for the nested EVPPI estimator. In the first case study of Strong, Oakley and Brennan, 1,000 outer by 10 inner runs gave GBP 351.92 for their parameter set 1 against a reference value of GBP 247.95, with an estimated upward bias of GBP 130.69. In the article's example a single inner run for each draw of A returns the EVPI of GBP 600 in place of the EVPPI for A of GBP 550. An estimate above the EVPI is a sign of Monte Carlo error, not a finding.

has description in the module Draws K values of the parameters of interest theta_i in an outer loop and, for each, J values of the remaining parameters theta_c in an inner loop, averages the incremental net benefit of the new option over the inner draws and keeps the larger of that mean and zero, the value of standard care. The average of the K kept values, less the larger of zero and the mean of the inner means, estimates EVPPI for theta_i, the double-loop scheme of Brennan, Kharroubi, O'Hagan and Chilcott and of Algorithm 2 in the second ISPOR report. The calculator form is written for K = 2 outer and J = 2 inner draws, with INB_kj the run at outer draw k and inner draw j; larger loops add terms in the same pattern, as the Excel and the Computational Function do. With more than two options the maximum is taken over the inner means of every option, and Strong, Oakley and Brennan note that the value is unchanged when net benefits are expressed relative to a baseline option. When theta_i holds every parameter the inner runs at each outer draw are identical and the estimator becomes the per-person EVPI of HE-FM-VOI-001.

Two-option CEAC at one threshold

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000202
Type formula
assumes Paired incremental results from one probabilistic analysis, Probability conditional on the represented uncertainty, Sign of incremental net monetary benefit classifies each draw
has calculator text CEAC = (1/N) * sum_(i=1)^N [1(lambda * Delta_E_i - Delta_C_i > 0)]
has common error note Classifying draws by ICER below the threshold. Counting a draw as cost-effective when its ratio lies below lambda misclassifies north-west draws, where a negative ratio means the intervention is dominated, and south-west draws, where the intervention is favoured only when the ratio exceeds lambda. In the first worked example the fifth draw, at £60,000 per QALY forgone, would be counted against the intervention and the CEAC would fall from 0.6 to 0.4.
Reading the CEAC as a probability of clinical benefit. A CEAC of 0.6 is the share of simulations with positive incremental net monetary benefit at one threshold. It is not the probability that the intervention improves health or saves money, and it says nothing about the size of the gain or loss in either group of simulations.
Treating the CEAC as a significance test. Requiring the curve to exceed 0.95 before adoption imposes a statistical convention on a decision problem. The adoption decision rests on expected net benefit, and the spread of net benefit bears on whether further evidence is worth acquiring.
has description in the module Counts the probabilistic simulations in which the intervention has positive incremental net monetary benefit at threshold lambda and divides the count by the number of simulations. The indicator 1(condition) equals 1 when the condition holds and 0 otherwise. Apart from exact ties, the comparator's value is the complement.

Two-option error probability as half the two-sided p-value of incremental net benefit

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000724
Type formula
assumes Symmetric test statistic for halving the two-sided p-value, Two options and a probability reading of the p-value
has calculator text P_error_p = p_two / 2
has common error note One-sample p-value of probabilistic draws read as the decision uncertainty error probability. Halving the p-value of a one-sample test of the mean of 1,000 probabilistic draws, with an illustrative mean incremental net benefit of GBP 1,000 and standard deviation of GBP 2,000, uses the standard error of the mean, about GBP 63.25, so z is about 15.81 and the error probability comes out at about 0. The spread of the draws gives about 0.30854, the upper normal tail at 1,000 divided by 2,000 (HE-FM-AN-004 read through HE-FM-CEAC-003, computed here for illustration). The p-value measures the Monte Carlo precision of the mean and falls as more draws are run, while the decision uncertainty stays the same. The halved p-value applies to a test whose standard error describes the uncertainty about incremental net benefit itself, such as a trial-based net benefit regression.
Sign of the estimate ignored when reading the p-value. Taking one minus the one-sided p-value as the error probability gives about 0.772 at GBP 30,000 per QALY, the probability that adopting is right. When the estimate is negative the new option is rejected and the error probability is still the one-sided p-value, the probability that the new option is cost-effective.
Two-sided p-value reported as the error probability. Reporting the two-sided p-value of about 0.456 at GBP 30,000 per QALY as the error probability doubles it, since the choice is wrong only when net benefit lies on the other side of zero, a probability of about 0.228.
has description in the module In a two-option comparison analysed by a test of incremental net benefit at a stated threshold, such as net benefit regression, the expected-value choice follows the sign of the estimate. Hoch and colleagues state that the probability that the new treatment is cost-effective is the one-sided p-value when the estimate is negative and one minus the one-sided p-value when it is positive, so in both cases the probability that the choice is wrong is the one-sided p-value, half the two-sided p-value that statistical software usually reports (derived from those statements). The result needs no normal distribution function. For a z test it equals the upper normal tail at the absolute statistic, which is the two-option normal error probability given by HE-FM-AN-004 read through HE-FM-CEAC-003 (derived). HE-ER-AN-007 covers the related slip of taking one minus the two-sided p-value as the probability that net benefit is positive.
has formalisation level catalogue record
has implementation Error probability from a two-sided p-value in one cell
has mathematical variable Error probability of the two-option choice from the p-value

has source in the module Hoch JS, Rockx MA, Krahn AD. Using the net benefit regression framework to construct cost-effectiveness acceptability curves, an example using data from a trial of external loop recorders versus Holter monitoring for ambulatory monitoring of community acquired syncope. BMC Health Services Research. 2006;6:68. Methods section, which states that regression programs report a two-sided p-value while a one-sided probability is needed, that it is converted by dividing by two, and that the probability that the new treatment is cost-effective is the one-sided p-value when the coefficient is negative and one minus it when the coefficient is positive. The same section states that the p-value of a parametric analysis is derived from a distributional assumption and that non-parametric methods like bootstrapping may offer better alternatives, and the Discussion states that a CEAC indicates a 50% chance of cost-effectiveness when the threshold equals the sample estimate of the ICER. That the error probability is the one-sided p-value in both cases, and 0.5 at the ICER, is derived from these statements. https://doi.org/10.1186/1472-6963-6-68

HEMA Report 2. Health Economics Methods Advisory, 2026. Two-option EVPI for a normally distributed incremental net benefit

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000654
Type formula
assumes Normal distribution of incremental net benefit for closed-form EVPI
Exactly two options for the one-dimensional normal EVPI
Mean and standard deviation of incremental net benefit at one threshold
has calculator text z = abs(mu_INB) / sigma_INB; pdf_z = exp(-z^2 / 2) / 2.5066283; EVPI_N = sigma_INB * (pdf_z - z * (1 - cdf_z))
has common error note Applying the normal EVPI to three or more options. Running the closed form on each pairwise comparison and adding or taking the largest result does not give the EVPI of a choice among three options, because the best option in each state depends on all of them together.
Using the Monte Carlo standard error as the spread in normal EVPI. Dividing the standard deviation of the five illustrative draws, about 0.2168 QALYs, by the square root of 5 gives the standard error of their mean, about 0.0970, and an EVPI of about 0.0133 QALYs instead of 0.0560. sigma_INB measures the uncertainty about incremental net benefit, not the precision of the simulation.
Using the signed mean in the normal EVPI loss term. For a mean of minus GBP 1,000 and a standard deviation of GBP 2,000, using z equal to minus 0.5 in the loss term gives about GBP 1,395.59 instead of GBP 395.59, overstating EVPI by exactly the absolute mean. The loss term needs the absolute mean.
has description in the module When the incremental net benefit of the new option over its comparator is normal with mean mu_INB and standard deviation sigma_INB, EVPI has a closed form, sigma_INB times the unit normal loss integral at z, the absolute mean divided by the standard deviation. pdf_z is the standard normal density at z, computed in the formula, and cdf_z is the standard normal cumulative probability at z, which the site calculator cannot compute and so takes as an input from NORM.S.DIST or a table. The form needs no draws and has no Monte Carlo error. For a given sigma_INB the loss term is largest at z equal to zero, where EVPI is sigma_INB divided by the square root of 2 pi, about 0.3989 sigma_INB.

Two-option incremental cost-effectiveness ratio

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000192
Type formula
assumes One comparator and two mutually exclusive options, Consistent analytical basis for the ICER, Ratio of expected values, Positive incremental effect for threshold comparison, Quadrant identified before interpretation
definition source the Source rows of the Functions and Formulae module record HE-FM-ICER-001
formalises model result
has calculator text ICER = (C_1 - C_0) / (E_1 - E_0)
has common error note Averaging ICERs across simulations. The mean of ICERs from probabilistic simulations is not the ratio of mean incremental cost to mean incremental effect, and individual ratios become unstable when incremental effects are close to zero. The ICER is formed from expected values, and expected net benefit is used to compare options under uncertainty.
Comparing ICERs of non-adjacent options. With several mutually exclusive options, ICERs calculated against one common baseline, or between options that are not adjacent on the frontier, can make a dominated or extendedly dominated option look acceptable. The pairwise formula applies to adjacent options only after dominated options have been removed, which is the sequential ICER on the cost-effectiveness analysis page.
Ranking negative ICERs by size. A negative ICER arises both when the intervention dominates and when it is dominated, and its magnitude carries no ranking information: larger savings push the ratio towards minus infinity while larger health gains pull it towards zero.
Reading a south-west ratio as cost per unit gained. When incremental cost and incremental effect are both negative the ICER is positive, but it measures the saving per unit of effect forgone. A value below the threshold then favours the comparator, so applying the usual rule reverses the correct conclusion.

Two-parameter Cholesky step for a correlated pair of normal PSA draws

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000725
Type formula
assumes Joint normality of the correlated PSA pair on the scale of estimation
Correlation strictly inside minus 1 and 1 with a stated basis
One fresh pair of standard normal values per PSA draw shared by all options
has calculator text L_21 = rho * s_2; L_22 = s_2 * sqrt(1 - rho^2); x_1 = mu_1 + s_1 * z_1; x_2 = mu_2 + L_21 * z_1 + L_22 * z_2
has common error note Drawing jointly estimated parameters as if independent. Setting rho to zero for the illustrative log rate and log hazard ratio gives the log of the treated rate, their sum, a variance of 0.05 instead of 0.03 (derived), a standard deviation about 29% too large. For the inputs of the computational function below the same omission moves the exact expected incremental net health benefit (derived from the log-normal mean of HE-FM-EV-004) from about minus 0.072 to about minus 0.047 QALYs per person, because the model is not linear in the parameters.
Using an upper triangular Cholesky factor without transposing it. R's chol returns the upper triangular factor R with R transposed times R equal to the covariance matrix, and Owen warns that failing to transpose it is an error hard to detect from simulation output. For the illustrative inputs mu plus R z gives draws with standard deviations of about 0.1414 and 0.1732 instead of 0.10 and 0.20 and a correlation of about minus 0.71 instead of minus 0.5 (derived from R times R transposed). The factor used must be the lower triangular L with L times L transposed equal to the covariance matrix.
has description in the module Draws two parameters that were estimated together, such as the log of a baseline event rate and a log hazard ratio from one survival regression, so that their correlation rho is kept. Two independent standard normal values z_1 and z_2 are combined through the lower triangular Cholesky factor of the 2 by 2 covariance matrix, whose entries are s_1, L_21 and L_22. The first parameter uses z_1 alone and the second takes a share of z_1 through L_21, which carries the correlation, and the rest through L_22. By algebra (derived here from the factor) the drawn pair has standard deviations s_1 and s_2 and covariance rho s_1 s_2, because s_1 times L_21 equals rho s_1 s_2 and L_21 squared plus L_22 squared equals s_2 squared. With rho equal to zero the step reduces to two independent normal draws.
