https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000955
Type formula
assumes Catchment membership by a hard travel-time threshold in the two-step floating catchment area
One travel-time matrix for both steps and residents placed at one point per neighbourhood
Potential access with equal weight for every resident in the two-step floating catchment area
has calculator text R_X = S_X / ((d_1X <= d_0) * P_1 + (d_2X <= d_0) * P_2 + (d_3X <= d_0) * P_3); R_Y = S_Y / ((d_1Y <= d_0) * P_1 + (d_2Y <= d_0) * P_2 + (d_3Y <= d_0) * P_3); A_1 = (d_1X <= d_0) * R_X + (d_1Y <= d_0) * R_Y; A_2 = (d_2X <= d_0) * R_X + (d_2Y <= d_0) * R_Y; A_3 = (d_3X <= d_0) * R_X + (d_3Y <= d_0) * R_Y
has common error note Bordered GP-to-population ratios read as two-step floating catchment accessibility. Counting GPs inside each neighbourhood gives A 8.0, B 0 and C 6.667 per 10,000 in the article's example, which ranks B, with no practice, as worst served. The 2SFCA ranks B best at 4.205 per 10,000, because its residents reach both practices within 30 minutes, and lowers A and C because their practices also serve B. The bordered figure, a plain quotient of the form of HE-FM-ACR-001, ignores patients who cross area borders, the weakness Guagliardo describes for supply ratios.
Each practice's GPs divided by its own neighbourhood only in step one. Dividing X's 8 GPs by A's 10,000 people and Y's 4 GPs by C's 6,000 gives ratios of 8.0 and 6.667 per 10,000, and B, which reaches both, then scores 14.667. The scores weighted by population add up to 41.33 GPs where there are 12, a mean of 11.481 per 10,000 instead of 3.333 (computed here), because GPs who also serve B are counted again. The step one denominator is every population within d_0 of the practice.
Single threshold travel time treated as settled in the two-step floating catchment area. Moving the threshold to an illustrative 20 minutes in the article's example cuts B off from practice Y, so B scores 2.667 and C 6.667 per 10,000 instead of 4.205 and 1.538, and the order of B and C reverses (computed here). Luo and Wang ran seven thresholds of 20 to 50 minutes and found a smaller variance of the scores at larger thresholds, and Wang 2012 notes that the right catchment size cannot be settled without real utilisation data.
Zero two-step floating catchment area score read as residents getting no care. After the article's consolidation neighbourhood C scores 0 because practice X is 45 minutes away, yet its residents may still travel there. The article puts the extra travel at 60 minutes per visit, GBP 15 at an illustrative GBP 15 an hour and GBP 360,000 a year over 24,000 visits, the patient time cost of HE-FM-PTC-001. A zero reflects the hard threshold, and Guagliardo notes that a study of spatial potential could not demonstrate or disprove a relationship with use.
has description in the module Step one divides each practice's full-time-equivalent GPs by the population of the neighbourhoods within the threshold travel time d_0 of it, giving the practice's supply ratio. Step two gives each neighbourhood the sum of the supply ratios of the practices within d_0 of it. Each comparison such as (d_1X <= d_0) is 1 when the travel time is within the threshold and 0 otherwise, so a neighbourhood outside a practice's catchment adds nothing to its denominator and takes nothing from its ratio. The result is in GPs per head of population, and the article reports it per 10,000 people. Neighbourhoods A, B and C of the article are 1, 2 and 3 here; more practices or neighbourhoods add terms of the same pattern, which HE-CF-ACCS-001 computes for any number of sites.

Full text read (PMC394340), formula images included. Subsection Two-step floating catchment area of the section Recent developments, which describes the provider-to-population ratio of each provider's 30-minute drive-time catchment, the summing of the ratios of every catchment over each population point, results in provider-to-population units, the artificially sharp catchment borders, Luo and Wang's sensitivity analysis of 20 to 50 minute thresholds, their plan to adjust for transport options and their demonstration that the method is a special case of the Joseph and Bantock improved gravity model. Section Measuring spatial accessibility describes the border-crossing weakness of supply ratios, and section Defining access states that a study of spatial potential could not demonstrate or disprove a relationship of spatial accessibility with utilisation or population health. https://doi.org/10.1186/1476-072X-3-3

Section The Gravity-Based Method and a Synthesis states that the population-weighted average of accessibility equals the physician to population ratio of the whole study area and that this applies to equation (4). Wang F. Measurement, optimization, and impact of health care accessibility: a methodological review. Annals of the Association of American Geographers. 2012;102(5):1104-1112. Section Health Care Accessibility Measures Synthesized, equation (2) for the 2SFCA with R_j = S_j over the population within d_0, the statement that the method's major limitation is its dichotomous approach, equation (3) with a general distance decay f(d), the statement that the best decay function or catchment size cannot be settled without analysing real utilisation, and the separation of place accessibility from individual accessibility. Section Optimization Models in Health Care Accessibility states that the weighted mean of accessibility under equations 1 to 3 equals the ratio of total supply to total demand. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3547595/

Undiscounted age-weighted years of life lost per death with a modulation constant

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000686
Type formula
assumes Modulation constant fixed within one set of estimates
Undiscounted age-weighted years over a single span of standard years
has calculator text YLL_aw = K * C / beta^2 * ((1 + beta * a) * exp(-beta * a) - (1 + beta * (a + L)) * exp(-beta * (a + L))) + (1 - K) * L
has common error note Undiscounted age-weighted total treated as the standard GBD 1990 figure. The standard DALYs of the original GBD combined age weights with 3% discounting, so a death at 5 in the article's illustration counts 36.44 years (HE-FM-AGW-003), not 84.07. The undiscounted age-weighted value is a component for comparison, not the published convention.
Weight at the age of death applied to every year lost. Multiplying L by the weight at the age of death, W(a) times L, ignores that the lost years are lived at later ages. For a death at 5 it gives 0.6787 times 75, about 50.90, instead of 84.07 (computed here for illustration), and turns the gain from age weighting for a child death into a loss.
has description in the module Integrates the weight of HE-FM-AGW-001 over the L years lost from the age at death a, which gives C/beta squared times the difference of (1 + beta a) e to the minus beta a and the same term at a + L. The modulation constant K mixes this with the unweighted L years, so K = 1 is the article's undiscounted age-weighted YLL and K = 0 returns the L standard years of HE-FM-YLL-001 for one death. The (1 minus K) L term is not printed in the sources cited, which give the K = 1 integral and the discounted form with K. It is derived here as the limit of the second term of HE-FM-AGW-003 as r falls to zero, and the numerical integral of HE-CF-AGW-002 confirms it. The whole expression is the r = 0 case of HE-FM-AGW-003, which cannot be evaluated directly at r = 0 because it divides by r.

Undiscounted DALYs of a cohort with deaths at one age and survivors living with a condition for a fixed time

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000644
Type formula
assumes Deaths at one age and illness of one length and weight in a cohort DALY scenario
Survivors outlive the period of illness in a cohort DALY scenario
has calculator text DALY = D * L + S * DW * T
has common error note Local survival in one scenario and the standard life table in the other. In the article's step 5 the 12 people saved are credited with 360 life-years under 30 years of local survival and 540 under the standard of 45 years. Counting the comparator's 20 deaths at the standard (900 YLLs) and the programme's 8 deaths at local survival (240 YLLs) credits 660 YLLs averted, more than either consistent choice gives (computed here for illustration). The life expectancy is chosen once for both scenarios and reported, and Airoldi and Morton trace the different rankings given by DALYs and QALYs to this use of life expectancy tables.
People saved left out of the survivors in the programme scenario. Keeping the survivors at 180 when the programme cuts deaths to 8 gives 540 DALYs with the programme in place of 552, so DALYs averted rise by 12 to 900 (computed here for illustration). The people whose deaths are prevented live with the condition and add YLDs, the mechanism behind Arnesen and Nord's equity critique.
has description in the module Gives the DALYs a cohort incurs in one scenario when D people die at once at an age where the standard remaining life expectancy is L years, and S survivors live T years at disability weight DW before recovering fully. The first term is the YLLs of HE-FM-YLL-001 and the second the incidence-based YLDs of HE-FM-YLD-001, so the result is HE-FM-DALY-001 for the cohort. The article applies it to one cohort with and without a treatment programme.

Unit cost of gross investment in health and the outlay for a target gross investment with schooling

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000736
Type formula
assumes Constant returns and fixed prices make the unit cost equal marginal cost
Prices of the period in which the gross investment is produced
Schooling lowers the unit cost of gross investment by the efficiency factor
has calculator text pi = exp(-rho_H * E) * (P / (1 - K))^(1 - K) * (W / K)^K; C = pi * I
has common error note Linear reading of the schooling saving over several years. Reading rho_H E as a percentage cut in cost is close for one year, 776.00 GBP against 776.36 GBP for 20 units, but the gap widens as the change in E grows. For four extra years at 0.03 the outlay is 800 times exp(-0.12), 709.54 GBP, against 704.00 GBP from the linear reading (computed here for illustration).
Price of medical care taken as the unit cost of gross investment. In the article's example the unit cost equals the price of care, 40 GBP, only because 2 times the square root of 40 times 10 happens to be 40. With a wage of 20 GBP and the same price of care the unit cost is 56.57 GBP, so using 40 GBP would understate it by 29% (computed here for illustration). HE-ER-DFH-004 makes the same point for the pure investment condition.
Wage left out of the cost of producing health. Own time is an input, so the unit cost rises with the wage. Grossman states that a 1 percent rise in the wage raises the marginal cost of gross investment by K percent; in the article's example a 10% rise in the wage, to 11 GBP, raises the unit cost by 4.88%, to 41.95 GBP (computed here for illustration).
has description in the module Returns the cost of one unit of gross investment at the least-cost mix and the outlay needed for a target gross investment. For the Cobb-Douglas form of HE-FM-HPF-001 the unit cost is exp(-rho_H E) times (P / (1-K)) to the power 1-K times (W / K) to the power K, derived here by putting the least-cost split of HE-FM-HPF-002 into the production function. Because of constant returns and fixed prices it is both the average and the marginal cost of gross investment, the pi_(t-1) that HE-FM-DFH-002 takes as an input. One more year of schooling divides the unit cost by exp(rho_H), the exact form of Grossman's result that marginal cost falls by rho_H percent per unit of E, and a 1% rise in the wage raises it by about K percent.

Grossman M. The human capital model of the demand for health. NBER Working Paper 7078. National Bureau of Economic Research, Cambridge, MA; 1999. Published as The human capital model, in Culyer AJ, Newhouse JP, editors. Handbook of Health Economics. Vol 1A. Elsevier, Amsterdam; 2000. p. 347-408. Section 2.2, the text after equation (2-10), which states that with linear homogeneity and prices independent of the level of the inputs the average cost of gross investment is constant and equal to the marginal cost; section 3.2, which states that if K is the fraction of the total cost of gross investment accounted for by time a 1 percent rise in W would increase marginal cost by K percent, and equation (3-10), in which the percentage change in marginal cost per unit change in E equals minus rho_H because a rise in E reduces the inputs required for a given gross investment; section 2.4, which reports that Ehrlich and Chuma introduce rising marginal cost of investment. The closed-form unit cost with the share terms is derived here from equation (5-3) and the least-cost condition. https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w7078/w7078.pdf

Unstabilised IPCW weight updated over one interval

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000523
Type formula
assumes No unmeasured confounders of censoring and the outcome, Positivity, every patient has some chance of remaining unswitched
has calculator text w_t = w_prev / p_t
has common error note Accepting IPCW results without inspecting the weights. Very high weights for a few patients are likely to lead to erroneous results; the article's three non-switchers weighted 20 make two-year survival swing from 0.605 to 0.505 with one extra death.
Dividing by the probability of switching. At 30 of 60 switched the two probabilities are both 0.5, which hides the error; at 57 of 60 the probability of switching, 0.95, gives a weight of about 1.05 instead of 20.
Truncating extreme weights without a sensitivity analysis. Truncating weights at a percentile, often the 99th or 95th, reduces standard errors but adds bias; the percentile chosen needs its own sensitivity analysis.
has description in the module Divides a patient's weight at the end of the previous interval by the probability of remaining unswitched (uncensored) through the current interval, given no earlier switch, baseline and time-dependent covariates and survival to the interval's start. Starting from 1, repeated division builds the product over intervals in the article's formula. Patients who cannot be censored in an interval keep their weight.
has formalisation level catalogue record
has implementation Unstabilised IPCW weight from named cells
has mathematical variable IPCW weight at the end of the previous interval, Probability of remaining uncensored through interval t, Unstabilised IPCW weight at the end of interval t
has module record identifier HE-FM-DCEN-001
has source in the module Bell Gorrod H, Latimer NR, Abrams KR. NICE DSU Technical Support Document 24: Adjusting survival time estimates in the presence of treatment switching: an update to TSD 16. Sheffield: Decision Support Unit, ScHARR, University of Sheffield; 2024. Section 4.2.2.1: truncation selects a maximum weight at a prespecified percentile of the weight distribution, often the 99th or 95th; as truncation increases the estimates become more biased through loss of information but standard errors are reduced; if weights are truncated, a sensitivity analysis should be undertaken around the truncation percentiles. https://doi.org/10.15131/shef.data.33850897
Latimer NR, Abrams KR. NICE DSU Technical Support Document 16: Adjusting survival time estimates in the presence of treatment switching. Sheffield: Decision Support Unit, ScHARR, University of Sheffield; 2014. Appendix A, IPCW: unstabilised weights are the inverse of the conditional probability of having remained uncensored until time t given baseline and time-dependent covariates, and past treatment history drops out of the switching model because a patient is censored as soon as switching occurs; section 3.2.1: non-switchers similar to switchers receive higher weights, the no unmeasured confounders assumption cannot be tested using the observed data, and the method cannot work if some covariate level ensures switching; section 4: IPCW reduces to simple censoring when all confounders are unmeasured. https://doi.org/10.15131/shef.data.33847621
Latimer NR, Abrams KR. NICE DSU Technical Support Document 16: Adjusting survival time estimates in the presence of treatment switching. Sheffield: Decision Support Unit, ScHARR, University of Sheffield; 2014. Section 6, step 4: for the IPCW it is particularly important to assess the weights calculated for each patient over time, since instances where certain patients are allocated particularly high weights are likely to lead to erroneous results; section 6, step 2: if more than 90 per cent of control group patients switch, IPCW is highly prone to bias given a sample size in the region of 500. https://doi.org/10.15131/shef.data.33847621

Utility of two conditions combined by the additive, multiplicative and minimum rules on a shared baseline

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000562
Type formula
assumes No utilities measured in people with both conditions, Shared baseline for both single-condition decrements
has calculator text U_add = U_0 - (U_0 - U_A) - (U_0 - U_B); U_mult = U_0 * (U_A / U_0) * (U_B / U_0); U_min = min(U_0, U_A, U_B)
has common error note Choosing the combination rule without testing the others. TSD 12 reports that no method is unequivocally supported and that all conventional rules produced some large errors, so the rule used should be stated and the others tested in scenario analysis; in the article the cost per QALY moves from 20,000 to 40,000 pounds with the rule alone.
Combining raw utilities as if the baseline were full health. In the article the multiplicative estimate falls from 0.525 to 0.42 and the QALY gain per case of B avoided rises from 0.875 to 1.40 when the baseline of 0.80 is replaced by 1; TSD 12 states that assuming perfect health as the baseline is inappropriate.
has description in the module When utilities exist only for people with one condition each, TSD 12 sets out three conventional estimates for people with both: the additive rule subtracts both absolute decrements, the multiplicative rule applies both proportional effects, and the minimum rule assumes no further loss beyond the worse single condition. With a shared baseline U_0 the multiplicative value equals U_0 minus d_A minus d_B plus d_A d_B / U_0, so with two positive decrements it is higher than the additive value by d_A d_B / U_0. TSD 12 advises the multiplicative rule when combined data are unavailable.
has formalisation level catalogue record
has implementation Combined utility under three rules from named cells
has mathematical variable Combined utility of two conditions under the additive rule, Combined utility of two conditions under the multiplicative rule, Combined utility of two conditions under the minimum rule, Baseline utility of people with neither condition, Utility of people with condition A only, Utility of people with condition B only
has module record identifier HE-FM-DISU-002

has common error note Treating repeated utility records as independent for the QALY standard error. An analysis that models visit records as independent and uses model-based (naive) standard errors works with a QALY variance of 0.015 instead of 0.03145. With 100 patients per arm the standard error of the difference in mean QALYs is about 0.0173 instead of 0.0251, understated by about 31 per cent, giving a confidence interval about 70 per cent of its proper width. An independence working model in GEE with sandwich standard errors, or QALYs calculated per patient before comparing arms, avoids this.
Using rho for the outer pair in the AR(1) QALY variance. Giving the baseline and 12-month pair the correlation rho instead of rho^2 turns the formula into the exchangeable one: 0.0325 instead of 0.03145 at rho = 0.7. Variance of the antithetic variates estimator with within-pair correlation

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000320
Type formula
assumes Mirrored inputs keep their distribution in antithetic pairs
Independent pairs and aligned random number streams for antithetic sampling
Sign of the within-pair correlation in antithetic sampling
has calculator text Var_anti = sigma2 / n * (1 + rho)
has common error note Comparing antithetic pairs with independent runs at unequal cost. The fair comparison holds the number of model evaluations fixed. Comparing 1,000 antithetic pairs, which need 2,000 evaluations, with 1,000 independent runs gives an apparent variance factor of about 0.178 instead of 0.3551 in the survival example, overstating the gain twofold.
Expecting antithetic gains for a symmetric model output. Outputs built from maxima, absolute values or squared deviations can be symmetric in their inputs, and pairing then doubles their contribution to the variance. In the article's extreme case for the expected value of perfect information, rho equals 1 and the variance is twice that of ordinary sampling, at a near-tie between strategies where the quantity matters most. A pilot run checks the sign of rho before the method is adopted.
Expecting large antithetic gains when rare events drive the model. When an event with probability p is simulated as occurring if U is below p, the two members of a pair cannot both have the event for p below 0.5, and the within-pair correlation is minus p divided by one minus p. For an illustrative annual probability of 0.02 the correlation is about -0.020 and the variance factor about 0.980, a gain of only 2%.
has description in the module Gives the variance of the antithetic estimate based on n model evaluations arranged as n/2 independent pairs. Ordinary sampling with n independent evaluations has variance sigma2/n, so the factor 1 + rho measures the gain: a negative within-pair correlation lowers the variance and a positive one raises it. Because rho cannot be below -1 or above +1, the factor runs from 0 to 2: in the best case one pair gives the exact answer, and in the worst case the variance doubles.

Reporting the vertical effect as the whole redistributive effect. V ignores horizontal inequity and reranking, which can only reduce redistribution. For the Netherlands in 1992 the guide reports a vertical effect of minus 0.0089 but a total redistributive effect of minus 0.0096.
has description in the module Gives the fall in the Gini coefficient of income that a compulsory health payment would produce through its progressivity alone, as the Kakwani index scaled by the average payment rate. It is the vertical term V in the decomposition of the redistributive effect into vertical redistribution, horizontal inequity and reranking. A larger payment rate magnifies the redistribution from a given degree of progressivity.

Wagstaff normalised concentration index for a binary health variable

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000607
Type formula
assumes Binary variable and large samples for the Wagstaff bounds
Same sample, weights and ranking for the index and mean in the Wagstaff normalisation
has calculator text C_min = mu - 1; C_max = 1 - mu; W = C / (1 - mu)
has common error note Applying the binary bounds to a count or continuous health variable. The bounds mu minus 1 and 1 minus mu hold only for a variable coded 0 and 1. For a mean of 2.5 outpatient visits a year, 1 minus mu is minus 1.5, which would put the upper bound below zero and reverse the sign of the normalised index. Non-negative count and continuous variables keep the standard index, and bounded scores need the generalised Wagstaff form or the Erreygers index with the bounds of the scale.
Comparing standard concentration indices of binary outcomes with different means. In the article's example the standard index of limiting illness is minus 0.25 and that of being free of illness about 0.0789, so the same distribution looks about three times more unequal when described as illness. Comparing immunisation, mortality or other binary outcomes across countries or years with different means needs a bound correction, and the report should state which correction was used.
Entering the mean of a binary variable as a percentage in the Wagstaff normalisation. With mu entered as 24 in place of 0.24, 1 minus mu becomes minus 23 and the illness index of minus 0.25 turns into about 0.0109, close to zero and with the wrong sign. The mean and the index must both be on the proportion scale.
has description in the module For a variable that takes only the values 0 and 1, such as being ill, immunised or dead, the concentration index is bounded below by the mean minus 1 and above by 1 minus the mean in large samples, so its feasible range shrinks as the mean rises (Wagstaff 2005). Dividing the index by 1 minus the mean restores a range of minus 1 to 1, so indices for binary outcomes with different means can be compared. The sign is unchanged: a negative value still means that the variable is concentrated among the poor.
has formalisation level catalogue record
has implementation Wagstaff normalised concentration index and binary bounds in Excel

Wagstaff two-group CES health social welfare with a group weight and curvature

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000683
Type formula
assumes Equal-sized homogeneous groups in the CES welfare, Group weight and curvature as separate value judgements
has calculator text W = (alpha * h_a^(-r) + (1 - alpha) * h_b^(-r))^(-1 / r)
has common error note Entering the Atkinson epsilon as the CES curvature r. The CES curvature and the Atkinson parameter differ by 1, epsilon = 1 + r, so the English median epsilon of 10.95 (HE-SR-ATK-007) corresponds to r of 9.95. Entering r = 10.95 for groups at 60 and 72 years with equal weights gives W of about 63.1817 instead of 63.3600, a more inequality-averse function than intended.
Outer exponent of the CES welfare written as 1 over r. Writing the outer power as 1/r in place of minus 1/r returns about 0.0153 instead of 65.4545 years for 60 and 72 years with alpha = 0.5 and r = 1, a value in reciprocal years that ranks distributions in reverse.
has description in the module Combines the health of two groups through a constant elasticity of substitution (CES) function, the iso-elastic form of Wagstaff 1991 that Asaria, Griffin and Cookson describe as the most commonly used in the health inequalities literature. The weight alpha pivots the welfare contours around the line of equal health and r sets their curvature. At r = -1 W is the weighted sum alpha h_a + (1-alpha) h_b, the inequality-neutral utilitarian case, and as r approaches infinity W approaches the smaller of the two health values, the maximin of HE-FM-SWF-003. With alpha = 0.5, W is the EDE health of HE-FM-ATK-002 for two groups with epsilon = 1 + r, so the isoelastic and CES families rank distributions identically. Unlike the weighted two-group social welfare of HE-FM-WE-004, whose weight on a group's QALYs is fixed, the weight here changes with the health gap (HE-FM-SWF-005).

Wald confidence interval for a binomial proportion

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000413
Type formula
assumes Large sample and probability away from the bounds for the binomial Wald interval
has calculator text p_hat = r / n; L_Wald = p_hat - z * sqrt(p_hat * (1 - p_hat) / n); U_Wald = p_hat + z * sqrt(p_hat * (1 - p_hat) / n)
has common error note Binomial Wald interval reported after zero or few events. For no events among 40 patients the Wald interval is the single point 0, and for one event it runs from about minus 0.023 to 0.073, below zero. In the article's exact calculation for 40 patients and a true probability of 0.02, the nominal 95% Wald interval covers the true value in about 55% of samples, against about 95% for the Wilson interval.
has description in the module The normal-approximation interval for a binomial proportion, the form most often quoted. It is symmetric about p_hat, has zero width when r is 0 or n, and its lower limit can fall below zero. Brown, Cai and DasGupta showed that its coverage behaves erratically and that the problem is far more persistent than had been appreciated. The general Wald interval for any estimate is on the Asymptotic Normality page (HE-FM-AN-001).

has common error note Requiring normally distributed patient-level costs. Rejecting a normal-approximation interval because individual costs are skewed misreads the requirement: the approximation concerns the sampling distribution of the mean difference, not the data. The real concern is a modest trial with a few very expensive patients, which can leave the mean far from its normal limit.
Using the patient-level standard deviation as the standard error. Entering the per-patient cost standard deviation of £6,708 in place of the standard error of about £600 gives an interval of about -£11,148 to £15,148 around the £2,000 difference instead of £824 to £3,176, so a clear cost difference appears uncertain even in sign.
has description in the module Subtracts and adds a multiple of the estimated standard error to the estimate. With z equal to 1.96, the 97.5th percentile of the standard normal distribution, the interval has approximately 95% coverage in large samples. The interval is symmetric by construction.

Weibull cumulative hazard and its straight line on the log-cumulative hazard scale

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000475
Type formula
assumes Weibull parameterisation stated before transfer to a model, Straight line on the log scale judged within follow-up only
has calculator text H_t = lambda * t^gamma; logH = log(lambda) + gamma * log(t)
has common error note Reading a gradient below 1 as a rising hazard. A log-cumulative hazard line steeper than 1 means a rising hazard and one flatter than 1 a falling hazard. TSD 14's illustrative example read a gradient below 1 after about five weeks as making an exponential model unlikely for that arm.
Taking a straight log-cumulative hazard plot as proof of the extrapolation. A good straight-line fit within follow-up says nothing about the tail. Flexible models also become linear in log time beyond the final knot, so their extrapolation resembles a Weibull whether or not that is plausible.
has description in the module Gives the cumulative hazard of a Weibull curve written as S(t) = exp(minus lambda t^gamma), and its natural logarithm, which is a straight line in log time with intercept log(lambda) and gradient gamma. A gradient of 1 is the exponential model with a constant hazard, above 1 a rising hazard and below 1 a falling hazard. Under proportional hazards two arms' lines are parallel, separated by the log hazard ratio. This is the scale of the log-cumulative hazard plot that TSD 14 uses as its first step in choosing survival curves.

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000224
Type formula
assumes Weibull distribution with a common shape
has calculator text HR = exp(-beta_1 / sigma)
has common error note Converting a time ratio to a hazard ratio without sigma. Taking the hazard ratio as 1 divided by the time ratio, about 0.667 in the first example, ignores the shape of the Weibull and is correct only for the exponential. The value with sigma of 0.8 is about 0.6024.
Mixing parameterisations from different software. Some programs report the log-linear scale sigma and others the Weibull shape, which is its reciprocal, and some report proportional hazards rather than accelerated failure time coefficients. Using a shape where sigma is expected, or a proportional hazards coefficient as beta_1, gives a wrong hazard ratio.

The Weibull shape parameter equals 1 divided by sigma, so the same result is TR raised to the power minus 1 divided by sigma.

Weibull log-likelihood contribution of a left-truncated record

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000543
Type formula
assumes Independent entry and one record per person, Weibull form for the survival curve from the origin
has calculator text l_i = delta_i * (log(k / b) + (k - 1) * log(X_i / b)) - (X_i / b)^k + (L_i / b)^k
has common error note Leaving the entry term out of a parametric fit. Patient F's contribution falls from about minus 3.71 to minus 4.32 when the 20 months before entry are treated as observed survival; across a registry such terms pull the fitted curve towards long survival.
Resetting the clock to entry for a model that starts at diagnosis. Fitting from entry removes the pre-entry time but estimates survival after registration, not after diagnosis, so the curve no longer matches a model cohort that starts at diagnosis.
has description in the module Writes the article's contribution, delta_i log f(X_i) plus (1 minus delta_i) log S(X_i) minus log S(L_i), for a Weibull curve with S(t) = exp(minus (t / b)^k) and density (k / b)(t / b)^(k minus 1) S(t). The last term, (L_i / b)^k, is what a fit without entry times leaves out. Summed over records and maximised over k and b it gives the left-truncated Weibull fit used for extrapolation; with k = 1 it reduces to the exponential case of HE-FM-LTR-003.

Weighted absolute-difference calibration loss for two targets

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000528
Type formula
assumes Each loss evaluation is a full model run, Targets on comparable scales or weighted to be so
has calculator text L = w_1 * abs(g_1 - T_1) + w_2 * abs(g_2 - T_2)
has common error note Assuming the best fit is unique. Alarid-Escudero and colleagues found two equally good-fitting parameter sets for a cancer model that gave treatment gains of 0.67 and 0.31 years; an optimiser that stops at one gives no warning of the other.
Setting target weights without checking which target dominates. Kong and colleagues combined 11 targets into one goodness-of-fit score by a weighted sum reflecting user-defined importance; the weights decide which targets win when they conflict, so results should be checked under alternative weights.
Treating the best-fitting parameter set as the full calibration result. Menzies and colleagues note that a single best-fitting set can be an important first step, but estimates of uncertainty around modelled results need a distribution of parameter values, as a probabilistic analysis requires.
has description in the module Folds the distances between model predictions and calibration targets into one weighted score for the search to minimise. The article's general form sums over J targets with any distance d; two targets with the absolute difference are written out here, and a single target is the case w_2 = 0. Each evaluation needs a full model run, so the loss has no formula or derivatives the search can use.

Type formula
assumes Weights chosen for the purpose of the segmentation, Standardising weights computed on the clustered sample
has calculator text D_ij = w_1 * (x_i1 - x_j1)^2 + w_2 * (x_i2 - x_j2)^2
has common error note Assuming equal weights give each variable equal influence. Weights of 1 leave each variable's influence proportional to its variance; in the example cost carries over 99.9 per cent of the unweighted distance between P1 and P5.
Standardising by default when only some variables separate the groups. Rescaling every variable to unit variance can hide two well-separated groups that one variable defines, so the weighting is a substantive choice, not a routine step.
has description in the module Multiplies each squared difference by a weight that sets the variable's influence. Each variable's influence on squared Euclidean distance is proportional to its variance, so weights in inverse proportion to the variance give equal influence; this is what standardising the variables does. Multiplying every weight by the same constant rescales all distances equally and leaves the grouping unchanged.

Weighted two-group social welfare and the switching weight

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000263
Type formula
assumes Linear weighting within each group, Weights are value judgements
has calculator text W_X = QA_X + w * QB_X; W_Y = QA_Y + w * QB_Y; w_s = (QA_X - QA_Y) / (QB_Y - QB_X)
has common error note Applying group totals when group sizes differ. Comparing group totals ranks options in the same way as QALYs per person only when the groups are the same size and everyone within a group is affected alike. Otherwise a Rawlsian or per-person comparison needs per-person values.
Reading a switching weight below 1 as favouring the better-off group. The switching weight only says where the ranking changes. Its direction depends on which option does more for group B; here Y does, so every weight above 1.2 favours Y and every weight below it favours X.
has description in the module Scores each option as total QALYs of group A plus a weight w times total QALYs of group B, where w is the value placed on a QALY accruing to the worse-off group relative to group A. A weight of 1 gives the utilitarian sum. The switching weight is the value of w at which two options X and Y score the same, found by setting their weighted totals equal; above it the option that does more for group B is preferred.

Welfare loss triangle of insurance-induced care

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000255
Type formula
assumes Demand curve measures marginal benefit, Linear demand between the two prices, Resource cost constant and fully passed to the uninsured price
has calculator text WL = 0.5 * (p - c * p) * (q_1 - q_0)
has common error note Counting the whole cost of the extra care as the loss. In the first example the extra 1.5 visits cost 150 pounds, but the patient values them at between 25 and 100 pounds each. Only the triangle of 56.25 pounds is a loss under the conventional analysis.
Treating all extra use as waste. The triangle values extra care by what patients are willing to pay at the margin. Care that insurance makes affordable, or high-value care that patients underuse, is not captured by that measure, so extra use is not waste by definition.
has description in the module With coinsurance rate c the patient pays c × p per unit of care that costs p to provide and uses q_1 units instead of the q_0 chosen at the full price. Each extra unit costs p but is valued by the patient at between c × p and p, so with a linear demand curve the loss is the triangle whose height is the price reduction p minus c × p and whose base is the extra use. The notation follows the moral hazard article.

Welfare-maximising uniform Pigouvian subsidy when public funds are costly

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000746
Type formula
assumes Concave net welfare with an interior optimum, Subsidy constrained to be zero or above
has calculator text Q_p = (a - c) / b; d_0 = m - g * Q_p; s_opt = max(0, b * (d_0 - lambda * b * Q_p) / (b + g + 2 * lambda * b)); W_opt = max(0, d_0 - lambda * b * Q_p)^2 / (2 * (b + g + 2 * lambda * b))
has common error note Excess burden charged only on the transfer to inframarginal users. Counting the excess burden on lambda s Q_p alone leaves out the part paid on the induced units, so the derivative loses its 2 lambda b term. For the article's curves the rate becomes 3 / 1.25, GBP 2.40, with a net gain of GBP 2,448 against GBP 2,727 at GBP 1.82 (computed here for illustration).
Pigouvian rate kept when public funds are costly. Setting the uniform subsidy at the external benefit at the efficient quantity, GBP 12 in the article's example, ignores Pigou's proviso. At an excess burden of 20p a pound it turns a net gain of about GBP 2,700 at GBP 1.82 into a net loss of GBP 82,800, as the article shows.
has description in the module Finds the uniform per-unit subsidy that maximises the net welfare W of HE-FM-PIGS-002 and the net welfare it gives. Setting the derivative of W to zero gives s_opt, which falls below the Pigouvian rate of HE-FM-EXT-002 whenever lambda is above zero and d_0 is positive, because each extra pound of rate is paid on every inframarginal unit as well as on the induced ones. With lambda of zero and a positive d_0, s_opt equals the Pigouvian rate and W_opt the deadweight loss of HE-FM-EXT-002. A subsidy adds net welfare only when the external benefit at the private quantity exceeds lambda times b times Q_p; otherwise the formula returns zero. The closed form is derived here from W and checked against the article's figures.

Section 3.7, Government Subsidies, which constrains the subsidy to be nonnegative; section 4.2, Targeting Subsidies, which states that authorities may face frictions in raising or dispersing public funds that make programme expenses a relevant consideration; and section 6, Conclusion, which states that with a monopoly supplier the per-unit subsidy needed for the first best can be prohibitively expensive and that, with even a small deadweight loss of taxation, such a subsidy would fail a cost-benefit test. https://www.nber.org/papers/w28085

Wilson score interval for a binomial proportion

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000414
Type formula
assumes Binomial count behind the Wilson score interval
has calculator text p_hat = r / n; m_W = p_hat + z^2 / (2 * n); h_W = z * sqrt(p_hat * (1 - p_hat) / n + z^2 / (4 * n^2)); d_W = 1 + z^2 / n; L_Wilson = (m_W - h_W) / d_W; U_Wilson = (m_W + h_W) / d_W
has common error note Wilson terms not divided by the denominator. Omitting the division by d_W gives about 0.0774 to 0.3186 for 6 events among 40 patients instead of 0.0706 to 0.2907, an interval that is too wide and shifted upwards.
has description in the module Inverts the large-sample test for a proportion instead of plugging p_hat into the standard error. Its centre is pulled from p_hat towards one half, it is asymmetric near the bounds and its limits cannot fall outside the possible range for a probability. Brown, Cai and DasGupta recommend it, or the equal-tailed Jeffreys interval, for small n.

Multiplying by 100 gives the percentage of work time missed. Hours missed for other reasons, such as holidays, are excluded from both terms.

Years of life lost from deaths in one age group under a standard life table

https://healtheconomics.wiki/ontologies/hemo/HEMO_5000602
Type formula
assumes One normative standard for every population and both sexes, Standard value applied to every death in the age group, Years of life lost counted without discounting or age weighting
definition source the Source rows of the Functions and Formulae module record HE-FM-YLL-001
feeds DALYs for a cause as the sum of its years of life lost and years lived with disability
has calculator text YLL_a = N_a * e_a
has common error note Comparing YLL totals computed with different standard life tables. The same 100 deaths at ages 75 to 79 give 1,285 YLLs under GBD 2010 and 1,719 under WHO GHE 2021, 33.8 per cent more, against 7.3 per cent more for the article's child deaths. A total should name its standard, and WHO states that its estimates for 2000 to 2021 are not directly comparable with its earlier DALY estimates.
Subtracting age at death from the standard life expectancy at birth. The standard value is the remaining life expectancy of a person who has already reached the age of death. In the GBD 2010 standard a death at ages 80 to 84 counts 9.34 years, whereas 86.0 years minus age would give between 2 and 6 years, and a death after age 86 would count nothing.
Using local life expectancy in place of a standard life table without saying so. Larson's worked example takes the local age-specific life expectancy of the person who died. With local values a death at a given age counts less in a high-mortality country than in a low-mortality one, which the LSHTM teaching module published by the IUSSP calls inequitable, so a study of YLLs or DALYs averted should state which life expectancy it uses.
has Content MathML <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><apply><csymbol cd="relation1">eq</csymbol><ci>YLL_a</ci><apply><csymbol cd="arith1">times</csymbol><ci>N_a</ci><ci>e_a</ci></apply></apply></math>
has description in the module Multiplies the deaths from a cause in one age group by the standard remaining life expectancy for that age group, the years of life lost per death in the standard life table. Summing the products over age groups gives the cause's total, as in the computational function below. GBD 2021 calculated YLLs this way for each cause, age, sex, location and year; GBD 2010 dropped discounting and age weighting.
